text: I was ready to give up on these expensive earphones because they kept disconnecting from phone calls and pausing the music. It is very difficult to place them in your ear correctly so that the sensors don't think you have removed them from your ears. What happens is that certain movements, such as chewing, clearing your throat, or even exercising, will cause the sensors that detects the earphones are in your ear, to disconnect the Bluetooth from phone calls or stop the music. I had constant interruptions using these to where I ended up going back to my older Bluetooth earphones with a wire connecting the two earpieces. The touch controls didn't always work because of the sensors thinking the earphones were not in my ear. Sometimes tapping the left one would pause the music, but tapping the right one would not start the music playing again. Then it would switch up and the left one would not work, but the right one would, all depending on which sensor it thought was in the ear at the time. But then, it hit me. Why don't I tape over the little sensors that detect if you are wearing the earphones. You can see this in the picture. Once I taped over them, the earphones do not lose it's Bluetooth connectivity and does not stop the music because I am eating lunch or exercising. This has been great! The only drawback is that the earphones are always connected to my device until I put them back in the charging case. Quick tip on raising/lowering the volume: when swiping up or down, use fast motions. If you do it slowly, it registers as a tap, which causes the music to pause or two taps which goes to the next track. If Samsung would reposition the sensors so that they are closer to the little speaker that fits in the ear canal, it would alleviate all of these problems. I can only give it 3 stars because of the sensors, which caused all of the issues I faced.

text: I was looking long and hard for a pair of on ear headphones for travel. I needed a pair that was small, compact, some sort of carrying case, and obviously had good sound. I new immediately to steer clear of Beats cause their sound sucks even though they meet my portability criteria. I looked also looked at Bose, Sol Republic, Sony, Sennheisers, and others. None of them could quite meet my needs. Then in my searching, I came across Logitech UE. I first saw these at a local Apple Store and was interested cause I never heard of them and they looked cool and were at a decent price. I saw these were being given pretty good reviews. Most people said they were definitely worth their price. So I went to Best Buy to go give them a listen. They only had these guys' big brother, the 6000s, out for demo, so I listened to those. I was pretty impressed with the sound of them. Bass was emphasized but not out of control like Beats and other headphones. Highs were also emphasized. After some listening straight from my iPod, I realized the big bros were colored to give that "V" EQ sound. The sound was good, but I really want as flat as a response as I can get. I also listened to all the other headphones, and still the Logitech beat out the others, even Klipsch whose sound was way too bass heavy and muddy for being that price and it being Klipsch. So I ultimately decided grab the 4000 at my local Apple Store since they were the best of what was available for around $100 and Apple's 14 day return policy which gave me 2 weeks to audition the pair. I was impressed with the features for the price. Detachable single sides cable with inline mic and controls for Apple devices, a carrying case, and a splitter to share a single source with 2 people. I really wanted a carrying case, but you have to pay nearly twice as much to get headphones with that, so it was fine. Now to the headphones themselves. Design: Sturdy plastic construction. Doesn't feel cheap or like it will break easily. It actually works out they're not collapsible to fit into a carrying case cause those designs are not as sturdy and much more susceptible to breaking. I like the glossy finish on the paint. Makes it flashy like Beats, giving you an aesthetic value. I got the white version; so it has a mirage of colors and looks really cool with the blue, black, gray, white, and chrome. The cups are very comfortable on the ears. I'm always apprehensive about getting on ear headphones cause I have a big head and ears so they usually get uncomfortable. These guys are always comfortable on my ears and I only start to feel them after a few hours of straight use. I'm pretty sure they have memory foam pads. If not, they're very comfortable regardless. There's also padding on the headband so it rests nicely on your head as well as your ears. Oh, I'd also like to comment on the apparent cable iussues. I have not at all had issues plugging the cable into the earpiece. Logitech may have taken care of the quality control issue since those reviews with this particular problem are a few months old. The cable feels really solid in its slot and I have no trouble pushing it in all the way. I've even ripped it out a couple times cause the cord got caught on stuff and it still fits perfectly. Don't let this apparent issue deter you from these great headphones! Sound: So now the most important aspect of headphones, their sound. When I first got to listen to these headphones, they sounded a little muddy with some highs missing and a prominent bass sound. Bass wasn't over emphasize and sounded tight and not uncontrolled. It was just that nice little boost you want for casual and not critical listening. I had previously read a review claiming the highs were too much and I couldn't believe anyone would say that because the one thing missing from the sound is the highs. I was slightly disappointed but it was still good enough for me to keep and I knew I couldn't get anything better without paying double the price. So fast forward to a few weeks later and I started to notice the sound changed. The lows tightened up and weren't as emphasized as before, the highs opened up and became present and even detailed, and the mids cleared up. The sound started to sound really good. I was listening to much of the same stuff I was when I first got the pair, so It wasn't the source material and I know it was the headphones opening up. So I would definitely recommend a couple weeks of break in for these guys. A lot of speakers require this break in period, so it's not a bad thing. Just play music with a nice dynamic range at just above normal listening volume for a couple hours a day and you'll have a really solid sounding pair of headphones. So in conclusion, these are a really good pair of headphones, especially given their price. They beat any competition in the price range. There's always better out there, but you'll have to pay a whole lot more for them. These are a great value!

text: PRO: Inserts directly into the ear without plugging into the ear canal itself, so it's great for eyeglass wearers since there is no "around the ear" loop to interfere with eyewear. PRO: It's literally so lightweight that I often forget it's even in my ear at all. Will not fall out, regardless of how you angle or shake your head. PRO: People at the other end of the call report good quality sound, doesn't seem to pick up on ambient noise too much. CON: Extended wear has caused my inner ear to become sore. I have tried a smaller eargel, but it's too loose. The large eargel is comfortably snug in my ear, but after a few hours (I'm on the phone all day long), my inner ear becomes painful and I have to remove the 925. Although the pressure from the gel is required for it to stay in the ear, it is just enough pressure to cause sensitivity and pain after about 4 to 6 hours of continuous wear. If you only need to wear it for less than 4 hours at a time, this unit is good. CON: Volume not as loud as I would prefer, even at the highest setting. I have no hearing problems, but even in moderately noisy environments, I constantly have to push the unit deeper into my ear canal to hear. In a loud environment, I can hardly hear anything the other person is saying. I'd like this unit to have a higher volume level. Great in a quiet setting, but not so great in noisy settings. CON: Battery dies after about 4 hours, requiring it to be recharged. This is a real problem for me since I am on the phone all day. I would almost need two of these to have one charging while the other one is being used. CON: Does not filter out wind when outdoors. Even slight wind seriously impairs the other person's ability to hear me on the other end of the call. I suppose this is a problem with nearly all earpieces, and this one is no exception. In summary, I rate it "okay". Nothing to write home about, but nothing to complain too loudly about either. I'm returning mine after having tried it for 30 days. I'm on the hunt for another unit.

text: To reiterate what others have said - Pros: - Sound quality - Immersive sound - Bluetooth or wired, they deliver equally as well Middle of the road: - Comfort: they pressed on my ears a little much but you should still be able to tolerate them on a moderate flight. Cons - Sound control is not very discreet: * 0-4 you get nothing * Past 50% becomes almost too uncomfortably loud Highly recommend! Here's a testimonial: I let my wife listen to them and she said I had to get her a pair of these! So there you go.... Now my lengthy review. The sound from these is spectacular. I ran them through their paces the first day I received them. From piano to classical, to rock, and everything in between. I've never heard Led Zepplin's "Whole Lotta Love" with such spacial definition and balance. I felt like the sound was passing through my ears and head when it went back and forth between the right and left channels. So I thought, what about Simon and Garfunkel. Again, I was amazed by what these headphones produced: the harmony of their voices was brought to life with "The Sound of Silence". And then the way they separated the percussion and guitar made me lose myself in the music! I didn't want to quit listening to Simon and Garfunkel through these, they sounded so good. The stacato sounds in "The Boxer" were delivered with precision. But I had to keep moving on, eventually.... Then I thought what about classical music? But before I got to full classical I decided to listen to Ólafur Arnalds. Again I was treated to some wonderful music when listening to several of his pieces. What amazed me most was the suttle background chatter in Nocturne in G Minor. The piano in "Words of Amber" was amazingly immersive. I could go on, but to summarize I thoroughly enjoyed listening to many of his pieces. Now back to classic rock: CCR never sounded so good! "Bad Moon Rising", "Heard It Through the Grapevine", "Midnight Special" and so many others sounded so full. Then you've got to take a listen to The Animals, Mammas and the Pappas, America, some Neil Young and so on. Everything I listened to from Country to Classical was phenomenal. Go listen to some Back, Beethoven, Liszt, Mozart (take Piano Concerto No. 21 for a spin!), Schubert and Tchaikovsky ("Hymn of the Cherubim" is superb) and you'll be immersed - you'll become part of the orchestra. The sound is so full and responsive. Oh, and don't forget to listen to some of Tina Guo's Cello! (I love "The Last of the Mohicans"). And some Cello from Gautier Capuçon, particularly "Meditation" - can bring you to tears - it's so moving; and his "Encore" sounds so precise. Again, highly recommend. Just by them already.

After my older model of earbuds died, I tried these, but ended up returning them and keeping a cheaper model, T9 instead, even though T9's sound quality for music is noticeably lower than these. Here is precisely why: PROS: - Excellent bass. Overall, good quality sound, especially for music. - Easy pairing. - Holds charge well. CONS: - When compared with Tozo T9, a cheaper model than NC2, the cheaper model has a better microphone. I tested it outside, in the street, with exterior noises present. The person on the phone told me that with T9, he could hear me well, and the sound of my voice was natural and clear even when there were background noises. The ANC was working well, suppressing external noises without muffling my own voice. But with these earbuds, NC2, my voice had a metallic sound and was fading in and out in loud surroundings. The ANC was muffling my own voice. - The touch controls are ridiculously sensitive. When a strand of my hair would touch the earbud, it would react to it as if I touched it with my finger. - The design is definitely not ergonomic. These buds are large. If you have small ears, like I do, the size of the attachment won't matter. The earbud itself sits rather uncomfortably in the ear. - Pairs easily, but sometimes glitches when connecting. For instance, when I get a phone call and my earbuds are in the case, I want to be able to quickly take them out and accept the call with earbuds on. But these are sometimes not quite fast enough when connecting. - Even though they are brand-new earbuds, I have to raise the music volume up to max in order to continue enjoying the sound when I am outside in loud surroundings. Customization of sound settings improved it a bit but did not fully solve it. I never ran into this with brand-new earbuds. Even my old earbuds have higher volume than these. Conclusion: They have a really, really nice bass. If you mostly use them in-doors in quiet surroundings and if their shape is comfortable for you, then they are probably a great fit for you. But I needed a pair of buds that will work best when I am walking in the street, with background noises. These buds failed the test. The music volume is too low, and on phone calls the mic and ANC are working against each other.

text: I have experience with high end headphones, but have even more with DJ headphones(4 years alone, with this pair). I've never really loved ANY Sony products, as most are for the masses, and not really catered for any specialty use. This model has honestly worked more than "good enough" for my DJ needs. While it isn't for audiophile listening, or reference-grade mastering work, the sound quality is very good. I am not sure what some reviewers here mean. I have never found the sound on this pair to be anywhere near muffled or veiled. The bass was clean, crisp, and very deep. The high frequencies are never harsh; they are rather laid back and balanced. The tonal representation and overall balance works VERY well for beat matching, and blending in sounds. Will you feel as if you're in the front row of a concert....or on stage, or hearing a singer breathing or spitting on their mic, probably not. You will feel as if you're in the center of the dance floor, which is what I am guessing its intended use is for. Accurate reproduction of the source is what you get, with a bit of dark coloration, rather than reference-quality neutrality. With the exception of earcup-padding deterioration (after 4 years of continual use...and serious abuse), these have never failed me, faltered, or fallen apart in any way. They have and do serve their purpose; (professional, bedroom DJ'ing, casual reviewing of material on your home system, game playing, or simply listening to a good tune- regardless of genre) with enough (coiled, and irreplaceable) cord length for all of the above. They're driven very easily, which is great for mp3 listeners with an I-pod.....or any other portable audio device/player. They're very user- friendly, as the cups move in most needed directions (perfect for DJ's, when in need of shouldering the phones during a mix, or folding a cup in... all the way- for simple one-ear monitoring). I found them to be extremely comfortable, enough for hours of work at a time, as well as hanging out on your recliner ....enjoying a CD. They're light enough to never be a burden, they fold away so you can store, or transport them wherever you wish. These headphones are simply an all- around great pair that you will not regret purchasing if you accept its limits, which are not many at all. I just ordered a pair of Denon d2000's for mid-level critical listening, I own Sennheiser 650's with Equinox cables for a serious musical experience, and these headphones will never be outdone for their special purposes. Very fair for their price, and well worth it. I'd spend $100 on these (if I ever needed to)in a second. Give them a try and see if it fits your bill. *no headphone amp required! If you want high-end, then be prepared to spend $350 on AKG, Senn, Grado, Proline, or Beyrdynamic, upwards to $4,000 on Stax ear-speakers + specialty cables (yes, you do need those also, $200+ on top of that). Good luck =0)

text: I wanted to give these wireless headphones 5 stars, mainly because the sound is really good for Bluetooth. I bought these because both pro reviews (e.g., CNET) and customers said the HK BT sound better than other Bluetooth headphones. I had considered the [[ASIN:B0081TH24O Parrot Zik Touch-Activated Bluetooth Headphones]] (the "Porsche" of wireless headphones), but they didn't match the sound of the HKs. In the end, I want headphones for their sound quality above looks or anything else. So, I went for the HKs (about half the price of the Ziks). Yes, the HK BTs sound really good for Bluetooth. But (and here's why they don't get 5 stars), when listening to Pandora on my iPhone 4, the wireless connection keeps dropping out (every 10-20 minutes). Other reviewers reported the same issue. That's a problem--something Harman Kardon need to fix right away if they want to stay competitive in the BT headphone market. One Amazon reviewer (or perhaps it was on the Apple site) mentioned that the HK BTs sounded even better than [[ASIN:B003IHUHGE Bowers & Wilkins P5 Mobile HiFi Stereo Headphones]] wired headphones (also fold flat and come in a travel bag). I have the P5s, and have enjoyed them for months. I compared the HKs with the B&W P5s, and, while the HKs do sound good--crystal clear mids and highs, and reasonably good bass--they do not sound as good as the P5s (P5 bass is fuller and richer, with really clear mids and highs). Listening to music, I prefer the P5s over the HK BTs. (Like most, if not all, Bluetooth headphones and earbuds, the HK BT sound is digitally processed, and you can hear the electronic "translation.") However, for watching movies on my iPad mini, the HKs work well (much better than the [[ASIN:B00AIRUOI8 JayBird BlueBuds X Sport Bluetooth Headphones - Midnight Black]], for instance). I do like the convenience and freedom of wireless, and so given HK BT's good sound (for Bluetooth), I'm on the fence about whether to keep them. I'm tempted to return them because (1) they drop the Bluetooth connection when listening to music on my iPhone; and (2) they are bulkier than the B&W P5s--i.e., not as comfortable to wear (a bit heavy) and not so good for travel. Recommendation: The [[ASIN:B008B10DDO Harman Kardon Premium Over-Ear Bluetooth Wireless Headphones (Black)]] are good-sounding wireless headphones. But if dropped Bluetooth connections will spoil your music enjoyment (you have to re-establish the BT connection, which is a pain), you might look around for something else. If HK were to fix the Bluetooth problem, I'd give these 5 stars. But because of dropped BT signals, they don't quite merit 4 stars; yet (because of good audio and impressive, spacious sound stage) they merit more than 3 stars. My "ideal"headphones would be a Bluetooth version of Bowers & Wilkins P5s. Also, I'd like to see Jawbone come out with either/both BT headphones and/or IEMs (in-ear monitors). I love what Jawbone have done with their [[ASIN:B004E10KI8 Jawbone JAMBOX Wireless Bluetooth Speaker - Black Diamond - Retail Packaging]]. By far the best sound of any small, portable speakers (for iPhone or iPads, etc.) -- wired or wireless! Their "Live Audio" software produces amazing surround sound from a tiny speaker. If you place the Jambox on your chest or hold up in front of your face, it's like having great-sounding, invisible headphones. Bottom line: 3.5 stars for the Harman-Kardon BT headphones.

text: The positive, first: these Yuin Pk3 earphones sound decent when they function. Now for the bad, which is overwhelming. I'm sure most of you earbud/earphone enthusiasts have encountered the problem, typical of cheaply made earphones, that through normal usage one of the audio channels just abruptly ceases to function. This usually happens when you're on an airplane, at the gym, or otherwise inclined to make a desperate attempt to massage them into working order. You twist the cord this way, you jiggle it back and forth, you do whatever you can to find that find the optimal cord geometry, etc. Eventually you get home and tape the stretch of cord near the input line into a certain position...and if you're fortunate your forty dollar earbuds work as before for a couple of more days. You finally heave them into a trash can and swear never again to do business with the crooked charlatans who built this textbook case of shoddily engineered earbuds. This is precisely the experience you're in store for with these Yuin Pk3 clunkers. I expect cheap manufacturing quality from $15 Radio Shack earbuds, but not from non-trivially priced buds from a company like Yuin that, for reasons mysterious to me, has a pretty good reputation. Well, you've been warned. You will be wasting your money on these. So far as durability is concerned, you're far better off with Radio Shack cheapies. My Yuin Pk3 buds bit the dust, after gentle use, within 3 months. AVOID.

text: I love everything but the "jog" button. Sound: 5 stars. Comfort: 5 stars. Can even sleep in them. May need some wiggling around to get fully over the ears and prevent fatigue when using for long periods of time. Connectivity: 5 stars. Quickly and easily connected to iPhone, Notebook, and Media Center computer. Technology: 5 stars. Latency when watching video is non-existent with iPhone, barely noticeable on Media Center PC, mild on Notebook (but improved when switched to High Performance power settings). Latency is generally more a factor of processor at the sound source than technology in the headphones. Usability: 3 stars. Actually, everything's fine until one gets to The "Jog" Button which has multiple flaws. 1. it's too sensative and wiggles too easily. To Pause/Stop a track, it requires great concentration to feel one's way around to find this button and then manage to press straight down without moving one way or the other and thus skipping or repeating the track instead of pausing it. 2. it's too close to the volume buttons. After several days of mild frustration, I've learned to slo_o_o_o_owly slide my finger up from the very bottom until I find the volume buttons. Then I slo_o_o_o_owly find the correct one to adjust up or down. Otherwise, I'm again faced with skipping to the next track every time I want to adjust the volume. This is especially unpleasant when watching Streaming movies as it generally stops the movie and forces the user to start over from the beginning and then scan to find where they were before their tragic decision to adjust the volume. This control should be moved far from other buttons. Better yet, the manufacturer could spend the extra few pennies on wire and put this control on the left earpiece where it can't be hit by accident. Of course, over there, maybe it wouldn't have to be a blasted multi-dysfunction "jog" button because there would be room to separate the functions to avoid unpredictable results. Overall, I love these headphones. I can get used to the controls but having to keeps it from a perfect rating in this reviewer's estimation.

text: I have purchased three (3) of these headphones over the last few years. The first pair worked well and lasted for about 2 years before cracking near the hinge area. That set failed in the same way recently (Feb 2020) so I followed the Amazon instructions and contacted Monoprice. I used their chat function (due to recent vocal surgery and treatments). The Monoprice agent was initially helpful but he could not provide support for a Monoprice product that was purchased on Amazon. I was given an Email (support.amazon@monoprice.com) that was supposed to go to a dedicated "team" that provides support for Amazon purchases. I sent an Email with all the required information and attached the photos that showed the failure. NO reply from Monoprice after several days. If you do not mind replacing them every 6 - 12 months, they might be a good purchase. The sound is very good and loud and I like the detachable cord feature. The headphones fit very tight initially but they do stretch out over time. If you have a large head, you might not like the fit. Once they stretched out, they tended to slide around a bit. If I ever hear back from Monoprice, I will update this review. Sound : 8 out of 10 Comfort : 5 out of 10 Reliability : 3 out of 10 Price: 9 out of 10 Support : 2 out of 10 Update - 3/24/2020 I resubmitted my email to Monoprice (support.amazon@monoprice.com) and got an automated reply with a case number. Next, I got an Email from a Monoprice product Specialist requesting a copy of my Amazon invoice and my shipping address. Next, I received a prepaid shipping label and I was instructed to return the product and all accessories. I dropped off my return at a FedEx location on 3/11/2020 and received a replacement product today (3/24/2020). Based on this experience, I have updated my review to 3-stars and the support portion to a 5. I still believe the product does not work well if you have to stretch it to fit your head. If you purchased this product thru Amazon,, try using the support.amazon@monoprice.com Email address. If you don't get a quick reply, I would try resending your Email.

text: I have always been more partial to the type headphones that don't have the silicone insert that sticks in my ear canal. I do have several different pairs of "noise isolating" earphones that do insert into my ear canals and wear them when noise isolation is needed. I could not call any of them comfortable. I would have to say that all I can get from in ear canal inserts is varying levels of discomfort. I have tried changing the inserts on some of mine to different types and sizes including the foam ones and none are really comfortable. Fortunately for me, most of my listening with earphones is done at the office or at home and it's quite enough at either place to get by without noise isolating earphones. At the office I still need to be able to hear my phone ringing so noise isolating earphones are not even an option. Several years ago most earphones were outer ear type so it wasn't hard to find something that fit well and sounded great too. I think most all the bigger name earphone brands have changed their high end models to some variation or another of in ear canal earphones making it harder for me to find a quality pair even if I am willing to spend the extra money. The AKG K311 sound very good for the cost. I have compared them to Sony MDR-ED12LP earphones and the sound and comfort is slightly better but only slightly so. The Sony MDR-ED12LP earphones are about half the price so I have to say they are a better value. I do like the way the AKG K311 fit in my ear. The flange part that fits in my ear is slightly smaller in diameter than the Sony MDR-ED12LP, is fully round in shape and has no sharp edges. These stay in my ears very well as do most all earphones of this type. They have a very solid build quality and I expect with a little care they will last. I would not hesitate to buy this model again. Both the AKG K311 earphones and the Sony MDR-ED12LP earphones sound quite a bit better than the earphones that came with my iPhone and any of my Sansa MP3 players.

They are insanely efficient - driving them from a smartphone or from an onboard sound jack or USB dongle is plenty adequate. Very detailed highs though everything can be a bit veiled and even sound a touch "below water" on some tracks. There is a sort of sheen to these that is excellent at preventing any harshness or piercing qualities to the upper-mids and treble detail areas, but at a cost that to me is a bit, well, irritating though it isn't a sound deal-breaker. These have a sparkle and slam that's unlike anything else in my house EXCEPT (and this will sound odd) the Blon BL-03 IEMs - these Phoenix cans sound like the Bl-03's big brother to my ears. Obviously there are large differences but the overall signature and presentation is quite similar. But where I love the Blons, these Sivgas take it too far for me. This is a hugely FUN headphone, occasionally sibilant but rich and buttery while still retaining some (slightly muted) sparkle, but there is a narrowness to the soundstage (IEM-like) and a coloration to the signature that would prevent me from picking it up often; if I want "fun" I'd reach for my Fidelio X2HR. However, comparing between the X2HR and the Phoenix is incredibly difficult to me; they're too different, particularly in the soundstage. Though I mentioned these can be driven without an amp, the darkness or slight veil of the Phoenix combined with their impactfulness and also combined with the narrower soundstage is all more pronounced when driving these from a low-power sources which culminates in a slightly claustrophobic-feeling sound for me when listening at lower volumes. Adding power via an amp (any of the small portables I have actually) and turning it up a bit, that feeling goes away entirely. The sound noticeably opens up. On acoustic tracks the bass emphasis and narrower stage seems to interfere with the imaging, the low-end really coloring and bleeding somewhat to the other instruments. Not horribly, but noticeable to me. Moving on to the fit: this is where they fall apart for me. I too had fit issues like all reviewers here thus far have mentioned, but bending and repositioning never fixes it for me. The ear-cups/pads are small, but not "on-ear", and they are shallow so my ear is actually touching the inside of the cans (which I think is a big part of why they can sound so impactful). I think these could really shine with a larger band and slightly different yolk and some larger/deeper pads. I'm just not willing to go to those lengths with this set. My head is definitely on the larger side but certainly not huge (my cap size is 7 1/2 if that's helpful), but these just don't quite work on it. They are not UNcomfortable but an hour is the *max*. That said, the *quality* of the pads is very good, very soft protein leather at the outside, very soft & smooth fabric for the inner ring that makes contact, and incredibly supple memory foam within the pad (almost too soft due to the lack of thickness so they compress almost completely when on my head). Finally, due to the small size, the protein leather and the extremely "cushy" nature of the pads where so much of your ear is in contact with it, they can get very warm like a heated soft pillow. Were I too try and keep these I would *have* do a pad swap of some kind, regardless of how soft and comfy these stock ones feel at the onset. Your mileage may vary. For size comparisons, my photos show them next to Fidelio X2HR (complete with the cat hair they constantly collect and store), AKG K712 Pro, Koss KPH30i and Sony MDR-7506. They're most similar in size and fit to the Sonys but where the Sony are comfortable to me for hours on hours with plenty of adjustment left, these don't last an hour on my head. Overall I don't think I'll be holding onto these personally but I'm absolutely CERTAIN they will make a great many people incredibly happy, especially if the fit works for them and based simply on house these impact in the low end and sparkle in the highs. The Phoenix are quite good, if not for me, and I certainly preferred them over the Sivga P-II by a large margin.

text: I hemmed and hawed about getting these cans for a while. Then, the price was reduced by $100 (I assume due to the introduction of the 400i and 560), and I could not resist trying them. Warning: this review is pretty schizophrenic. That's because I have very mixed emotions about the HiFiMan lineup, and these phones in particular. Out of the Box ------------------ Upon receipt I found the shipment packing to be very good, but the actual product packaging to be disappointing: just a simple cardboard box. When I pulled the phones out, they had a quantity of some sort of powder (proved NOT to be Anthrax) on them, which was no problem to wipe away, but did not add to the joy of receipt. Construction ---------------- Moving to construction quality, I'd say they are solid, but not luxurious at all. They are quite heavy, and you need to be prepared for that. The earpieces are infinitely adjustable, which is nice, but I do worry about them getting loose over time (probably not worth worrying over). The cable attachment mechanism is a mini-coax style, which looked like it would be cool, but is really kind of a pain. The cables come straight out of the bottom of the earpiece bodies, and with the stiff stock cables, can make for a kind of annoying fit as they sometimes rub against your shoulders. Sound (what really matters) ------------------------------------ Sheesh, with all that complaining, why did I give these things four stars? Well, they sound really great, plain and simple. I don't find them to be what I consider neutral, however. My impression after lots of listening is that they have good bass, and a slightly sucked-out midrange and a tilted-up treble. If you like that sort of sound, you'll LOVE these. They are very detailed and have an airy presentation (possibly due to the treble lift I detect). I have run them with a Schiit Magni and currently a HiFiMan EF-5. They mated well with both, IMO. I was well and truly impressed by the sound I got from the phones for my first months of ownership. But then I got a pair of the cheapest Audeze LCD-2 B-stock (at about 2.5x the cost of the HE-400). The HE-400 are now NOT my best-sounding cans, by far. But for 300 clams the HE-400 sound pretty darn good, and they are planars. They are the cheapest planars, in absolute dollars, you're going to find. A Bit More Complaining ------------------------------ Well, not complaining, but food for thought. Lately I have wondered about the true *value* of the HE-400. Yes, the LCD-2 cost about 3x as much, but they are MADE IN AMERICA. The Audeze also blow the HiFiMan out of the water in luxurious feel, materials, accessories, and out-of-the-box experience. The Audeze Pelican-like travel case is very nice. The Audeze cables are better (IMO) and the cable entry on the LCD-2 is appropriately angled. The leather is nicer, the connectors are better, the plug is better, etc, etc. What bugs me is that I guess I might expect a Chinese product to have provided close to the same construction quality and features as the Audeze, but for 1/2 the cost. Instead we get a much more cheaply-constructed product, with not extras, and worse sound, for 1/3 the price. I'm also not convinced the construction quality goes up as you go up the HiFiMan scale. So, in the end, I guess you're buying the *drivers* with the HiFiMan, and you're buying the "whole package" with the Audeze. Something to think about, IMO. If you simply can't (or won't) afford the high price of the Audeze planars, then the HiFiMan offerings are definitely a good option. My opinion is that you should at least consider holding off, saving your pennies, and getting a pair of Audeze, even used. All that said, I look forward to someday trying out the HE-400i and/or the HE-560, since HiFiMan has addressed some of the HE-400 in those 'phones (with an attendant price hike). UPDATE ===== I have had my neighbors Sennheiser HD-600 for a couple of weeks now, and IMO, they blow the HE-400 out of the water for neutrality. After listening to the Senns for a while, I almost can't stand the HE-400. It sounds very nasal and odd with a lot of material. I definitely would recommend the HD-600 or HD-650, over the HE-400, to anyone looking for a $400-ish headphone.

text: This is the 3rd Soundpeats products I own. I was quite excited about this new ANC earbuds that I have been waiting for quite awhile. Overall, I am more disappointed than impressed. Things I am impressed with: 1. The ANC is ridiculous for a $50 earbuds. I have tested many pairs TW ANC earbuds from $40 to $200 (from MPow X3, Tozo T9, Boltune, Edifier, Aukey, Anker Air 2 Pro, Galaxy Buds Pro, etc). This pair knock everyone of those out the door. It's so strong that it almost give me a nausea feeling. I can ride the subway train going through the undersea tunnel and still have 70% of noise block out, which is crazy. The Mic work really well too, compare to other earbuds, it doesn't have that static feedback sound when you talk. On top of that, it tells you what mode you are in. 3. Comfortable as always. I haven't have a pairs from Soundpeats that I would complain about comfort, although I wish it didn't stick out that much. 4. Great improvement on video latency. One of my biggest complain from the previous model was latency while watching Youtube. This doesn't seem to be a problem so far My biggest disappointment is the sound. Maybe because it's not the dual dynamic drivers, it just doesn't sound that good compare to all the Truengine models (I owned the SE and SE 3). The entire sound profile is very flat. It lacks the crisp and clarify when you listen to vocal or instruments. It lacks the punchy bass when you listen to Hit Pop. I also didn't get the fun dynamic sound when you listen to EDM. Honestly, I am so shock about this since all previous Soundpeats earbuds sound great. I am having a hard time debating whether I should keep it for the ANC or return it because of the disappointing sound.

I've heard some people claim it takes 500 hours to break in - but who has time for that. Besides, even if the bass opens up, I am not convinced that would cure the hyper-crisipness. There seems to be a big trend to acheive an open, non-headphone soundstage. One way this is done is by using large earcups surrounding the ear. The other seems to be to hype the highs. Sure, you hear more detail, and its easy to get seduced by the big, juicy soundstage. But If they go too far it is just not natural. text: I tried the EM1 because frankly, I always thought Simgot's stuff looked cool - the styling drew me in, but I wasn't sure what to expect. They arrived a few days ago. Took a few photos of them with my Susvara Prion4 cable - I own Double Helix Cables and play around with the full spectrum of gear, from reasonable IEMs like this to unreasonable planars and electrostatics. I think their colors go well with my titanium connectors... In the package: They come in a sturdy hard box with foam cutouts for everything - the IEMs, cable, owner cards, and a carry bag full of two types of tips, one promising a brighter presentation than the other. The IEMs from the outside: They have a nice clear smoke color that I opted for, with a metal plate on the outside and an overall teardrop shape. They use extruded sockets which work with regular cables but are breakage resistant when used with the stock cable. The fit & feel: One of the most comfortable UIEMs I've ever worn. The preferred tips were the warmer medium size. The cables have a springy earguide that stays put behind the ear. The unique shape of these IEMs gets them pretty close to a custom fit feel. The sound: Treble is crisp and light but a little forward and edgy with the wrong tips. Using the warmer tips was the right plan. These have an upper-neutral overall quality to them, but paired with substantial, impactful bass. The mids are sweet and natural and the bass quantity is just right - it's shocking that a single dynamic is producing more pleasant, impressive bass than my 12-driver customs from other brands. The soundstage could've been a little bigger, but they have an intimate, front-row quality to them - I don't expect single DD to sound like a massive stadium. I drove these with my Hiby R3 for now and they make a terrific pairing at ~$250 combined price. Conclusion: I will be keeping these for sure! Now I need to try the rest of the Simgot lineup...

text: If your a musician or home studio engineer and you are looking for a solid pair of headphones that you can both track and mix with, look no further than the ATH-M40X series. I have sampled the entire ATH series as well as other similarly priced headphones, and out of all the one's I sampled these have the flattest and most honest frequency response of any headphone at the same price point. I plugged them into a CD player and listened to various artist's from Pink Floyd, to King Diamond, to AC/DC, Led Zeppelin, and others, and found that these are the first headphones that I ever owned that actually made me smile. The audio is very clear, and concise. The bass guitar comes through clear and clean, not boomy or punchy. The highs are angelic in frequency, not tinny at all to my ears. All the instruments sound even and not in competition with each other, even in the mid's, every tone and nuance is complimentary to the point you will hear a lot of things you may have heard before, but never really noticed until you heard it through these. These work perfectly and flawlessly from my Fender amp, to my Roland Octa interface, to my MP3 and CD players without the need for a headphone amp. The Slapper case and polishing cloth was an awesome bonus and more realistic value with this package. The Slappa is a high quality and very resilient soft interior case and will protect your investment for years to come. The seller at Butterfly Photo was kind enough to package a polishing cloth to keep the cups clean and separated when stored in the slapper, so the cups are not in contact with eachother when stored in the slapper... Protecting my investment after all is more important than a headphone amp I'll never use. As for the con's, I recommend ATH M50X's for DJ's and audiophiles as the bass of those is more punchy than the M40X's. These cans do clamp snug and tight around the ear, and that might be an issue for those looking for something comfortable or fashionable, more so than a workhorse... One thing is for sure these things aren't going to fly off your noggin if you spin off into a long head banging session. Build quality is excellent, considering it's mostly plastic and metal, but the materials are high grade for what they are and durable. Though design is a bit weird as the cups tend to have a life of their own when manipulating them. All in all, these are a great set of can's and are the best of the best when considering a set for tracking, monitoring, and mixing. UPDATE; 3.30.17 - Went to put these on my head and the left cup broke off entirely in my hand, the head band just snapped off the cup and smarted me up side my head pretty hard! After examination the cheap plastic plate which secures the head band to the cup FAILED. I've treated these things with extra care like no other headphones I've used before, and was surprised and disappointed that this happened to my favorite pair of headphones. I will be returning these to Audio Technica customer service to either fix, or replace them. For a $100 pair of headphones they should not have failed like this.

text: Sony is always leading the way for electronics.. that may be my personal opinion but I’ve also had Sony products since 1995 and I am the type of person that when I see a brand that works, I do not stray away. Regardless.. these are the flagship TWS earbuds around.. I am being unbiased when I say mehh… I will keep this review short. Sound quality/Call quality.. extensively great.. having the adjustable EQ, makes it so much better to enjoy music that you love. I listen a broad spectrum of music and they do not disappoint by any means. They can provide clean and clear bass when you want them to, or be bass heavy. Just slide that “Clear Bass” to the right and you’ll not be disappointed, as they still provide clean sound that’s totally not overpowered with the bass all the way up. Even at flat, the highs, mids and bass tones are natural and warm.. they are rich. Though these don’t provide a soundstage like over the ear headphones do which may be a downfall to some people. The call quality though, is to me, better than the top of the line Jabra 85T.. I have had those before myself, and was let down. People can hear me very clearly, rarely do I have to repeat myself if not at all. Voices are clear, they’re not muffled or sound far away by any means, which me being a trucker, having the cleanliness and clarity is a must have when on the road. It is very weird though, when you do receive a call, the sound changes I’ll explain that below. Sound modes.. the ANC, I hardly ever use because they seal in your ear well enough that ANC, in my case, is almost obsolete. I wear them in off mode every day.. they provide enough seal and passive noise reduction being “in ear” more than let’s say Apple AirPods Pro, that you won’t need ANC. Transparency mode is really nice to use. If I’m out and about running errands, I leave the transparency mode on so I can hear what’s around me at all times. Sometimes though, with certain sounds, or wind it can sound like you have a solo cup over your ear so not everything is going to sound clear. I usually take one out when I am talking to someone to be courteous, because they do give you a sense that you’re talking too loud when in reality you’re not talking loud enough which can make people have to ask you to repeat yourself. Overall, the ANC is great, it’s not something I use or care to truly use unless needed but it’s a great feature to have if you like to use it. Li Ike I mentioned above, it does have this sound mode that turns on when you receive a call. It’s not transparency mode, but it’s like a hear your own voice mode. For some reason the volume every time I connect these earbuds the ringer is on the lowest volume setting. The only way I know I’m receiving a call is when the sound mode changes from off, to the “hear your own voice” sound mode. It goes from hearing barely anything to like a 50% transparency mode that makes it sound like you’re in a tunnel. Battery life… This is the flagship of any earbuds… I’ve worn these for 10-12 hours some days, and with the sound mode in Off, they did not die or reach “low battery”.. I had them at 60% battery life one day, and 8 hours later the voice prompt finally said “low battery” and that was at 20% battery left in both earbuds. They do last a very long time. Mind you I have mixed usage.. music, movies, phone calls/etc, and they still have outlasted any other pair I’ve had. I cannot speak for battery length in ANC/transparency mode, but I can say that they do outlast anything. Tap control… be weary, that while they are functional, you have to tap the earbuds just right for them to recognize the functions you wish to have them perform. They seem to be proprietary to the center of the earbud, as I’ve tried tapping just outside the center and nothing happened. This may be cumbersome to a lot of people who like having tap controls.. I barely use them except to change sound modes, and play/pause whatever I’m listening to or watching at the time. Comfort… this is a let down… I’ve been wearing AirPods Pro’s since they came out. To me, they are the most comfortable earbuds I’ve had. And I declare that to Apples design of the tips and earbuds to your ears rather than having an eartip contour or expand your ear canal to fit.. while these do have comfort, the foam tips, they aren’t gonna last long and while they provide comfort, it’s just not enough. I ordered a pair of Eartune U-Ellipitical eartips that changed everything. To anyone looking for better eartips, the Eartunes are what you need, as they are designed with a more oval shape to contour to the ear canal a lot better. With the ear tip change, they will however, these earbuds still provide discomfort elsewhere.. where they sit in your ear overtime will cause a burning sensation.. the first few days wearing them I had to take them out after a few hours because my ear canal, and the area where these sit were making my ears burn pretty bad.. I still have some days where I feel some burning, it’s not as bad but it’s still enough where I find myself taking them out for a while to give my ears some relief, and that’s where a lot of other earbuds may prevail in comfort compared to these. Overall, if you’re a sound guy, you want top of the line ANC, and a superior battery life and can live with small discomforts.. I highly recommend these for you and they will not disappoint. For those who are looking for an alternative in comfort and comfort being a priority, compared to the Apple AirPods Pro’s, or equally comfortable earbuds, these are not for you.. while the pros may trump the downfall in regards to the small issues in comfort, the comfort may trump the pros for others. Please understand I changed eartips to one’s more similar to the Airpods, but still experienced discomfort. If you’re looking for a balance of everything a TWS can offer/may have to offer, these are definitely a great pair, I just think that maybe the price should be a tad bit lower and I would wait for the next time they go on sale. Update - 12/5/22 After doing some research I found a set of eartips that I recommend for these, Eartune Fidelity U-Ellipse. I highly recommend these to a seriously great extent because they have changed the game for me, and I can comfortably wear the WF-1000XM4s over 10 hours without any issues of burning, itchy or etc. If you purchase these earbuds and the eartips above, you will not be looking for another pair of earbuds for quite some time.

text: Updated review²: Well, they broke. I used these for at least 8 hours a day, at least five days a week, since I purchased them since July. That's a little over five months of very regular use. I loved these things, they're by far the most comfortable, best sounding, and best battery life TWS headphones I've used, which isn't a small number in my search for "The One". I thought these were that. But, today they finally gave up on me. Like so many other reviews, one of the ear hooks snapped off, making them unusable. They were never abused, the ear hooks were never bent out of shape or yanked, it simply snapped off today when I adjusted the bud in my ear. I almost want to buy another pair because I love them so much, but seeing as that appears to not be an uncommon fault, I'm going to have to pass and find something else. And that makes me very sad. Updated review: Much better! A replacement set came in, and these do not have the same issue as my original pair. The same pros as earlier still apply, these are insanely comfortable. Now that I can hear what they sound like, I can say they're pretty good in that area as well. They have the usual JLab sound profile selections, a JLab tune, balanced, and bass boost. I prefer the JLab signature, it's punchy, has good bass, and is fun to listen to. Balanced is also good for certain types of listening. Bass boost is a bit too much for me, and that's coming from someone who likes bass. The main reason I wanted to try these was for the battery life. I'm on the road for work often, and listen to a lot of audiobooks and such, and it's been a struggle to find a device that will last me a shift, sound good, and be comfortable. These give me the audio quality and battery life of using a Bluetooth dongle and a preferred pair of IEMs, but without having to keep a Bluetooth dongle in my pocket all day (difficult to make phone calls that way). I'm usually left with 60% battery after a day of work. That's putting them on at 7:30am, and listening to them until around 4:30pm. I've kept them going until 8:00pm or so, and there was still plenty of battery left. If I had to make a complaint, it would be that I'm not a fan of their case charging method. I prefer a standard micro USB or USB C port, instead of the built-in dongle they chose. I have a feeling this will be more prone to failure, depending on your charging situation. The bji-directional USB plug they used is nice though. As a side note, these do fit a little weird. I have many pair of TWS devices and wired IEMs, and I've always been a medium tip person. These, however, I have to use the large pair that was included to get a proper fit. So that's a little odd. One the plus side, that left the medium pair free to use on a different set of IEMs, and that's where they live now. Original review: Well, these fit amazing and are super comfortable. Unfortunately, that's as far as my experience with the product goes, because the left side will not power on once removed from the charging case. It lights up, indicating that it is charged while inside the case, but once removed, will not function at all. I've initiated a product replacement and will update once the next set is in.

For a few years I had been using my Plantronic headphones, which were about $100 cheaper than these but sounded wonderful, were incredibly comfortable, and were super easy to use. I figured if the Plantronics could be *that* good for *that* much cheaper, these would really be something special (especially since a lot of brands don't make high-end on-ear headphones). The truth is I just don't understand where the money is going here. They are very durably built, for certain. They have a great weight to them, and while the Plantronics were kind of flimsy plastic, these seem to be very study aluminum. But beyond that, there is nothing here that justifies the price. The sound is fine, but noticeably underwhelming compared to my similarly-priced Bose over-ear headphones, Beats over-ear headphones, and the much cheaper on-ear Plantronics. They don't bring out anything exciting in the music the way the others do. In terms of comfort, they aren't necessarily uncomfortable, though they do get a little tight on the ears after prolonged use. However, they certainly aren't discernibly more comfortable than cheaper models. Additionally, there is something about the design that, if you're walking around on a relatively windy day, you get a lot of hissing in a way I haven't experienced with many other headphones. Most frustratingly, the controls are not intuitive. Because they are touch-sensor and not buttons, you have to remember the controls, and you have to be precise about your movements in a way you don't have to with buttons. The feature that pauses your music when you remove the headphones would be great if not for the fact that, often, it reads that you have taken your headphones off when they haven't moved at all, and they don't start back up on their own even after adjustment. There is a similar problem with the Plantronics removal-sensor, but it isn't as consistently wrong or difficult to fix. Overall, these are okay headphones that in no way approach the price that they are charging. You can do better for cheaper with Plantronics, or for about the same price with Beats or Bose. I wouldn't waste time with these.

text: In writing this review, keep in mind that I'm comparing this set of headphones to 6 other ones: Sennheiser HD 280, Sony MDR-7506, Sony MDR-V6, Sennheiser HD HD202, Sennheiser HD201, and Monoprice MEP-839. The first 3 can usually be purchased for $60-$90 (depending on which headphone and if you can find it on sale) and are used by many as studio monitors. The latter 3 are all ~$20 headphones and sit in the same category as the JVC HA-RX500. Of course, as we all know, whether you like a particular pair of headphones depends on what you plan on doing with them and what you listen to. Personally, I listen to a mix of music ranging from classical to pop to dance. I'm not what one would deem a "bass head" - I like my headphones to faithfully reproduce the entire audio spectrum. Knowing my requirements, the way I would rate my headphones would be Sony 7506 = Sony V6 > Sennheiser HD 280 > Sennheiser HD 201 > Monoprice MEP-839 > JVC HA-RX500 = Sennheiser HD 202. In my comments below I make deliberate use of my adjectives (i.e. excellent > very good > good > average). Not surprisingly, the more expensive headphones sound the best. The Sony 7506/V6 have very good bass and excellent mids and treble frequencies which help bring out vocals. The Sennheiser HD 280's have excellent bass (better than the Sony's) and very good mids and treble (but not as good as the Sony's). Of the ~$20 headphones, the Sennheiser HD 201 has the best overall balance with very good bass, mids, and treble - its main deficiency is that it needs more power to drive; they are noticeably quieter than the other headphones at the same volume setting. However, once you turn up the volume, I feel they are the most balanced of the $20 headphones. The Monoprice MEP-839 falls next in terms of audio balance. It has very good bass and good mids and treble. It doesn't bring out mids and treble as well as the HD 201, but it is superior to the JVC HA-RX500 and Sennheiser HD 202. When compared to the 7506, V6, and HD280 I feel the bass is a slight bit muddier - with the more expensive headphones, the bass seems cleaner and has more of a punch. That said, the MEP-839 low frequencies extend as deep as the HD 280 and more than the 7506/V6. The reason I rate the MEP-839 bass as very good, instead of excellent, has to do with the fact it sounds a bit "muddy". The MEP-839's are relatively easy to drive and don't require the volume to be cranked up. Finally, there are the JVC HA-RX500 and Sennheiser HD 202. I feel these 2 are pretty similar in audio quality. They both have very good bass with average mids and treble. The HA-RX500 is more comfortable than the HD 202, primarily because they are circumaural and sit around your ears instead of the supra-aural HD 202 which actually rests on your ear. I can see why bass heads would like the HA-RX500 and HD202 - they emphasize bass over the mids/treble. That being said, I prefer my headphones to be balanced.

text: Note that the same headphone can be gotten for 30$ less. It's called Ex1 by Fiio. It's the exact same thing, but rebranded and even improved a bit in the durability and sensitivity area. Don't know why the price tag on this hasn't changed, but they're still great for the value at 100$. I didn't know until it was too late and already got my titan 1s. Very nice sounding earphones. I bought this hoping I'd get the most natural sound I can possibly get. If you go on innerfidelity.com to find the measurements for Dunu Titan 1 it shows some of the flattest frequency response I have ever seen in a headphone. However they didn't tell you what earphone tips were used in the measurements, and tips happen to matter a lot in this earphone. If you use the stock tips you will get ear resonance at around 6-8khz, as confirmed by a guy named Speakerphone ([...]). The resonance will be removed by triple flange tips ([...]). So I recommend getting those. Also be careful not to clog up the holes on the front of this thing. It changes the sound a lot if you do. They serve to prevent resonance and give the "open back" sound.

text: I mainly wear earbuds when listening to music and instructional videos on my computer. Plusses: * awesome cord that is woven fabric type (not plastic coated wire like other earbuds). I have not seen this type of cord on an earbud before, but it is great - flexible and does not tangle up. * silver metal reinforcements on the plug end and at the "V" where the two speakers come together into the main cord * nice slider to adjust the length of the two speakers, stays in place * very nice bass sound Minuses: * static! and "rustling noise" when using these on my computer, I can hear static (I think from the hard drive or fan running). Also, as others have mentioned, if the cord is jostled, the noise is transferred and heard in the headphones. This is a big minus for me. I have not tried these on an iPod, so I don't know if the static problem would be as extreme, but I think the noise when the cord moves would still be an issue. * not comfortable! these buds seem soft at first, but hurt my ears after a short time listening (10 min or so). I determined it is probably the soft bud part since when I replaced the Philips bud and tried my Skullcandy clear softer bud on the Philips product, the comfort was much improved. Maybe the material the Philips bud is made of is harder material that is designed to be "sound isolating", but it is extremely uncomfortable. The pain in my ear lingers for long after removal (with the Skullcandy there was no pain). I tried two different sizes of the Philips earbuds and the pain did not improve. * different size earbuds are different colors. The medium is green, but the small size is red and the large is black. Using the red buds results in a non-matching set and is pretty ugly - it would be better if all were green or black (or neutral clear) to match the green cord. * specked appearance is not really that speckled. Only the tiny about 1" part connecting the roundish black plastic bud part to the cord is black speckled with green. It is not even visible unless looking up close. I have debated what star rating to give this product. I love the quality tangle-free cord and solid connector that should last. I hate the uncomfortable ear buds and can maybe live with the static (hoping this might be just due to my computer). I decided to give a middle rating of 3 stars. I plan to buy an extra set of Skullcandy silicone earbuds and use them on these Philips earbuds to improve the comfort.
