text: *** UPDATE ON OCTOBER 18 (2017) *** Grab a chair! This is going to be an in depth review. Most of you that are reading this review are fans of Knowledge Zenith, as am I, and you're wondering if KZ has managed to outdo themselves, yet again, but before we get started on the ZS5, there are some things you need to know. About Me: I tend to prefer a relatively neutral sound signature with a slight emphasis in both bass and treble, which is basically a mild "U" shaped sound signature where midrange frequencies are left intact and unaffected. I find that an absolute neutral sound signature usually lacks enough energy for the genres I enjoy most, which are Classic Trance and Progressive (early Tiesto, Markus Schulz, Otello, DT8 Project), Chill Out, Breakbeat (Hybrid & Burufunk Remixes) and 80's & 90's (New Order, Secession, The Cure, Siouxie & The Banshees, Depeche Mode). Sure I listen to Shania Twain, Sade, Bach, Ella Fitzgerald and everything in between, but as of late the bulk of my listening pleasure is focused on the aforementioned genres. About IEMs: Take note when you read IEM reviews that when the reviewer gives his/her opinion regarding the sound that there are many factors that shape the final sound an IEM delivers to one's ear. Those factors include: 1 - Shape & size of reviewer's ear canals. (shallow/deep, wide/narrow) 2 - Shape & size of eartips (round/cone, single, double or triple flange) 3 - Materials of eartips (silicone/foam) 4 - Shape of IEM (and/or angle of nozzle) can cause fitment issues for some. 5 - Source (quality of DAC in smartphone, laptop, digital audio player) 6 - Source (power rating) is it amplified/unamplified. 7 - The IEM itself (driver flex/trapping air in canal causing muffled sound. 8 - The Reviewers ability to hear all frequency ranges (age plays a factor). Most consumers are unaware of how much weight each of these factors hold in rendering a final verdict. This is why there is such a wide variance in not only ratings, but the description of an IEMs sound. An unaware consumer purchases a perfectly fine IEM but has difficulty keeping the IEM in the ear or he/she does not satisfactorily seal the ear canal with the included silicone eartips (this is a common occurrence) and the consumer summarily dismisses the IEM as sub par. Another consumer purchases the same IEM but experiences a perfect fit and seal and has nothing but praise for the same IEM. Sealing the ear canals AND HAVING THE EARTIP FIRMLY AFFIXED to the IEM nozzle is the only proper way to use in-ear monitors. I can think of no audio equipment that is subjected to such praise or ridicule as the in-ear monitor. As if that's not enough, there is no "one-size-fits-all" when it comes to IEM eartips. Materials (silicone/foam) have different dampening effects on final sound. Shape of the eartips (olive-shaped, cone-shaped or other-shaped) can have different dampening effects on final sound based on how much space is between the IEM nozzle and your eardrum and how well the eartip has sealed the ear canal. The aperture of the eartip's opening (wide-bore/narrow-bore) will have dampening effects on the final sound. The easiest way for you to experience the different effects I am discussing is to take your current on-ear earphones or over-ear earphones, pick a song full of energy, put the earphones on and let them sit naturally over or on your ears. Listen to the music for two minutes. After two minutes, using your hands, slightly press the headphones closer to your eardrums. Notice the change in the sound. Is there more/less bass? Is there more/less treble? Did the vocals slightly slip forward/back? Consider that on-ear and over-ear headphones have a driver that sits approximately 1 1/2 inches to 2 inches from your eardrums and by pressing the headphones 1/4" closer to your eardrums the sound changed. Now consider that an IEM driver sits anywhere from 3/4" to 1/4" from your eardrums and the slightest changes (angle, depth, shape, material) can have up to three times more of an effect due to the proximity of the IEM to the eardrum. For this reason, I think it is wise to invest a nominal dollar amount on different eartips to find an eartip that works well for your particular ear's anatomy. This way you experience everything the earphone tuner intended for you to experience. Some IEM manufacturers supply multiple sizes (S/M/L) and/or materials (silicone/foam) of eartips to increase the odds that the consumer achieves a satisfactory seal, but even this is not foolproof. If this information holds any interest for you, there are a plethora of aftermarket eartip brands to look into, such as "JVC Spiral Dots", "Spinfits", "Comply Foam Eartips" or "Znari Foam Eartips", "Creative Aurvana" and others. If you really want to fine tune things, then you might find yourself doing what I do, which is scouring Amazon for inexpensive earphones that appear to have silicone eartips that have a shape that typically work well with my ear's anatomy. In the case of the ZS5, when I used "Znari Foam Eartips" I rated the ZS5 an "8 out of 10". When I pulled the blue Whirlwind Silicone Eartips from my Knowledge Zenith ED8 IEMs and installed them on the ZS5, the rating jumped to "9 out of 10". From an "8" to a "9", just by changing the eartips. A word to the wise is sufficient. The Knowledge Zenith ZS5: Typically, my KZ reviews start off with me discussing how Knowledge Zenith has several lines of IEMs, offering specific sound signatures and/or fashions (wires worn over-ear or wires hanging directly down). All of that still holds true, but I have to say that once KZ released the ZS3 and ZST, they silently moved further up the food chain. When Knowledge Zenith released the ZS3 "with detachable cables" in June 2016, there was nothing in the sub-$20 category that could touch it's sounds quality so long as you knew how to moderate the bass response via eartip size (see my review). Three months later, Knowledge Zenith released the ZST with it's detachable cables, which, again, nearly dwarfed everything else in the sub-$20 price bracket at the time of it's release. The ZST still sells quite well for an IEM that was released one year ago, and rightfully so. NOTE: For those of you that don't know, there is a quiet storm taking place in the IEM (and Audio Gear) market which we hobbyists affectionately refer to as Chi-Fi (Chinese Fidelity). In essence, the sound quality of audio gear coming from some Chinese manufacturers (Knowledge Zenith, Fiio, Monoprice, Shanling and others) is improving and progressing at a quickening pace. Some brands deserve as much attention as the established brands, if for no other reason than the value proposition in a global economic downturn where one typically receives less for their hard earned cash. In the midst of an unavoidable global economic upheaval, Knowledge Zenith is one such manufacturer that consistently offers exceptional value for your hard earned cash and the KZ ZS5 is evidence enough that the changes in the world of audio gear are reaching a feverish pitch. Knowledge Zenith's previous offerings, for the most part, resided in the sub-$20 price bracket, and most of the those offerings can be found by clicking my name at the head of this review and scrolling through the reviews to get a better description of each in-ear monitor (KZ and others) that might cater more to your preferences. This ZS5, however, has taken a hop, skip and a jump into the $40+/- price bracket....and while I will admit that I was skeptical, I can tell you unequivocally that Knowledge Zenith has MOSTLY accomplished what they set out to do. What do I mean by MOSTLY? It's become clear to me that the ZS5 has to be a "Beta" model, an interim model or even a test run. The following anomalies and abhorations will paint a clearer picture, so let's just lay this stuff right out on the table. Shortly after Knowledge Zenith released the ZST Colorful Edition, we (hobbyists) were teased with two up and coming IEM models. The first was a "Campfire Audio-inspired" design known as the "ZSR Pro" which, according to KZ's own photograph and specs, was to have a total of 10 drivers (4 balanced armatures & 1 dynamic driver per side). The second, and lesser known of the two, was an "Audio Technica E70-inspired" design. Many of us waited months for an aluminum shelled 10 driver IEM from KZ. After SIX months of rabid speculation, Knowledge Zenith released a PLASTIC shelled "Campfire Audio-inspired" ZS5 at a whopping $40+/-. I could not muster the words to express my disappointment. PLASTIC?! FOR MORE MONEY?! KZ, a rising star on a roll, consistently offered well tuned quality METAL finished housings on most of their IEMs. Why regress to PLASTIC shells, especially ON THEIR FLAGSHIP MODEL? To add insult to injury, the included detachable cable that was thrown in....FOR THEIR FLAGSHIP MODEL....is not designed for the ZS5 at all. The cable was designed for the ZS3. Note the angles of the stepdown molding on those cables. That stepdown angle was specifically designed for a perfect flush fit for the curvy ZS3. What could be sadder? Well....that would be the "square peg in a round hole" connection. Apparently, the ZS5 flagship didn't deserve its own cable, but whoa there Nelly....don't trail off just yet. I'm not even done yet. The ZS5 promotional photo showed the ZS5 with a crossover which is a key ingredient in multi-driver IEMs. Why? Because having all four drivers putting forth full spectrum frequencies from top to bottom (20hz to 20khz) tends to cause resonance issues in the frequency response you actually hear. Guess what? NO CROSSOVER. WTH?!?! What has happened to my favorite Chi-Fi brand? Needless to say, baffled and bemused, I barricaded myself in my man-cave, assumed the fetal position and reached for my pacifier. In the ensuing weeks I poured over multiple reviews that praised the ZS5's sound quality, but I just couldn't pull the trigger on the ol' "square peg in a round hole" IEMs..... that is UNTIL I caught a glimpse of the braided silver plated upgrade cables you see attached to my ZS5's in the photos below. Truth be told, "IF" I was going to pick them up I had to put my order in quickly because, lo and behold, Knowledge Zenith has chosen to revise the configuration of the balanced armatures in the ZS5. Instead of the original configuration (1 BA in the nozzle and 1 BA in the main cavity of the ZS5 shell) KZ has now chosen to place both BA's in the nozzle. Hmm, in light of everything I mentioned earlier regarding how minute changes can effect sound I knew I'd better order sooner rather than later if I wanted to receive the ZS5 in it's debut configuration, so what you see in the photos below is indeed the ZS5 in it's original release configuration. There has been much praise of the ZS5 sound signature when the ZS5 is paired with foam eartips. I have Znari Foam Eartips and Comply Foam Eartips, but I just can not abide the dampening effects present in foam eartips. I always feel one step removed from the music. Conversely, silicone eartips ALWAYS give me a presentation that I deem "true" to the IEM, and in the ZS5's case, the best silicone eartips (to my ears) are the Whirlwind eartips that KZ offered with their ED8 and ED10 IEMs. In light of the near $40 pricetag, it would be wise of KZ to offer its Whirlwind eartips (S, M & L) with the newly designed KZ ZS6. (Red Tips for the Black ZS6), (Black Tips for the Red ZS6) & (White Tips for the Green ZS6). At the very least KZ should continue offering them separately here on Amazon and if they are currently low on stock, KZ should ramp up production. Tennmak also offers Whirlwinds (See photo below). In fact, at near $40 Knowledge Zenith should be including all three designs to give the consumer an optimal chance for a satisfactory experience with their flagship IEM. Pairing: If you've read my review of the ZST, you'll be familiar with my rule of thumb when it comes to IEMs that sport balanced armatures. That rule is "for a full-bodied sound, use a low impedance source with a well regarded DAC and sufficient power". The ZS5 sports not one, but two BA's. In my estimation, having multiple balanced armatures may introduce impedance curves and/or render the ZS5 quite sensitive to your source (phone, laptop, DAP, etc). If your main source is a standalone smartphone I would stick to the ZS3, ED9 or UiiSii Hi-805, unless your phone has sufficient power with an exceptional DAC or is tethered to a low impedance portable amp. A great DAC and more power will likely give you a smoother response. It's not a hard and fast rule, but I find it to be true more often than not. The ZS5 sounds quite anemic and thin when coupled to my power-EFFICIENT ZuneHD. On my ZuneHD, rating on a scale of 1 - 10, the ZS5 bass was 5 out of 10 while the mids & treble were pushed to the forefront presenting a bright and analytical sound signature. When I coupled the ZS5 to my Fiio X3(i) the sub-bass & bass of the ZS5 woke from their slumber and breathed unrestrained life into the music. Not only was the presentation full-bodied, but now it was a more balanced presentation (though not flat or neutral). With foam eartips and narrow-bore silicone eartips the ZS5 had somewhat of a dual personality. Sometimes the music was crystal clear and inviting while at other times there were hints of lower frequency resonance that would ruin the experience. It didn't happen often, but it did happen. With the KZ Whirlwind Silicone Eartips resonance issues were harder to detect due to it's wide-bore aperture slightly diffusing the lower frequencies. With this set up (Fiio X3i - ZS5 - Upgraded Cable - Whirlwind Eartips) I was quite surprised at how well the ZS5 performed considering all 4 drivers were firing from top to bottom (20hz - 20khz). Again, with the wide-bored eartips the bass remained quite deep and quite natural and eartips with a more narrow bore seem to give the ZS5 a dual personality, where the bass could go from perfection on one track to slightly boomy or unrefined on another track, but bass was consistently well done with the Whirlwind Eartips. Let's hope the new ZS6 "WILL" include a crossover and thus eliminate the resonance issue present in the ZS5. Bass: 8.5/10 (most of the time), 7/10 (some of the time) Midrange & Vocals were natural and just south of centered. There was admirable weight in male vocals and female vocals were transparent and velvet-like, but truth be told, I prefer a little more presence in the midrange. It's why I love the ZS3 so much. Here's hoping the midrange on the ZS6 will have more presence. Midrange: 8/10 Treble was never ahead of the mids or bass. Diana Krall's "I Miss You So" and "Maybe You'll Be There" are tracks that I know are prone to sibilance, but I experienced none. Personally, I think the treble is well judged (never bright, never lacking). I'd love to see KZ carry this into the new ZS6 because those triple vented faceplates will give the treble more breathing room. Treble: 8.5/10. Soundstage and imaging are impressive. The ZS5 soundstage is a bit wider than the ZS3, but there is a trade off. You gain width on the ZS5, but you lose the ZS3's silky warmth in female vocals and you lose some weight in male vocals. In fact, the ZS5 actually loses some resolution in comparison to the ZS3 due to the ZS5 presentation being a bit more diffuse. The ZS5's mids are good, but I noticed the difference right away. The presentation as a whole is slightly more diffuse and leans more towards an over-ear headset than the typical in-ear presentation. I did not say that the ZS5 sounds like an over-ear headset, but the ZS5 LEANS toward an over-ear presentation. How much does it lean in that direction? Let's call it 25%. That's enough to set the ZS5 apart from just about any budget-fi IEM you can shake a stick at.......and then some........for $40+/- mind you. I was quite skeptical and, truthfully, quite miffed at KZ for offering a half-baked IEM to pacify KZ fans while their mad scientist concocts their next line of IEMs for the informed enthusiasts. The truth is that the ZS5, in its original release configuration, though it is not perfect, may just be that rare IEM that defies logic and becomes an instant collectible once the debut configuration is sold out. Can't explain why it works so well and don't know how it works so well...but it just does. I'm glad I gave in and finally picked these up before they vanished. Test tracks were the following: Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong - "Gee Baby, Ain't I Good To You" Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong - "Learnin' The Blues" (test shouty mids on trumpet) Diana Krall - "Maybe, You'll BeThere" (sibilance test) Diana Krall - "Baby, All The Time" (sibilance test) Nina Simone - "See-Line Woman (Masters At Work Remix)" Shania Twain - "No one needs to know" Tim McGraw - "She Was Mine For A Little While" Tears for Fears - "Woman In Chains" (test Clean bass/test vocals w/ Oleta Adams) Morcheeba - "Blindfold" (test clean bass) Massive Attack - "Teardrop" (test Clean bass & guitar presentation) Portishead - "Roads" (test vocals & resonance on note holding texture on keyboards) Schiller - "Under My Skin" (test clean bass, vocal presentation and micro-details) Beth Orton - "Central Reservation" Beth Orton - "Daybreaker" Metallica - "Nothing Else Matters" Dream Theater - "Pull Me Under" (test for body, crunch and micro-detail) Tourniquet - "The Hand Trembler" (coherency in a busy and layered performance) Tourniquet - "Where Moth & Rust Destroy" (coherency in a busy and layered performance) Jackson 5 - "I Want You Back" (test for imaging and separation) Secession - "Magician (Pecky Plus Mix)" (male vocals/lower mids vs upper bass) The Church - "Under The Milky Way" (test for acoustic guitar presentation) Al Stewart - "Year Of The Cat" (test imaging, Soundstage & Tonal balance) America - "Tin Man" (test imaging, Soundstage & Tonal balance) Otello - "Masterworks Collection: Rabbit Hole" (handling complex bass & drums) Otello - "Masterworks Collection: Las Vegas" (handling complex bass & drums) Otello - "Masterworks Collection: Downtime" (test clean bass & vocal presentation) Antonio Vivaldi - "L'Estro Armonico" (test for shouty mids/violins and timbre) The ZS6 should be on my doorstep in about a week and I'm expecting an improved soundstage and a near holographic presentation due to the triple-vented faceplate. With dual balanced armatures in the nozzle it looks like I'll have to order two more pairs, one Green and one black, so I can modify and experiment in order to shape the final presentation. The Red ZS6 will stay stock. The Green ZS6 will be opened in order to reposition the BA's so they fire directly into the ZS6 cavity instead of directly out of the nozzle. The Black ZS6 will be opened in order to slightly dampen the BA's at their nozzles. Regardless of the results, I know they won't sound like these ZS5's, because the ZS6 is a semi-open design. Part of me is thankful, but in a begrudging manner. In fairness I have to give credit where credit is due. Knowledge Zenith did a good job on tuning the ZS5, occasional resonance aside, and they've surprised me yet again. *** UPDATE October 18, 2017 *** Reading my original review above, you will recall that I found the ZS5 to be "laidback". You will also recall how much emphasis I put on tip rolling. After listening to the ZS5 for two weeks I had decided that they are a very good IEM, but probably wouldn't get more than 20% playtime because I prefer more presence and energy for the genres I enjoy most. I have several pairs installed on other IEMs because I enjoy them so much. In fact, I had stashed this last pair only to be pulled out for a special occasion. Funny things is I was listening to the ZS5's and had literally just decided that I needed more energy and I'd probably spend more time with my ZST's or Magaosi M3's to get it. Just then, out of the corner of my eye, I caught a glimpse of my favorite silicone eartips. My eyes widened, I jumped up and extracted them from their case and installed them on the ZS5 and .... CHEEZ & RICE!! ... REALLY?!?! Yes! Absolute perfection! I mean everything is near perfect: Bass (9), Mids (9), Treble (9), Soundstage (10) and what makes it all gel together (for the genres I enjoy) is PRESENCE (9). My ZS5 no longer sounds "laid back". No, these really hit that sweet spot of being out of head, yet still having direct presence ..... all for the want of an eartip! Dang, should've ordered two pairs of these. Dang! Dang! Dang! KZ, you need to revert back to this original configuration for the ZS5 because these are EPIC for $35! EPIC! *** END UPDATE *** If KZ is reading this, I do have some constructive criticism. If, ....scratch that....."When" you decide to alter a KZ model that has already been released to the public, PLEASE...change the color of the modified release in order to avoid confusion and/or frustration. It would be so much simpler if the ZS5 in its new configuration would be offered in two new colors as opposed to the original configuration colors of blue & gray. This way everyone knows exactly what they are getting. As it stands right now, if I ordered another ZS5 today, I'd have no idea (and your sellers would have no idea ) which configuration would be received. That is unacceptable. A new configuration or revised edition should rightfully warrant a new color. If, on the ZS6, you choose to revert to the original ZS5 configuration (with 1 BA in the cavity and 1 BA in the nozzle) then perhaps discontinue the Red, Green and Black and offer three new colors for the revised ZS6 (Silver, Bronze and Gold). Before I forget, those new ES3's sure would look nice if they were offered with wood coloured faceplates and French vanilla bodies, similar to the "TFZ 1 series with wood finish". I'd buy them! P.S. - YINYOO AUDIO is a top notch outfit and I highly recommend them. Received my ZS5's within ten days. Hope this was helpful. DocHolliday

text: Like most everyone, I'm spending a lot of time on Zoom etc., and these were an asked for gift to help make the experience less stressful. The highlights are: - Outstanding audio, both for listening and for your voice during a call. - The noise cancellation is astounding, better than the Panasonic's these replace and even the QuietComfort 35's that I use occasionally - They are lightweight but don't feel flimsy -- PACKAGING -- Most expensive consumer devices come well packaged these days and the 700's are typical of that. The case is kind of egg shaped, and bigger than I expected, but it does have a neat little flap to hold the USB to USB-C cable and audio plug cable. The case is solid and should stand up to being in your luggage for when we find ourselves flying places and needing in-flight noise canceling headphones again. There is no charger, but the USB to USB-C cable means you can plug in to an existing charger, of which you are likely to have numerous. I use my Samsung phone charger and its USB-C cable because that's always set up in the bedroom, so the Bose cables stay in the case most of the time. -- THE APP -- Here is one flaw, which starts with the requirement to download the Bose app before you can use your headphones. I get everyone wants to harvest your data these days, but come on Bose, they're headphones! I could live with some dumbed down features without the app, but this is is overreach. Also, the app itself is not particularly useful. If it added a lot of functionality to the headphones, I'd possibly feel the value prop. As it is, most of what it can do is one-time setup related and occasional firmware updates, so it's then just wasting space on your phone. -- BUTTON CONTROLS -- Once you accept that, you have to live with what are fussy touch controls and poorly placed physical controls. I'll talk the physical controls first, which are two small buttons on the right ear cup and a larger one on the left ear cup. Even being mindful, I find it too easy to depress them taking the headset on and off. So, I frequently turn them off, then take them off, and inadvertently turn them back on again without noticing. I've burned through a few podcasts that way, as they play, unlistened to, in the background. The most other *really* annoying aspect of the physical buttons is the mute. When you're in a call on your phone, and you mute the microphones, the headset tells you. But it does not do this with Windows PC VoIP apps like Zoom or Teams. It makes the mute button way less useful because you don't know if you have or haven't. Mute isn't useful if Bose take the word literally in the UI. Noise cancellation has a dedicated button with three presets that you can change via the app. The defaults are zero, five, and ten, which I've not bothered to change and would be interested in knowing how many people do. A long hold on this button shifts into "conversation mode", which seems to pause audio on a phone and turn off the noise cancellation so you can interact with others. It's a good idea, but I find it faster to just pull the headphones down than wait for the long press to activate conversation mode, and I've now had enough feedback to know that others do too. -- USE WITH PCs -- The PC experience is poor and that's really disappointing. I've set my headphones to shutdown after 20 minutes of no activity, and initially, they would do this when connected to the PC and in a Teams call. That was a surprise, took me a few calls to understand the headset had turned off and not just lost Bluetooth. A firmware update solved the problem, so I am hopeful a firmware update can solve the mute mute button as well, but Bose seems to be ignoring all the programmatic power available in Windows 10, which is disappointing. -- TOUCH CONTROLS -- At least the physical controls offer tactile feedback. I find the touch controls a hit and miss affair. They are based on taps and swipes of the front area of the right ear cup and so far I've managed to mostly master a double tap to pause a podcast or music. On my phone that is. The double tap does nothing with content coming from the PC. I can somewhat control volume as well, which is a swipe up / down on the ear cup, but honestly, it's not consistent and I get frustrated trying to use it so I don't bother much. -- SOUND QUALITY -- In terms of sound, the 700's are smooth without too much bass. Indeed, if you are looking for bass, these probably are not the headphones for you. My Apple earbuds go down deeper than the Bose, but I'm okay with that because my head banging days are well over. What is awesome is the audio when you are in a call, which really is my primary use case. The noise cancellation allows for your voice to leak through, so you can hear yourself talk without too much else intruding. Note though, that the noise cancellation does not mean that sounds around you are not sent down the wire. I was copying files off a failing hard drive that has a high pitched buzz and while the 700's eliminated the disk whine for me, people on a call I'd joined could hear it loud and clear. One thing I have noticed when connected to my Dell XPS laptop is crackle. I mostly listen to music on YouTube when I'm writing my novels, so it _could_ be the source, but I tend to listen to the same albums and don't recall any crackle prior to the 700's. Note that I've only used the 700's Bluetooth connected, I've not tried them connected via the audio jack, so can't say if that degrades the experience in any way (apart from the obvious of being physically tied to your device). -- BATTERY LIFE -- Battery life is reasonable. After a recharge I'm told I have 19 hours available. Using noise cancellation turned up to the max burns battery faster than having it dialed back, but I hardly ever dial it back and so far I'm recharging about every third day and usually there are still a few hours left. You get told battery life when they power up, but you can also query it with a long touch on the right ear pad, which I often trigger when I'm pulling them down off my head. -- CHARGING -- I've updated my original review to note that if you plug the USB cable in to charge the headphones, they stop operating. It seems unlikely, but they can't multitask (charge while you use them) like most electronic devices, which is annoying. -- COMFORT -- Sadly, no over ear headphones that I've ever worn seem designed for glasses. These are not bad, but after an hour-ish the press of the glasses arm into the side of your head starts to hurt. That's a hard one to engineer out, but if someone does, I'd be happy to hear about it. Apart from that, they are light. But I will admit, they don't seem to want to stay in place and once I yawned with them on they fell off the back of my head (and onto the floor. Fortunately, nothing seems to have broken!). So I am constantly jostling them back into place as I wear them. Do I do this more than with my Panasonic's? I'm not sure, to be fair. It feels like I do, but it may merely be the physiological impact of expecting the Bose to be more comfortable. -- SUMMARY -- For the price, I was expecting quality and from the reviews, best-in-class noise cancellation. I got both of those. The noise cancellation really is amazing and if that's what you are looking for above all else, these will suit. But there are niggles, and the interaction with PC apps is a major one for me, as are the controls, and esp. the mute button behavior on a PC. The requirement for the app may also be a showstopper if you find such things overly intrusive. And given that the app itself is not very featured, that seems a fail. On the plus side, I am hopeful Bose respond to the mute button with a firmware update, we'll see. They have responded to the shutdown timer already, so these are not expensive 'set in concrete' devices that you buy and the vendor never improves. We'll see. In the meantime, I'm happy enough with my 700's ability to shut out the world, and that's not a bad thing in our pandemic-inflicted times.

text: While I will agree nearly point-by-point with reviewers regarding the sound reproduction of the AH D1100s (bass can be a bit thick, works better with an amp), I must add yet another incident where the product delivered was not 'built to last'. In fact, this model appears to have, in the experience of a number of posters in internet (hi-fi and other electronic product) forums, myself included, a common structural defect. I can't tell if this is a design, manufacturing, or quality control problem. But nevertheless, it is *clearly* not an isolated issue. More specifically, the issue regards the swivel arms that critically attach the cans to the headband. The lightweight plastic from which these arms are made have, in several discussions, lasted as little as 9 months before cracking. In my case, I didn't notice any cracks until, in the 13th month of using them (only at my desktop at home) a large chip of the plastic splintered off the left swivel arm. The arm could no longer reasonably support the left can and very quickly broke upon using them the next time. Note that these headphones had neither never left my desktop nor been otherwise mistreated in any way (no accidents, drops, nada). I also inspected the swivel arm of the right can, Very minute cracks could be seen spreading from the midpoint of the 'C shaped' arm. These were quite subtle, but with only a very minor bit of torque applied, it was evident that these fractures were displaced, meaning they were critical structural failures and would not last long under the moderate tension from normal wear. I called Denon support about this, and spoke to a rather prickly representative. I informed him about the issue and the incidents that I had read in discussion forums on this product. He implied that the cans were mistreated, that he had owned a pair of these for 9 months, and he would do nothing to inform his company that there could be a quality flaw that hasn't been examined. He especially didn't care to help solve this issue as my headphones were *just* out-of-warranty. Such fanatical service this Denon corporation.... (in comparison, I've seen far better from Sennheiser folks lurking various forums and answer to defects with a nice degree of transparency). I sent the headphones to PanurgyOEM, who is the primary repair service for warranty and out-of-warranty repairs for Denon. PanurgyOEM was fully aware from my report that the issue was the broken piece on the headband. They still charge a $29.00 'evaluation fee' which would be applied to the labor cost for a repair. Nearly 1 month after sending the cans for repair (this is far too long, given I sent the item 2 day FedEx and confirmed date/time of receipt), I received a rather belated and shocking estimate from them. Here is the breakdown: - $72.86 for the headband (they only replace the entire thing) - $29.00 for labor (already charged as the above mentioned 'evaluation fee') - $20.00 for shipping (??? what do they use, Singapore Air?) - $12.00 for materials(??? really? a box and cushioning? I know, it must have been the expense of the surgical suite grade clean room they use to send the precious devices that have been contaminated by the humans...) Total, a mere $133.86 - FOR A HEADBAND!!! I bought the headphones for $120. Since my purchase, there has been a markup of these cans to $199 (as of 9/22/2012). At either cost, this is NOT an economical repair, especially given internet reports that this issue has *repeated* after repair. The cost of repairing headphones should arguably come at the expense of the audio technology, not a headband. A PanurgyOEM representative interestingly input their definition of 'economical' as the price of repair that meets or exceeds a *current* list price of the cans, not the price at the time of purchase. Show me a headphone which appreciates in value. In the end, PanurgyOEM was kind enough to tell me that if I want the headphones back even without repair, I must pay $32.00 (itemized above). Let's see......$61.00 to have *NOTHING* done to repair the product. No highway robbery there.... In sum, I think it's safe to say that I would urge *extreme* caution in buying these headphones - if, and until the structural integrity of the headband is in some way improved by Denon. Otherwise, you could be faced being scoffed at by a swarthy Denon rep, or mugged by the repair man in New Jersey.... 2 stars for nice audio, but durability factor and expense to service renders them problematic given the price point.

text: The sound is pretty incredible for the price. I A&B compared them to my Sennheiser HD 558's and preferred these. The bass is a fraction of the 558's but it is very tight and doesn't bleed into the midrange. I prefer these for gaming due to the low clamp force and oversized pads. They are excellent for long sessions without feeling fatiguing. Now there are some issues, mainly with QC. I returned my first pair because the left channel was noticeably more quiet than the right, got the replacement pair and they sounded excellent but the adjustment strap on the right side has no clicks. It freely slides from the 2 position to the 5 position by it's own weight. I am waiting on my THIRD pair of these. I really hope I just had a bad streak because I really like the sound that these put out. They are bright, but not irritatingly so, and above all provide great clarity for gaming. They won't be the best for all kinds of sub-bass heavy music but they are more enjoyable than the veiled sound of my sennheisers, even if you have to give up a bit of soundstage and bass. SIDE NOTE: I do NOT recommend these with the v-moda boompro. I know it's compatible and very easy but the QC on those is just as hit or miss. The first mic I used had a lot of white static noise in the background, and the replacement sounded great, until I found out that the volume slider controls both the headphone audio AND the mic audio. This is a massive design problem because it basically makes it so that gaming at an acceptable volume makes the microphone hard to hear. It also draws power from the right channel making the left cup noticeably louder. I would rather deal with the extra cables on the modmic.

text: My 5-star review is simply based on the price and value for these headphones. I was torn between these and the ROCK Zircon, so I ended up buying both the ED9 and Zircon. Being a musician, producer, and audio enthusiast, I can confidently say that the ED9 are better than the Rock Zircon. In my opinion, the ED9 are more balanced and have a better gain stage. When I say "balance" I don't mean there is no sub-bass because there is plenty. While the ear buds themselves are a bit heavy and the design isn't as sexy as the Zircons, these headphones outperform the Zircon on audio quality. The Zircon has too much of an increase in the sub frequency which ends up muddying up any mix. I could go on about some of the other flaws about the Zircons, but let's stick to the ED9s. If you're looking for headphones to use while doing cardio or any other physical activities that requires the cable moving, I wouldn't recommend the ED9. If you shake the cables while the earbuds are in, you'll get A LOT of cable noise - it's almost like the sound of wind in your ears. I don't believe these are being marketed as performance headphones, so I'm able to look past this flaw. These are mainly for when you're stationary, doing work on the laptop or desktop, etc. If you're on the fence, just buy them. They're so cheap compared to other headphones on the market that are lesser quality.

text: My cell phone is my only phone so I use it constantly. For perspective, my past and secondary headsets have been Jabra BT250's and a Nextlink AX2 -- both of which go in the ear (not on the ear). I got the Nokia BH-900 at Best Buy for $110 - definitely on the high side but the headset is the whole user interface for the phone once the call is placed - so quality is important to me. Overall, good noise cancellation, good sound quality both incoming and outgoing, typically good Nokia fit and finish. Pros: * solid construction - plastic with touches of black chrome - feels solid but not too heavy * sliding boom moves microphone closer to mouth as well as answers/ends a call * unique (to Nokia) ear hook is secure and comfortable once you figure out how to attach (for me, pointing the boom down to 6 o'clock and lowering the headset on my ear, with the rear/lower hook going behind my earlobe, then rotating counter-clockwise to 4 o'clock got a secure fit that made the headset unnoticeable once on) * volume control was able to amplify a caller's voice significantly loud enough - rocker switch enabled easy fine tuning Cons: * Ear hook design took me a day or two to perfect how I put it on -- easier to leave it on than take on and off * Definitely not the smallest headset * Sliding boom is a potential point of failure Overall, great headset with premium price - time will tell if it delivers its full value.

text: EDIT: These lasted almost 4 months before they stopped turning on. The light is purple when it tries to charge. Very dissapointing. I guess that's what I get for trying to go cheap. My Bose SoundSports went bad after about a year of moderate use and I needed something to replace them. Unwilling to to spend over $100 on something that might go bad in a year I went on the search for some cheaper headphones. After searching through product reviews and YouTube reviews I stumbled across the Dudios Zeus and have to say I am pleasantly surprised. I'm no audiophile but I do like my music to sound decent while I'm working out and the sound out of these are pretty darn close to my Soundsports. The bluetooth connection is good and it pairs with my phone quickly. I haven't tested the distance but I've been able to walk across the room in the gym and didn't experience any dropped signal or stuttering. The build quality on the earbuds themselves is ok, not great but ok. The control box and the wire feel like the cheapest parts. The wire feels flimsy, like if I tugged a little too hard I'd get a short easily and the control box feels like it's made of really cheap plastic. The set came with a couple clips to clip the wire to the back of your collar and I was very nervous putting it on the wire. I felt like it would snap the wire if I pulled too hard, and I did have to pull a bit to get it on. The clips are cheap and broke within a few days of use. Like every other set of earbuds it comes with multiple sizes of ear inserts. The "wing" is a bit odd but it does help hold the earbuds in place although a standard sweep design would probably feel more natural. I am dissapointed in the battery life. I only got 4-5 hours on a charge and while it reported I had 20% left, it died in the middle of my workout. When they worked I got 12-15 hours on my Soundsports. The best thing about them is the cost. It's hard to beat $28 for some earbuds that actually sound good. PROS: Excellent Sound Quality Good Bluetooth Connection Price CONS: Middling Build Quality Poor Battery Life

text: I purchased these headphones to use with my Waterfi iPod shuffle (which is awesome btw). The sound quality isn't amazing (I would not choose them over my day to day headphones when listening to music outside the water); but honestly, you don't really notice the slight decrease in sound quality after being in the water a few minutes. I have found that they stay in my ears pretty well with vigorous lap swimming even when my swim cap is not pulled down all the way. I discarded the plastic attachments as they were uncomfortable, and I have been fine without them. Given that they come with about 4-5 different size/shape ear-bud fits I would recommend them to anyone looking for a "good" waterproof head phone. *Manufacturer Please Read This" The reason I am not giving these headphones 5 stars is due to the cord being way , way too long for most practical purposes that people would use waterproof headphones for. Think about it: for water sports you don't want to create drag by having cords hanging about, and people are usually attaching them to devices on the back of their goggles (especially for swimming) or on their upper arm. So why do you need 3.5-4 feet of cord in headphones that are advertised to use for water sports?!? Right now, the most laborious part of my pre-swim workout routine is winding the damn cord of these headphones around and around and around and around my goggle straps till it's not flailing about anymore. I like these headphones, but as soon as another company is smart enough to make a pair with swimmers in mind by having a shorter cord I will re-evaluate my customer loyalties.

text: I had high expectations for the Powerbeats Pro, and have ended up highly disappointed. Fit If there's one good thing I can say about the Powerbeats Pro, is that they don't fall off like AirPods, EarPods and most wireless and wired ear buds do. The Powerbeats Pro come with four pairs of ear tips in different sizes. Too bad none of them actually fit my ears. I wish Apple would just make their current AirPods with an ear hook to prevent them from falling off our ears. Anyway, the ear tips included with the Powerbeats resulted in either flat out pain or discomfort. After trying out all four pairs of ear tips, I ended up going back to the medium ones that come installed out of the box. Sound Sound quality in ear buds is directly related to their fit and how well that fit can create a seal. Needless to say that I cannot get good sound with the ear tips that don't cause me pain, and I can't get good sound quality for too long with the painful ear tips. The end result is ear buds that sound like the cheapest earphones you can buy, except that the Powerbeats are not cheap at all. Battery life If the Powerbeats Pro are supposed to have better battery life than the AirPods, I seriously don't want to imagine how awful the AirPods can be. The Powerbeats Pro can't even stand a whole day without needing to recharge, and that's regardless of whether you use them a lot throughout the day or barely at all. Yes, even in Standby these ear buds suck a lot of battery. Don't forget to take the oversized case with you, because you are definitely going to need it before you come back home.. Pairing Don't be fooled by the super quick and simple iPhone pairing process the first time you use the ear buds. If their batteries reach near 0%, the ear buds lose their pairing and you have to re-pair them by long pressing the pairing button on the case. I'm seriously debating whether or not to return these ear buds. They are not worth the money I paid for them. I'm already talking to people I know against buying them.

text: It is with regret that I write this review. I wanted so badly to like these earbuds, and expected to based on others' reviews, but they were simply miserable for me. I'll start with the pros, which earned the earbuds one star: The build quality and craftsmanship are quite impressive. They are stunning to look at and hold ... everything from the differential colors for the left/right buds, to the in-line controls, to the case and ear tips are impressive. But, unfortunately, that's where it ends for me. These are, without a doubt, the most uncomfortable things I've ever put in/on my ears (and I once had to go to the ER to have a rock removed from my right ear). I could not get a good seal without pushing tips all the way into my ears, which created discomfort after about 30 minutes of using them. Anything longer than an hour caused significant pain that lingered after removing the buds. Some of the ear tips fit perfectly fine, but whether due to the weight or the design, they simply weren't comfortable. Now about that weight; these buggers are heavy … very heavy. Not only are the earbuds themselves heavy, but the over-the-ear cables are significantly heavier than any others on the market. While that may indicate durability, it also translates to discomfort. Because the over-the-ear cables are metal, they rubbed the top of my ears, which over time became less than enjoyable. I think the main problem here is that the in-line remote is metal and the cable is fairly thick, which causes some pull and tension over the ear. However, even with the clip, the metal-on-ear contact was uncomfortable. I compared the sound to two sets of earbuds I previously purchased. The first was a high-end pair in the $350 range made by a company that begins with K and ends with h. The sound from the other earbuds was noticeably better and richer, which isn't surprising, considering the price difference, components, and possibly the purpose of the two pairs. However, I also compared these (RHA) to an older pair of earbuds by the same company mentioned before, but that were a quarter of the price of these. The only difference between the two pairs was that the highs from these (RHA) were slightly less shrill than my old pair. That is, they sound perfectly fine, but are underwhelming. Also, as others have mentioned, they are bass-heavy, and the filters did little to adjust that imbalance for me. Again, while these are extremely well made earbuds, attractive, and seem superbly durable, the durability comes with a cost. Weight certainly trumps comfort, which is something I'm not willing to put up with. Hopefully others will have more luck with them (and it appears they do), but these simply are not for me.

text: This is more of a first impression, and I have only an hour or two on these. I'm running these through a Soundavo HP-DAC1, to a S.M.S.L. mini tube amp. Out of the box, with the stock tips I was thinking, "Ok, they sound good, but it's going to take me a hot minute to get used to a flatter sound signature again". I listened to them for a bit, enjoyed them, and then decided to try out some of the other tips. It seems like the tips are all "medium", just different styles of medium. The red ones that came on fit me great, and I grabbed the yellow pair to try next and... WOW. With the default red tips they sound like what you'd expect a flatter signature to sound like. Flat. Well, these aren't quite flat, not in that boring way some headphones are. Highs are relaxed, mids sound great, bass pretty weak (no sub bass at all). Then I tried the yellow, more ball shaped tips. These have a stiffer inner wall compared to the reds. I still get an amazing seal (and believe me, these things seal great due to having quite a small body size, smaller than the images lead you to expect). And, there's the bass! Now we're talking. With these tips they have a fuller, more "fun" sound. The bass has been brought up, not to an extreme extent, but the rest sounds much the same. I like that the highs aren't crazy with these. Too many headphones try to create a "detailed" sound by boosting the highs, which leaves them almost unusable to me, because I'm very sensitive to highs, and especially sibilance. Nothing will make me take a headphone off faster than a hot S or T sound, it's like being stabbed in the ears. The highs with these is pleasant to listen to. I'm listing to a couple tracks that normally make my head almost explode, Marilyn Manson's If I Was Your Vampire, and Kittie's Funeral For Yesterday. Very tolerable with the Salnotes Zero. The high hats in Funeral For Yesterday starts to edge into that space of "I want to rip the headphones out", but never quite gets there. Detail is alright. I'm definitely missing some things that I'm used to hearing. Marko's bass lines in some Nightwish songs, such as Bare Grace Misery, aren't as easy to pick up on as I'm used to, but that was with the default red tips, maybe the swap will bring those things back out. (Listening again with the yellow tips, and this is the case.) These are very comfortable. As I mentioned before, they're a lot smaller than they appear in the images. This leads to a snug fit in the ear. They're very lightweight, as well. They fit in a way that I call "disappearing" when you're wearing them, you really can't tell they're there. I use games to test imaging and soundstage. Gaming is my primary use for my audio devices after all. Currently my game of choice is Star Citizen, so that's what I used. Soundstage isn't terribly big. It isn't "in your head", but it isn't wide either. Imaging is great though, I can clearly tell if something is to the sides, up or down, or behind me. If I had to give a real complaint, it would be the the L and R labeling on the wire is difficult to see! Overall these are pretty great. A steal at $20.

text: Background – My natural preference is a warmer sound. If a company can't make the 'detail' show up without making the headphones screechy, I’d rather they just tone down treble all together. The IE60s have no problem in this department. I am starting off this review as such because it’s important to understand when a reviewer says they love the sound; I think the reader should know what type of sound the reviewer naturally prefers. Someone who prefers "bright" or treble-filled and detailed sound may consider the amount of base in, say the KEF M200s too much for example. This is the perspective I’m coming from. I recently purchased and am returning both these and the KEF M200s. I hope that this review helps anyone considering either. Check out my review of the M200s if you would like to know more about those. Case, Cord, Accessories (5/5)– The Sennheisers have the best accessories, most thoughtful case, and a good selection of ear tips, very thin but strong cord that does not tangle, and make the best presentation. It’s incredible how much consideration went into making the case and presenting it to fit the headphones. The best feature of the case for me, is that it has an area devoted to wrapping the cord. This should be standard in all IEM cases, what a great idea! The cord may be the best I’ve seen on any IEM, maybe even better than the Bose MIE2 (it’s a thick cord). Even through the cord for IE60s is thinner; it also seems to be very sturdy and doesn’t get tangled up easily. Fit (3/5) – The IE60s need to be crammed in your ear in an unusual way (for me). Check out Youtube videos of people wearing them, it looks fine but it’s not always easy to get them in your ear like that. Hey, pushing $250 plastic headphones against your ear to force them in the right position isn't a great plan for longevity. I guess the people on Youtube were able to get the motions down, so it could just be me. Once in your ear though, they are comfortable and much more so than bigger IEM’s like the KEF M200’s. Sound (2/5) – The IE60s are for me a bit of a paradox. On one side, for my musical preference the Sennheiser IE60s don’t give the right kind of sounds in the right amounts (more on that later). From this perspective, I find them overpriced. On the flip side, comparatively I found them the best to live with (partially for the case, cord and accessories). The IE60's do have a warm sound without the annoying screechy highs; however paradoxically they didn't have much base. It seems like they can produce base, but are tuned not to. Maybe I didn't wear them correctly? However for $250, the headphones should be easier to put on and achieve the best sound then this situation is currently. The base does exist, but it runs away and hides quickly. This means that much of the music I listen to all of a sudden lacked emotion (vs. KEF M200). Dubstep in particular was awful. I tried using different tips with various degrees of success, but overall, the sound itself can't hold a candle to the KEF M200s. Add to that, the KEF's are $50 less expensive, and aren't plastic. I did find the sound coming from the IE60’s the least distracting and most pleasant for in-office use. However, I can't justify $250 for using headphones in the office. Even with cramming, the IE60 does fit way better than the KEF M200s; my ear was relieved not to be violated by the KEF Conquistadors for a change. However, the sound out of these IE60s... I mean, why do they say on the box that it has good base extension? Take a look at the KEF's if you want a good warm sound that pounds when you want it to, and gives you detail when your least expecting it. An interesting fact about the sound is, while I’m no audiophile, I think that the IE60s sound was the most correct if that makes any sense. The sound was also the most detailed, accurate, and purposeful I think I’ve ever heard in a headphone. When music begins to get complicated, there is not just separation of instruments, but there is a sense of the instruments being located somehow next to and around you. It’s for this reason I’m not giving these a 1 star rating. This type of sound I’m sure has its suitors, and to them these are fantastic sounding IEM’s and more than worth the price. I found the description on the packaging to be a bit deceitful. Yes there was warmth in that you didn’t get Montezuma’s revenge when music began to throw high notes in the mix, and yet, the base wasn’t present enough, and didn’t extend low enough for the music to be enjoyable. For some tracks I believe the lack of base extension took the essence of the music away when compared with the KEF M200s. Conclusion – Perhaps if you prefer classical music these are awesome IEMs? Perhaps if you are used to the way these fit in your ear, or have an ear shaped in a way that complements the way these were designed then these will be fantastic IEMs for you? For me, I find returning them a bit sad; because had they included better base and perhaps an easier fit, I could happily live with these no problem. I have never seen such attention to detail given for IEMs and it doesn’t seem like a gimmick to me. For someone these are very good IEMs, just not for me.

text: Arrived in a slim flat box, I was expecting these headphones to have a very travel-friendly footprint. Typical for other Beyerdynamic headphones I have tested, I never take with a grain of salt their "writing on the box" since they are usually accurate about describing a sound signature and headphone features. The packaging box had a lot of info about specifications, accessories (in this case a singular "accessory"), and magnetic folding cover to reveal the actual headphones under a see-through display screen - always an enjoyable unboxing experience. Out of the box, you find a pair of DTX 350p and a draw string storage bag (the accessory). This is probably going to be my only negative comment/suggestion, but I truly wish they would have included a large/wider storage bag. I do understand they are trying to keep the cost down, so no fancy case. But considering how great these will be when traveling, a good storage case would be important. Headphones itself have a very solid plastic build, with only a metal band going through a headband. I do have to admit, from the first glance they look identical to P21 in terms of a design and overall dimensions. But the build quality is night'n'day. There is no creaking when you twist and rotate DTX 350p, the folding joints are not as loose, and adjustable headband has better latching control to stay in place. It really felt like a premium quality over P21. Also, earpads in DTX 350p are softer, bigger, and plushier. The build and earpads improvement alone justifies $20+ difference between DTX 350p and P21 models. The design details are the same where earcups rotate 90deg to lay flat on the surface and fold inside of the headband to occupy a minimum space. Cable is flat, soft, and easy to manage while being tangle free, and it's attached to each earcup. Also, I sensed no microphonics effect. The headphone plug is gold plated and has 270deg angle, similar to some other Beyer IEMs. Inside of the headband at the top, you have a soft layer of foam wrapped in the pleather similar to earpads. In combination with a comfortable clamping force, these headphones feel very lightweight and provide decent noise isolation. Keep in mind, this is on-ear design which sits on top of your ear, so it's tricky to get isolation right. Here, it felt perfect and rivaled even more expensive models from V-Moda (M80 and XS). Of course, don't expect the same comfort and isolation of T51p, but we are talking about DTX 350p which is 4 times cheaper. So how do these sound? That's where a thought crossed my mind about $69 DTX 350p being a "giant killer", except Beyerdynamic is usually on the other side of the fence being a "giant" lol! I often use this term when I compare some budget priced in-ear headphones that come close in performance and design to a more expensive brand name ones. With DTX 350p I was hearing a rather well balanced sound signature with a little bit of v-shape and enhanced (but not overpowering) bass. Starting with a low end, bass has a deep sub-bass texture with a nice rumble, and a fast mid-bass punch to drive the beat. I guess it will be unfair to compare it head-to-head with Tesla drivers of T51p, but for sure the bass was more articulate and better defined than in M80 and XS. There is no spillage into lower mids, everything was under control. Mids are clear and detailed, warm and smooth, and a little bit recessed but not too much back to still enjoy presentation of vocals. Treble is crisp and extended, yet smooth enough without a hint of sibilance. And to top it off, soundstage has above the average width with an average depth which is expected for on-ear closed back design. Overall, I was very glad I got an opportunity to review DTX 350p which quickly got elevated to the top of my favorite affordable "on-ear" headphones. On-ear design usually doesn't get as much attention while being stuck between in-ear and full size over-ear, but I think they deserve more credit because of being more portable than full size and offer better isolation and fitment than in-ears (especially for those who hate eartips). DTX 350p has a great sound signature that will suite any music type because it has a well balanced sound with a nice low end and a clear upper mids. It's also very convenient when you are traveling since it occupies very little space and offers a decent passive noise isolation when in public, though you are still aware of surrounding. Considering their price of only $69 - its one heck of a bargain!

text: I own three iPODs and listen to music about 3 to 5 hours a day. It helps me concentrate when working (i do some graphic art work) and block out noise and it puts me to sleep a few nights a week when I have trouble. I listen to everything from "fuzz" (white noise) to classical music, jazz,rock, bluegrass etc. so I guess i am a good "reviewer" and I felt obliged to pass along my experience as it has been fairly costly to obtain and could save others a lot of time not to mention money. So here's my take. By the way i am also a product design engineer, not that it helps me be a better consumer but rather i tend to see things more analytically than many consumers. So much for qualifications - this is still just my opinion - Having lived with ultimate ears super.fi pro 5EB (excellent bass) and before that the ultimate ears pro 5 both for a couple years now,AND having to replace the thin cord set on both three times - the last time - I opted for a pair of Shure E500PTH's their best earphones instead. My reasoning was based on my previous experience with Shure's most excellent V15 type III series of stereo phono cartridges (what are those) from back in the days of "record players". Anyone who could make such a tiny transducer that produced superb sound from plastic discs with bumps on them surely could make one of these ear buds. I also thought about there industry standard microphones. so I ponied up the $500 and gave them a try. Well lets get the audio performance out of the way -I must note that It is hard to do A/B comparisons because you can't just switch between speakers. Changing involves pulling these guys out of your ear canal and stuffing the other set back in which is a bit distracting from your sonic memory BOTTOM SOUND LINE - Yes they have excellent clear solid sound and decent bass response as I expected for $500 and they seem just slightly "cleaner with more separation both voice and instruments" than the UE 5EB's but with less bass (that's what the EB stands for i think - extended/enhanced bass so no big surprise there) BUT the differences are small and once I start listening with either one the music is so clear and enjoyable I forget any differences. But i prefer the Shure's HOWEVER just as critically helpful in delivering that awsome sound was I suspecct the volume control. Since the frequency response of your ear varies with volume you can "tune in" the best sounding sweet spot by adjusting the volume - and with your iPod up all the way this control can either whisper or blow your eardrums out. (in fact Shure puts a warning paper in the box advising you to listen at the lowest level - which sounds the best anyway to me) LET ME QUALIFY THAT - They sound really really good once you get the right sealed foam piece on the earbud so your ear canals are really isolated. I have one ear canal slightly bigger than the other so it took a while, but i guess everyone's ears are different both individually and in pairs which is why they give you so many different sleeve. Just like ultimate ears (UE), they come with an assortment of different sizes of foam and soft rubbery "sleeves" as they call them, to help you get that fit right. One thing they do have that ultimate ears doesn't is a moldable foam material on some of the sleeves that slowly re-expands when you squeeze it so it creeps shut and since it's solid I imagine it blocks out sound more effectively than the rubber umbrella design. Another difference is the heavier three piece cord - UE's have a single thin and very light weight cord with a right angle plug that goes into you iPod at one end AND at the other end(s) a stiff bendable wire sleeve at the earbud which bends around your ear and KEEPS the cord over your ears. The right angle plug keeps close to your iPod and out of the way and it is harder to accidently pull out like if you drop you iPod (heaven forbid - I do it almost once a day with no problems). They are very comfortable to the point that you forget there is a cord and that you have earphones on! AND IF THEY GO BAD since the cord plugs into each earbud assembly right at the ear - YOU CAN UNPLUG THEM and replace them, Lucky for me. The cords are only about $20 instead of the $100-150 for a new set of earphones. Shure E500PTH uses three pieces - 1. a short headset cord that comes together at chest level under the chin ending in a female mini stereo jack plug 2. a 2 inch long thumb-wheel volume control which has male and female ends and a short cord ending in a bulkier right angle jack 3 a 2 foot or so long standard male/female straight steros mini jack cable that plugs into your iPod and of course sticks up an inch and a half or so bulging above your pocket and adding that extra length to your iPod Now i guess you can plug number 2 and 3 in reverse order so the handy compact right angle plug on the volume control is at your iPod but that puts the bulky volume control right there also since the cord it has is very short (about 4 inches from angle plug to volume control) ANYWAY - I thought the idea was to put the handy volume control right under your chin so you can just reach up and turn it down (or up if you like the next tune) which is what i like about the Shure E500PTH's On the downside Shure E500PTH uses no such bendable sleeve - the wire is molded into the earbuds so i guess if it goes bad after the 2 year warranty your out the $500 but it seems more durable than the UE's. Because the cord just winds over the ear, I found the cord kept falling from around my ear and pulling at the earbud unsealing it until I pushed the cowboy-hat-like rubber cinch that holds the two cords together, up tight under my chin. Yee-Ha with a strangle hold - well it isn't really that uncomfortable but you feel it up under the chin like a cowboy hat cord. BUT this stiff bendable wire that keeps the UE's cord over my big ears is right where my UE's cord frayed and broke down so maybe this could be a hidden drawback for UE's Shure E500PTH's heavier bulkier cord, while more durable, is always there making its presence known, with the volume control dangling from it. I guess that's the trade off and why my UE cords eventually broke - and in fairness I should mention that I frequently fall asleep listening to my ipod in bed so there's a cord stress test. After listening to the Shure E500PTH's for a while and adjusting the volume with each song, I put my UE's (the 5EB) back in and they seemed to have a stronger bass but very similar sound not noticablly worse or better -both excellent. so i guess if i could put UE's feather light cord on Shure E500PTH's earbuds and add a magic lightweight volume control AND make the cord DURABLE - NOW THAT WOULD BE THE ULTIMATE EARBUDS

text: Bought these primarily for running/working out. They're comfortable and for this purpose the sound is fine. They won't win any audio awards, but I'm not mixing down studio tracks with them, either. When running, the music is just fine. I can hear the world around me at the same time. Primary reason for getting these, right? I thought they'd be a good all around headset to replace my (hated) Galaxy Buds Pro. Here's the parts that aren't great: Audio books/voice: at any comfortable listening level they buzz against my cheeks in an uncomfortable way. It's weird it doesn't happen with music, but with voice alone it does. Also, others can hear what you're listening to. It's small, tinny, and quiet, but it's not silent. Not an issue when running alone, but in a group or if watching a movie on an airplane, just be aware. Also, when connected to your phone without audio signal, I think they go to "sleep" and then wake up when signal resumes. So if using during GPS navigation, the first word of each direction is lost as they're waking back up. So instead of "turn left at Abby road" you hear "eft at Abby road." or worse... Instead of "in 500 feet turn right" you'll hear "feet turn right." If you have music or an audio book or phone call going (ie consistent signal) this doesn't happen. Very small nitpick. I'd much rather use these instead of those blasted ear plugs, especially when running (one always comes loose). So as a one trick pony they're awesome. They're not a full replacement for Bluetooth phones, though.

text: This is a difficult review to write... As someone who has been deaf in one ear since around age five or so (mumps), and who loves music, plays bass and guitar, I was intrigued when I heard about Yuni. I'm so glad I read the reviews, and thus knew what to expect as far as 3D printed build quality - otherwise the disappointment would have been extreme when it arrived. It's too bad - great idea, and it works; especially for guitar, where I was able to hear tones and nuances I never could before (this on a Cort/Manson Matt Bellamy model). Bass was a bit thin, but fine. If the build quality was better, I'd be stoked. In fact, I'd be willing to pay more for better construction. So, there's my problem. I'm so glad someone is addressing the needs of people like me that I want to support them. I also understand about economies of scale (no pun intended) and need for keeping costs down. Having said that, a bit more attention to quality would have resulted in a more satisfying product. So - I do recommend Yuni, but with a caveat - it works, but you will be disappointed in construction if you like the feel of quality. PS - Using fabric tape, some material and a bit of creative aftermarket DIY, I was able to make it more robust. Still wouldn't drop it, though...

I think the sound would have been fine, if I could have got them to go in my ear far enough to block out any other normal sounds. In the next thought I figured if I tried the smaller rubber ear part,(even though I don't think it would make it go in my ear any further)but as soon as I took it out of my ear and looked at it (not even trying to take the rubber part off yet) the ear piece popped apart. Of course my first thought was oh crap, these are super cheap, and thought well if they pop together maybe I could reinforce them some how so I could still use them, but after looking at them further, I see that they are so cheaply made that the effort to repair them is not worth it and probably will not work or hold anyway. I would not buy these ever, ever, ever again. They remind me of the super cheap toys you might get out of a gum ball machine or the cheap toy section at a swap meat. I have never written a poor review on any product before, I can usually find something good about most things, but the only thing good about these is well, ummm...they had an awsome clamp on the cord that would have been nice for jogging if it wasn't closer to the plug rather than the ear parts and not so cheaply made that I don't think would last more than a couple of runs at best.

text: READ THIS REVIEW, in it's entirety. It will help. Let me start by saying that after going through 3 different BT headphones, I researched BT headphones for 2 months before deciding on the JLab GO headphone... With that said... My initial impression was less than excellent. The right ear bud was defective, HOWEVER, JLab customer service was AMAZING, and sent me a new pair under warranty, with NO ISSUES... Even sent me a new set BEFORE they received my defective set. LIKE WHOA! 5 Stars for JLab customer service. Special thanks to Brandon and Stephanie. (Shameless shout-out) Now, sound quality between my car and my iPhone is exceptional. The only issue I have is when I'm on my bike. When my iPhone is in my pocket and I am pedaling the audio will cut out. But, if I have my phone in my backpack or in my arm-band, audio is perfect. Also, I'm by no means an "Audiophile", however, I LOVE great sound quality, and I know the differences between crap and quality. Call quality is on par with other BT devices that support this function. Normal quality. Secondly, JLab needs to provide an assortment of ear-bud covers. The ear-bud covers that come with the unit are inefficient and produce a ton of wind noise at higher speeds... crap, even low speeds with strong headwind. I feel that with an ear-bud cover that enters deeper into the ear canal will reveal deeper, MUCH more prevalent Bass and increased sound quality in ANY situation. JLab is working on a solution, and will provide previously purchased headset users with an option to buy these bud covers at an extreme discount. This is from the "Horse's mouth."... CAN'T WAIT! Thirdly, pairing is a breeze! I've owned 3 other BT headphones (Motorola, Sony and Beats) and they were much more complicated to pair with any BT enabled device, COMPARED to these headphones. Range is excellent. I can navigate most of my home (2300 Sq Ft, 2 level) with very little audio interruption or interference. Obviously, glass and metal doors seem to cause issues. Fourth comment is about the battery and usability. Battery seems to be very good. Although I charge my unit daily, I also use my headphones more than most would use a set. I use mine at work and at home through out the day. The first 2 or 3 charges seemed to yield low levels of battery life which concerned me, but after cycling the battery between full charge and depletion, I've noticed huge gains in battery life. This is consistent with Lithium batteries. I get between 7 and 10 hours out of the battery through constant use. Case and point, I listened to my iPhone music library 3 days ago, uninterrupted for nearly 9 hours, and still had enough juice for the bike ride home (25 minutes avg). And the headphones never died or faltered. Who knows how long they might have gone. My final issue comes when streaming a movie with OS X or Windows 7 (WMP or VLC Player). Audio is very low quality, and often static filled, or even inaudible. Unless stationary, the average user will be very disappointed with the quality, but the power user will be able to manipulate the streaming bit of the audio; being much easier on a Mac. Some movies or videos have different bit rates and will need to be manipulated, accordingly. But it really only takes 2 minutes to get perfect sound quality. However, this is a disadvantage for the average user. A simple Google search will yield a ton of great info. Hit me up if you can't find anything. I'd love to help, but I do not have the time to prepare a write up strictly for this review, on the matter. Overall, I am extremely pleased with the purchase. I find the headphones VERY comfortable, even forgetting that they're still on my head when the sound is off. I LOVE how they disclose information such as proper Burn-in procedures and proper cleaning and storage on their website and in the manual. text: These headphones were VERY disappointing, considering the price I paid. Without the Active Noise Cancelling (ANC) they sound good. Not audiophile quality but the bass comes through fine, as well as the treble and mid. The headphones are light, fit all the way over my full-sized ears, and are comfortable, too. I can enjoy music for an extended period of time with these headphones (with the ANC turned off.) All that said, you can get something just as good if not a bit better without ANC a little cheaper. The ANC by itself does pretty well too. It cuts down outside ambient noise as well as any other headphones or earbuds I've had that included ANC. It's great for getting rid of that annoying blowing sound if you're listening to headphones with a fan blowing on you. Here's the bad news, though: The headphones fall flat when you use the ANC while also listening to music. Ugh! Epic fail! When you turn on the ANC the quality of your sound instantly plummets to something just terrible! Highs and lows are chopped away out without mercy, and I think the sample rate of the output is way below CD quality. Overall the experience is little better than if you were listening to music via an old-style landline telephone. I was frankly shocked at this result. I've had several ANC headphones and ear buds in the past and never experienced this before. I'm almost certain that when the ANC is off the headphones simply pass the analog signal from the source to the (pretty good quality) speakers. When the ANC is turned on, however, it appears the little embedded computer has to kick in and digitize the sound from the source, digitize the ambient sound coming from the little microphone, calculate a "negative" sound from the mic input and blend that with the newly digitized source sound, then finally convert this new blended digital signal back into analog for the speakers. And do it all quick enough to avoid any noticeable delay. Probably, the electronics on these headphones is doing a very poor job digitizing the analog source sound. But that's just a guess.

text: So I used to believe Tranyas sounded the best in this price rage sub $50 price range. Well let me tell you that I purchased 5 earbuds including the Soundcore Liberty Pro 2s and Grados MT225 - which I ultimately kept the Grand and Soundcore (both received rave reviews on YouTube reviewers). That said, the FIIL T1X TWS sounded absolutely amazing in comparison and easily was the best value. I would even go as far as saying that the FIIL sounded nearly as good (or close in sound quality) as the Grados that cost 4 times as much, believe it or not. Both the FIIL and Grado played the music loud and had very distinct crisp high and lows. However, listening very closely, the Grado's just as a bit of an edge when it came to a more slightly more clean sound. The Grados and the FIIL T1X's both had narrower soundstage than the Soundcore -- this is where the Soundcore shined above the rest. But the Grado definitely placed emphasis on the vocal being more pronounced and forward sounding - more than the Soundcore, but similar to the FIIL. The Soundcore, because of its app to customize the sound, I believe has the best, refined sound all around. If it was for the app that also allowed you to, in effect, increase the volume, the Soundcore would have been returned only for the low volume issue. But again, the app resolves this issue. From a bass standpoint, I would not call one better than the other, just different. From preference, I would say the Soundcore bass is my favorite (sounded slightly more refined -- perhaps because you can customize the sound with the EQ in the app), and the the Grado had a more "natural" deep bass sound. I also auditioned the Monster Clarity 102 Airlinks and the Tranya T10s. The Monster Clarity sounded decent but was a step below the three referenced. Sounded a but less of a soundstage and less distinct clarity between instruments. The Tranya T10s sounded the worst of the five. I have yet to have delivered the Sennheisers and the Cambridge Audio, but once I do, I will see if these replace either the Grados or Soundcores that, at least at this moment in time, I intent to keep.
