text: My wife and I have been shopping for wireless headsets to use with our iPhones for a good while and had pretty well settled on a couple of brands in the $150 to $200 price range when I came across the Anker Soundbuds Slim+. The price seemed too low for me to believe they could be any good, but as I have been very happy with Anker chargers and USB data port, I decided these were cheap enough to take a chance on. Less than 24 hours after mine arrived my wife insisted I order her a pair as well. The Soundbuds Slim+ are light enough and fit so comfortably in the ear it is easy to forget you are wearing them and the extra hooks and buds provided assure almost anyone a comfortable fit. The magnetic back is really convenient to keep them corralled when they are hanging around your neck and the case with its carabiner clip is generally a $10 extra at this price point. Initial pairing was easy and since then they pair quickly and reliably every time they are switched on. While I might wish the controls were a an inch or two further down the connecting wire, the operation is intuitive enough that we caught on quickly. Most surprising of all is how good the sound is. It is not the equal of a $300 over the ear set of headphones, but for normal day to day listening they are better than "good enough" and at this price point that is amazing. When flying I generally use over the ear headphones with active noise cancelation and while these do not have active sound cancellation, switching to the next size larger bud does an amazing job of shutting out environmental noise; close enough to my active noise cancelling over the ear headphones that the difference is academic. As to my wife's reaction, she just keeps saying, "Thank you, thank you, thank you!" So I will say, "Thank you Anker for a good set of Soundbuds at an amazing price."

text: With thousands of reviews on these headphones there isn't much I can say that hasn't been said. However, I'm actually fairly dissatisfied with these buds. Just to call out a few items that make me want to return them: *Case - this is a pretty bulky case, carrying them in your jeans pocket is not the most comfortable or discrete. *Functionality - you can use the right bud or the left bud independently, but there's a catch. You need to separately pair the left bud creating a completely different profile. So while you can use that left earbud solo, don't plan on switching them back and forth like the high-end players. To use the left you must first seat both buds in the case prior to pulling out the left bud. To connect the right you must seat the left and right, then you can do the right. Going from stereo to right solo bud is easy peazy or vice versa. Not exactly the way I hoped it'd work. Also, the buds are not touch, the mechanical click button on the buds drive me crazy. Who honestly enjoys pushing something into your ear, or double or triple clicking for that matter! My eardrum feels like it's getting beat up just changing the track. *Call Quality - pretty much trash. There is zero ambient noise reduction. Every little scrape and shuffle blasts through the mic and your friend on the other end will ask you what you're demolishing when you simply turn on the faucet and run some water. No joke, it picks up and amplifies everything. Even the super low hum of the mini fridge in my office I was told sounded like I was driving in a car. That's unfortunate. I do recommend them for music listening in stereo (as long as you don't mind jamming them in your ear to press the buttons, but call quality is a joke and I'd steer clear if that's on your checklist. Beyond those few gripes, the earbuds are good sounding. It's just not that comfortable or enjoyable to use.

text: At $300 you really need to know what you want out of your headphones. If you're looking for noise cancellation with a little more low end "thump" the Bose QC20 might be for you. I purchased them on a whim expecting fantastic sound from a Bose product only to be disappointed. Turns out you're losing sound quality and paying for the best noise cancellation found in in-ear headphones. I, however, would prefer to have superior sound and am willing to settle for noise isolation. I ended up buying the Shure SE425, also $300, after reading a million reviews. They have fantastic clarity and will bring new light to the tiny details of your music that you haven't heard before (also missing from the Bose QC20) and while they don't have heavy bass (don't buy if that's really what you want) they have enough bass (the way music is meant to be listened to) with the proper seal in your ear. Don't get me wrong, if you're used to headphones in the $20 - $100 price range you will be more than pleased and impressed with the sound quality of the Bose QC20, but at $300 I wanted to make sure I was getting the best sound quality (clear & accurate) my money could buy and you won't get that here.

text: I picked these up for $21. I'll say that at this price, you won't probably won't find better but I'll stop short of saying they are very good sounding. The sound quality is good for casual listening. If you want high quality headphones, check out the [[ASIN:B007BY3POQ Sony MDR-ZX600/BLK Over the Head Style Headphones]] which are similar but better sound quality, construction, and comfort (but 3x the price.) Like the ZX 600 and 100, these have a balanced frequency response. These do not have heavy bass or enhanced bass (there are other models for that.) Sound Quality: The first thing I noticed with these is that the treble range is really lacking. You get very well proportioned/even frequency response from sub-bass all the way up to low-treble. It's the mid-treble and very high treble which are quite weak. So you won't hear the hiss of a singer singing an "s" or crystal-like crash of symbols. Instead you get a more muted sound. I'll stop short of calling it muddy, because it's not muddy. Muddy is when you get too much mid-bass and no mid-high end. But with these you'll get very even bass and mids. My best comparison is "FM Radio" where you hear it all in full detail, but that crisp high isn't there. Since the bass response (the whole low end) is really good in general, that's probably why so many people are impressed with these. They hear deep and punchy bass and think that's very good not noticing the lack of high end. My [[ASIN:B004U5DH9W Sony MDREX58V/RED In-Ear Headphones]] ear-buds actually sound better but in a differt way. They have strong deep bass and crisp highs at the expense of the mid range. I was expecting full size headphones to sound better at a similar price. Over all I'd say these are "pretty good" for $20. Now I have the more expensive [[ASIN:B007BY3POQ Sony MDR-ZX600/BLK Over the Head Style Headphones]] and I've listened to the cheaper [[ASIN:B004RKQM8I Sony MDR-ZX100 ZX Series Headphones (White)]]. While the 100 were surprisingly good for the price, these are better and I would recommend them over the 100. The 100's lacked not only highs, but had weaker lows. Neither the 100 or these 300's come close to the 600 which will cost 3X which is what you should get if you're looking for high quality. Now hyper critical analysis aside, they do sound good. Very good bass, mid, and the lower end of the highs. It's like these just need a tweeter or something. Generally they are balanced, clean, and pleasant sounding and you can listen for hours not hating the sound and feeling like you're just missing everything. Recommendation: I would highly recommend these at under $25. I listen to them for hours and fully enjoy the sound. I have the more expensive 600 but I use both models at different times and unless I'm really looking for a guilty pleasure of hearing a favorite song in best quality, these are totally fine. As far as I can tell the [[ASIN:B00BN0N058 Sony MDR-ZX300IP/B Headphones with Microphone for iPod/iPhone/iPad, Black]] are the same headphones with mic/remote and they are not worth $50. I would like the IP model since I use a headphone but MSRP is overpriced for how they sound. On sale for maybe for $35 or less, then yes and they'd become my primary headphones. So if you want very good sound, upgrade to the [[ASIN:B007BY3POQ Sony MDR-ZX600/BLK Over the Head Style Headphones]]. If you want casual, beaters, or headphones for your kids, podcasts, or flying, they'll be satisfied with these. (If you're primary thing is podcasts, then I'll say these are definitley for you.) Cord length is pretty short. Great if you have your device close or a portable player, but you'll need an extension if you're trying to use it in-home with equipment. They are on-ear headphones that put pressure on your ears. Like all other headphones of this style that will cause some soreness with prolonged use but generally no more than any other headphones this style that I've used. If you think that's an issue, look into headphones with a larger earcup that surrounds your ear and doesn't sit ON your ear.

text: We've been having a whole lot of fun with these headphones. Bass is great (IMPORTANT- Give your headphones time to break in before you judge the bass). The headset is comfortable to wear and adjusts quickly and easily. Sound leaks out if you have it too high, so not a good device to use in a library or other places where silence is mandatory. The microphone sits on the right ear piece facing forward. The quality is about equal to having your phone on speaker and walking 5-10 feet away to talk. You can hear the person you are talking to just fine, but they might have issues understanding you clearly - especially with other noises going on around you. Pairing to all our MAC products was a breeze. No issues at all. The Quick Start Guide will put you on the right path to managing your headset easily. The volume button controls volume up and down, mute/unmute calls, and skip forward/back for songs. The call button controls answering/ending calls, reject incoming calls, switching calls, redial and play/pause music. With only two buttons to work with, you won't have a lot of fumbling with your headphone to figure out what button to push/move when needed. Your LED indicator light keeps you apprised of low battery, pairing and whether or not the headphones are on and connected to a device. If the headphones can't make a connection, they will shut off after a bit. You can opt to plug in the audio cable when your battery is low, but be sure to turn off your headphones first before doing so. All in all these headphones work well for our family. The only downside was the audio quality on calls. Thus why I rated it with four stars instead of five. The $99 price tag with free prime shipping might seem high... but consider the brands this wireless bluetooth headphone is competing with and decide then if it's worth it.

text: When I bought these earbuds, I didn't expect much, but these surprised me with their full-bodied, wonderfully rich sound. They have very-noticeable, deep bass which won't drown out your awesome mids and highs. The tremble is unbeatable at this price. This is probably because of their frequency range, 12 to 22,000 Hz. Most earbuds around this price don't have that good of frequency response. If you're wondering what frequency response is, well it's the sound they capture and put into your ears. The lower Hz means the bass. The higher Hz means the highs. They also have a neodymium magnet, one of the best you can buy. What a magnet does is they determine how good the overall sound quality is. These earbuds also have a silent cap, a cap with no outside holes, just the holes you hear sound out of. This means you won't have to turn up the volume on your player so much, and that you don't hear much outside sound either. I think this is great for mowing or any other noisy activity. They also come with a nice twist-up, compact case. I can slip these headphones easily into my pocket or anywhere else. These earbuds don't have the best comfort but, they're very comfortable when it comes to earbuds when I use the earpads. On top of it all, the quality is the best thing about these earbuds. I think they will last a long time. I hope this review was helpful to you, thanks for reading.

text: EDIT 11/1/2019: I was looking at my profile and noticed this old review and realized I needed to update it. I did eventually get my hands on a working set of actual Airs (I believe I wound up just ordering directly from the company to get exactly what I wanted). They have been awesome, the sound quality is great for bone-conducting headphones and the battery lasts a good long while. I enjoy being able to control the volume, pause the audio, or skip to the next track from the headphone buttones themselves rather than digging the phone out of my pocket. If I lost or broke these, I wouldn't hesitate to order another pair immediately! I will say the call quality as a phone headset leaves something to be desired, but that is not why I ordered them, and I would definitely recommend it not be why you order them either. It's nice to be able to use them for that purpose rather than dig your phone out to answer a call during a run or while bicycling, but it's a compromise solution at best. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I've had Trekz Titaniums for over a year and a half now, I wore them when I ran or rode my mountain bike. Great headphones, I've really enjoyed them. The sound isn't perfect, but that is the sacrifice I gladly made to be able to hear car traffic or bicycles overtaking me when running on trails. However, I recently finished a run, wiped down my Titaniums and tossed them on my passenger seat. Sometime between then and when I grabbed them that evening to take them in to charge, the band right behind one of the earpieces cracked, leaving that speaker kind of floppy. I have no idea how, I assume it got wedged in the crevice of the seat and I set something on them. It was definitely my fault, because they weren't cracked when I took them off. So, bummed, I came to Amazon (where I got the first pair) to order another. Upon searching them up, I see that Trekz has a new design called the AIR that they claim are not only lighter and sturdier but sound better as well! Now, the weight of the Titaniums had never really bothered me, but lighter is better when it's hanging from your head. And while the sound quality wasn't terrible, it could definitely be better. But the biggest reason I decided to go with the $50 more expensive AIRs is that they claimed to be sturdier, with a titanium band all the way around. That seemed like a great idea to me, considering why I was back in the market for headphones. So, after determining that the standard Airs were out of stock for weeks apparently, I went ahead and ordered this pair with some goofy reflective tape I absolutely do not care about for an extra $10. They duly arrived two days later and I eagerly took them out of the box (side note: the packaging is a little much, AfterShokz). They are definitely lighter and lower profile than the Titaniums I was replacing, yet felt fairly sturdy. I plugged them in and fully charged them before pairing them with my phone. After charging and pairing (which was as easy as could be) I popped them on to see how they sounded. Initially, I was quite impressed with the sound. They definitely seemed an improvement over the Titaniums. You're never going to get good in-ear earbud quality from bone-conducting headphones, so get that idea out of your head. You are sacrificing some sound fidelity to get the sound through your skull rather than blocking your ear canals, so you can still hear what's going on around you. Nevertheless, I was happy. Then, I switched over to some jazz with a little bass and noticed that the right speaker was buzzing terribly with the bassline. I pulled it away from my ear, and the left side sounded great. Put the right back on my head and it sounded like a blown $5 speaker from a blue-light special. I switched the equalizer setting, which seems to pull most of the bass out, but it still buzzed and now neither speaker sounded very good. So, now bummed that I have received a defective pair, I package them back up, request the return with Amazon and print off the shipping label. However, I am impressed enough with the one good speaker that I decide to go ahead and order another pair right away, so that I will have them by the weekend. I trust Amazon isn't going to screw me over on the return so I just purchased another pair rather than waiting for the return credit. Two days later, on Friday, I receive my 2nd pair. I open the Amazon box and immediately realize that I am looking at a pair of Trekz Titaniums, just like the pair I broke. I am initially cross with myself, thinking I must have somehow ordered the wrong thing. But then I remembered clicking the "Order again" button from my AIR order. So I log in to Amazon and sure enough, I did order the same exact Trekz Air headphones that I'd received the first time. Only this time, I'd received a pair of Titaniums, which sell for $50 less than I was charged! Wondering how this could have happened, I look all over the box for an inventory sticker, and found it stuck to the plastic shrinkwrap (which I had thankfully not immediately ripped off of the box before realizing it was the wrong product). Right there on the paper inventory sticker, it said "Trekz Air" headphones. Ironically, the sticker was placed over the bar code on the actual product box, but didn't cover where the box says "Trekz Titanium". See the attached photo, assuming I uploaded it correctly. Somehow, they've labeled their Titanium inventory with the stickers meant for the Air headphones. OOPS! I looked at the shipping label on the Amazon box, and it says "AfterShokz" above the return address. But, it's the same return address in Lexington, KY that the first box had, and that one says Amazon Fulfillment. So I don't know who screwed up the inventory stickers, but if you order a pair of these, you better make sure you get what you paid for, and not a pair of Titaniums that should have cost 2/3 the price! So, now I am shipping back two pairs of headphones, one defective and the other not even what I ordered, and I still don't have a pair to wear - or do I? Turns out duct tape was sufficient to temporarily fix the old Titaniums for now, so I've still got tunes for the trail. Nevertheless, I intend to order YET ANOTHER set of Airs, because the sound out of the left speaker of the first pair really did sound nice, and they were incredibly light. If I ever get a fully working pair of actual Air headphones, I'll update my review with my thoughts on how they actually sound in stereo!

text: The Brainwavz M1 earphones are good sounding for their price and come with a lot of accessories. Included with the M1's is a hard carrying case, 1 set of Comply foam tips, 6 sets of silicon ear tips, 1 set of bi-flange tips, and a shirt clip. The clean, balanced sound from the M1's is very similar but not as pleasing as the sound quality from the more expensive M2's and the M3's, which are my go to earphones from Brainwavz. While I'm happy with the sound quality from M1's, my biggest complaint is the construction which feels cheaper than the $40 price point. SOUND QUALITY & COMPARISON: In addition to the M1, M2, and M3 earphones, I also own the Brainwavz Delta earphones which retail for $20. The sound from the M1's fits between the Delta's and the M2's, as the price does also. The M1 earphones produce a full range of sound with a nice, deep bass. While the sound from the M1's is noticeably richer than the Delta's, it isn't as detailed as the more expensive M2's which have a brighter sound with tighter bass and crisper highs. What really shines to me with the sound quality from the M1's is their balance. The sound is exquisitely balanced much like the more expensive M2 & M3 earphones. The M1's also offer very good clarity although I do hear some harshness in the highs at higher volumes similar to that with the M2's but better controlled than the Delta's. The same harshness, however, isn't present with the M3's. From that stand point, the M3's are clearly superior to the M1 & M2 earphones. BUILD QUALITY & COMPARISON: As mentioned in the first paragraph, my biggest complaint with the M1 earphones is their construction which feels cheaper than the $40 price point. The M1's are very lightweight due to the thin cord and smaller metal housing. This is the main upside to the construction. The aluminum housing of the M1's is noticeably thicker and more durable than the housing on the Delta's but not as nice at that on the M2 or M3 earphones. Unlike the Delta and M2's or most other earphone I own, the M1's do not have any silicon wrapping around the cord where it goes into the housing for added durability. Additionally, I'm not a big fan of the cord on the M1, M2, & M3's, which all have the same style of cord. The cord, even though it is suppose to be tangle free, gets tangled on me more so than my other earphones. This is likely because there is no pulley to keep the two ends of the y-cable together which prevents those ends from getting tangled with the rest of the cord when not in use. The other thing I don't like is when uncoiling the cord for use it doesn't go straight like other earphone cords. It still has a defined coil to it. SUMMARY: Listening to music with the Brainwavz M1 earphones, they clearly offer a good amount of bang for your buck, producing a full, balanced sound in a small package. While I'm pleased with the sound quality from the M1's, their construction could clearly be improved upon. Comparing the M1 earphones to the M2's, the M2's offer a step up in build quality with silicon wrapping around the cord where it goes into the housing and a larger more durable metal housing. In addition, the M2's produce a brighter sound with tighter bass and crisper highs. What you get by stepping up to the M2's makes them worth the extra $15 spent. I actually prefer the build quality of the Delta's to the M1's due to the slightly thicker cord that doesn't tangle, the cord pulley, and the silicon wrapping around the cord where it goes into the housing. On a positive note, the M1's are very lightweight which is great if you are active while wearing your earphones. Additionally, the M1's come with a surprisingly large amount of accessories; the most useful is the hard carrying case. The M1's are nice earphones for the price, just not quite nice enough to deserve 5 stars when taking everything into account. Note: A product sample was provided by the seller in exchange for a fair, unbiased review.

text: I wanted so badly to like these. I think there is a real market for discreet over-the-ear headphones. They just weren’t for me. It took about 10 minutes of playing with them to know that they would not suit my needs. PROS 1) They seem high quality, despite what I felt was a poor amount of online credibility to speak to their “high-ended-ness.” However, I was pleasantly shocked by what I received - a really high quality cardboard box with high res-printing with clean edges. That experience was consistent throughout - everything was really nice. It was like the first time I held an iPod back in the ‘90s in the sense that there was an irrefutable craftsmanship to it that extended all the way to the packaging. That is not something you get with rando junk in my experience. Since I have been traveling the world my entire life and my parents trained me on how to identify wastes-of-money, I feel like that is something that should not be discounted. 2) The sound quality was way better than I was expecting, including the clarity of the Bluetooth signal as I distanced myself from my phone. I mean, duh, it’s not going to soundproof the user from the world bc there is obviously no seal between the headphones and the user’s skull, but the sound delivery is quite effective. I like to listen to music at a low volume, but I was still able to hear the music and just the music despite the noise of multiple two-stroke engines in the vicinity. I did not attempt any calls, but I did listen to hip hop, folk, Hawaiian, jazz and rock songs to see if there was my difference. There was not. (I really should have tried one of the dubstep songs my brother made - I’m serious - but like I will address, they just weren’t physically comfortable.) 3) I love that there are physically differentiated buttons for each function. I had a pair where you pressed different zones to achieve different effects and I was always making a mess of things. 4) Like I said, this is a market that needs to be addressed. In-ear buds are all wicked uncomfortable for me and most over-ear headphones are really an advertisement to the unsavory characters of the world that you don’t have your guard up. And if you wear them around your neck like mini-speakers, let’s be honest: you’re a jerk. CONS 1) This is the money shot for me: they are just not comfortable!!! I have an insanely huge head - I literally outgrew all of my mom’s hats and helmets before I was 8 years old. So maybe I’m the jerk here. But even extended all the way, these pinched the sides of my head so, so badly. text: I'll try to be short and simple. Get them for the ANC and sound quality, not for anything else really. Pros: 1. ANC is amazing, when I first put these in I thought I went deaf lol. I was actually shocked and gasped when I turned it to strong. It may not block out every single noise but the ones that does let through are crisp and clear such as people talking in close proximity or rain drops ( writing this review I'm not hearing the thunder storm but I am hearing a few rain drops that sound surreal and movie like. 2. Sound quality is pretty good ( may also tie into point above) audio is just clean and crisp. 3. Design is pretty, really pretty especially in person Cons 1. Design, earbuds are a bit large. They're borderline comically toy like cheap large. They're not heavy but I thought they would be smaller, they look smaller in the pictures. 2. Build quality, don't get me wrong these are very solid and it seems like high quality plastic all around, but that's the problem. I thought this was metal but it's actually plastic. Considering the price I would have expected some form of metal even if the carrying case had metal accents (especially considering my previous headset was cheaper, had wireless charging and was fully wrapped in metal {except the wireless charging area obviously}) 3. The app is pretty rudimentary. Outside of seeing battery life and adjusting what the touch points do ( also extremely limited) the only other real thing you can do is switch the ANC/transparency modes Issues 1. Battery drain Not sure if this is a bug with mine or what, but I was able to use the earbuds for about 6 hours with ANC on as advertised before the battery reaching 10%....but only the left earbud. The right earbud was at 40%. I thought it was an error with the first charge cycle so I charged to full again and in writing this review the left earbud is registering 10% lower than the right already. Now considering I got these earbuds yesterday, I'm ruling out uneven battery wear. THIS IS AN ACTUAL ISSUE 2. Battery life Considering the large size ( something I realized after buying it) I would really have expected longer battery life, again considering my previous earbuds were less than half the size and had much longer battery life ( I had them for a few years that's the only reason I replaced them tbh cause they were old and battery was now bad among other things) 3. Google assistant doesn't seem to be working. That is I can't say "Hey Google" to activate my assistant hands free. Which then leads me to having to use one of the only 3 touch controls as an assistant button. However, once assistant is activated, it does pick up with I'm saying very pretty ok. Feedback: It's only been one day but I think most of the issues can be solved with firmware and app updates.

text: This is my second pair of Avantree headphones. The first pair is pretty much useless due to the button covers becoming too squishy, thus not allowing them to be pressed against the actual contacts within the headphone. I contacted support but they said they were out of the warranty and left it at that. Other than the squishy button problem, I enjoyed the sound produced from the headphones. They produce decent bass for me (compared to typical wired headphones supplied with cell phones) and the the mids and highs are good enough (I'm certainly not an audiophile). Nothing mind blowing, but good enough sound while working out. The bluetooth works well and has decent range. I can leave my phone in my bag at mid-court while playing basketball and never lose reception while running all over the court. The battery no longer holds a charge and they have to be recharged after about 3 hours of use. My second pair is on par with the first pair, although they don't have the button problem. They sound is the same (in my opinion), the bluetooth range is the same (pretty good) and the battery life has died off just like the first pair (about 3 hours of playtime). These are about 16 months old so I won't waste my time with customer support. I'll probably end up upgrading to JLabs or Jaybirds for my next set and will give a review/comparison at that point. Overall I guess I would recommend these as a budget headphone, with the caveat of you get what you pay for: average sound, decent hardware (that may fail over time) and questionable battery life. Basically, you should probably consider these disposable (like so many other cheap/generic made in China hardware) and expect to buy a new pair every year. Not necessarily a bad thing, but the way things are nowadays. I'll move onto another brand shortly just to see if the premium price is worth it.

I primarily use then during low impact excercise (weights, indoor rowing, indoor cycling) so I can't speak to the security during more strenuous activity (running, outdoor cycling, etc.). The tiny button on the earbuds are not convenient, and it's challenging to adjust volume by tapping the earbuds. They aren't terribly responsive. I agree with other reviewers regarding battery life and chargning features. The battery life is TERRIBLE and they do not charge quickly. If you don't leave them constantly charging when not in use, you will be lucky to have 10% battery life when you go to use them. The charging station is bulky and inconvenient, and it needs to be laying fairly flat so the earbuds don't fall off. I like the carrying case, but wish that you could charge through it, like you would with Apple airpods. If you are looking for this style earbud, I would suggest waiting for Bose to resond to customer feedback and redesign them a bit.

text: As an engineer and sound designer I need compact head phones that will travel easy and allow me to mix or create on the go. I had been wary of earbuds but read some good reviews about this one, so I decided to give it a try. The sound is pretty clear, I will give them that, but that clarity doesn't overpower what's wrong with them. First, the bass is practically non-existant. I know its real hard to get a full bass out of small headphones, but this is why I bought the more expensive model. Second, the high-mids are a little shrill and overpowering. I tried doing some EQ work to get the sound to be where I wanted it, but they didn't respond very well at all - forget boosting the bass at all, the buds can't handle it and the overall sound will just distort. Third, once these things have been in your ears for more than 20 minutes, you'll start getting a headache. Wonderful. My advice? Look elsewhere for earbuds, or stick to over the ear. These are definitely not worth the price paid at all.

What i mean by this is, when im done with the buds and put them away I place them back into the case which is magnetized so you can feel them sort of "pull" the buds into the case as you are putting them in which turns them off, the problem is, from my experiences at least, the slightest jostle to the case un-seats the ear buds in the case from the contacts for a brief moment, turning them on and making them re-connect to whatever you had them last paired to. An example I can give, which had just happened to me a few minutes before writing this review, I had received a call on my phone (which is what I have the buds paired to normally), my buds were in their case, over on my desk which I had taken off of charging and left over there. I go to pick up the call and try to talk to the person only to realize I could not hear them and was confused, I look at my phones screen and realize my ear buds, which I remind you were still in their charging case, were currently connected to my phone, I had to turn off the Bluetooth to my phone to be able to talk to the person. text: I absolutely love JBL products. I have a set of club pro ear buds and I also have a huge party box. Those two items sound awesome so I was very confident that these ear bugs would also be awesome. I was getting them to wear when I lift weights, jog, and mow the yard because the silicone nubs would help them stay in my ears. When these arrived I was super excited. I immediately got them out and started to try to pair them. I had an extremely hard time pairing them to my phone... the same phone that my other two JBL buds and speaker pair with flawlessly. I finally got them paired and realized the left earbuds wasn't working. I asked uncle Google for advice about these earbuds because at this point I've been messing with them for over an hour trying to pair them and get the left ear bud to work. The problem with the left earbuds is that it apparently was dead because the connection points in the earbuds weren't making contact with the charger. I had a difficult time getting them to settle in and seat correctly in the charging case. I finally got the left ear bud to start charging. Fast forward a few hours to give them time to charge properly I get them out and tried to pair them. I couldn't get them to stay turned on and when I finally got them to stop automatically turning off, which is easy to tell when they turn on, off, and pair because there is a very distinct noise JBL products make when they turn on and off and they make a bleedeebeep (yeah bleedeebeep, you read that correctly) noise when they pair. I finally got them to stop automatically turning off but found that I had to go into my bluetooth and forget them on my phone and pair them again because they just wouldn't connect. Finally after 5 hours of fussing with these silly things I got them to charge, turn on and stay on, and pair with my phone so I could actually test their sound quality, which I was 100% sure would blow me away. They absolutely failed to meet the mark. They didn't cancel noise very well and they wouldn't get very loud in the way that it almost sounded like the music was playing through a membrane that slightly muted the sound and the equalization was off. Hey! It's a JBL so it's no problem because they have an app that I already have that will link to these things and I could mess with the equalizer, sound quality, and make them louder or at least adjust them so that I got the most out of how loud I could get them. Couldn't get them to link to the JBL app and I messed with that forever with absolutely no progress and uncle Google had nothing for me on this issue. I also noticed that they suction into my ears really easily which causes a vacuum affect and completely deadens the sound. Again, not a problem because they sent three different sized earbuds to change out and three different inside ear nubs that hold the earbuds tightly into my ear. As with everything else with these earbuds so far switching all of these pieces up to try to get the perfect fit, comfort level, and to keep them from suctioning into my ears was a waste of my time because nothing made them fit well enough to keep them from sectioning into my ears, or create a fit that was good enough to increase the volume, sound quality, or noise cancelation feature. After about 6 hours I was very confident that these earbuds where not worth a third of what I paid for them. I had a $25 dollar pair of off brand ear buds that I used to workout and mow in that worked a lot better. Still love JBL products but these earbuds are not good. I only gave them a 2 star rating because I know that JBL makes awesome earbuds and speakers and I give them the benefit of the doubt and assume I must have received an absolute lemon in ordering these earbuds. I've had them a few months now and, unfortunately I have yet to fiddle with them enough, or find out secret information, or connect them to the app so that I can adjust sound quality, noise cancelation and the terrible fit well enough to fix any of their issues. They work but they are almost unusable because they don't sound good, sound loud enough, cancel outside noise well enough to hear them when I mow. I also continually have to readjust them so that they don't suction into my ear and completely cut out their sound so I can't lift weights in them because I actually have to move my head a little here and there or change positions or move my eyes or have a slight breeze hit me doing any working out. They have sat on my nightstand for about the last three weeks and I've gone back to my old off brand ear buds. I know you're wondering why I don't just use my club pro ear buds and the answer to that is they fit in my ear really good and connect to the app so I can adjust their equalization to boost sound quality and volume and test their actual fit in my ears but they don't stay embedded in my ears all enough doing intense movements. I can go for a walk with these or ear them around my house cleaning but they vibrate loose when I mow (I don't have a bad mower either, it's a new zero turn but mowing is what it is and can be very bumpy at times no matter how good your mower is) and I almost lost one under the running mower and decided it's time to get more heavy duty ear buds so that I don't have a bad accident with my club pros. I hate to say it... I wouldn't recommend purchasing these ear buds because there's just way too many issues with them. I do still hope they were just a bad pair of these and the rest are as awesome as all of their other speakers and earbuds.

text: The new Denon flagship headphone looks great, sounds very good and is packaged to make a big impression, particularly when given as a gift. The memory foam leather covered earpieces are very comfortable although the overall headphone is heavy and is inclined to slip with any significant head movement off the vertical. Ultimately, I returned these and bought the new [[ASIN:B00858I4F2 Denon AH-D600 Music ManiacTM Over-Ear Headphones, Black]] from Amazon for 1/3 the price. The specifications are almost identical, including the size and composition of the "Nano-Fiber" drivers and the glass fiber molded ear hanger (frame). The only specified differences for the D-7100's over the D-600's per Denon USA's web page are an extra 2dB/mWatt of sensitivity (slightly lower input will provide a louder sound) and a extra 5 grams of weight, accounted for by the fine looking Mahogany Wood earpieces that are replaced on the AH-D600's with silver moulded plastic. The D-7100's also include a headphone stand that is not packaged with the D-600's. I listened to both these 'phones using a standard iPhone 5 output from the mini headphone jack and alternating with my [[ASIN:B0042KVX2S Denon AVR-4311CI 9.2 Channel Network Multi-Room Home Theater Receiver with HDMI 1.4a]] using the provided 10 foot standard headphone connector. For both the D-7100 and the D-600, the two provided cables give you a quick switch from in-line iPhone controls and microphone to the home system connection. In both cases I was using 256 bit ACC file formats, which are not the audiophile's preferred lossless files, but realistically what many of us have readily available when using iTunes and iTunes match music data. I really like the look of the D-7100 wooden ear-cups and the silver trim over the D-600's black and silver with contrasting stitching. If they were $100 more than the D-600's, I would have kept them for aesthetic reasons alone. As it was, with Amazon selling the the D-600 for exactly a third of the D-7100's, I kept the D-600 and returned the D-7100. To my ears, there was not a significant difference (your mileage may vary, as outside of specifications, sound quality is very subjective). I plan to use some of the money saved for a Schiit Asgard headphone amplifier, which I fully expect would significantly improve the sound from both of these low-impedance headphones. At the price point of the D-7100, there are several other top-of-the-line headphones that the audiophile websites rave over. I'd look to those when spending $1200 on headphones and make sure to have a headphone amplifier for serious listening. For me, the Denon D-600 provides a very similar sound stage to the D-7100s at a bargain price.

text: Monster NCredible NErgy In-Ear Headphones are a solid set of earphones for their price. Being a multiple earphone owner, including Monster's Beats By Dre, these are not the 'greatest' earphones but are a great choice for 'portability.' The Control-Talk feature is a positive for sure, as is the cord design, which doesn't tangle like say traditional iPod/mp3 earphones. As far as the sound, it is more 'balanced' than Beats By Dre solo headphones, but perhaps this is a personal preference given the style of music you enjoy. For hip-hop, one may enjoy the surging bass of Beats By Dre and dislike the balance of these headphones, which includes more treble frequencies and less 'subwoofer' bass frequencies. That is not to say that the bass is not within these headphones, but the sound is less weighed down by bass and is 'wider' you might say. My personal opinion is that these are great for portability and yield a better sound than regular old rinky-dink earphones. If you are aiming for a higher quality sound or a more professional sound, opt for more expensive headphones that will provide that ideal sound. I prefer my Beats By Dre, which are more expensive headphones, but these are ideal for more portable events than taking my bigger Beats By Dre Solos.

text: FIT: The fit of these is great. Although always subjective, but being on the picky side, I must admit that I was pleasantly impressed with the way these fit. BUTTONS: Feels good to the touch. In addition to the buttons on the headband, there are additional buttons. It emits a click-like sound. You can move to and from the next song by hitting the forward and back buttons once each. It can be held down to raise or decrease sound. The power button in the middle also functions as a pause and play button. I have not yet experimented with accepting or declining a phone call using buttons. You'll just have to get used to not being able to independently feel the buttons. BATTERY: Prolonged battery life. Funny how it seems to live longer than my phone! I use my phone a lot, thus it doesn't last as long as it ought to. I'll provide an update with the average number of hours I managed. BLUETOOTH: Thanks to Bluetooth, I was able to put my phone down, go outside, and reprimand my dogs for bothering the neighbors. My phone and headphones are uninterrupted by one wall. PHONE CALL: I've already had a call through this set. Both the caller and I could clearly hear each other. What a wonderful benefit. AS A SLEEP MASK: These can be worn over your eyes to serve as a sleep mask. In contrast to the other set the store sells, it is not completely dark. But it's wonderful for on-the-go brief naps or meditating. SOUND: Overall, excellent sound. The speakers are placed close to your ears. Although noise will still be audible, the volume increases sufficiently to enjoy music and phone calls. I appreciate it because I require their hearing for the purposes for which I utilize them. It is important to be cautious when walking outside. I detest having to take out my earplugs while delivering meals to clients or restaurant hosts. NOTE: My phone came with an app that degrades the sound quality. Motorola G Stylus is what it is. The audio produced by the app is crisper and louder. I believe this will significantly impact how much you like using these earphones. Before giving up on this set, try downloading an app to improve the quality. I'm going to buy more to give as presents.

One drawback another review had mentioned, which is why I am dropping a star, is if your laptop or phone is being charged and you have the noise canceling on, there is a seriously bad low end hum. I am assuming it is picking it up from the AC somehow. Not a deal breaker for me, but annoying. This happened with S7 Edge and a late model ASUS laptop. Unplug the power, buzz is gone. Even with the laptop unlpugged, there is still a slight low end hum. Plug the charger in, hum is back. I may look into an EM filter or something to see if I can find a workaround. text: TL:DR These are fantastic low abuse, everyday listening ear buds. Not optimal for exercise/gym, sweating use. This is a great system for the average person but will disappoint an audiophile. Bass is very pronounced and fun, mids/highs not as balanced. Battery life however is indeed astounding. FULL REVIEW: I'm a video editor and often need to edit/review outside of my studio. I have used my ATH-M50x for almost 15 years so I'm very acquainted with the sound but was tired of bringing them around everywhere. I've had a pair of cheapo Ankers that I CANNOT BEAR to use outside of biking, battery dies all the time. Wanted a stylish, functional pair of buds for general listening and on the go editing. Big Audio Technica fan, was excited to discover they had a line of in ear products. This pair seemed the nice in between in regards to their high and low end models, battery life seemed out of this world compared to majority of other brands which was a big draw to me. First listen, pretty much all the reviews about the heavy bass are correct. It is huge and the highs were noticeably diminished, muddied compared to my old M50x and ATH-ES7. There was a noticeable hiss/high frequency coming from the right bud as other people have said (though definitely less pronounced than the hiss in my Anker's). I was initially so disappointed I was going to send them back and started looking for other options. Two things happened. One, it seemed to me that I would need to spend an additional $100 to get something somewhat satisfactory to the audiophile and was back to 6 hour single charge battery life. I personally was not needing these to be my GO TO audio listening experience. Secondly, I just started using them and I actually really enjoyed them. For someone who listens to EDM and cinematic music I grew to really enjoy the bass. My ears attuned to the high frequency to the point it doesn't really bother me now. Spotify has a built in equalizer that I use to balance. They work really well for zoom calls and for casual listening and even for video editing they've been perfectly adequate. Extremely portable for traveling and again the stellar battery, not to mention aesthetically I think these look the best of all their models. So I've decided to hang on to them. I've only had them for a month, the left bud has indeed turned off once randomly during that time. Buttons aren't amazing to access but they are functional. I've worn the medium rubber tips and that's been perfectly fine for me for my typical 5 hour continuous use. Volume levels do feel a bit constrained on the louder end, and yes the app is unfortunately still not great and not really necessary apart from updating the firmware (which you should do, helped with the frequency). They do seem somewhat delicate so again low-abuse product, office, plane, etc - I would not bring these hiking, biking, running, or in rough weather. We'll see how they hold up over time.

text: I read and heard the hype of noise-cancelling headphones and how they will make my life much better. So, i went out and bought/researched most of the top selling headphones. The Aiwa model (HP-CN5) is the most value priced. But, it has a buzz when you turn on the noise-cancellation, and i certainly think that most of the noise-cancellation is being achieved by increasing the volume than anything else. Also, the battery slot is awkwardly placed above the left earpiece, and it thus constantly budges against my head. The Sony MDR-NC11's are quite uncomfortable, and cost nearly 3 times as much as the Aiwa model. The manual said that the noise-cancellation will work only if the earbuds are fitting "snugly," and from my experience it seems that the snugly fit of the earbuds is what cancels more noise than the noise cancellation technology. I must say, however, that these are the most stylish, sleek and portable headphones of the lot. Sadly, their noise cancellation is nominal, and not worth it for the pain of "snugly" fitting earbuds for extended periods of time. The third model i tried was the Sony MDR-NC20, which is the most expensive of the lot. It is definitely more comfortable than the previous models, and also has passive noise cancellation due to the closed loop cushion design around the ear. However, it will get uncomfortable when worn for long durations due to the small earcup design. In Summary, all three of these headphones cancel noise by adding a "buzzing" sound when noise-cancellation is turned on, and by increasing the volume of the music if plugged to a CD player. I would suggest using your money on a better CD player, and get comfortable headphones without the noise cancellation feature. Let me suggest Koss UR-20 or Koss UR-30 for beautiful sound quality and comfort, and the Koss THE-Plug or Sony Fontopia for ear bud type models. All cost less than 50 bucks! Enjoy, and i'll head to the stores to make all the returns! :(

text: First the good: These sound great, there isn't much to complain about the sound quality. In comparison to my QC35's, they are slightly better. The noise cancellation is basically the same in most situations, and the build quality is good. It's nice having a 3.5mm jack on each end, which wins points. The bluetooth connection handling, in my opinion, is better than the QC35 because I don't get constantly bombarded with voices reading out long device names. It's also nice to be able to turn off noise cancellation. However, there are some questionable design choices and unacceptable performance issues that made me return these cans. The gesture based controls are a pain in the ass and not too intuitive. I like to rest my hands on my headphones sometimes or reach to adjust, and that causes the MDR-1000x to perform random actions, including turning off playback, stopping music, and crazy stuff with volume. That's just poor design and I wish there were discreet physical buttons. The earpads are uncomfortable in that I can't feel that they're there, so I always think they're not covering my ears when they are. They otherwise are less stick (if that's the right word) than Bose ones, so this is just a minor subjective quip. The ambient noise passthrough is terrible and gimmicky. Sure, I can hear people talk when its on, but I can also hear people's feet scraping against the floor from 30 feet away, and the random small noises that are usually drowned out by background white noise are now noticeable. And now the dealbreaker: The noise cancellation is good if you like not moving. In most cases, it has indistinguishable performance from my Bose headsets, except when I'm on the road. If there is even a slightly bumpy ride, the NC (mainly without music playing) goes insane and starts hissing obnoxiously in my ear. There was no way to remedy this, and since I'm trying to eliminate distractions, this is plainly unacceptable. How am I supposed to nap or enjoy music on a long bus ride while listening to highly compressed snake rap? I'm typically a Sony fan, so I'll be awaiting for when they return to physical controls and address this problem with their NC.

text: EDIT: Ok so, as I had said in my original review, these earbuds are great, and I rated them 4 out of 5 stars. I liked them so much that I bought another pair for my brother as well. HOWEVER, about two weeks ago, I received an email, presumably from the sellers, asking me to take down my review in exchange for a "refund" of $30, explaining that 4 out of 5 stars simply wasn't a good enough score. Now this incident alone won't change my rating since I still loved the product, but I wanted to alert potential buyers that the overall ratings for this product might have been artificially inflated by the seller. --- Pros: +Cleanest and most modern design out of any earbud I've tried. The material is mix of plastic and mostly aluminum. Very nice +Bluetooth pairing is great. Pairs quickly. These earbuds support both mono mode and stereo mode, so you can listen with each earbud interchangeably. +Great battery life. After a month of regular use, I have yet to use up all the battery in a single listening session. +Earbuds are easily accessible because of the open design. The lack of a lid also allows the case to be the smallest I've tried. +Audio sounds great. They're no comparison to higher end earbuds that I've tried (Momentums, MW07+, Klipsch), but they hold up really well for their price. +Comfort is a 5/5 for me. They fit well and don't irritate any of the usual parts of my ears that get sore from the other earbuds I've tried. +Some reviewers have mentioned the app not working well. It's honestly been great for me. It crashes on occasion, but the functionality is perfectly fine. They recognize the earbuds quickly and will then show the battery life for both earbuds as well as the case. They also have a fully adjustable equalizer (although through testing, I've found that the equalizer is somewhat atrocious and does not seem to work well). For those who are concerned with low bass from the lack of a seal, there is a bass boost option, which is what I personally use. Additional features include the ability to turn on Full Control Mode, which I'll get into in the next bullet. +The base controls aren't great. Double tap for play and pause, and hold for voice assistant. However, once you turn on full control mode in the app, you get additional controls added on top of those. Single tap and triple tap on the left earbud for volume, and single tap and triple tap on the right earbud for skip and previous track. They're not the most intuitive control scheme, but I'm still glad they're there. Cons: -While the open design is great, there is some cause for concern since dust and small particles can easily get stuck in the case. In addition, it definitely is possible to shake the earbuds out of the case. However the force required to achieve this is pretty high and I've never had this issue in real life testing. -Due to the unsealed nature of these earbuds, sound isolation is pretty poor. Don't get these if you need to block out a lot of outside noise during commutes (train rides, planes, traffic) -Indicator lights are great. Both earbuds have a single indicator light as well as one on the case. They work fine, but they don't show much. White continuous light means its charging and blinking white light means they require charging. Blue means they're pairing. That's basically it. No different colors to show battery level, so if you need that information, you'll have to either use the app or hope that your phone shows the battery life of your bluetooth devices. Overall a great pair of bluetooth earbuds that sacrifice some audio quality for portability, design, and ease of use. Great cheap alternative to Apple Airpods

text: My initial thought was to just get some inexpensive noise cancelling (NC) 'phones to tone down the din on a plane trip to Australia. Researched and researched and researched before buying the Gorsun M98 from Amazon. I tested the M98 in my home and car, switching back-and-forth with Bose QuietComfort 35 IIs (widely considered one of the very best NC models, as it should be for $300). The M98 is a tad bit heavier than the 35 II, but not objectionably so, and seems to be of good quality (hinges, extending detents, plastics). Ear cups are comfy around my big ears, and I find the headband padding a bit more cushy than the 35 II. The M98 clamped to my head a touch more than the light-touch 35 II. Appreciate the included long audio & charging cords (Bose only had a short charging cable), airplane headphone adapter, basic carrying bag, and excellent 60 days free refund and 24 month guarantee too. For all this, under $60, the Gorsun M98 is a solid performer. It had very good low-frequency NC, mid- and high-end attenuation was a bit less complete than the 35 II and there is a slight bit of hiss (commonly found in NC headphones). Overall, an impressive NC showing, considering the M98 is 1/5 the price of the 35 II. Battery life seems good, it's easy to connect, and I like that noise cancelling can be activated separately from bluetooth (saves battery). Bluetooth range seems good too. So why did I send the M98 back? Sound quality. Even before comparing with the 35 II, I could tell the mids and highs were quite muted/muddy, with heavy skewing of sound toward bass. Imaging wasn't as spacious or separated either. Finally, the M98 needed more volume from input devices to put out the same amount of sound compared to the 35 II. All *totally* understandable for the price, but after much consideration I decided to splurge for the best. If one wants effective low-end noise cancellation, the Gorsun M98 is a solid choice. These headphones may be cheap, but they don't look/feel it, and have a super return policy and warranty to boot! (I'm a tough grader. 3 of 5 is excellent for sub-$60 NC headphones in my book.)

text: I've been using a pair of Shure 530s for two years and two months now. Before that, I had Etymotics ER-4Ps for something like 2-3 years. I had learned to really like the ER-P4s, despite their heavily attenuated bass (though I admit I am no bass freak; I prefer to most natural sound possible). But I fell in love with the Shure 530s at first use. I currently use them with a Cowon iAudio7, which despite being a year or two old, is still an audiophile's portable player. I don't play lossless rips like FLAC, but I do rip high end, like OGG 256kps ave (VBR). I play a wide variety of music. With those particulars, I found the audio difference (between the Shure 530s and the ER-4Ps) was striking. (I need to add that I had taken excellent care of my ER-4Ps, so the difference cannot be explained by misuse.) I've often checked back with my old Etymotics (stored in "like new" condition) but I just can't enjoy them anymore, now that I know what I am missing. Besides the missing low frequencies, the ER-4Ps are just too bright (and I even like bright). The ER-4Ps remain an excellent earphone, but given how much I listen to earphones, and how much I love music, the 530s are the best investment I've made yet in my musical life. I see some reviewers reported their 530s "breaking" after nominal use. I can only speak for my own use, and can't rule out them getting lemons, but I'm inclined to suspect the handling was less than optimally careful. Way too many people pretty much toss these sorts of things around like footballs, and then rant when they miraculously break. Anyway, I probably average 5-10 hours a week on them. Never had any trouble with them at all. I always treat them with kid gloves. I remove them by pulling on the body of the ear piece, and never by the cord. I clean the foam plugs carefully with alcohol wipes once a week (exterior, not the interior), and change them out periodically (never had the use the earwax removal tool: kinda think that you only need that if your hygiene is lacking, but maybe I'm just fortunate). I never store/transport them in a way that they can be crushed. And when stowing them in the provided carrying case, I make sure the ear pieces won't be impinged upon by the little nub that sits in the middle of the carry case (not the best case design; but it may have been improved by now). I did own a much cheaper (~$100) pair of Shure earphones (I forget the model number) that I handled just as carefully, but which nonetheless went part-dead on one side suddenly one day. Never could figure out why. No blockage. No parts feel off/out. No tank/drop/crush/etc. But my 530s are still going strong.

text: I've had my R/80's for 21 months. They worked fine (and produced adequate sound) with moderate use--not used on a daily basis, almost never stretched (I wore the coil around my neck attached to a 2oz mp3 player), removed from the house only on very rare occasions, etc.--for about 18 months. At that point I started to get a crackle as the cord weakened internally. It wasn't too bad, just something that happened when I moved and stretched the coiled cord every once in a while. I just used them through it. Now, a few months later, I can barely get sound to come out of them. "No problem," I figure. "The cord is replaceable after all. The headphones themselves are perfectly fine, and I can just have Koss send me a new cord. Their warranty is touted as good all the time, right?" WRONG. Koss got back to me with their solution today. Send them the headphones (shipped at *my* cost, which is about $10.50 for USPS "if-it-fits-it-ships") AND a check for $9 and they'll consider sending me a replacement about a month later. They want me to spend about $20 (look up top for how much a brand new pair would cost)and be without the headphones in the interim. And they of course don't guarantee they'll handle the request. (Though I suspect they would, to be fair, it's OBVIOUS that the cable has failed.) All to replace a single cord that costs pennies and should not have failed were it properly constructed. A cord which only a Koss customer with a viable set of headphones has any use for. I have a much better solution. Let everyone know what a terrible warranty Koss has, and that their gear DOES wear out even if you're not a HEAVY user. Oh, and buy a new pair of AT's from Amazon. If past shipping speed is any indicator they'll be here by the end of the week, and I'm not even a prime member anymore. So, in the end, if you want a pair of headphones that you know you're going to throw away, buy these. (And be aware that the more stress you put on the cord by stretching it or taking it into rough environments, the sooner it will break.) If you want a pair of headphones that you're actually going to keep, go with a different company. Or, spend hundreds of dollars on a pair from Koss so that when they ask you to pay them for the privilege of fixing their broken junk it's not such a huge percentage of the brand new price.

text: The first thing you notice about the AKG K323XS A in-ear monitors (IEMs) is the size. These headphones are small, very small. I have a number of IEMs and these are probably the smallest, even smaller than the Klipsch X10s. AKG does provide four sizes of tips (Extra small, Small, Medium, and Large). I usually use the large sized tip with IEMs, but even with the large tips, I am unable to develop a good seal when inserting these into my ears. A seal is very important; without a good seal, noise isolation is virtually non-existent, and bass will be lacking. That's exactly what happens when I use the AKG K323XS A headphones. I have found that I need to push these into my ears and far as they can go, and then pull back slightly to develop a seal. Unfortunately, the headphones do not stay in place (while walking and certainly while running) so any seal that may have developed is lost if you move too much. Despite the small size, the headphones seem durable, with a relatively thick cord that will likely stand up well with usage. The one-button remote worked fine with my Android phone. Bottom line, for the price these are decent headphones, as long as you sit and don't move around too much. The sound is very balanced, although highs seem to be too shrilly, and they seem durable. I prefer at least a little bass, and the small size and shape of the headphones, while great from a comfort perspective if you planning on using these for a long period of time, makes it hard if not impossible to develop a good seal.

text: I did not get my pair from here but I noticed there isn't many reviews on the SHP9600 so I figured it would be worthwhile leaving a review. I also own the SHP9500, X2HR and owned the X3 for a brief period. Right off the bat I would tell people to wait. I imagine the price will fall to the $90 and below range in another 6 months or so. I already see a closed back gaming version of this headphone called the Philips G6105 which can be ordered overseas right now for $130 and that has rgb, a mic, and a built in dac/amp with eq presets. If they can add all of that for the same price as these they definitely have the headroom to lower the price of these back down to where they should be. Strangely when I first starting typing this there was a discount lowering the price to $100 but after going back to see what the original price was to confirm what I put as a headline I don't see the discount anymore and they are $130 again. If you aren't like me and don't have an addiction to buying headphones wait for these to hit $90 or below. Anything more than that and you're better off getting the X2HR. I read one review saying " It sounded like put my hands over my ears and compared to the 9500s." I find that to be a gross exaggeration. Personally I find the SHP9500 to sound too thin for my liking and always thought the best description of those would be that they are an imitation of an "audiophile" sound. By saying that I mean they make what you can hear obvious giving a false impressing of more detail. It has a brightness that make things that don't normally stand out stand out. There is no extra texture or nuance to the sound. By comparison the SHP9600 is a more traditional sound. Rather than trying to trick you into thinking it is more detailed than it actually is it goes for more of a forgiving sound. I didn't find them to sound muffled like that other person at all. To my ears they sounded like the SHP9500 with the annoying and occasionally painful treble fixed. Despite all the graphs I see showing the SHP9500 to be well behaved I find them to be sibilant at times and some sounds can get a "piercing". I let a certain reviewer persuade me and it was one of many regretful purchases. The SHP9600 would not have been a regret if that is the sound I got back then. The SHP9600 seems to have fixed that and are a much more enjoyable listen as a result. The SHP9600 also has more bass but that isn't saying much since I find the SHP9500 to be well below average there. To me all those changes sound great but it seems more of just a change in tuning and not any real improvement in quality over the older SHP9500. It is definitely a more pleasing listen though. The problem lies with the current price of the SHP9600 and the X2HR. With the SHP9600 being so close to the X2HR in price you have to compare them and that is where things fall apart for Phillips. The X2HR offer a rather unique experience with a soundstage that wraps around you in a way not many headphones can replicate. Other headphones do that as well but there is something different in the way the X2HR does it and it turns the X2HR in to an experience. Even though the SHP9600 costs roughly the same you don't get an "experience" when listening to them. They are good headphones but just like the SHP9500 there is nothing about them that makes you think "I need to hear this song or watch this movie on my SHP". To be fair most headphones that make me think that cost me much much more than these but the sub $140 X2HR gives me that feeling. On top of the X2HR offering an "experience" while the SHP9600 doesn't they also seem to offer a quality improvement over the SHP9600 as well. The sound of the SHP9600 seems loose in comparison. While it has improved bass over it's predecessor it still lacks the texture and control of the X2HR. I really can't think of a reason to buy the SHP9600 over the X2HR. Maybe an argument could be made that the X2HR can sound a bit fatiguing on the occasional song but that same argument can be said for the SHP9500 to a much greater extent. With all of that said these are better than the SHP9500 but I also feel like I was mislead and overpaid for the SHP9500. These sound like what that reviewer said the SHP9500 sounded like. At $90 buy the SHP9600 but at it's current price buy the X2HR and enjoy a unique experience with better quality sound. Don't even think about the X3. If the X2HR didn't exist then maybe the X3 could be priced at $300 and be a good buy but there is almost no sound difference at all between the X2HR and the X3. That same reviewer that got me to buy the SHP9500 also claims the X3 is "a few percent" better but that is also what you get when you go from single ended to balanced. If you listen to the same headphone just one pair single ended and the other balanced you will think there is a difference. It will be even more so when using a different dac and amp for each like he did. In my experience using the same gear for both there was no difference outside of the balanced difference. Single ended on the same gear they sound virtually identical. No improvement in quality at all which is why I got rid of them while I could still get my money back. If you skipped past all the rambling just buy the X2HR and pretend the SHP9600 and X3 don't exist until their prices drop way down.

text: My old Sennheiser PX-100s were finally dying after about five years and it was time to find a new pair of jogging/traveling around headphones. The PX-100s were great, but with the success of that product Sennheiser changed the headphones somewhat and jacked up the price so I figured it was time to tryout their Koss counterparts. I'm a big fan of the PortaPros, they have punchy bass, mid-range is good and the treble is not too piercing. The result is a very good product, though I have to admit I don't like the sound quite as much as the Sennheisers. I think that the main problem is the bass, it's good, but the Sennheisers had a dynamic, fat bass sound that the PortaPros can't quite reach. I'm a fan of a variety of music, and in rock and jazz tunes this slight deficiency is not apparent at all. With electronic music and, in particular, hip-hop, the limits of the bass show up. I should say that I do have perhaps an over-fondness for low-end sounds so it's possible that you'll like the fact that the bass isn't as strong with the PortaPros. I will also say that while I don't like these PortaPros quite as much as the PX-100s, I don't think that the PX-100s are worth their new $50 price tag and I would purchase these Koss headphones again if giving the choice.

text: I put these headphones through their paces on "The Ultimate Headphones Test" web site. I was able to hear the low frequencies as soon as the web site said I should have, and I could tell the headphones were vibrating at frequencies lower than that. I can't speak for the high frequencies; both these headphones and my excellent Bose earbuds kicked in between 17kHz and 16kHz, which I think says more about my hearing than the headphones. I was very impressed with how the headphones sounded on the binaural test. I had just read that I was about to listen to the sound of people knocking on doors; like the doofus I am, I got up and answered the door when I heard the sound. So I think the headphones pass the "realistic sound" test. I listened to some Gotye and Kimbra tracks, as well as a recording of Maurizio Pollini playing the piano and some of Ellie Goulding's electronic stuff. On Gotye's tracks, I noticed a certain static that I'd never heard before. It wasn't like it was supposed to be there. But then again, switch to Ellie Goulding and it's not there. On the piano music, I also noticed a little ambient white noise that I didn't notice before. So the headphones seem to emphasize white noise in certain cases. I experimented with the iTunes equalizer and found that driving the bass up all the way produced distortion and muddiness without a lot of resounding bassness. So if you're looking for good dubstep headphones, probably no. Comfort level is okay! They go over pretty much my whole ear. They do make my ears warm. They do a little bit of noise blocking -- better than my Bose earbuds, which are designed to partially block noise. I got these for a weird reason -- they're the headphones frequently seen on Martin Freeman (Watson in the BBC Sherlock series and Frodo in "The Hobbit") when he's bumming around on set. I figured a film star could afford any headphones and chose these because they were good. My deduction: Martin Freeman doesn't like dubstep?

text: Let me start with a couple of statements/disclaimers first: 1) my English is still rough around the edges, so - sorry for that in advance. 2) I won't talk about burn-in and the wonders of soundscape which opens after that; I could be able to talk about that if I'd done the following: hi-end source, 2 indistinguishable sets of h-phones, one - burned in, another - just out of the box, blind test, select the best sounding pair - that would be fair. Otherwise, while I may understand the mechanics behind the burn-in - after all the headphones is an electro-mechanical device of sorts - changes in the current are converted to the physical movement of the membrane, it needs to loosen up before revealing its pure beauty, but we shouldn't forget the psychological factor of just getting used to something new and recognizing it as something familiar (and pleasant). So - while there're grounds to mention the burn-in, its importance may be slightly overrated. 3) I'm not a hardcore (or even softcore) audiophile, nor I listen to audiophile-grade records; I bought these headphones mainly for office use, with the source being either the iPod or the lap/desktop. My musical taste is heavily oriented towards electro and indie/alternative with a hint of rock/classical (several examples would be: Underworld, Laika, Cocteau Twins, Grimes, Course of Empire, TV On The Radio, Elbow, you got the drift; hiphop, dubstep and other bass-heavy styles are rare entries in the menu). Given that, I'm also not capable of discussing the soundstage and instrument placement; there is basically no such thing in the electronic music. All in all I could see myself as a regular John Doe, wanting to enjoy the music just for his own pleasure. With this said and done, now to the actual review. *** Sound See above - neither of sources can be considered hi-fi; this is important while evaluating the actual sound. Proper approach would be to use the proper source, unfortunately this is not possible at the moment. Pros: * the depth, breath and width of the sound is really, really good. I haven't listened to higher-grade h-phones, so can't compare, but I do like what I hear * the sound is very.. precise; there's an Ordnung here. It can be plus or minus, depending on how you look at it. * the detalization is unbelievable - it is worth going through the collection just to find out - ooh, so This is how it is supposed to sound (again, keeping in mind the capabilities of the playback devices) * it is a pleasure to listen to mids and highs, the sound is neither harsh nor overly bright, no listening fatique whatsoever - at least at normal listening levels Cons: * while mids and highs are brilliant, I'd appreciate a bit more in bass department. Don't get me wrong - the bass is there, all right, it's precise, tight, well controlled, not boomy, but it's pushed too far to the "background". Bass guitars, bass drums, even snares are.. a bit too far away. Probably it could be remedied with an amp. * .. no, there are no other cons. Maybe the aforementioned precision could be an issue for some, I see where the argument about lack of emotional involvement (lack of bass, perhaps?) could come from. Overall, I'd say, this is a precise and faithful instrument, trying its best not to stand in the way or change things. *** Looks and comfort Pros: * Earpieces are really comfortable, at the moment I've spent about four hours non-stop with these, and I can go for hours more, as it seems. I can't say that it's "like nothing at all" because it isn't and there are no headphones out there that would feel "like nothing at all". not wearing headphones feels "like nothing at all". but these indeed are comfortable for long periods * velour!! thank you, Sennheiser, for that! faux leather is the devil's invention - unless "sweaty ears" is one's style and preference. it looks like they could pick up a bit of dust but that's expected - and not evident after a day of use. Cons: * you may need to spend some time adjusting the position of the headband on your head; this is not the most comfortable headband out there (although much, much better than older AKGs I've had a chance to try - these had really _horrible_ headband; what good is the quality of the sound, if after 10 minutes it felt like they were nailed to the top of my head). so far the best in this department has been a pair of old Technics RP-500; the headband on those so far has been the most comfortable of all, although those Technics were lighter, so that also had an impact on comfort. The headband of the HD598 is very close, but tiny bit not as good. Earpieces of the HD598 are better, though. * the cable may be a bit too long for office use, although it can come in handy if you're using it with an [under]desktop. Cable should be perfect for home use, I presume. * be careful with 6.3>3.5mm adapter; it works fine, but the whole setup is rather big; if you are not careful enough, you can damage it (I would bet on bent 3.5mm plug). a shorter version of the cable with 3.5mm plug would be a welcome addition to the lineup. Neither: * I like the looks, but I think it might not be for everyone. * these are open headphones, so they will leak a bit of sound if cranked up, but that's expected. to complain about that is the same as to complain about the hair getting wet, when driving a cabrio with the roof down during the rain - well, it just happens to work that way! So far my colleagues haven't complained. Overall - I like these headphones. I'd give them 4.5 stars if that would be possible, or 9/10. There are some things to improve, but for the money - I haven't listened to competition, but these seem to be hard to beat. They seem to be placed in that sweet spot of price/performance, after which a relatively tiny bit of improvement will cost you a fortune or two. To recommend these or any headphones to others is the same as to recommend a wife/husband - what works for one may not work for others and vice versa; listen, compare, get what you like the best for the money you can afford to spend. Personally, these work for me and I'm glad I got them.
