text: I've been using these wireless SleepPhones for a year, and can't do without them. I'm sensitive to sounds and even light snoring drives me out of my mind. Soothing sleep music plus the muffling effect of the headband helps block it all out -- but the thought of tossing and turning with wires wrapping around my neck wasn't appealing! Bluetooth to the rescue. As others have said, this product feels a bit slapped-together, an ingenious but kludgy solution. Recharging is especially annoying; you practically have to disembowel the thing to charge it, and I'm kind of amazed mine still works after doing that hundreds of times. But it does work, and there's simply no comparable product on the market. The key thing to know: **Do not set your device to play continuously all night long.** If the headphones run out of power, they don't just shut off. Alas, a loud recording speaks straight into your ears, awakening you to tell you it is powering down. (Huge, huge design flaw, please fix!) But frankly, it's probably not a good idea to play music continuously all night long anyway, right? Just set your device to a timer or sleep mode and let it stop after 45 minutes or an hour. If you wake up during the night you can start it again.

text: I am a musician and audio enthusiast. My normal listening gear includes Sennheiser Momentums, KRK Rokit 5 monitors, and ELAC B6 speakers. I had 3 pairs of Nox Audio Scouts dual driver earbuds before this, all of which unfortunately broke. As Nox is out of business (no surprise since their products clearly don't last even though they sound great), I had no choice but to look elsewhere to replace them. I listen to an extremely wide range of music, from Tchaikovsky to AC/DC to Zedd to Adele and generally enjoy speakers or headphones that are able to present a wide range of music well. After listening to them for over a month now: Pros: -Fantastic dynamic range, especially for a pair of earbuds -Bass extension is incredible and very detailed -They sound 'airy' and open compared to other earbuds -Treble sounds detailed, controlled, and sweet -Carrying case looks pretty cool -Build quality feels superb Cons: -Vocals can sound recessed, especially on busy tracks such as on Mr. Brightside by the Killers. I usually prefer a more forward/prominent mid presentation -Mids could be sweeter sounding -Earbuds are large and may not be comfortable for everyone -Can expose weaknesses in your DAC, for example, these earbuds don't sound very good plugged into my Thinkpad, but sound great plugged into my Samsung Galaxy, iPhone, or my desktop headphone amplifier at home I think these earbuds really shine with instrumentals or other types of music that are instrumentally driven. If you primarily listen to vocal work, I would imagine there are better earbuds out there. Either way, I doubt you'll be disappointed by these, especially for $100.

text: My first Superadio III was purchased in late 1993 (...) The FM sensitivity was great as I could pick up weaker stations from Cookeville and Livingston, Tennesssee from my house in Murfreesboro (80 to 95 miles). The same could be said in the other direction Huntsville Alabama and Chattanooga. On AM, I received Louisville, KY and Memphis, Tennessee in the daytime (200+ miles) and Cincinnati, Chicago, Des Moines, Detroit, and New York City by night. Sound quality was VERY GOOD and tuning was generally accurate for an analog dial. Earlier in 2004, I bought a second one. (...) No substantial changes from appearance or sound performance are noted. However, tuning distant stations seems a bit more difficult with the newer radio. Also, tuning contains more inaccuracies on AM. Furthermore, plastic knobs seem more flimsy which means they must be treated with extra care to avoid breakage and premature wear. Both radios are manufactured in China, so it is possible they may have come from the same factory. My eleven year old GE Superadio III, in my judgment, has the better overall quality. Verdict: if a no-frills radio (e.g. no dial light, digital presets, or shortwave) is what you desire, look no further. It is the best value around and produces excellent sound. If one is particular about dial tuning and cabinet durability, examine carefully and buy from a store that has a good return policy as an exchange may be required to get a accurate tuning dial. If a high end radio is what you desire and need, consider a CC Radio or a Bose Wave Radio (about $169 and $349, respectively) over the Superadio III.

text: These are a nice step up from the wraparound bluetooth headphones I had before due to the convenience of them. They take up much less real estate on my head, which also makes them easier to shove into a pocket when I'm not using them. The charging storage case is one of the best features of these, because it means they're charging when not in use and you're on the go so they're ready to go when you need them (misery is being halfway through a workout at the gym and having your earbuds die). The bluetooth range is also impressive. The built-in mic works great. I've had a number of phone conversations with people while driving, walking around my apartment, and walking outside. The only time someone complained about the audio quality was when I was outside, and that was probably due to wind. For gym workouts, these have been great. I can stop/start music by pressing the right earbud and skip forward and backward by using the left earbud. Accessing Siri can be done play pressing and holding the right button and then I can speak my commands. The buttons are big, too, so gone are the days of me having to try to use long-holds, quick presses, and double- and triple-clicks to do various functions on tiny buttons. Okay, now for my gripes... First off, I hate that I can't adjust volume from the earbuds. I can only do that with my phone or by using Siri through the built-in mic (which is not going to happen at the gym, where I'm most likely needing to raise and lower the volume). I miss the volume control on my old bluetooth headphones. Second, the bass doesn't sound as deep to me as I would expect on JBLs, especially at this price. Of course, this is subjective, and it's also possible that I need to swap out the earbud tips for a better seal. Or, maybe JBL decided to do me a favor and not blow out my eardrums with too much bass resonance. Third, the earbuds are supposed to power up and connect to phone when they are removed from the case. In most cases, they do. In other cases, one of the earbuds won't power on automatically and has to be manually turned on (holding the button for a couple of seconds). And, sometimes one or both won't make the bluetooth connection and have to be powered off and then on again. It happens enough times to be frustrating. Overall, though, I really like these. They're super convenient and look cool enough that I had someone at the gym asking about them during my last workout.

text: After reading all the praises and positive reviews Hifiman's newest budget iem, the RE-400 waterline garnered, I decided to purchase a pair for the everyday abuse. It was hard to predict what to expect before a firsthand experience, so I must say I was shocked when I opened up the package once I received my order. The packaging is modest yet practical, a small brown box containing the hard cover with the ear pieces and accessories, plus a hard carrying case. Sliding open the plastic case, one will find the ear pieces, three pair of ear tips, a wire clip and a user manual and filer replacements. For the price, this sound equipment is exceptional to behold even before one is ready to try them. Once connected to a good audio source, the sound quality it produces is astonishing, the gear definitely lives up to the hype. The frequency range is well extended, with sparkling treble, though a bit rolled off, and very fast, deep, punchy bass. "Beats" by Dr.Drae, or Sennheiser IE-8/80 fans may be disappointed, these phones are no bass monsters. What they offer instead is crystal clear, slightly warm and very detailed sound, with reasonable sound stage. Nothing I ever heard in this price range comes even close. For those who are decided to try a pair of these, a set of Comply Comfort tips are also recommended. The factory installed double flange tips do isolate well, but they tend to create air pressure, and somewhat uncomfortable to wear for long sessions. All and all, this audio gear represents true innovation, incredible performance and the best value at an incredible price. Strongly recommended.

text: I had high hopes for the Echo Buds 2Gen but they let me down on just about every category. My grades: Fit: (C-) I got one to fit well and pass the sound test. Neither did well on the sound test with the optional wings. On the right one, I never got better than a "Fair" fit rating. It doesn't fit well and is not secure in my ear. The wings don't seem to help. Sound Quality: (B+) I have several truly wireless ear buds, mostly because I'm still looking for the perfect pair. My favorites so far are the 1st gen Air Pods. The sound quality of the Echo Buds is better than those and nearly as good as the Air Pods Pro. I had hoped that it would be better (since newer) but I think the Air Pods Pro still provide better sound. Noise Cancellation: (D) I really can't tell when noise cancellation is on or off. Perhaps it is the poor fit or perhaps it is poor quality noise cancellation. Either way, these do not provide decent noise cancellation, making them just another set of poorly fitting ear buds to me. Ease of use: (D) The Air Pods play/pause/answer/end all with a double tap (or Squeeze on the Pro). The Bragi were pretty cool with head movements, but also needlessly complicated. (I suspect that the Echo Buds are really the next gen Bragi ear buds since Bragi sold out of the consumer market). The Echo buds require you to memorize one tap for play pause media and 2 taps to answer a call. It's just dumb that way. The Apple buds all recognize that if a call comes in when you're listening to media one command pauses media and answers a call. If you're on a call the same command ends the call and starts playing media (if paused for the call). If listening to medial the same command plays and pauses, so you only have to remember one command to execute any of these actions. Amazon's system is needlessly complex, (just as the Bragi system was). Battery life: (A) I think I get about 5 hours of listening to audiobooks. They charge reasonably fast. This feels like the right metrics for truly wireless ear buds. Build Quality: (A) I think they are solid and well built. Not well designed, but well built. Charging case: (A) Charges wirelessly on a normal Qi Charger or using a cable. Charging is fast enough and easy enough. Alexa: (C-) Although it is true that the Echo Buds will summon Alexa to execute commands, I've had a few instances where it wouldn't execute a command because the phone was locked. That's just dumb. Also, when the echo buds can't execute an Alexa command, they take priority so none of your other devices will execute. You need to take them out, put them in the case and wait a few seconds to use Alexa from another device to turn on lights etc. When they work it is a nice feature, but about half the time I wish there was a way to disable Alexa on the echo buds and just use the normal echo devices I usually use. Bluetooth: (D-) Simply put, these are the worst BT Ear Buds I've ever used. If they lose the BT connection (e.g. leave the phone in the house and walk into the yard) I have to reconnect them manually. When they reconnect, the play pause commands may not work and you have to go to your device, unlock the screen and go into the app to resume playing media. Often I receive complaints about the sound quality on the other end of the call going in and out as if my phone has a poor signal, until I put the echo buds in their case and then the sound quality becomes perfect through the phone's speakers and mic. If you take the echo buds out of your ear, they may continue to play music or the call you're on and they may not. Sometimes they switch back and forth on their own despite making a specific choice on the phone for the audio source for a call. As far as a device for making and answering calls go, these are terrible. Apple watch compatibility: (F) It's possible that I missed a setting somewhere, but so far I have yet to have them work with content or calls from the watch. Price: (B) Not the cheapest but fairly reasonably priced, although I would probably pay more for Air Pods. They just work better on an iPhone. Overall grade: (D+) I think if they fit better, if the BT worked better, if noise cancellation was noticeable, if they were easier to use, if they worked more cooperatively with other echo devices... really any one of those things, I would have given this a grade of average. If they did all of them they would get a great grade. Failing in all of these important areas, though, makes the Echo Buds Gen2 a product to stay away from. I may give the Jabra or Samsung products a try next in my search for a really great pair of truly wireless ear buds, but the Echo buds have been the worst of all of the ones I've tried so far.

text: I got a pair from the Kickstarter campaign and my husband had to get his own. I would recommend the Dash to anyone looking for a new Bluetooth stereo earpiece or fitness tracker or portable audio player, especially if they wanted a single device to do all three in a tiny package. I use mine primarily for Bluetooth audio, occasionally taking phone calls. I had been searching for years for the "perfect" earpiece and finally feel like I've found it. My first requirement is that it be wireless. With long hair, I ended up yanking anything with a cord out a least once every time I used used it. The second requirement is that it is comfortable to wear, including how easy it is to put on/in and how securely it stays put. The third requirement is that the audio needs to be clear, both for listening and speaking. Until now, I had found only one other device that even came close to meeting all three basic requirements. Wireless is easy. Getting something I could wear that had decent audio capabilities seemed impossible. I have small ears and couldn't get anything to stay in my ear without a loop unless it was painful to wear for more than an hour at a time. Even the ones that fit over the ear weren't always secure. The ones with good audio quality weren't easy to put on while driving and I couldn't wear them long enough for 'in case a call comes in while I'm driving'. Plus the whole being distracted thing. The few that I did find comfortable to wear had horrible audio quality. Even from the big names. But mostly I just never found any that were comfortable. I tried all the ones my husband got and didn't like any enough to steal them from him (and I had high hopes for the Jawbones... :-( ) I didn't really expect the Dash to be any different, to be honest. But what's another few hundred dollars on another one at this point, right? Surprisingly, the Dash is not only comfortable to wear, it stays put. They need a good 'seal' for noise blocking and don't come out until you take them out. I even tried it showering. I can wear them until the batteries die, although sometimes my ears do get itchy. (It is important to insert them with the little twist, as described.) The audio is good and, OMG, can be changed with updates, which the manufacturer periodically puts out. I found the listening quality pretty good from the first version and it's only been improved. My callers tell me the speaking quality is now up to par (unless I'm in a high interference area, when switching to the phone doesn't help all that much, either.) I'm thrilled having just my basic requirements in the same set of earphones, so everything else is a bonus for me. I particularly like the pass through audio. With the noise suppression, I can ignore everybody until I want to hear them ;-) and switching is just a swipe over the sensors. Gestures are being added, so maybe soon I can just nod my head or something. However, as amazing as these are, there are some technical limitations. Bluetooth frequencies don't travel through water, which means you can get signal interference from your body. Because they're tucked inside your ear, and only the right Dash receives the phone connection, you usually can't wear your phone in your back left pocket outdoors. And some phones have crappy antennas, which becomes very apparent with these earpieces.

text: When I first saw this I was excited, because the QC-15s have a few cons (Bulkier, doesn't work without battery). So this was like the best of passive noise canceling (like my -now stolen- etymotic) plus Bose's active noise canceling tech, which, at least on the QC-15 is superb. I am an Android user (and have a series of iOS + Apple products like this very Macbook Air). I develop software so I need iPhones, iPads and Androids. When I got my QC-15, I remember going to an App Store with my MBAir to try whether the mic would work when connected in the computer. It did, so it was awesome, because I could use it to Skype with people without using the integrated mic in the computer while wearing the awesome headphones. I later gave my QC-15 to a very good friend who couldn't afford them and decided I was eventually going to buy new ones. I finally got these new QC20. As an Android user, I picked the Android version. That was my first mistake. I'll summarize the pros/cons: Good Things: - They are light and very portable. The battery doesn't really bother much (but it has a few caveats). - Moderately easy to fit and less tiring (for me) than the full in-ear-canal (Etymotic stuff). I flew 16 hours straight and they didn't really cause a major problem (tho I could feel them by the end). - Easy to sleep with these on a plane while tilting your head. Still some vibrations can be heard, but with the others is really hard for obvious reasons. - The USB charging is nice (Boeing 767-400 have USBs on every seat so you can watch the TV while not draining your battery). - The new "Aware Mode" is also a nice thing, but on a plane it will not necessarily be loud enough to hear a person talking to you. You have to turn it on-off when you want to use it, because when that is on, the cancelled noise is nowhere near as good as when it's off. - The sound is good, but these are not top of the end headphones. The idea is for sound to be acceptable in noisy environments. It's certainly not the best sound you can get, but it will be probably the best isolation in certain environments. And the combination of both is extremely decent. - You can use them even when turned off as regular headphones. - The cable is nice and doesn't create the annoying sound (known to Etymotics and such) when hit by objects or your own body. Now the Bad things: - With the 3 sizes (S-M-L) ear tips, you might not find an appropriate one for your ear size. Mines (I was using Med) would slowly pop out after a few hours. Not a big deal, but I wish Bose would offer more choices (Like Etymotic does). - The battery is not heavy, but heavy enough to cause disconnects if it hangs from a loose plug (like on a plane where the plug is abused a few times a day). - The position of the battery in the "cable" is a win-loss situation. Sometimes you feel like it's great and sometimes you wished it where somewhere else. - The Amount of cable after the battery could use a few more inches (it's really really short) so you have to basically "stick" the battery with your phone and every time you hold your phone, you have to hold the battery or it bother you all the time - The Android/Windows version only comes with 1 button (plus the button to activate aware mode). The button serves as a play/pause on any app that is registered to operate with media buttons (most should anyway). But it has no volume controls (lame). The iOS version of these controls in the QC15 work on Android (the volume doesn't but the play pause does, so you get the same functionality). On the plus side, the QC15 buttons (for iOS) work with a Macbook so you get a Mic, mute, volume keys and this is why I'm returning my QC20. I use a Macbook Air and I need the headphones + mic for Google Hangouts or Skype. It doesn't work for some reason. The MIC works on my Nexus 4 tho (but no mute which would have been great). - Since the buttons are not interchangeable (like in the QC-15), you're stuck with what you got. I'd get the iOS -EVEN- if you have an Android device (don't know about Windows). - The tips (rubber?) are very weird and fit ok, but they are "fragile" (I almost broke one trying to remove it) DON'T PULL. Read instructions. - For obvious reasons, you can't detach the cables and use the noise cancel feature alone (like in the QC-15) Conclusion: These are great headphones if you travel a lot (especially on short trips where you don't carry a lot of stuff and you have limited space in your bag). They win the size war vs. the QC-15. I've compared the noise cancellation inside a 737-900 mid-flight side by side. I asked a fellow passenger for their QC-15 and tried one after the other for a couple of times. The sound isolation is pretty much the same, I'd say the QC20 have a little but more mugginess to voices because they are somewhat in-ear and provide more passive isolation. But the "real" engine noise was cancelled by both in a very similar way. If anything, the QC20 wins by a small margin. The sound quality is hard to compare (especially in a plane!) but with the QC-15 I had to turn my volume all the way up. With the QC20 it was 3/4 (for the same volume experience). I don't know if this was because of the battery or what. All in all, these are expensive headphones that I can only recommend if you travel a lot and don't want to carry extra batteries or don't want to deal with the "big" QC-15. The battery is not replaceable so I guess that could be a factor. It lasted through two flights: 8 + 4 hours with no problem whatsoever, but then again, Bose claims 16 hours. So… which one do you get? It really depends. If you're looking for portability, you won't look back, the whole thing is really light for what it does! If you hate in-ear stuff, go QC-15. If you want sound quality, get an AudioTechnica or similar :) If you don't mind carrying AAA batteries around and want to use the noise canceling feature without carrying a cable and stuff, the QC-15 can do it. If you need Macbook (Air/Pro) microphone compat, get the iOS version (even if you have an Android phone). Note: I haven't tested the QC20 iOS version, but I did have the QC15 iOS version and it works on both android (as a mic+play/pause) and on Mac (as Volume+mic+play/pause). The volume controls won't work on Android and that's why the presumably sell two versions, so you don't get controls that don't work… I assume the QC20 will have a similar behavior. But you should dbl-check. I will be personally getting the QC15 again instead of these (which I am returning as we speak). What would I like to see improved? More ear tips Ability to detach the whole battery thing and use them as regular earphones. Volume buttons for Android (that also work on Macbooks!) Battery should be replaceable, otherwise you're going to have to throw the whole thing away in a few years. Better price, 200 dollars would be better.

text: The Sony XBAH1 Hybrid 2-Way Driver In-Ear Headphones are a decently-made set of earphones (or IEMS) for the price, which has currently dropped a bit under $100. But due to their treble-heavy sound I can't recommend these at all. Build and fit - good. The XBAH1s seem to be well constructed of plastic, and they come with a long 48" flat cord that seems resistant to tangling. A small fabric carrying pouch is included, along with a selection of silicon ear tips. (Note that I almost always toss the included tips and use a set of Comply foam tips.) My only complaint is that these are built similarly to other Sony earphones, and stick way out of your ears. I much prefer either a smaller overall size or a style like the [[ASIN:B004SNCZ3K Creative Aurvana 3 In-Ear Headphones]] that is designed to not stick out so much. Sound - too much treble (and I like treble). The bass is the best part of these - if you prefer you bass to be accurate and not boomy. It reaches down to 30 Hz or so before tailing off, and is not unnaturally emphasized like so many headphones these days. These will not appeal to bassheads, but are good for those seeking accurate bass. Sadly the treble is not accurate, but is really pushed up around 4.5 KHz, creating a rather uncomfortable mid-treble heavy sound. I also noticed that the treble tailed off quickly after 8 KHz or so, so the high treble is lacking somewhat. I typically enjoy a bit of treble "sizzle", but the mid-treble emphasis here just became tiring after a while. Conclusion - well constructed earphones, good accurate bass, but too much treble. For my listening tastes I prefer the UE 700 (now discontinued) or the Aurvana set (not perfect, but better than the XBAH1) mentioned above.

text: So, initially, if you are going to be using these as a primary headphone/earbud device and want GOOD quality sound this device is NOT for you. The sound quality is by no means bad, but for the same price, you can get much better sounding headphones or ear buds. Now onto the meat of the review The entirely wireless design is AWESOME. These earphones fit perfectly under over-the-ear style headphones or even ear protection for those who work with heavy machinery, or in loud environments. The noise cancellation is there, its not great, but its there. The battery life is ABSOLUTELY AWESOME. 5 charges on the case and a five hour charge gives you about 25 hours advertised, I'm averaging roughly 20 hours before I need to charge the case. so for me, roughly a week. Pairing is pretty smooth with a few minor drawbacks (see the end of the review). And in my 6 months of ownership, I've dropped these things a number of times, and only twice has the earbuds themselves split open, but they just snapped right back together no problem. Now, the not so good things. If your case dies, you run into a number of problems, 1: The headphones won't turn off when you put them in the case, 2: The headphones wont turn back on once removed (if they had turned off inside the case). Now onto the design of the case itself, rather strong plastic, I haven't cracked mine yet, but if you drop it, your case will open and will likely spew the headphones. The "door" or "lid" of the case is sometimes hard to get off, the plastic is very smooth and I sometimes cant get a grip on it to get it off. Now the headphones themselves, like i said before decent sound quality but little to no bass (which is to be expected from such a small device) and every now and then the right earbud will stop playing audio for 2-5 seconds and then will resume playing again (This is while connected with the L earbud, and the Left one will still play audio the whole time). The metal mesh that sits inside the rubber cushion, easily fell out of one of my earbuds, it would be nice to see a bevel that held that in. The same goes for the rubber cushions, there is no lip/ridge/bevel/divot, anything to hold the rubber on, on a number of occasions i have had the rubber stay in my ear when i took out the headphones, and had the rubber come off in my pocket (when not inside the case)

text: I loved my Backbeat Go 2 ear buds; nothing fit my ears better. When the true wireless bug finally hit me earlier this year, I did a LOT of research and it came down to the Backbeat Fit 3200. Of course they were backordered for MONTHS when I wanted to place my order in early January, so I borrowed my sister's Powerbeats Pro earbuds while I waited for my BB Fit 3200s to arrive. I am thankful that I had the chance to test drive something else, because it gave me a great baseline to compare the two and the BB Fit 3200s REALLY shine. They fit my ears more comfortably than the stiff Powerbeats, as the flexible over-ear design doesn't dig into my skin. They come with comfortable and easy-to-swap buds that fit perfectly in my ear and make for better bass and overall sound quality than I noticed with the Powerbeats. I could wear them for a few hours at a time and not noticed any soreness in or outside of my ear, which is huge for me. When I am biking, lifting, or swinging the kettlebells around, I don't notice any white noise or wind picked up through the mics. They STAY. PUT. no matter how much I sweat or how much I move. They are reliable and sound great no matter what. Awareness Mode is great when I need to quickly switch from "shut out the world" mode, and it lets me keep my music playing quietly in the background while picking up conversation through the mics. Voices sound a little mechanical, but clear. Overall, I am SO happy with my purchase and glad that I waited instead of buying something else on the spot. I only have a couple incredibly minor complaints, which might be deal breakers for someone else but weren't enough to have me return them. PROS Awareness Mode Noise cancellation Sound quality Super comfortable Waterproof (limited) Tap features Immediate pairing to my phone out of the case Secure nicely and effortlessly in the case Quick charging CONS USB-C would have been awesome The zipper on the case is a little tedious; the Powerbeats Pro magnetic case was nice! A larger profile than I anticipated, but not terrible I wish the Tap features weren't so limited, or that there was a physical button for volume. I really want to be able to control the volume with a tap or button press, but also assign Tap functions to one of the earbuds.

text: I purchased these based on my past experiences with Sony, and partly due to the rave reviews these buds received. Had these now for about a year. I received the earbuds and was comforted by the smart packaging. It didn't take over 5 minutes to remove the components, download the associated application, and have these deployed and playing in my ears. I have been using Sony wired buds for years and assumed the same hybrid bud would be the appropriate one for the XM3's...nope! The ergonomic approach and fit requires a larger bud. which is important for proper ear seal and noise canceling. The fit and comfort are dependent on your understanding of the XM3. There is a video demonstrating the proper way to insert and fit your buds. I find them to be very comfortable and secure in all aspects of daily activity. The sound quality of the XM3 is surprising. I realize everybody's taste and expectation are different, so I won't get into exactly how I reached nirvana with these, but you will have to experiment with the EQ to achieve the response you are looking for...out of the box, the buds are set completely flat. I like more of a base thrush with crisp highs, and it took my a good day to hit my sweet spot. The take away here is: I was able to hit that sweet spot with Sony's wireless buds. My musical taste has a wide range, from classical to electronica, and the XM3 delivers in all genres. Out of the box, the XM3 are preset to acclimate the phones based on your activity. So, If your sitting listening to music and decide to go for a walk, you will hear a small notice (bell/gong) notifying you that you buds have automatically changed their setting for the specific activity you are engaged in. My issue with this is that these buds were notifying me every few minutes of a change, which would mute my media. At first, I didn't know what the heck was going on, but I knew I didn't like it! I disabled this feature...at least for know. Controls are a bit over-sensitive..unless of course, you want to change the volume, which seems to take a bit of effort to get these to respond to your command (Tap for more, Hold for less). Phone connectivity and call quality are very good, with the exception of those pesky over-sensitive controls not responding to your command to answer/drop the call. Hear is the bog rub, the mic picks up so much backround noise, its almost impossible to use these on business calls. I find that earbuds are noise canceling by their nature and the XM3 are excellent if you want to shut out the world. I think there is a bit of a fidelity trade off, though. You will notice a noticeable drop in dynamic range while using noise cancellation. Activity...This is really my only rub. Sweat and moisture are a real problem for these buds. Battery life? All day. Sony produced an outstanding set of wireless buds that really sound awesome.

text: [[VIDEOID:fb279d66a58ca758b3d51e1e9fb067bc]] An Active Noise Cancellation Headphone sells on amazon for around $80 or higher, which gives this pair a stance point greater than others as it is priced for $60. Built Quality: The Quality with which these headphones are built is very promising, a soft and smooth feel with black matte finish makes these headphones well worth the buck in terms of the feel and texture. The sound was instantly boosted and amplified, this amplification also brought about a change in the frequency response as it now played higher frequencies, the vocals were much clearer. Here making a loud and clear statement (no pun intended), ' Use these headphones with the noise cancellation on'. Noise Cancellation: The noise cancellation works like its supposed to, it cancels out the 'noise' but don't go about buying these thinking that it will cancel out the voice of an annoying person, as no headphones can do that. Battery: The only place where it lacks is in the fact that these headphones aren't rechargeable, a good pair like these should have a rechargeable battery, maybe the first version? In conclusion, these headphones have a lot to offer all that's in the way might be the flick of a switch, after that its simply amazing and can even be compared with some high end headphones. I recommend these. text: I am currently a/b-ing Sennheiser's new MX-450's against last year's MX-500's, and am of the opinion that the MX-450's represent a uniform and decided step backward for Sennheiser. The MX-450's are nowhere near as refined, open, transparent and detailed as the 500's. The 450's boast the new "Basswind" system, but this seems only to amount to bass that sounds artificially inflated, but which is neither as accurate nor as extended as the bass from the MX-500's. The lower capacitance of the 450's (16 ohms) lets them play louder at comparable volume levels than the 500's (32 ohms)--which may account for the marketing bullet "Powerful Stereo Sound." Not surprisingly, I found the 450's more fatiguing than the 500's. In addition, the cord on the 450's feels flimsier and tends to twist and gnarl more readily than the better-behaved cord on the MX-500's. Lastly, and to put it extremely politely, I think the cord rewinder that comes with the 500's is much more sensibly designed and user-friendly than the one with the MX-450's. Actually, I wanted to get ahold of the MX-550's to do a strict comparison between lasts year's and this year's marketing equivalents from Sennheiser, but couldn't find the MX-550's stateside. Aside from the inline volume control (on the 550's), the specifications for the 450 and 550 are exactly the same, though. As you've probably already guessed, I overwhelmingly preferred the MX-500's in every department. Sure, they cost a few dollars more than the 450's, but it is money well-spent, with the return in musical enjoyment far outweighing the minimal bump-up in price. Unfortunately, it seems that with the MX-450's Sennheiser spent more time and energy coming up with catchy advertizing jargon than they did formulating a functionally better product design. So, if you truly value value and a faithfully delivered musical signal, bypass the MX-450's and go sraight for the MX-500's. The latter are destined to be a classic; the former perhaps no more than an iteration. POSTSCRIPT: After an extensive break-in period, the MX-450's sound a little less strident in the high frequencies. All-in-all, a midrange-forward and tonally/spatially confined presentation compared with the MX-500's. The MX-450's are at their best with pop and vocals, providing some nicely rounded midrange "nibble" on the ears. I'll therefore reliquish another half star: ***1/2 (still rounding down to 3). Associated Equipment: Panasonic DVD-S47 player Gilmore V2-SE head amp DakiOm feedback stabilizers ErnieM PCK13 power cords Fro-Zen interconnects PAC digital (RCA line) filter Marigo Labs Signature 3D (cd) mat Powervar ABC-400 ac conditioner

My first, a Motorola H500 was purchased a little over a year ago and was by far my favorite and most expensive, and would be one of only two but I could not get a replacement earhook for it since the original broke less than 6 months after purchase. This should have put up a big red flag for me with Motorola. In a pinch, I bought a cheap Plantronix 270 which was all I could get in a pinch locally. This turned out to be a great investment, I absolutely love it. It has great features, an astonishing battery life of as much as two days even with my extremely heavy work usage and decent sound quality in both directions. But I am a very heavy user and have to change out some days; which led to my buying my third bluetooth in less than a year when Motorola made the offer to sell me an H270 when they could not replace the earhook. I hate the Motorola H270 and except for the money I am out, Motorola refuses to refund me, am grateful only for the fact it rarely works. It is such a miserable piece of equipment and I would not recommend it to my worst enemy. The H270 finished off any good will with Motorola. The Motorola H270 chronicly has a broken earhook, my ear canal is chronicly sore with this device which even caused a raw calus when it worked for 6 consecutive weeks. It also has the habit of frequently disconnecting from my blackberry device and requiring connection to the charger briefly (plug in, pull the plug) to get it to reconnect even with a full charge; in short the Motorola H270 is junk. Now for my latest and second most expensive aquisition, the Blackberry HS700 which I purchased to serve as the second to my primary cheap Plantronix 270 of all things. I paid considerably more for the BlackberryHS700 and was excited about having a bluetooth that would fully integrate with my Blackberry device. I was also enthusiastic about the promised noise cancelling features. Unfortunately this bluetooth has not lived up to any of the promises. While my Plantronix will go for up to 2 days of my very heavy usage, the specs are stretching it when they say the Blackberry HS700 talk time is 4 hours, I am lucky to get that. I had hoped this was a CYA. BOOOOO. The second problem is the okwardness in turning the divice on and off. You must insert and twist the outside only. The problem is it does not fit in the ear tightly enough and I would imagine would be painful if it did, to hold the stem while the outer switch part moves. You have to try to squeeze your fingers past the lip and hold the stem with one hand and turn with the other or turn it on before putting it in and hope you don't turn it off while trying to position it. The sound quality is ok on my end most of the time though getting the thing to stay in my ear is very iffy which frequently results in interupted calls. The sound quality on the other end, forget noise cancelling I have to make sure my office door is closed at all times, cannot have the radio on (had to have office sound system disconnected to my office) or TV sound on and in the car it is awful for the receiving person. Yes, I am a stickler for keeping this thing up against my cheek for those of you other noise canceling users, I have no problem with my other noise cancelling bluetooths as previously described. The fit has been a major problem as I said I have had a terrible time keeping the device in despite spending weeks experimenting with the 5 diffent earbuds and the hingeless earhooks force the device out of noise canceling position. The voice activation system is complicated; apparently too complicated for the device. When instructing call (name) it will frequently reply calling (number) and do so without confirmation. You immediately hear ringing as it has called some person you don't even know, so embarassing. I have stopped using the hands free dialing. The speak "answer" to answer a call is unrealable. I often lost calls saying answer repeatedly and now use the answer key on my blackberry when using this bluetooth which defeats the purpose; there is no touch answer. When I received this device I made it the one I started each day with for four weeks in order to give it an honest try. I have now returned to the cheap plantronix and resort to the Blackberry only when the Plantronix battery dies. I was really looking forward to having a Blackberry Bluetooth that would take advantage of all the great features of the Blackberry device I so love. Very disappointing.

text: These are an update to the Sony Wi-C300 Bluetooth headphones that they introduced a little over a year ago. When those were introduced, I wrote that they were a steal: Great comfort, excellent Bluetooth performance and decent sound at a very good price. They are not the best sounding Bluetooth headphones I own, but they are the most comfortable to wear, and I find myself using them very regularly, even a year later (and they still work great). I was excited to get these, as they improve a things things about the previous generation while maintaining all the other advantages (and even carrying a cheaper list price). Happily, these don't disappoint. They are just as comfortable as the previous generation (can be worn for many hours without discomfort), the battery life is FAR better, the cord is better, and even the sound quality is better--although I would still call the sound overall just decent. So let's break it down. In terms of sound, what you get here is clear highs, very agreeable mids, and limited bass. Compared to the previous generation, the highs are a bit more accentuated, and all the instruments and vocals are well articulated. With respect to the overall sound, these sound less congested on complex music than the previous genreation. There's still a SLIGHT bit of harshness at higher sound levels. But, they remain easy to listen to. As with the previous generation, the mids are much better balanced in these than in many earphones--even some costing many times the price. The bass is the weak link: There's not much of it. What you hear in the bass region is fine, but limited bass is a deal breaker for you, these won't be your earphones. It seems the bass may have been ever-so-slightly improved over the previous generation, but the difference isn't huge. The sound, on the whole, is detailed and pleasant. I find these easy to listen to for very extended periods. But let's be clear: These are not audiophile headphones. To be honest, few Bluetooth headsets offer an audiophile experience, and the ones that do are very expensive. But these are headphones you can listen to for a long time without feeling the need to rip them off--and that in itself is a win in this class. One thing I like a lot about this earbud design is that the earbuds are small and light. Because these are single driver earbuds, and because there's a separate battery pack on the cable, these fit very well inside the ear canal. These are FAR more comfortable to use than most in-ear headphones, as a result. You only get three sizes of silicone earbud covers to choose from in the package, but I find the mid-sized ones (that come installed by default) to fit just fine. You don't get any clips to go in or around your ears, so while these are extremely comfortable, they won't stay in under conditions of stress. So these are probably not the earbuds you'll want if you engaged in any aggressive sports activity. . The battery is charged via a USB-C port (see photo). This is an upgrade over the previous generation, which used a more fragile micro-USB port. The package includes a standard USB-A to USB-C cable that can plug into any compatible USB charger. I like that MUCH more than the proprietary chargers that companies like Jaybird use. It means that I will never worry about losing the charger. They take about 3 hours to fully charge (about 1 more hour than the previous generation) and I got somewhat over 13 hours on a full charge, which is terrific and about TWICE what the battery life of the previous generation. The ergonomics are satisfactory. There are two "bulbs" on the cord connecting the left and right buds. One bulb contains the battery, and the second bulb houses the controls (on/off/Bluetooth_pair, volume up, volume down, pause, skip forward, skip back). Like most earbuds, there are three buttons, and all do double duty depending on how long you hold them. The weight of everything: earbuds--cable, two bulbs--is quite light, and you quickly forget you're wearing them. These headphones have fixed the assymetry issue of the previous genration and have greatly increased the length of the cord connecting the headphones. With the previous generation, although they are sold as "behind neck" earphones, I found they were too short to be worn comfortablly that way, so I wear them with the cord in front of me. With this new set of headphones, the cable is about twice the length and comfortably fits behind the neck. That's a much appreciated improvement. The buds announce power on, when a Bluetooth connection is formed, and when you power them down. Bluetooth performance itself is excellent. Pairing was fast and reliable every time I turned them on--a rare experience with inexpensive Bluetooth headphones. And they held a good Bluetooth connection even across the entirety of a floor of a large house. I would even say that Bluetooth performance was surprisingly good, far better than some more expensive Bluetooth headphones I've used. These headphones feature Bluetooth version 5, whereas the previous generation featured Bluetooth version 4.2. This should translate into both more stable connections and better battery management (allowing the doubling of run time on a single charge, as is seen). Based on research, it appears that Sony has updated the Bluetooth module in the headphones from the Airoha AB1522 v 4.2 chip in the WI-C300 to the Realtek RLT8763B v 5.0 chip in the WI-C310. Comparing these to my other favorite mid-priced Bluetooth headphones, the Jaybird X2, I find these Sony headphones to be considerably more comfortable, and only modestly inferior in sound quality. I actually like the balance of highs and mids on these better than the Jaybirds. But the Jaybirds can deliver better bass (when you can properly seat them in your ears) and the highs are a bit nicer. Given the very reasonable price, these are a relative steal compared to the Jaybirds and others. There are cheaper no name Bluetooth earbuds, but in my extensive experience with those off brand earbuds, they are mostly horrible (bad sound, bad ergonomics, bad Bluetooth performance). This WI-C310 set, along with the predecessor, the WI-C300, are the first Bluetooth headphones with a list price in this range that I would strongly recommend. Inside the package: You get the Bluetooth earbuds headset, three pairs of silicone tips (small, medium [pre-installed], large), a USB-C cable, and an instruction booklet. The USB charger is NOT included, but any standard USB charger will work. In summary: Pros: Terrific Bluetooth pairing and excellent Bluetooth range Very comfortable in the ears Standard USB-C charging port Quite decent balance of highs and mids 13+ hours on a charge (rated for 15 hours) Long cord fits comfortably behind the neck Attractive price Cons: Limited bass No clips to keep in your ears during aggressive sports Differences between WI-C310 (this headphone) and predecessor WI-C300: Bluetooth: WI-C310: Version 5.0 (bettery battery life, better connections) WI-C300: Version 4.2 Lenth of connecting cord: WI-C310: 34" (fits better behind neck) WI-C300: 22" Charge port WI-C310: USB-C (more durable) WI-C300: micro-USB Sound quality WI-C310: Similar, but less congested on complex music WI-C300: Similar, but more congested on complex music

text: I tested the senheiser 598, ath ad900x, Sony mdr7506, & these. These were a good middle ground of all of them. Loved the brightness & detail & price of the Sony’s, but didn’t like the cheap flimsy-ness, & the non existent clamp of the headband......Liked the detail, open sound stage, build quality, & comfort of the senheisers, didn’t like the light clamp, & just couldn’t justify $200 for them.....the ath900xs was just bizarre, very very light, “air” is an apt product line name for them, like the soundstage and detail. But lacked any low end punch. & unless you have a pumpkin sized head they slide down your head to where the tops of your ears are holding the weight of them. Even with trying the zip tie mod on the “wings”. If they’d increase tension in the wings I might have chosen them. So went with the hated m50xs. Ignored at 1st because of all the bad reviews/opinions. But they were in my price range so I thought I’d try them. I personally feel they took most of the good outta all these. Good clamp, but can be uncomfortable after awhile. I have a small slender head so I can see how melon headed ppl would not like them. Good detail, but not great. Good punch but not muffled. Needs a little eq for my taste. Very hot. Detachable plug which is nice, however both these and the senheisers have notched plugs so you turn the plug, then pull. Which to me defeats the purpose of having a removable plug. I thought it was for if you got the cable tangled on something & stood up, it wouldn’t tear the cord, it’d jus pull free. I guess mabey easier for transporting. All in all, for the price I’m happy with them.easy to drive. Big sales so parts are available, highly modifiable.....on a side not it cost me around $20 to send the other 3 back, even with prime. So keep that in mind if auditioning. Also the ad900xs I got from a camera place in jersey mabey? And took forever to get here to Las Vegas. I watched them through package tracking & they kicked around Jersey for a week before being shipped, then suddenly was here. I’ll probably not order anything that far away again. Anyway that’s my 2 cents. For this price range for closed backs, get them.

text: 3 stars may not seem very high, but these are actually the best running headphones I have had. They fit on securely and are very comfortable, more so than others. As a runner, I always go for the neckband headphones cause they do not fall off the ears. These pair last longer than any other type of headphones I have had, but they do eventually die. I go through a pair every 3 months, now, I am a pretty avid runner and I run almost everyday, so for most recreational runners, these will be fine and last a while. What makes these headphones disappointing is that despite the claim of being "sweat proof", they fall short. They work great for spring/winter/fall running, but it is very hard to run with these on in the summer when it is hotter and I sweat more. They often stop playing in one or both ears and then later they are able to play in both ears again. But overtime, the volume goes shorter in 1 ear and you start to hear your chest beating more and audio consistencies. They have a slow downward progression, right out of the box though they are great. I have bought 5 of these and I do go through them. When they work they are fine, but nothing else comes close. Exercise headphones are just a repetitive investment for high intensive athletes because there are simply no holy grail headphones that are foolproof.

text: These are comfortable, good-sounding earbuds that don't fall out of my ears the way some earbuds do (for example, the standard Apple earbuds just do not stay in my ears). They sound good too. I compared them to the Apple earbuds and to Klipsch Reference S4 In-Ear Headphone, and these sound better. The noise canceling electronics are housed in a little cylinder that has a clip for clipping it on your clothing. The designers made a big mistake in not making the cord from the noise-canceling unit to the earbuds long enough, so you can't really clip it to your belt if you are a normal-sized adult - you have to clip it to someplace higher like a shirt collar or shirt pocket. On the plus side, the noise-canceling unit is easy to turn on and off, and has a long battery life and is light and compact and easy to store. These earbuds probably don't provide the total noise-canceling experience you'd get with earphones that cover your ears, but the noise canceling feature does make a difference and for earbuds the sound quality is good. Over all, a good value here.

text: I've had the Soundpeats True Free+ earbuds for a few months. Here's what I think: 1) If you can get them at or below $30, they're probably worth it. The sounds acceptable. You can do calls in a pinch and if you're in a relatively windless, quiet place. They stay in place unless you're vigorously moving or sweating. 2) The range is very good. I can use them all over my home without losing connection, including when my source device is on another floor or different room. 3) The BIG DOWNSIDE is that the buds often disconnect, and they don't reconnect unless fully removed from device history on the source and re-set using a convoluted process. The single reason I don't rate them higher or use them more often is the pairing is very inconvenient - literally have to do the remove-reset-repair process every time I used them. These are NOT pickup and go earbuds. Would I recommend them? Only if you're listening scenario is for long sessions/periods AND you don't mind the remove-reset-repair process every time. This is the only brand/pair of earbuds that I have this issue. I've never had it on even old BT 3.0-4.2 earbuds. Not sure what's going on here. I want to like them more than a 3, but I can't given the significant pairing flaws. Instead, I just use them when I have to do something that's going to take a couple hours or so when I can use them until they lose charge. Then I do the reset after they recharge. So close Soundpeats. So close.

text: TL;DR: If you're thinking the "superior" sound will make up for the functionality of the Airpods Pro or the Galaxy Buds, be prepared to be very disappointed. I have no idea what Sennheiser is trying to do with these earbuds. The max volume on these is frustratingly low. They sound pretty good at max volume; which I would describe as "office listening" but if a song comes on and you're into it, there's no "turning it up." I have tested these with my Macbook, iPhone, and iPad, doesn't matter. I even dug up my old Samsung Galaxy s10+ just to make sure the volume problem wasn't Apple-specific. It's not. And before you ask, yes I disabled the "Headphone Safety" on the iPhone and Samsung. Not my first rodeo. The EQ, like with most Bluetooth earbuds, is laughable. Anytime you adjust the equalizer the overall volume drops 20 dB so it is completely pointless. (Unless riding in an elevator was the best "concert" you've ever heard.) Pairing with my devices went ok. Like many others, I had problems. For some reason, these earbuds pair left and right separately. When initially in pairing mode they are named MOMENTUM TW 2. There is only one option, but once they pair you have MOMENTUM TW 2 and LE-MOMENTUM TW 2. I'm guessing the "LE" stands for left? I'm no engineer but that seems like an extra "point of failure." I know Sennheiser makes good products, or at least they used to. That's the reason I even gave these a shot. This is the first Sennheiser product I've ever purchased, and I bought them KNOWING the issues many reviewers pointed out. I could get past all of those issues if they sound great. Unfortunately, Sennheiser failed. Any manufacturer out there can make a "bassy, punchy robust" sounding earbud at a low volume. I don't know about anyone else, but isn't the point of spending the extra money to get a better, louder sound? I'm not expecting a concert in my ears for $250 but shouldn't I at least be able to say "whoa, these sound great! Hey, you've got to hear these!" "Those Germans, they did it again!" With these, I'd prefer not to offer them to a friend to hear them or know I purchased them, because I'm actually embarrassed. Sennheiser, if you're listening: If these can get louder, update the firmware and "unlock" them. If in fact that is the case, and you sold these to deliberately max out at a dB that prevents my eardrums from harm, shame on you. I'll do what I want with my eardrums thank you. And don't give me the lawyer bs, that lawyer is going to make you obsolete. I doubt Steve Jobs cared about some hippy lawyer telling him the screen was too bright "someone might go blind." Bottom Line: If Sennheiser just went with a great-sounding earbud rather than try to tack on a bunch of crappy features, these might be worth it. As they stand, if I had to do it over again, I wouldn't pay more than $80 for these.

text: Quality: Haven't had long enough to speak to durability, although build quality is decent. Cables are fairly thick and strain relief on buds and jack seem very robust. The wood aspect is cool, but honestly fairly subtle once they are in your ears. I ordered the orange version. Wish cables were a solid color and didn't have the grey stripe but I don't hold that against them. Sound: Very bass heavy. Like "punch you in the ear" bass heavy. But they do sound good. Definitely better than the Monoprice 8320s I had (which I felt were great for the price, but were flimsy and pretty disposable). Full volume on these is very loud compared to my Advanced M4 earbuds but sound is not as balanced. For those wondering, what "balanced" means, I'm referring to the lows, mids, and highs all being output at comparable levels. On these Symphonized ear buds, the bass is MUCH louder than the mids or highs (although they are fairly clean). The upside of this is that bass heavy music still sounds great at low volumes, but at high volumes the bass can get uncomfortable (not deafening, but just too much). Honestly, a good equalizer (even in software) can help counteract this (I tried) but if you plan to use these on a variety of devices, then an equalizer won't always be an option. Bottom Line: If you want cool looking ear buds that sound pretty good and don't cost too much, these are a good choice. Wouldn't recommend for classical music, jazz, audio mastering or any genre that wants balanced sound. If you listen to a lot of hip hop or EDM you'll probably like these. Personally, I'm happy with my purchase, but glad to have some more balanced options available. I'm still trying to decide if this pair or my M4s will become my work earbuds, or my "everything else" earbuds.

text: I ordered these earphones to help minimize office noise, and used them to tie into my desktop computer system. The first week the noise cancellation worked fairly well, and the office chatter going on around me was cut by about 50 percent. The second week of use I could hear the click when engaging the noise cancellation, but it seemed like the noises were not cancelled, but rather they seemed like they were somewhat amplified. The design of the earbuds and cords themselves could use a little improvement. I noticed a couple of other reviews that indicated they didn't fit inside the ear canals of some of the users very well. I had the same problem. My $10.00 Panasonic ear buds fit nicely, but the Quietcomfort 20 earbuds didn't fit well with any of the 3 sizes of included attachments. Another issue that I noticed is that the plastic volume button where the two cords connect to a single cord didn't have any strain reliefs. The cords coming out of the buds have strain reliefs, and the cord going into and out of the noise cancelling on/off switch box have strain reliefs, but not the areas going into and out of the volume control area. I probably wouldn't have thought twice about this, but the reason my older Bose non-noise cancelling earbuds needed to be replaced was due to no strain reliefs coming out of the buds. Why not include them on all areas where the cords enter a piece of plastic on a $249.99 product? After a bit of use, I also didn't like the fact that the USB charge cord was only about 12.5 inches long. I have a USB plug in on the side of my computer monitor. The cord was barely long enough to reach the charge port on the On/Off box. This cable is way too short for anyone wanting to plug into an outlet adapter or a CPU, and then route the cable to a nearby table without the On/Off box dangling. Even adding 6-8 inches of cable would help. Speaking of cable length, another annoyance is that the plug-in end of On/Off box only has about 3 to 4 inches of wire coming out of it. Unless you have the perfect scenario, the weight of the On/Off box is likely going to hang from the plug in, rather than resting on the desk surface. This could have been easily fixed by adding another 4-6 inches of wire, or moving the box up the wire another 4-6 inches. The 3-4 inches of wire and plug-in aren't very robust, so I doubt the wire and plug would last long after hanging in various positions. Because of this issue with the noise cancellation not working properly, and the small design issues, I ended up returning my earbuds. I understand that defects can happen with any and all brands, but the design issues should have been easily identified by anyone testing the product for a period of time in different scenarios. At $249.99 I'd like to not only get good noise cancelling technology, but I want the materials to last, and the design to be well thought out.

text: If you travel by plane you already know what it's like watching a movie with the 'free' headset while competing with the cabin noise, it's a close call of whether to even bother. Slip on a noise canceling headset and you suddenly enter another world, a very quiet world, and watching the movie becomes a pleasure rather than a chore. Or plug it into your IPod and hear the music as clear as you would at home. From the reviews I have read, not all noise canceling is created equal, the cheap ones don't get good reviews, but I have owned my own pair of Sennheiser PXC for a couple of years, and have bought them as gifts for three friends, these are the real deal. The sound quality is great, the noise canceling works, and they fold up into a very small package for easy travel. The minus is the wires, wires everywhere, because the noise canceling electronics are enclosed in a cigar shaped unit that is attached in line to the headset wires. In practical use it's fine, you just clip the cigar onto a piece of clothing and forget about it, but it can seem a bit of a mess at first. The plus is that the actual headset itself is much lighter and much more compact than it would be with the electronics built into it. The cigar also has an on/off button, so if the batteries start to die (2 AAAs, they have a tremendously long life, far longer than the specs would have you believe) you can simply turn off the noise canceling and still listen as if they were normal headphones; the quality is not nearly as good in this mode, but still good. If money were no object I would probably do a close comparison with the Bose III headset, those are much more expensive, but fairly compact too, with comfortable over the ear pads, but for the amount of use I give mine (mostly for travel) the price difference wasn't worth my giving them consideration.

text: KBEAR KS2 The KS2 is a hybrid IEM with a 10mm Composite Diaphragm dynamic driver producing the low to mid frequencies and a balanced armature for highs. The shells are polycarbonate which the manufacturer apparently used because it helps quell internal shell resonances. It is light and very comfortable with a metal nozzle that features a prominent lip to retain the tips. No tips left stuck in ear! The cable is replacable and works fine though a bit tangle-prone. KBEAR has many beautiful replacement cables available. Now, about the sound. I must admit upfront that I changed tips early on. There was just a bit more treble than I wanted so I used tips with a smaller bore and now they sound great. I also replaced the cable with a 2.5mm balanced one to use with my Hiby 3 PRO'S balanced out. It didn't make any difference tonally but, it benefits from more power from the balanced output. I always replace the cable just for this reason. The Bass: The bass is quite powerful and punchy. There is plenty of low/sub bass with a reletively fast attack and a slightly slower decay. This gives you the punch of a kick drum but also caters well to electronic music with sub bass boom tracks. It has massive punch and will produce a physical sensation if turned up. You can feel the bass! It does a good job on most all genres of music, but loves synth bass! The mids are mildly V-shaped with the bass and treble boosted. This makes it a fun sounding IEM! There is sufficient detail in the mids and there is a prominent lift of the high mids. These are surprisingly revealing when you don't boost the bass and treble on your plater too much. Vocals are crisp and intimate. Treble is most definitely elevated. It does not produce sibilance in my experience but will definitely reproduce any sibilance present in the original mix. If its a bit too bright, try using tips with a smaller bore to even things out. I like sound these make when the treble us tamed slightly. The mids start to really pop out. The soundstage is about average width and decent depth. The vocals sit right up close while instruments sit back slightly for a nice layering effect. So, am I happy with the KS2? Yes. I especially like it on electronic music and hard rock. It gas a rounder bass tuning than I am used to, but I really love that on sub bass hits! It will serve me well for electronic music.

text: I was very excited to test and review the Senheiser Ambeo smart headset. I had heard a lot of good things about the Ambeo so I was pretty sure they would be good. I unpackaged the headphones when they arrived, plugged them into my iPhone and played a song. They were the worst sounding headphones I’ve ever heard! I thought maybe the eartips were too small even though they felt like they fit pretty well so I changed them to the large eartips. BOOM! Excellent amazing sound! It’s very important that if they don’t sound like you think they should that you go up to the next size eartip! They sounded superb but the highs were just a little to,prevalent for me. I adjusted my EQ. On my phone and much better after that. You see, all music will sound different depending on the source. Through a phone will sound different than a home stereo and you must find the right EQ combination. Once I did that I was very pleased with how they sounded. One thing I noticed right away is how loud the Ambeo headset is. And I like that! I want to be able to jam sometimes. I hate it when headphones just don’t go loud enough. Not the issue with these. They are very comfortable and the ear hooks feel great and really keep things in place. I love the noise cancelling. I love the noise amplification as well. If you are at work or driving and need to be able to hear what’s going on around you just kick in the amplification mode and you’ve got music and surrounding noise. Or, kick in the noise canceling to shut out the world. One thing I didn’t like was how big the controls are. In the pictures the controls look small but in reality they are pretty big. The whole control module fits in the palm of your hand. I was hoping they would be smaller and less in the way. Not a huge deal though. That’s why I gave them 4 stars instead of 5. The dual mics on each earpiece record video in natural 3D sound which makes it sound way more realistic. The Ambeo’s Are great for V logging or just general video recording. It’s nice to be able to record in stereo! The headset is stored in a small nylon bag. I was hoping for a small crush proof box that I can throw in my pocket and not have to worry about them being damaged but in reality I don’t travel with them that much and a bag is fine. The Sennheiser app has an equalizer so you can adjust the settings and that is important. Once you equalize you have total control over the sound. If you are serious about video I really think you would love these! Senheiser usually does it right and they did pretty well with these.
product_title: Sennheiser AMBEO Smart Headset (iOS) – Active Noise Cancellation, Transparent Hearing and 3D Sound Recording

text: All I can say is WOW!!! It took me a while to warm up to ear buds that actually go in my ear. After getting a job working in a noisy environment I took to them quickly over wearing earplugs all the time. Over the years I've tried countless ones from the cheapest of cheap to expensive ones like Sure and I thought some were better then others but none of them to me were worth more than the cheaper ones. Out of all of them (and we are talking dozens of them!) none of these have ever Wowed me until now. I ordered the Ultimate Ears a month or so ago as an X-Mass present to myself, I got them and tried them and was impressed with them but as others mentioned they are a little bulky and even after trying the medium and small ear cushions they still never felt right and found myself fumbling with them all the time. I finally popped on the large cushions and all I can say is Oh My God these things are AWESOME!!! I know that fit is key for any of these type of ear buds to work properly and always try all of the various cushions that come with each of the buds I've bought in the past but through that the mediums were the right size for me only they just weren't staying in place, boy was I wrong. The only reason I didn't give these 5 stars across the board is I feel that the cable is a little flimsy on the jack end and can see that being an issue over time. I would prefer to see it be a 90 degree angled one (which they do include with an extension but it then becomes to long and catches on things which is an issue when you have them behind the ears / head. The second complaint has been mentioned in that they are quite large which I am sure is what is required to make the amazing sound reproduction. These are not for everyone, if you have small ears or don't like that feeling of something in your ears / tight seal required you won't ever enjoy these at their full potential. If you think that you can deal with the items I've mentioned then by all means invest in what will probably be your last set of ear buds EVER!!!

text: These are my gazillionth replacement Apple Ear Pods. They never last more than a few months. Sometimes one ear pod stops working. Sometimes both. Sometimes the sound fades or totally cuts off during use. Sometimes unplugging and re-plugging the lightening plug makes them work again. Sometimes it doesn’t. It’s extremely annoying that Apple makes these so junky the past several years. The first pair I owned at least lasted a couple of years, but those were the ones with standard 4mm, not lightening, plugs. These can only be considered disposable. Apple could do better. They just choose not to. Why make these good when you can make them so bad a person gives up and buys the $150 or $250 Air Pods or Air Pods pro? Then they have to keep buying those because they’re so easy to lose. There’s no reason *not* to be cynical about this. Yes, you could buy a lightening to 4mm adapter and use any brand of ear pods. I have one. But that’s just awkward, unplugs too easily, works inconsistently, and is one more tiny junk electronic to try to not lose. I hate that they got rid of the 4mm jack after iPhone 6. Can’t charge phone and use pods at the same time without buying an adapter and those are crappy too. Blech. 😠 Sound quality isn’t even worth considering. It’s meh, period. Good enough for phone calls but not for music.

text: EASE OF USE/CONVENIENCE: These headphones were a breeze to pair with my iPhone, and I was using them immediately. I love with the wirelessness of it. Not only do I love being able to move freely without the annoying cord snagging on everything, but it allows me freedom of movement (up to 35 feet) even while my iPhone is charging. SOUND: The sound is great, including the bass. Being earbud headphones, they also offer good sound isolation. When I first took these running, I noticed an annoying popping sound in both ears and thought it was the tugging of the cord (which is somewhat heavy to improve durability and minimize tangling) against the ear pieces. However, I later realized that it was my earrings, which are very small hoops, hitting the ear pieces. So ladies (and/or gentlemen), if you run with earrings, keep this in mind! IPHONE COMPATIBILITY: If you're used to the functionality of the headset that comes with your iPhone, you will find this headset somewhat limited. For one thing, although it can jump tracks forward or backward (using the volume buttons), it cannot fast-forward or fast-reverse. As someone who listens to a lot of audiobooks, this is an annoying omission. Also, accessing Siri is somewhat tricky: You have to hold the "talk" button just long enough to get the "pairing" tone, then release the button and wait a moment for the "Siri" tone. Hold the button too long, and the headset powers off. BATTERY LIFE/CHARGING CASE: Fully charged headphones will give you about 4.5 hours of listening time before needing to be recharged. This is true whether you buy/use the charging case or not. The charging case is basically a portable charger, allowing you to charge your headset on the go, without a wall-based charger. It still does not allow you to use your headphones for more than 4.5 hours without stopping to charge. So when the product description talks about 14.5 hours of listening time, it does NOT mean continuous listening time. It means listening and charging, in intervals, for a TOTAL of 14.5 hours listening time. If you're interested, here's the math: A fully-charged headset gives you 4.5 hours of listening time. A 20-minute charge will give you another hour of listening time. It takes 90 minutes to reach a full charge; leaving it longer on the charger will not increase your listening time beyond 4.5 hours. A fully-charged charging case can deliver about 200 minutes of charge, or another 10 hours of listening time, but not more than 4.5 hours at a time. In conclusion, the charging case is an attractive and portable way to carry and charge your headphones. If that is worth $20 to you, go ahead and buy it. Otherwise, it doesn't add much functionality to the headphones. There is no case or charger that is going to let you listen more than 4.5 hours without having to stop and charge. No matter what, when the headphone battery is dead, you HAVE to stop listening long enough to charge it, whether with the case or with a wall charger.
