text: Listening to music is subjective so here is the type of listener I am and if you are similar, this review might help you out. ME: I am not an audiophile. My ears are 40-ish years old and I believe I have typical hearing. I travel on a long haul flight about once a year. I was looking for over-the-ear (OTE) headphones that I would use 85% of the time at home and 15% of the time when travelling. I had some ear buds and on-the ear headphones I had used on previous trips but decided it’s time to go OTE with some real noise cancelling. I wanted to go wireless and I know the limitations of Bluetooth. Frankly, I don’t find the Bluetooth experience that terrible (see sentence #1 – I’m not an audiophile). I watched a dozen video reviews and read the same number of reviews (you know, “best wireless headphones of 2016!!!”). Obviously, everyone pointed to the Bose QC35’s as the best noise cancelling headphones on the market. The new Sony MDR1000X headphones were equally regarded (if not, better by some people). I picked FOUR headphones to try. Let me put my subjective assessment of their sound later. ** ROUND ONE: Sony Noise Cancelling MDR1000X ** I picked these first because they had all the nifty features. Specifically, you could swipe the outside of the ear cup to control your music (skip, back, volume, etc.). It was a bit finicky. They were very comfortable. Noise cancelling using the vacuum test was quite impressive. Helpful voice prompts. Modern design. You can turn the noise cancelling on or off. They are plastic and leather or “leather” – not sure – but they feel very premium. The most expensive of all the headphones I tried. ** ROUND TWO: [[ASIN:B01E3SNO1G Bose QuietComfort 35 Wireless Headphones, Noise Cancelling - Black]] ** The venerable QC35. I had to try them. I mean – every headphone is being compared to them. Somewhat old school in their design and controls. Not particularly good looking. However, these were definitely the most comfortable of all of these headphones I tried. They just fit great with the tilted ear cups. Noise cancelling with the vacuum test was as impressive as the Sony MDR1000X. Helpful voice prompts. The noise cancelling is always on. Controls are buttons and you’re going to have to spend some time training your fingers to feel and use them. Also very expensive but about $50 less than those Sony’s above. Bose has a quaint little phone app to control some basic settings on the headphones – no equalizer or sound quality controls. You’ll know these are plastic but the ear cups are soft, comfortable fake leather wrapped cushions (see comments below for info on the ear cups). ** ROUND THREE: [[ASIN:B01CQXGM5K Sony H.ear on Wireless Noise Cancelling Headphone, Charcoal Black (MDR100ABN/B)]] ** I guess this would be the “cheap” pair in the bunch. At the time, about $100 less than the Bose and $150 less than the Sony MDR1000X. Also comfortable and bit smaller than their Sony big brother. Noise cancelling was good but not as good as the two above. You can turn the noise cancelling on or off. One glitchy thing I experienced was they wouldn’t always automatically connect back to my phone (Nexus 6P). The others did. I like the basic control toggle that you can feel, click forward/backward or click down in various combinations. You can find it easily by touch. ** ROUND FOUR: [[ASIN:B00SNI44CQ Sennheiser Momentum 2.0 Wireless with Active Noise Cancellation- Black]] ** Unique retro look and unlike all of the above, they are made of metal and leather. Very premium. I think the only plastic is in the round knobs that hold the ear cups. I am actually not sure if those knobs are plastic, could be metal. Noise cancelling is very good but not quite as good as the top two. It is always on, no switch. It’s a toss-up as to whether they beat or just meet the H.ear model. These seem to fit the least tightly. They just softly press against your head (and I have a bigger head). The ear cups are leather wrapped, soft cushy material. If you have a small head, there may be issues with fit. These aren’t tight. The only other pair I wanted to try were the Plantronics Back Beat Pro 2 that were recently released. Amazon didn't have them. Best Buy didn't have them. I didn't like the way you turn them on/off though. CHARACTERISTICS OF ALL OF THEM… --- All of them come with a corded option in case the battery dies. No noise cancelling without battery power though. --- I experienced no problems with the Bluetooth connection on any of these. --- Your ears will get warm after a while with all of them. I was able to go the longest with the Bose before I started to feel it. ---- All of them have sound leakage. All of them have enough that its noticeable in a quiet setting. This disappointed me but then I thought about the fact that on a plane, the engine noise is going to drown it out. ---- They all have battery life that is going to last an entire long haul flight including the waiting when connecting flights. I’m not going to wear them continuously. So… why did I end up with the Sennheisers and not those amazing noise cancelling masterpieces? Sound quality. The Sennheisers sound great. They were the last pair I tried. I put them on, played various types of music and quickly realized they were the way to go for me. NEED THE BEST NOISE CANCELLING? If you need headphones primarily for transportation situations where noise is a problem (planes, trains, etc.), get one of the top two (I would pick the Sony’s). They have outstanding noise cancelling capabilities. Don't get me wrong, they sound pretty great too. NEED BETTER SOUND QUALITY AND OCCASIONAL NOISE CANCELLING? If you are like me and the majority of your usage time will be in environments that aren’t noisy (like at home), get the Sennheisers... and the build quality, wow! If those are out of your price range, the Sony H.ears are a good alternative. They also sound better than the two big guys. I got them when they were $229. I had a friend try the top three and he picked the H.ear model as the best sounding. He didn’t get to try the Sennheisers. TIP FOR ANDROID USERS: I tried a few equalizer apps. I chose an app called “Equalizer FX” by devdnua and it further improved the sound of my streaming music. Hope this helps someone out!

text: As with any product these seem to have their fair share of negative reviews and for the life of me I cannot understand why. Everyone has their own opinion on what "good sound" is and for me it's these headphones. I have a pair of Sony WH-1000XM3's that I use on a daily basis for when I'm outside the house and before I bought these I though they were awesome, and for noise canceling and portability they are however these Fidelio's wipe the floor with them in every other meaningful way. I've owned these for two years now and they still look and feel brand new thanks to the superb build quality. I'm sure that spending more money can get you headphones that technically sound better with more even response curves but when I put these headphones on and listen to some of my favorite songs they send chills down my spine. I listen to a lot of different genres and I have yet to find a situation where I've been disappointed with how these sound. Bass is well defined and slightly forward but not overdone, mids are ever so slightly recessed but vocals and guitars still sound excellent. Highs are perfectly balanced and well controlled, no harshness to them at all. The real reason to buy these however is the sound stage. It's as if you were listening to music in a large room. The music isn't in your head, its around you and all of the instruments are separated perfectly. You'll discover parts of songs that you didn't even know were present before because everything is so wonderfully detailed. I think even for $300 I still would have been extremely satisfied with these headphones. Pick them up, give them a try and if you don't like them send them back but I think that these are the right headphones for a lot of people.

text: I'm normally much more detailed with my reviews, but I'm going to keep this short and honest. I ordered these almost exactly a month ago. The sound hasn't been bad at all considering the price, and I am not a person who abuses his headphones, so these have not been tossed around or neglected. Today the left ear went out on me, which tells me all I need to know about the quality of this product. I saw some questionable reviews before I had purchased, but I figured I would try these out for myself. I've learned my lesson, and now I want to help you save your money by politely recommending that you invest in some better headphones than these. I hope sharing my experience helps! Also, just as a side note, before purchasing these headphones I found a lot of reviews of this product questionable, saying that it is the best headphone they've ever purchased. I still decided to go through with trying these out, and in all honesty, these are average/mediocre headphones. I can say with confidence that if these are the best earbuds anyone has ever bought, then this must be the first pair of earbuds they've ever owned. It's just a bit sketchy is all so beware. UPDATE: I wrote my original review a couple of weeks ago and just wanted to provide a quick update. I had failed to mention that because of the deal I found on these headphones at the time of purchase, I decided to get two pairs in case I really liked them, or in the event that one didn't last. Since the first pair lasted just under a month, I've moved on to the second pair, and a couple of weeks in I can tell the same issue is starting to happen, with one of the sides crackling (music not played at maximum volume), and sometimes cutting out completely. I just wanted to reiterate my original review and advise against purchasing this product. It's worth putting the few extra bucks toward a better quality pair. Also, I noticed that nearly immediately after my review was posted, that the first person to see my review marked it as unhelpful. I found it extremely odd considering I gave an honest and unbiased review of my experience with the product. It's almost as if the seller might be monitoring the reviews or something to that affect. In any case I'm not going to make a big deal of it, but this just added to the "sketchy" nature of the past reviewers saying these were the greatest ear buds ever. Again, I hope my experience having owned two pairs of these helps, but if you still decide to gamble on these I hope they last longer for you than they did for me. Going to reach out to the company regarding their limited warranty to see if I can't get a refund. SECOND UPDATE: I reached out to customer support and told them about my experience with the first pair of headphones. They sent me a new pair without hesitation. I can appreciate that they replaced the item for me, and the headphones have been working fine to this point. With that said I've added a third star to my rating. Perhaps my experience was a fluke, but I will write another update if I run into any issues with my new pair.

text: I was initially hesitant to purchase these based on the mixed reviews, but after using them for a week, I can safely say that these are much better than I had hoped. FIT: The earbuds come with three sizes of ear tips. I'm using the large tips and they stay in my ear fine during walks and runs. That being said, I am actively looking for a replacement set that will create a better seal. So far, I've found that Comply makes a replacement set of foam tips, but haven't taken the plunge yet. The housing connection to the tips is quite large; one of the largest I've seen on a set of earbuds. This makes the eartip's shape fairly rigid, which can make fitting it in your ear--and keeping it there--more difficult. CONNECTION: I have been using a Google Pixel to transmit audio to these 'phones, and haven't run into any large connectivity problems. The buds have no trouble staying connected to my Google Pixel while walking or running upright. That being said, I've found that if I bend down to tie my shoe and end up blocking line of sight to my phone with my body, the earbuds have occasionally lost connection to the phone. If I go to wipe my brow and cover my left ear with my hand, the connection to the secondary (right) earbud will sometimes fade. At the very least, I can say that the manner in which audio cuts in and out is pleasing... it's not abrupt or static-y, but a gentle fade in and out. The connection resumes immediately when I remove the "obstruction" (whether it's my hand, body, or whatever.) I haven't tried another pair of no-wire earbuds, so I have nothing with which to compare this behavior, but it seems inoffensive and acceptable for something so early in this new tech space. SOUND: Overall resolution is quite good given the circumstances, but these will not knock your socks off. They rely on standard Bluetooth protocol (no aptX support, as far as I can tell), and the sound quality reflects that. Highs: I found that they have fairly substansial roll-off at the top end. There's some sparkle / clarity there, but it quickly disappears. Details are acceptable for this price point, once you factor in the tech aspect of these buds. Mids: The strongest aspect, in my opinion. Guitars are expressed decently; voicing at least sounds correct. Details are there. Good. Bass: Bloated, but not completely overpowering. There is some definition at the low end. All of the people leaving reviews about the lack of bass, claiming that there isn't enough room to create lower frequencies, etc. simply aren't getting a good seal from the eartips. (See above, FIT.) They are sitting mere millimeters from your eardrums; they don't need a large chamber to create sufficient bass. I've adjusted the bass down a bit at the source to try to counter some of this bloat. If you're a "basshead" [read: like overpowering bass and don't care much for clarity], a little EQing should allow you to get what you want. OVERALL: Very pleased with these, if only for the portability this provides. Connection strength is good, and when it does cut out because of obstructions, the disconnections are not abrupt. I haven't worn them for more than an hour at a time while exercising, but they haven't died on me yet. Sound quality is pretty good for this price point, but won't hold a candle to a good, cabled set of headphones. Since you're looking at this page, you're obviously in the market for truly wireless headphones, so I'd say take the plunge and buy these. Much better than some other reviewers have suggested.

text: As a big fan of the MS400 series that these headphones are replacing, I was extremely disappointed. This is a clear downgrade from the MS400. When it comes to sound quality, these head phones are comparable to what you might find at Best Buy for under $50. These head phones have no bass and the lows are nearly non-existent, removing all the power from your music. Dance music that sounds lifeless and tinny, rock and roll with no punch, and classical music that lacks depth; this is what you can expect from these headphones. The MS400 were a masterpiece and as soon as I returned these for a refund, I ordered a pair of MS400 from e-bay. Why did Phiaton replace the venerated MS400 with this garbage? My guess is that, because the MS400 was originally targeted at the $250-$300 price range, they cut less corners in production and put together a better product. The $250 price point proved to be too high and Phiaton ended up lowering the price, finding its sweet spot at the $150-$200 range. But when it came time to make a new generation headphone they started out aiming at the new price point and cut corners accordingly. The MS400 can easily stand up to headphones in the $400 range. The MS430 is outdone by many $50-$100 headphones. I hope Phiaton will bring back the MS400.

text: I have been on a neverending quest for earbuds since I purchased my iPod. I don't know if my ears are weird or what, but all the ones I have tried before (the Apple ones being the worst) fall out of my ears very easily. I would be sitting at my desk, simply typing, and before I knew it the earbud would just slide out of my ear. It is so annoying to be constantly pushing earbuds back into your ear all day long. After searching high and low, and spending more money than I thought I ever would on various headphones and earbuds, I found the Sennheiser MX55V Stereo Headphones w/ Twist-to-fit System & Volume Control. These headphones have been a godsend! They fit in my ear and they stay put! I seriously thought it just wasn't possible, but these do. Now, I only gave them 4 stars because after extended wearing my ears are sore afterwards. They take some time to get used to and you have to try different 'positions' to get the fit that suits you best. I wasn't sure how to wear them when I first got them either, they should come with more detailed instructions. So, there is a little pieace over the actual speaker- this piece wedges in and holds the headphones in place. This is where the 'soreness' comes in. My ears, and probably most people's ears are not used to having something in that area of the ear, so, like I said earlier, they take some time to get used do. But the bottom line is that these work great. They have NOT FALLEN OUT ONCE! The difference between this model and the green MX75 (besides 20$) is that the MX75s are sweat resistant. It looks like they come with same items and are almost the same headphone. FYI- both the MX55V & the MX75 come with different pads & fittings to ensure they fit your ear perfectly. I did have to change from the pad it came with to the smallest one. Also, I LOVE the volume control. Basically about midway down the wire there is a small piece with a cool looking slider. The slider allows you to lower or raise the volume (not fully but within a certain range of the volume you previously set). This is great, because I do not have to fumble for my iPod in my pocket (or worse remove the earbud) when someone at work asks me a question, now I can just use the slider to lower the volume. The sound is good on these I have no complaints, but I am no audiophile either. If you have read this far into the review then I assume you are serious about buying these- and you should. If you have tried all the rest and are now ready to get a pair that truly fit, then buy these! Just remember, they take a couple days to get used to, so do NOT give up on these guys. Seriously, the best thing to do is play around with them and find what works for you- that's what is great about these customizable headphones!

text: Grado headphones are so widely known in the audiophile community for so many years there isn't much new to report. Yes they have issues that can be mildly bothersome, but the 325e's have such superior sound for such little relative expense that the small issues melt away. Buy the expanded 3rd party foam earpads (Earzonk work well for me) and the extension cable, and add the costs together and the Grado experience is still as good as cans costing twice as much or more. Their output is incredibly well-balanced, has remarkable breadth and depth in the soundstage, and does not add anything to a recording: it never highlights bass over mids or highs over mids, etc... just reproduces what is in the groove faithfully, which is the highest complement one can give any headphone. If you have a low budget, go for the 80s and you will be sonically happy wel beyond the cost. If you want near perfection and a nice comfy leather band buy the 325s. Also, if you are using a digital source? BUY A DEDICATED DAC/AMP. Because although Grados will do fine on straight line outputs, they like the extra power and really sing with more headroom. I recommend you spend the small extra to introduce a tube amp into the chain (I like the Bravo Audio box for value, looks, and sound) - if you love music, you will not be disappointed. Lastly, if like me you like to spend local and support small business? These are handmade in Brooklyn by a real family business: not some conglomerate that bought the name. text: This review is of the Sony WH-CH520 Wireless Headphones Bluetooth On-Ear Headset with Microphone, Black. They're especially good in lower bass ranges, and I can hear the higher tones well, too. Sometimes I need to listen to music to destress while at work/lunch and these don't let me down. When I want an excellent audio experience, I switch to my Simgot wired IEM/earbuds. I read another review of the battery life being low. The headphones that I received have performed well. I used them for 10-12 hours -- 2 hours at maximum volume -- and then left them connected all night. I put them back on pressed the power button to turn off then back on and it's still saying the battery is "fully charged". I repeated virtually the same thing the next day and the headset is still reporting significant battery life. I only use them with my PC so is the lower battery life something that happens while using them with an iPhone or Android? Don't know. It might be that that pair got past quality control. Positives: Volume is plenty loud on my computer. I listened to Leo Moracchioli's Africa cover, and Kid's Cover 45 & 2 by Tool. Both sounded great! The WH-CH520's sounded good listening to songs like Maroon 5's Girls Like You, and Ed Sheeran's Shape of You. If this is the type of music you listen to, then these headphones ought to be a good choice, too. Well balanced: quite good sound reproduction for the price and for them being Bluetooth. I have 3 pairs of Bluetooth earbuds and they don't sound as good as the Sony WH-CH520s. The padding on the earcups and headband is soft and the material is buttery. It very comfortable except when I have to wear my nighttime glasses that have thick arms. Flawless on Zoom calls, Podcasts, and YouTube. Negatives: There's no way to see if they're on or off just by looking at them. You have to press the power button. The blue LED turns on once while turning off. While turning on the LED flashes slowly few times, then flashes quickly a few times and then goes dark. It has flashed slowly after that for a while. I'm pretty sure that means it's ready to pair. Could be wrong. Conclusions: All-in-all I'm very happy with these headphones. They will get a lot of use. If the headphones you receive perform as well as these, I can highly recommend them. =========== Just as an FYI: I have *not* used any of the following because the headphones are working fine for me, but I went to Sony's website and found the following specifically for the WH-CH520: Great sound quality customizable to your music preference with EQ Custom on the Sony | Headphones Connect App. Boost the quality of compressed music files and enjoy streaming music with high quality sound through DSEE™ Digital Sound Enhancement Engine (DSEE) restores the harmonics and liveliness lost during typical music compression, for a more authentic performance. text: Cambridge Soundworks was a premium computer speaker brand many years ago. Co founded by and based on principles of sound engineer Henry Kloss (cofounder of KLH, Acoustic Research, Advent), Cambridge Soundworks was to the computer desk and portable audio device, what Bose was to home theater. That is until the market shifted to price, over performance, then Cambridge Soundworks all but disappeared. Now reborn like a phoenix as Oontz, can the company that wears that proud name today still be a contender in the tight audio market? Is premium sound still their focus? The battery is charged by the battery inside the charging case and the charging case is charged by any standard USB charger. Both can be charged simultaneously. Battery life is shorter than other second tier devices that have passed through my hands in the last year. This is due to the physically smaller size of the device compared to similar priced products most likely. So it stands to reason that the battery is physically smaller. Does this affect audio performance? No. Even though this is priced lowest price tied with one other true wireless ear bud I've tried, the audio performance of the Cambridge Soundworks Oontz True Wireless is the best. The sound approaches top tier and surpasses a few that are more gimmick than substance. Sound is slightly mid heavy but not so much that highs and lows are lacking. Picks brushing on guitar strings and amazing bass fingering and slapping is easily heard. Like many similar products there are no extra fancy features. The buttons are too easily pressed, but this is a common problem with all the true wireless ear buds I've used. The smaller size makes for a more secure fit or a better fit for those with smaller ears. Downsides include the inability to add custom memory foam ear tips and have the charging lid close and the before mentioned slightly shorter that others battery life. However many other ear buds also cannot be fitted with memory foam tips and have the lid close as well. The only real problem I see with these is the lack of any type of charge remaining indicator in the charging case. Other wireless ear buds universally have 4 LEDs on the case to indicate remaining charge left in the case to charge the ear buds, on the Oontz there is only a single LED that is not easily seen and can only give a low battery warning. If you are out and about, the low warning may be too little too late. If you can charge your charging case religious and don't plan to use your earbuds for more than about three hours at a time, these are an exceptional buy.

text: I left a lengthy review comparing the Jabra Evolve2 85 (E285) vs Bose Quiet Comfort 35 II (QC35II) vs Bose Noise Cancelling 700 (B700) vs Sony WH-1000XM4 (SX4) (in order of when I received them) for the E285. This is a shorter version of that review, mostly focusing on QC35II and E285. This was almost entirely written up during the week I had all four headsets for direct comparisons. Microphone and Playback QC35II recordings were consistently louder than the E285. But the E285 did a far better job of removing background noise, as evidenced by my recordings while drumming. Muting can be done with the QC35II but it was much more difficult than just raising/lowering the boom arm of the E285. Audio Output - DISCLAIMER - I'm not an audiophile E285 and SX4 audio sound better than the QC35II but primarily because I can use an equalizer and increase bass (obviously this is the most important factor). Even if the QC35II had better hardware, it’s not as accessible and therefore is a moot point. Win for SX4. Runner up is E285. Brand Bose: wanted my location and would ask for it every time I open the app (and wouldn’t allow usage without accepting beyond the standard Bluetooth connection process). These are headphones. You don’t need my location. Jabra: doesn’t require my location. Instead, it lets me know if I desire to give it my location, it will use it to locate my headphones. No, but thank you for giving me an actual choice! Win for Jabra. Runner up is Sony. ANC When standing in front of running water, QC35II had slightly better cancellation, but not a noticeable difference without actively concentrating. When playing on a drumpad, the E285 did a noticeably better job than the other headsets. It sounds like the pad is being muffled (which is what I’m looking for), whereas the others don’t quite succeed. During testing of the QC35II, whether ANC was on/off, there was a ceaseless light static (with no audio playing). I thought it quite odd and luckily, it didn’t happen again, but I suppose it could. With the QC35II, when the drum pad was hit, there was a tang sound, like the residual sound from tapping on a pan, as opposed to the muffled thumping the E285 gives. Perhaps with a constant noise the QC35II does a slightly better job filtering, but the E285 does a better job with impact noises (or maybe it’s just higher frequencies). In addition, the hear-through function of the E285 is awesome. With the QC35II ANC off, it sounds like the microphone is picking up sound and then replaying it in the speakers. In contrast, the E285 hear-through, which has adjustable levels, almost makes it sound like you’re not wearing them (tested at maximum hear-through). Win for E285. Runner up is SX4. Connectivity The E285 and SX4 have longer ranges than the QC35II. The E285, most of the time, reconnects automatically when coming back into range. QC35II, SX4, and E285 have a 3.5 mm jack. Why doesn’t the B700? Because it sucks. Double-connection to my PC (independent of range): E285 is easier because it’s just plug-and-play, no downloads or “connecting”. The QC35II and SX4 are only Bluetooth, so you have to do the standard “add device”, etc. An added feature of the Jabra is Jabra Direct, a software you can download to better manage your Jabra. It gives you a few more options and is worth using, in this writer’s humble opinion. Response time: the QC35II and B700 have a slightly faster response time when pausing media than the E285. The SX4 is the fastest, though we’re talking minute (not 60 seconds) differences. The E285 is on the cusp of being slow enough to be annoying, but not quite. The E285 and SX4 also have the cool feature of pausing media when the headphones are removed from your skull. Again, the E285 feel lack-luster in comparison because they take approximately 4 M-I-S-S-I-S-S-I-P-I seconds to pause, whereas the SX4 is half that time. For the E285, I’ve noticed the ear detection only works properly when playing music from your phone and not the PC. When using it with the PC, if I remove the headphones, the music will pause as it should. But it doesn’t resume when I put them back on. If I pause the music with the button, then remove the headset, it resumes. Again, cool feature, but needs work, especially when using it with the PC. App connectivity: some issues with E285. Some issues with SX4. Some issues with QC35II (Bose Connect). LOTS of issues with B700 (Bose Music). Unfortunately, apps are prone to some bugs every now and then. I can’t say which of the two (Sony/Jabra) had more, so neither bothered me much. Win for SX4 (better media response time). Runner up is E285. Voice Assistant Couldn’t even get B700 to work. First off, I have to change the “action” button from ANC control to activate voice assistant (so you can’t have both functionalities at the same time). However, once button mapping was adjusted accordingly, I click the button and it says “open your Google Assistant settings”, with no further instructions. I open the Home app, and once again, no further instructions, so I didn’t get it working. I didn’t spend anymore time on it because in contrast, the E285 and SX4 worked exactly as expected. No setup or anything, I just pushed the button and my assistant came up. The caveat for the E285 is you have to pull down the boom arm to use the feature (you can still press the action button with the boom arm up and have the assistant prompt, but because the arm is up, the microphone is off so it’s pointless). Perhaps Bose has better functionality when used with Alexa, but I use Google so I’m not bothering with testing that. Tie between E285 and SX4. I know this is extremely nit-picky, but the Bose assistant’s voice is far more annoying than Jabra or Sony. She sounds like an actual robot as opposed to someone I wouldn't mind meeting. Controls The QC35II and E285 have essentially the exact same button layout and functionality. The key difference is the action button on QC35II. It can be EITHER for voice assistant or cycling through ANC. On the other hand, you can access both functionalities on the E285, with the caveat of lowering the boom arm first for the voice assistant. The other difference is placement of the power button. On the QC35II, it’s a lateral switch on the side of the right ear cuff. On the E285, it’s a vertical switch on the bottom of the left ear. I literally don’t have a preference between the two. However, I do have a preference for the other buttons. While in the same place (the action button on the QC35II is in the same place as the ANC cycling button on the E285), the QC35II has a much more noticeable difference between the volume buttons and the play/pause, which I like better. All the buttons are bigger and more defined, plus the volume buttons are slightly raised, making it even easier to know what you’re pressing. On the E285, the buttons take up less surface area and are rather flat. Muting is definitely easier with the E285 because you simply raise or lower the boom mic. Though it also takes a little longer. The QC35II is more annoying because you have to press two buttons at the same time (the volume buttons). Win for SX4 (touchless controls are better). Runner up is E285. Comfort and Style I prefer the QC35II. Though I’ve been wearing the E285 for a little over an hour and was so comfortable, I had to look to my left to see which headset I wasn’t wearing. So both are very comfortable, but for comparison’s sake, it’s a win for QC35II. Runner up is E285/SX4 (just as comfortable). Extra The E285 has the hear-through feature, which I really like because I use ANC only when there are sounds I actively don’t want to listen to, like from mine or my roommate’s drumming, running water, laundry, phone call, or pooping with the fan on. Other than those times, I want some awareness of my surroundings because there’s nothing more frustrating than trying to get the attention of someone with headphones on (especially at work). In addition, the E285 and SX4 have ear detection (discussed previously). The E285 has a great way of handling multiple calls with its huge button on the right cuff. You can switch between two phone calls by putting one on hold and accept/end/reject calls using it. This is RARELY used, but it's cool. Issues My biggest issue was trying to connect QC35II with my Google Assistant. Besides that, functionality of the QC35II was pretty much flawless. Speaking of Google Assistant, there’s some variability with functionality with the E285. At the very least, the action button on the arm activates the assistant. But sometimes the input for said assistant is on the phone rather than the arm. Most of the time it works as expected. I think the additional connection to the PC adds complexity that needs to be vetted out for seamless functionality for the E285. Final verdict, best to worst: E285, SX4 (killer - no mute function, worse hear-through), QC35II (killers - older BT connection, worse audio, poor ANC). Literally wouldn't buy B700. UPDATE: It's been several weeks since I returned all but the Jabra Evolve2 85 (I use it 3-10 hours every single day) and my final rating is four stars while the QC35II I gave two. When the E285 works, it's great. But it doesn't work all the time, unfortunately. Even so, the E285 is better in just about every way. Stronger connection, more functionality, better app, better audio, better background noise removal (though the QC35II you could maybe argue is better at ANC, but not during a call). As far as functionally using the QC35II, I would give it three stars. But I give it two because the Bose app REQUIRES your location and that is absolutely ludicrous. It's a pair of headphones. You don't need my location. Note - if muting yourself directly from your headset isn't important to you and you're not typically in a noisy environment during calls, then I would honestly recommend the Sony WH-1000XM4.

text: These work well for the majority of my needs, which is sitting in my office on video calls, and the sound quality is very good and people can hear me well in most cases. Like just about any Bluetooth device, when the battery starts to get below 50%, there is an echo, but this is not unique to these earbuds. The good news is that the battery lasts through multiple calls, back-to-back if necessary, and they seem to charge very quickly in the charger/storage container. The noise canceling is OK, but not great, for instance, if outside with a little wind, but not bad for indoors. The biggest problem I have with them is that I can't get them to stay in my ear if I'm moving around much at all. I've tried just about every different ear bud that come with them, which are several, and they always work out of my ear when I'm moving around. A second problem is that the button to hang up is right where I naturally put my fingers on the ear bud to reposition them securely in my ear and if I'm not extremely careful, I accidentally hang up the call. This happened 3 or 4 times when I first started using them but I've learned to carefully grab the sides of the earbud in a pinch-type grip to reposition them in my ear. text: Edit: Even months later these headphones are by far my favorite audio product ever. Nowadays I use these headphones with 12" retina Macbook, iPhone 6S Plus, and Apple Watch, and the wireless audio performance is absolutely fantastic on any of the devices above. Although I am pretty careful with my stuff anyway, it is also good to note that the pair still looks like new, thus the build quality is just about as durable as it can be. I would recommend all Mac users to download Bluetooth Explorer app made by Apple. The app can be used to force Mac's Bluetooth audio output to go through with AptX codec, which is a slight improvement over SBC codec that is being used by default. All the listening I have done with P5 Wireless has been in wireless mode and thus I’m not going to compare how do they sound wireless versus wired. After all, why would one buy wireless to listen with a wire when wired can be had for $100 less. Music I listen to is streamed from Apple Music (presumably 256kbps AAC) through either iTunes on 13” Macbook Pro (Early 2015, OS X 10.11 Beta) or Music app on iPhone 6 (iOS 9.0 Beta). My choice of wireless headphones and listening equipment probably confirms that I’m not very hardcore audiophile. Connectivity: P5 Wireless was easy to pair to both of my devices. On the bottom of the right side of the headphones there is a power switch / bluetooth button. Sliding the switch turns headphones on and off and pressing the button for 2 seconds brings P5 Wireless to pairing mode. First thing you pair P5 Wireless to becomes a “master device” and short press of the bluetooth button will connect to this device. With other paired devices it is required to go to bluetooth settings and reconnect whenever you want to use headphones, but going through pairing process is not necessary. According to B&W, P5 Wireless can remember 8 devices at once, but I do not have more than 2 so I can’t confirm this. After connection is established in between of device and P5 Wireless the connection is very solid. Connection does not stutter or anything until I go to the opposite corner from an iPhone or Macbook Pro in small/mid-size Floridian home with pretty open floor plan. I doubt there will be any issues with the connection in any normal situations. While connected it is also possible to control music playback with volume up, down, and play/pause buttons. They work well, but I prefer to control through the device I’m using instead. Design: Aesthetics are very subjective thing, but I personally like the way P5 Wireless looks and feels. They’re mostly made out of leather and metals, but rather than having chrome ring familiar from P5 and P5 S2 in between of ear pad and ear cup there’s a black plastic ring, which accommodates all the buttons. I’m not too big fan of plastic, but this strip seems sturdy enough and is probably a necessity to achieve stable bluetooth connection. These are also pretty comfortable headphones for me to use–more comfortable than P5 or P5 S2. However, since I’d rank P5 to be the least comfortable and P5 Wireless to be most comfortable, I suspect that my head is just getting more used to the feel of these headphones over time and they’re in fact just about equally comfortable when compared to each other. Regardless, although I don’t have much experience with my P5 Wireless I bet I can wear them for long hours without significant discomfort. Sound: Unfortunately sound is the hardest thing for me to really review since I have nothing really to compare these to. Of course I have had some other headphones too outside of B&W offerings, but it has been so long ago that I can’t possibly remember their sound. Additionally, I have nothing to do direct comparison with since I always sell, dispose, recycle, or give away my previous stuff before buying new. In fact, besides some furniture, all of my stuff fits in the cargo area of Mustang, so I really don’t have too much stuff… Regardless of lack of comparison I can still say though that P5 Wireless sounds very good. Judging by the sound I couldn’t really tell they are in fact a wireless pair of headphones. Mid frequencies are probably their strongest point and vocals sound fantastic. Highs are pretty good too, but sometimes a bit too bright to me. I personally set EQ to bring highs slightly down. Bass in these headphones is something I like very much too. To me it feels like that the bass would be “under” or “behind” the vocals, while still having quite good presence. Out of my memory P5 Wireless bass seems to be less powerful than it was on P5 S2, but I can still very much enjoy EDM and other bass heavy music I tend to listen to. EDIT: Sound has changed quite a bit after using more of these headphones. It might be due to mysterious burn-in, which I do not really believe in that much, or ear pads have now had more time to form a shape better to my ears. It may also be just me getting used to the sound, but again, I used to own P5 S2, which sounded almost the same to what P5 Wireless has now become. Anyway, bass has now got off of the background and instead is very present in the listening experience. I love the bass of these headphones now as I did with P5 S2 too. In the beginning treble was too sparkly or sibilant, but now it's no longer an issue. Mid frequencies are still fantastic and the vocal reproduction of these headphones is hard to beat. Soundstage is not too big, but it's sufficient or even great for an on-ear headphone. All in all, I'd recommend these headphones to just about anyone looking to drop $399.99 for their listening experience. While many wired options might be more accurate sounding, P5 Wireless is joy to listen to with wireless convenience. Finally, these also sound great from any modern bluetooth capable source, so buyer doesn't have to worry about impedances or other technical stuff–they just work! I bet that simplicity and convenience with this great sound cannot be beaten by anything on the market today.

text: Judging by the other reviews, there seems to be some confusion as to the purpose of these ear buds. They are designed to listen to music in high noise environments. They are not meant to be 'normal' ear buds that you wear while working out or around the house. I was looking for something that I could wear while mowing the lawn that would offer good hearing protection, allow me to listen to music, and work with safety glasses. When I first set out to find something that fit those criteria I thought it would be easy. Boy was I wrong, I went through several things before I finally found these. Pros: -Block a lot of background noise. Either 20 or 29 db depending on the ear tip that you use. (Plain, foam hearing protection give about 29db of protection) -Replaceable/interchangeable tips. As mentioned above, there are options with the ear tips that you can use. One is more comfortable and the other offers more noise blocking. In either case it's nice to be able to replace them if they become dirty or worn. -Nice sound. I am not an audiophile, so my standards might be lower then others, but I find that these sound pretty good. I have used bad headphones in the past where the poor sound quality bothered me, that is not the case here. -Volume control. I use my phone to stream music while I cut the grass, it's great to not have to pull my phone out of my pocket to adjust the volume. -WORK WITH SAFETY GLASSES. Sorry for the caps, but I can not over state the importance of this (at least to me). Muff style hearing protection doesn't work well with safety glasses (or most regular glasses) because the arm of the glasses interferes with seal of the muff around the ear. This gives a place for outside noise to leak through which lessens the amount of noise that they block. Since these go in your ears you can still wear glasses without them causing problems. -Comfortable. I don't have any issues wearing these for 90+ minutes at a time. They are also cooler to wear then muffs. Cons: -Volume control is big. I think the reason it's so large is that these ear buds have some noise limiting electronics built in. This doesn't cause any problems while I'm riding my mower, but may bother some. -Replacement tips are pricey. $20 for 10 pairs? You SHOULD replace in-ear hearing protection regularly since it's effectiveness will go down over time. That being said, I have used my current set for over 50 hours of use and they are still going strong. SAFETY CONCERN: Again, sorry for the use of caps, but this is important. The whole point of these is to be able to listen to music while blocking out a lot of outside noise and they do a darn good job at it. The problem with that is that outside noise can let you know danger is coming. I know that my wife has tried to yell for me while I was mowing the lawn and I couldn't hear her at all. (Didn't notice her until I saw her.) I'm also wary when I am near the street since there is no way to hear a car passing by and I am concerned that I would have trouble hearing a car horn. You just need to think about where you are wearing these and be mindful of the fact that you won't hear everything you normally would. Conclusion: These ear buds aren't perfect for every situation but they suite my needs very well. They allow me to comfortably listen to music while mowing the grass and wearing safety glasses. I spent a lot of time looking for a product that would allow me to do this and have finally found it. Things I tried that didn't work: (I didn't want to bog down the main body of the review with this stuff.) -[[ASIN:B004U4A5RU Howard Leight 1030110 Sync Noise-Blocking Stereo Earmuff]] The problem with here was that these didn't work with safety glasses. A lot of noise bled through causing me to turn the music volume up which pretty much defeated the purpose of trying to protect my hearing. I tried to buy different safety glasses with thin arms, but none of them really worked. -[[ASIN:B003EM8008 Panasonic RPHJE120K In-Ear Headphone, Black]] I tried wearing these under plain earmuffs and had all of the above problems. (I really like these earbuds though. They sound great for the price.) -Noise cancelling headphones. Didn't stop nearly enough of the outside noise to be at all effective. I have a pretty cheap pair, so maybe more expensive ones would work better. Update 6/3/14 Some Quick Points: -I've owned these for around 2 years now and I still love them. I can listen to music at a comfortable volume while mowing the grass and wear sunglasses while doing it. -I haven't had any trouble with durability, but in fairness I only use them riding the lawn mower, weed whacking, and using the snow blower. I'd guess I'm up to 200 hours of use or so. -I saw a couple other reviews mention some trouble they had with volume control, what I do is turn the volume on my phone up to the maximum and then use the in-line buttons to control the volume and that seems to work pretty well. -I lost the shirt clip that came with these, but managed to find a decent replacement. [[ASIN:B0006H5IC2 Plantronics clothing clip]] -If these ever break I wouldn't hesitate to buy another pair.

text: I own both the open and closed back version of this pair of headphones and wanted to do a quick comparison to help anyone trying to choose between them. I've owned the 598SE for about 1.5 years and just got the 598Cs a few days ago. Build Quality: Both have good build quality but I would say it's a bit better on the 598SE. The plastic feels slightly higher quality and the earpads have a more premium feel. That's not to say the 598Cs feel cheap. They still live up to Sennheiser quality. Comfort: Both are quite comfortable and I have no problem wearing either of them for many hours at a time. The only difference is the 598SE have less clamping force because a tight seal isn't necessary. It's not a problem with the 598Cs thought because they have enough padding to be comfortable. Sound: This is where the headphones vary significantly. The open back 598SE's have a noticeably larger soundstage and a richer overall sound. If anyone is unaware a larger soundstage means it feels like the music is coming from all around you instead of feeling like it is right inside your head. This can be good for pinpointing certain instruments or voices and leads to a "fuller" sound from your music. The closed back 598Cs still have an impressive soundstage considering they are closed back. It's better than any other closed back headphone's I've tried. One thing that I consider an advantage with the 598Cs is the amount of bass. I found with the 598SE's that the bass was almost non existent and lead to some songs feeling stale or boring. The small bass increase in the Cs makes for a big difference when listening to bass heavy music (pop, hip-hop, etc...). The overall sound quality on the Cs is great on its own, it just lacks clarity in the mids and highs when compared to the 598SE's. Portability: The 598Cs win this by a huge margin. Being that they are closed back means you can use them in public without hearing much of what is around you or disturbing others with your music. I still wouldn't crank the volume too high or you will find that some sound still leaks but as long as you are listening at a reasonable volume it shouldn't be a problem. The 598Cs cable is thinner in comparison but has a play/pause button built in making it better for mobile use. I also found that the 598SE's couldn't get loud enough plugged in to my phone but that depends on which phone you have. It seems like the Cs are focused on portability whereas the SE's are meant to only be used at home. Overall I think both these headphones have a place and offer different functionality depending on what your needs are. If you want to listen to music on the go then the 598Cs are a much better choice whereas if you just want great sound and don't care about bass then the 598SE's are definitely a better option.

text: I really wanted to keep these. Their sound compared very well against my Sony MDR-7506 studio monitors (look them up if you don't know what they are). Their bass is a bit muddier and the trebles don't sparkle quite as much as the Sony, but they beat out all the wired in-ear earphones I own (mostly cheap ones) for sound clarity. The Sony has a very flat frequency response, and the LG's response was very similar. That's good if you want to hear the sounds naturally, bad if you want deep thumping bass as is the trend nowadays. (The bass boost function makes almost no difference. You'll find it difficult to tell the difference between bass boost, normal, and treble boost.) The other features are great too - long battery life, lots of physical buttons and controls with clear orientation, lightweight and rest comfortably around the neck. The silicone earpieces are strong and wrap onto the earbuds really tightly. While changing them to get a better fit, I used enough force to tear the silicone apart on all the other earphones I own. But these held together like a champ. Range is about 20-25 ft from my laptop before the signal starts breaking up. So what's the fly in the ointment? They hurt. If you look most earphones, the part that sticks out of your ear is offset from the part that rests inside your ear canal. This is because your ear canal is angled relative to the outside of your ear, and offsetting the exterior part allows you to rotate the earphones until you find a good, comfortable fit. Not so with these. The exterior portion is a straight metal tube directly in line with the inner portion. If you have smaller ears, the edge of this metal tube will jam up against the folds and flaps of your ear. You don't notice it at first, after 15 minutes it's annoying, after 30 minutes it's painful. And because it's a straight tube, rotating it doesn't change the profile in any way. The only way I could get a comfortable fit was to angle it such that the silicone no longer made a good seal, and I lost the noise isolation. For me that defeats the whole point of buying in-ear earphones (I already own a pair of on-ear bluetooth headphones). So reluctantly, I'm going to have to return these. I spent a lot of time researching different bluetooth earphones before settling on the LG. These were the best match for my needs. Unfortunately, I can't use them if they leave me in pain. (Almost forgot. The microphone is worthless. My friend could barely understand me while I was using it. So disregard these if you were hoping for a combo music-listening phone-talking headset.)

text: I like these a lot and I can tell JBL put a lot of good engineering into these. I just hope I need to get used to these; if I can't get used to these in a couple weeks I might return them. I like the sound quality and the options for the noise reduction, ambient play through, or none. This works well. I like the battery life for such a small headphone and the charging case is small, compact, and sturdy. I have no problem carrying these around all day. The idea of the charging case in general is genius. The charging case is nicely built and functional. It has magnets in the case that draw the earbud into the correct spot every time. That works so well I am impressed. It is sturdy and not too large so I feel comfortable carrying them in my pocket. The sounds falls into the Pro and Con category, but mostly Pro. The Con with the sound is that if you don't seat the earbud into your ear perfectly it cancels the sounds or you get intermittent sounds when you jaw moves because of the way it slightly moves the ears. Once seated and secured the sounds is great, clear, and fast enough to keep up with the music playing on the device. Cons: There is no way to control the volume from the earbuds and there is no software option to go back to the previous song. These two aspects are deal breakers for me. I thought these options were pretty standard in today's environment of headphones. The buttons are weird and I hope it is just hard to get used to for me. I learned that if you push the button in an upward type manner you can have more control because you are supporting the back of the earbud with your earbone. Kind of weird because it feels like if you want to push a button you have first to first have stable control of the outside frame of the earbud. Taking the earbuds out of the case can be frustrating if you have no grip on your fingertips. The earbuds are nicely constructed, round, and smooth. This leads to slipping when you go to take them out of the charging case.

text: My last headphones before these were sony XB90ex, so my review will be loosely based on comparison with xb90. Firstly since I paid $50 more than xb90ex (95$) my expectations were bit high. xb90 had 16mm driver and I really liked it and the second I put h1 in my ear and pressed "play" I felt that they were small 9mm drivers, don't get me wrong, I didn't literally feel the size of the driver but it has somewhat thinner sound, the sound that you can tell it comes from earbuds, which wasn't the case when listening to xb90. Soundstage: xb90 had huge soundstage so the first thing that disappointed me when I tried XBA H1 was the soundstage. while it's still larger than low-priced headphones(< 70$) it is nowhere as wide as xb90's (though it's better than ex310's) . On the other hand instrument separation is very good, I would say better than xb90, highs and lows don't distract each other, I think 2-way drivers have something to do with this. Bass: compared to xb90 subbass somewhat lacks, generally bass is good and high enough for me and majority of listeners but that subwoofer feeling of xb90ex is gone. Midbass is punchy and fast, slightly better than xb90's. Overral bass is almost as good as xb90's Mids: Mids are definitely front-oriented, bright and clean.female vocal is really joy to listen. I think generally this is easiest area for IEMs to perform and there is no point to talk much about it. In one word, mids are very pleasant to listen. Highs: before burning in, highs were harsh, bright and there was sibilance, after burn-in the harshness smoothed and sibilance faded away (not completely though), in fact it got too smooth for my taste. Arguably inferior performer compared to xb90ex in this area, which had very smooth but bright treble. The good thing is that it's smooth and quality is good, it's just not bright enough for me. Amplifier: I used them on my walkman x1050 which has excellent sound quality and regardless its age it's still one of the best sounding PMPs. Since the impedance of the headphones is 40 OHM which is much higher than most earbuds (majority have 16-24 ohm) I thought amplifier would be necessary but the deference isn't that much, Even without amp these earbuds sound good. Without amp the sound is somewhat hollow though, with amp it gains some midbass and sound gets more full. Conclusion: The headphones are good but very overpriced IMO, Overall I would take xb90ex over H1 without any second thoughts, they are overall at least as good performers and much cheaper than these. I think real price of these should be $80 or at most $100 because of style (they are really attractive in terms of appearance). one more thing, the left headphone is slightly quieter than the right one but I'm the only one who notices it (difference is almost negligible) but still if there wasn't this problem I would have given 4 star rating. This review maybe was too critical, they're not bad at all, at least instrument separation and "attack" were excellent for the class. Thanks for reading.

text: Another set of earphones for the ever growing collection. That collection spans everything from the Ultimate Ear 10's (list price around $400) to a wild variety of low end stuff by Koss, JVC, Sennheiser, Sony, Altec Lansing, MEElectronics, and many many more... So what's the skinny on these? Packaging: Nice package. Really nice case. Look substantial. Fit and finish: Seems reasonably well made. About par for the course with more expensive earphones. The cable is thin and flexible. It doesn't scream audiophile, but looks can be deceiving, and in this product category you're mostly looking for longevity, not huge and heavy. Ear-fit: So-so. These come with multiple adapters to fit your ear. I found one pair of silicone adapters that were probably the best of the lot in my ears. Not the most comfortable headphones I've ever used, but they stay in and aren't painful over long listening periods. Sound: OK, forget everything else. This is where it's at, especially when you're paying what these cost. And here...something of a disappointment. The low end bass is fine: Tight and strong. Not overbearing. Fairly neutral. Perfect for my tastes, but will be seen as deficient if you're the kind of person who likes a lot of boom-boom-boom! Mid range: Goosed. Unfortunately. I like a nice, neutral midrange, and find an emphasized midrange really muddies up the experience. These are definitely goosed. They're very much, in that respect, like the similarly priced Monster Turbine in-ear earphones, much liked by some, but not by me. The treble sounds a bit rolled-off on these, yielding some loss of breath. The upside of the treble roll off is that they can be less fatiguing with some types of music. But again, that's a deviation from "natural", which is what I prefer. The treble roll-off and the midrange goose combine to create a sound profile that I would classify as acceptable, but not really of audiophile caliber. On the whole, these aren't bad earphones. Not at all. The packaging and the package are pretty substantial. But the sound quality just isn't, in my opinion, at a level that justifies the price. In this sense, they are comparable to the Monster lines of in-ear headphones. It's worth noting that those have their fans, and I am sure people who find that goosed midrange profile delightful will be similarly pleased with these. I, personally, prefer a neutral profile (I can modify the sound through a graphic equalizer in/around the source, if need be).

text: ok I've written and deleted reviews for the he400 for months now. I just never seem to make up my mind about these headphones. so whats the problem? well it's a massive case of a love/hate relationship. before I get to all that, some details first: all my headphones (he400, dt770 pro 250, hd598, and ath m50x) are run through either a fiio e12 or a schiit modi with a vali or magni. I stream spotify premium (320kbps quality streaming). so what's the deal then? lets get the hate out and be done with it. there are a few things I just HATE about these headphones, and they have nothing to do with sound. yes these headphones are heavy, but that's not my problem. they're just not fun to wear. mine came with both the velour and pleather ear pads and I found neither to be comfortable. they're stiffly padded, and the materials that touch your face are low quality. I know i'll have dissenters, but I personally cannot stand either set of pads. now on to the headband....it's awful! it's stiff and thinly padded. I get a sore spot on the top of my head when listening for more than 30 mins. so every point of contact with my head is uncomfortable! but my complaints don't stop there...the cables! they're stiff and inflexible. they're very high quality, just unwieldy in use. and finally, I find adjusting them to be an exercise in frustration. I just cant seem to get that perfect fit. whew glad I got that off my chest! sounds like a whole lotta hate! especially for a 5 star review, no? well in the end sound quality is my first concern, and in that regard these are hands down the best sounding headphones I've ever listened too. there's lots and lots of detailed reviews of their sound signature and quality, so i'll be brief. they're hyper detailed, offer an excellent soundstage, have hands down the best bass I've heard from an open headphone, and just seem to sound good no matter what I throw at them. they can be a tad bright at times, but that's ok, it rarely gets excessive. I really cannot make any major complaints about the sound of these headphones. they awe me on a regular basis, even after months of listening. they're just that good! these headphones do need an amp, despite the arguments to the contrary. sure you'll get sound plugging them right into a phone or computer headphone jack, but they wont sound anywhere near their potential. the schiit modi/vali stack is quite good with them. but the magni also pairs very well with them as well. the vali is a bit more lush and analog sounding, whereas the magni is a bit colder and more digital sounding. its more detailed though... either way I think you'll like those amps with the he400. my fiio e12 does an admirable job powering them as well. it drives them with authority, but is less detailed than the schiit amps. soundstage with the fiio is also inferior to the schiits. so that's the basis for my 5 star review. despite many comfort and design issues, I just cant score them down when they sound so darn good for so darn cheap. and being the resourceful guy I am, I found a few workarounds for my hate items. /> those are the ear pads from the he400i model, they're called focus pads. they're the best $40 I've spent in a long time! they're so so so much more comfortable than either stock pad the he400 comes with. they also sound really darn good. so my suggestion, if you don't like your stock pads, get those focus pads. they're made of much higher quality material, and the cushions are much more pliable, like memory foam. /> that's basically a scarf for your headband. it's not the greatest looking thing, but it gets the job done. it's softer and offers much better padding vs the stock band alone. that eliminated the sore spot on the top of my head from the headband. so after all those comfort mods, I no longer hate wearing my he400. I don't really love wearing them either, but indifferent is better than hate, right? so if you want world class sound, and you're ok with some minor issues, give the he400 a try. I really cant put into words how good these headphones sound. they make all my other headphones sound like toys in comparison.

text: You gotta love it when you get a pleasant surprise when you buy something. I'm a rather serious audiophile and I have a nice collection of top notch headphones/earphones. For full size cans, I have a pair of HD650's, which are quite amazing. For earphones, I have JH Audio 13v2's, Westone UM Pro 50 SE's and Shure 535's. All three of these are amazing in their own ways (JH Audio's best overall of them). I bought these for one reason - I wanted to have a pair of full size headphones that were easy to drive. I didn't want to spend a whole lot - $300 was about all I wanted to put into this. The mighty Sennhesier HD650's fully deserve their stellar reputation - they are awesome. But they have a big catch - you need to be tethered to a powerful headphone amp to get the best out of them. Without proper amplication, they sound hard as soon as the volume goes up. I like full size cans over iems because they they are so much more comfortable and easy to deal with - and they don't have that "underwater" sensation you get with earphones. I have an Astell & Kern AK120ii DAP and my ideal would be a set of full size cans that had sound quality at least comparable to the HD650's but that could be driven straight out of the ak120. The ak120 alone can't drive the hd650's ( at least not very well). Based on reading a million reviews, I decided to go with the Phillips X2's. It was between the x2's and the Audio Technical MSR7's. I was hoping for parity at best with th hd650's, and frankly I didn't think I would even get that - I thought anything I chose would still be a cut or two below the hd650's. Well, I was wrong. To my astonishment, these x2's are actually better than my HD650's. And my JH13's, and my UM Pro 50, and my SE 535's. Pretty much everything - transparency, clarity, sweetness, coherency, etc. Although they dig nicely down into the deep bass (deeper than the hd650's), this is the only area where some of the others beat them. The JH13's and Westones have more bass power. But none of them can match the incredible sweetness of the x2's. They are simply incapable of sounding harsh or hard. The better the recording (especially DSD's) the more they reveal. They are the best I have ever heard on massed strings (so hard to get right). The air they put around instruments & voices is the best I have ever heard. The second I put them on (before any break in) I just went "ahhh". They just get everything right. Yes - they are quite easy to drive. But they still do benefit from amplification- they love both my Ray Samuels Predator and my Peachtree Shift. So there you have it - if you are an audiophile looking for high quality, easy to drive full size headphones, look no further. I'm pretty sure you will love these. Great job, Phillips!

text: The bass boost is extremely picky. I actually thought my headphones were broken, because it wasn't working no matter what. It wasn't until last night that the bass finally engaged on the extremely low notes in Viktoria Modesta's "Prototype." I have my slider all the way up and the bass boost never engages, unless the note is extremely deep. It's essentially useless on anything that's not full of super low notes. The sound is fine, but I do wish that the bass boost was more consistent and less picky about the notes it chooses. Especially since sometimes it will boost a not once, but then ignore the same note a few seconds later. On certain songs it just goes on and off. It sounds like my old Skullcrushers did... when their mini subwoofer was broken. Just with better regular sound. That's the biggest plus. When the bass boost isn't doing anything, it sounds almost like normal headphones instead of a tin can. I only paid $32 thanks to the lifetime warranty on my Skullcrushers. If I had paid the full $99 (+ tax and shipping, so more like $103) I would have sent them back immediately. I expected the bass to work like on my old headphones, and vibrate every note baritone and below, but they obviously don't do that. Maybe if I had the volume high enough to deafen myself, it would work. But I'd rather not ruin my hearing for the rest of my life. My left ear has problems enough as it is. At least they look cool. (I got them in "bunny teal" from the Skullcandy website.) I enjoy them for the most part, despite the inconsistent bass, but as with the old Skullcrushers, I would never recommend them to anyone. I only continue using Skullcandy headphones because the lifetime warranty allows me to get new pairs for next to no charge (other than shipping). As a whole, the brand's products tend to be extremely prone to breaking and malfunctioning. In addition, while the battery is not in an awful place, it is a little inconvenient to take the pad off of the ear cup and put it back on. The battery slot is somewhat tight, as well. Not too much trouble putting the battery in, but a little harder to take the battery out. I had to use my nails, and nicked myself on the finger trying to pry out the battery. It works best to grab the negative side since it has that little groove on the bottom of the battery. The bass slider is easy to move if you push on the top or bottom edge with your nail but difficult to move if you attempt any other way. They fit comfortably, for the most part, and in fact the ear cups completely surround my ear rather than sitting on top of them, which I am not used to. At first it felt like they would fall off because of the additional weight in the ears and because of the surrounding squishy stuff laying against my skull instead of my ear. But they stayed on. Long story short, these are not worth the full price unless you listen exclusively to the kind of EDM that is bass heavy to the point of ridiculousness. I tested them on several songs off of Minaj's Pink Friday and on a Japanese rock song that is quite bass-heavy, and it engaged on none of them. If you are set on these headphones, try to get them on sale. EDITED after a month: These are actually quite uncomfortable the longer I wear them, and hurt both my ears and my head, and sometimes if I wear them for too long they even make my teeth slightly sore. They hang heavily, pull down on my ears as well as push the speaker against the shell of my ear, and the pad on the headband is also not very comfortable due to the angular, uneven surface. It's come to be that these headphones are becoming more uncomfortable than earbuds, which is problematic for me because earbuds cause me some definite pain. If it gets worse, and I expect it will, I will have to buy a different pair of headphones before these ones even break. The sound continues to be fickle and bass only engages if the notes are very low, or if you decide to turn the treble down a lot in EQ and listen with a high volume. The vibration is pretty picky too, if you turn it down much it just stops working. But if it's up all the way it can be pretty uncomfortable. Also, if the cord in the jack on the headphones gets twisted, it may make the sound go weird. I do not like these, except aesthetically, and will not be purchasing them or any other Skullcandy product again.

text: These are decent headphones for the money, but there are several things wrong with them that would prevent me from either buying them again or recommending them. First, the good: The sound quality is pretty good. Out of the box they are EQ'd "flat", so you may have to mess with your phone's onboard EQ to get them to sound the way you want. This for me is not a deal breaker, although on an iPhone it makes podcasts sound hollow since the onboard EQ doesn't work beyond the music app. The fit is also good, there are several foams included to fit the size of your ear canal. They also stay on thanks to the wrap around thingy. They charge fast, and they hold a charge for a long time. Ok, the bad: I can not for the life of me figure out how to use the controls outside of making it pause/play. There is theoretically a way to fast forward, rewind, etc but the sensitivity of the "buttons" on the buds is so touchy that all I can do is make it stop or go. This also extends to putting them on, taking them off, or adjusting them. They inadvertently pause or play without intention. This is actually my second pair. The first pair I get seemed to disconnect/break up while playing music. I figured that maybe it was a bad pair, so exchanged them for new ones. Nope, the problem persisted. It turns out that the bluetooth reception is poor, so they only work without disruption if my phone is in my right pocket. This isn't that big a deal you say? I have kept my phone in my left pocket for over 20 years and at 50 years old, having to change my pocket paradigm is super annoying. I, however, do not have the patience to go through the exchange process again so I am going to let it ride. For these reasons, I would not get these again, even for the price. They are however acceptable enough to keep until they die because the good outweighs the prospect of having to get something else at this point. So yes, I am keeping them out of apathy.

text: These headphones are everything ear buds are not: they're comfortable, rich in bass, and keep noise out the old-fashioned way, by encircling the ears with large sound-insulating pads. They produce a big, strong sound from MP3 players that tend to be underpowered. In a departure from the more rigid headsets of the past, the earpieces swivel on the headband so that they may be packed flat in a briefcase or perhaps alongside a laptop in its case. The flat, very flexible wiring, resists tangling; and a three-ft. extension cable is provided should you want to use these in your recliner next to your home stereo system. But there's a problem: the engineers have overshot the mark in battling the scourge of tiny sound. The bass is impressive, and mellow can be good up to a point; but unfortunately, the bass bias is so strong that the overall sound is muddled and unclear. Although I would not go as far as to say that single-driver systems are incapable of producing deep bass without sacrificing mid-and-upper-range clarity, these headphones could certainly use the addition of a tweeter. Curiously, the uppermost frequencies, which produce the characteristic overtones of instruments and voices, are still present. Usually I have to run my iPod in bass-boost mode, but with this headset I have to switch to bass-reducing EQ, and still there is too much mid-bass mush. Plugging into my home stereo system the situation is even worse, although there I could probably skew the EQ enough to compensate. A treble boost at the sound source is needed to make speech fully intelligible. The overall sound is pleasant, if dishonest; and the noise-insulating quality of these `phones prevents the sounds of the outside world from overwhelming the weak treble. In spite of my disappointment with the unbalanced frequency response, there may be occasions when I will find these useful inasmuch as my primary alternatives are various pairs of tinny-sounding miniatures. Call me Goldilocks, but I'm still waiting for the headphones that are "just right."

text: Bought 1MORE PistonBuds in July 2022 based on strong positive reviews at Wirecutter, Consumer Reports, and Amazon. After a mostly good start, things went downhill, eventually ending in a refund. When earbuds arrived, their LEDs never came on, no matter what I tried, even though user manual said they should. Main section of user manual failed to mention that earbuds and case should be fully charged for two hours before first use, which only came up at the very end in the troubleshooting section. Even when I put the earbuds into the plugged-in charging case, their LEDs still didn’t come on the way they were supposed to. Only after several minutes in powered charging case did red LED on each earbud turn on, indicating that they were charging. Appears that batteries in both earbuds were completely drained on arrival. Once earbuds were fully charged, setup went smoothly, pairing them with my Mac laptop. Fit of earbuds in my ears was surprisingly comfortable (soft silicone, plus good ergonomic design), and felt very secure. Sound quality at my usual low volume was pretty good, although highs were not quite as bright as I’m used to with earbuds, and bass only seemed a bit heavy on tracks that were already inherently bass-heavy. Really liked how smoothly earbuds worked in routine use, powering on and reconnecting to laptop when removed from charging case, and powering off and immediately recharging when returned to case. After about a month, pairing with my laptop became increasingly unreliable, with only temporary relief from un-pairing and re-pairing. Not long after that, even successful pairing still left only one or the other of two earbuds working. (Later discovered that other reviewers had had this exact same experience.) At this point, I contacted product support at the 1MORE website, and they didn’t offer any troubleshooting advice, but did send a replacement set of earbuds, after I returned my original set at my own expense. The replacement earbuds I received also arrived with completely dead batteries in both of them. Once they were fully charged, the right earbud had persistent clicking and buzzing noise all the time while powered on, whether or not I had audio playing. Nothing in my setup had changed, and the left replacement earbud didn’t display this behavior, suggesting that the right replacement earbud was defective. I contacted product support again, and once again they didn’t offer any troubleshooting advice, but this time they offered a refund along with return shipping at their expense. I took them up on their offer, even though *I would have preferred to have a working set of PistonBuds that I could have relied on for the long haul*. Noticed that both the original and replacement earbuds showed a manufacture date of 2021.04 (18 months ago), which may explain why all of the earbuds’ batteries were so deeply discharged. Leaves me wondering whether deeply discharged batteries could have played a role in subsequent improper behavior. Went back to Amazon reviews of these PistonBuds, looking specifically at the most recent ones, only to discover that more than half of those most recent reviews report quality and/or support issues. This appears inconsistent with the high global star rating Amazon displayed when I bought these earbuds months ago, suggesting a significant recent decline. Disappointed that apparently something has gone wrong with what had been a good product. Two stars for good overall experience (when it worked), and for absence of resistance from support for either replacement or refund.

experience_rationale: Initial charging problems and eventual pairing issues led to a refund despite early comfort and sound positives
