text: I purchased these based on the price and the fact that they have noise reduction as nothing else in this price range has that. They are decent earbuds and the sound quality is solid but there so many little issues that add up to a subpar experience. Pros - Sound quality is decent. - Noise reduction works well, if not in a windy environment. (see below) - Battery life seems similar to other earbuds and the case helps. - Quite comfortable and I have never felt like they would fall out. Cons - The touch controls are super finicky. Sometimes they work, sometimes they don't. For them to work it seems like they need a super solid tap/touch, which isn't the most comfortable thing when you have these shoved in your ear canal. They are unresponsive to light gentle touches. Adding swipe gesture controls would be so much nicer. No idea what the touch sensor hardware is like but perhaps this could be added in a software update. - The app is meh and required for nearly all settings. On Android, it places a persistent notification, but touching it does nothing. It should at least open the app to the Echo Buds page. Quick toggles on the notification itself would also be super useful. - Noise reduction works great, but it is by no means noise cancellation. The one issue, if you are outside and there is a slight breeze the noise reduction will actually make this noise louder. It's trying to cancel a sound (wind across the mics) that you can't hear and introduces more noise. If there is any wind, you are going to have to turn off the noise reduction. - They aren't vented, which can help with passive noise reduction, but also give you that uncomfortable plugged ears feeling. - The case is a bit large compared to other similar earbuds. Overall they are just okay, fix the issues above and these will be amazing.

text: These IEMs are pretty fantastic for the price. I am on my second set after a year where I absolutely abused the previous set in the gym. I don't mind spending $20 per year for IEMs if they hold up to abuse and sound as good as these do. I have cycled through dozens of IEMs over the past decade and nothing beats these for the price. Are they the best that I own? No. Do they compete with my set of Philips Fidelio S2 for which I paid six times as much? Absolutely. The Brainwavz Delta are well-balanced IEMs with a neutral sound signature. They can sound a bit harsh in the midrange, but I paid $20 for them; I am not going to complain. Frequency extremes are rolled off and the bass does not possess the depth as in other IEMs. The manufacturer had to make compromises to ensure that these came in at a reasonable price point and their choices were judicious and appropriate. Of particular note is the build quality. I use these almost exclusively in the gym and the only weak point seems to be the strain relief at the 3.5 mm connector. One earphone was going out in my old set when I bent the cable a certain way so I bought these. Not a big deal. I work out for 90 minutes per day, including running 4 miles, five days a week. I have never had a set of IEMs that held up for three months, even those costing upwards of $100. These lasted a year. You cannot purchase another set of IEMs that comes close to the value equation with this set. Yes, there are some that sound better. Yes, there are some that are cheaper. The Brainwavz Delta falls on the inflection point of price vs. quality and I recommend them as even a primary IEM for anybody who desires a neutral and clear sound signature. Highly recommended!

text: I LOVED my H7s before this. And I suppose this review is technically for the H9, but B&O customer service said the H9i has the same supposed "non-issues" that my H9 has... It's a real bummer, because I love the company and love their sound signature, but this really killed it for me. So much for buying a full home theater setup from them, which I was about to do... When I got my H9s, I was happy overall, but right away I noticed a popping sound every time audio started and stopped playing (i.e. changing songs, pausing music, or, most annoyingly, browsing on Apple TV, where between each little chime from switching icons, it would pop on and off). At first, support was very kind. They did have me jump through a bunch of testing hoops, but that's understandable. At the end, they said there must be an issue with these, as this sounds like strange behavior. They said to send them in and not to worry...and that they'd fix them, etc. So I sent them in...only to have them later tell me they couldn't see anything wrong with them. I told them to please check again. Again, they said they couldn't see anything wrong. The support office told me they'd try to have it shipped to them so they could see for themselves, since the testing facility didn't have Apple TVs to test (even though it happens with anything). But they couldn't get the package in time before the testing facility sent them back to me. I kept writing to them after I got them back, as it still had the issue, of course. Then, the next person (this is months later now after all this) is telling me oh, that sound? That's NORMAL. That just happens because power is coming on and off in the headphone. I told them this did not happen with my H7. And if I was told this was normal from the start (instead of everyone saying I'm crazy and there's no sound), I would have returned them. Except now I can't because I'm past the return date. This is ridiculous. For a headphone this expensive, it shouldn't be normal to have a distracting pop every time audio starts or stops or every time you change a song or every time you scroll over a menu item on a connected device. And they won't do a thing. My girlfriend's Bose headphones don't do this. And the ANC is better (obviously). Honestly, I really wanted to like these, but I wish I kept my H7 headphones. But even then, I feel like I can't trust B&O now. These aren't cheap. Such a letdown. Other than that, yeah...nice leather, classic B&O sound when they're not popping. But what a pain.

Don't synch it using the bluetooth discovery method. If you do so it will function like a regular bluetooth headset and some features will not work correctly (such as on screen indication of your volume level, battery life gauge, the mute button, and on screen display if your mute is on or off). The only complaint I have is that the "headset speaker" is sort of big and the rubber ring that goes around it isn't very soft and can hurt your ear after less than 30 minutes. The noise cancellation does work, so if you buy these because you're around loud machinery or don't want to hear a screaming child next to you then they do their job. text: Summary: it is an extremely affordable earphone, that sounds great, very portable, feels sturdy, and has better sound quality than what you can get at the gas station or at your local retailers. What is it? This is what is referred to as an IEM or in-ear-monitor. It is different from an earbud in that it goes in your ear rather than hang on the ear. The advantage to this is that sound doesn't leak, you can listen to your content (ie. music, movies, phone calls, podcasts) without worrying if the person next to you will hear it too. Where is this product coming from? This product is sold by a reputable Chinese company who ships it to you at no extra cost. I have bought other products from this company with an overall positive experience. Although, tracking is no up to date through Amazon the tracking number provided can be searched on many websites such as 4PX or ParcelApps.com. It takes time for it to be shipped, but it has never taken more than a few weeks once it does; which considering from where it is coming from it's impressive. Who are they? Moondrop is a company that specializes in Chi-Fi (Chinese Fidelity), they are a company primarily focused on audio quality. For this same reason even though the Quarks feels light and plasticky, the cable feels smooth and everything about its design is deliberate. Why buy these? As mentioned, Moondrop, is a Chi-Fi company, even so it is shocking how well they sound for the price. They have no business sounding as good as they do. The bass is well controlled and won't rattle your head, the mids (instruments) sound clear and the highs (vocals) do not feel harsh on your ear drums. Because they are light they are easy to carrying around and do not irritate the ear like some of the larger earphones do. For their price they make for a great stocking stuffer, or even as back up earphones if you already have a good pair. I have praised them long enough, but they do deserve it. Moondrop knew what they were doing and their 2 years of research and development for this product shows. My only complaint is that due to their size they will fall of my ears, to be fair it is mostly the left side and I might need to change the size of ear tip. The build also feels cheap, again they cost $13 or $15 (with a mic), but they also feel durable even if you were to throw it around (please don't). I ordered a second pair with the microphone, when I ordered the first time that wasn't available, to use with my phone which still has a headphone jack. It is a good gift, for others or yourself, it is a great value for the sound quality at this price. Again, even as a backup earphone you will not regret buying it.

text: I am not a big music geek. I don't know what people mean by highs, lows, mids. I don't care. I will make this as simple and as layman as possible because that is all I know. This pair was mediocre at its best. A little headphone history before I start. In the past I have owned Moshi Vortex (my favorite pair ever) and Monster DNA (2nd favorite). I am very rough with my headphones so after about a year of use both of them fell apart. When I researched in-ear headphones, I decided to go with the pair with the highest Amazon rating. I looked it up, these looked the most attractive so I ordered it immediately. I looked at the reviews off of Amazon, they were not so great but they all praised the customer service. When it came in the mail, I opened the envelope, to my surprise, it was in a zip lock -ish bag. I didnt care because it was the sound that matters. I took it out of the case thats bigger than my phone itself, and there it was, the beautiful obsidian black color. The kevlar coating gave the wire an amount of stiffness that it almost looked like the wire was a living snake. It was beautiful to say the least. I was happy. So I plug it in and play some of my favorite artists as an inauguration ritual. Dance In The Dark by Lady Gaga I pick. My smile turns immediately to a frown. What? Why does the sound sound so.... 'warm'? I guess what I am trying to say is bass heavy. But it makes me feel uncomfortably warm on the inside. So I rush to the equalizer settings and turn it to Electronic to give it some treble. It is still pretty bassy but I guess I will settle for it. Professor comes into the class and I pack it away. After class, I am now walking back home. My ears hurt from how heavy the headpiece is. Reminds me of the Moshi I owned. But unlike Moshi, its not just the headpiece that's heavy, is the mic and the middle thingy with J4 on it as well. I guess I am going to have to use the clip huh? I use the clip and it restricts my head movement. Every time I try to look around, My headphone comes off or pull son my shirt. Later that night, I go out on a run, and the headpiece keeps getting displaced and trying to fall off while hurting my ear. Alright, I am done. I am ready to settle because I did make an impulsive decision, but not to THIS extent. So I returned it and accepted the financial penalty/fees. Music is an important part of my life and I need it the quality to be acceptable if not perfect. This was not acceptable. Tl;Dr Experience Level: Amateur Pros: Excellent build quality. Cons: Heavy head piece. Clip restricts head movement Bass heavy (not in a good way, in a treble damping, listening to music under water way)

text: Where to start...I researched online between these, the Bowers & Wilkins P5 Wireless and the Sennheiser Momentum Wireless and ended up purchasing the H8's due to their relatively good reviews and super looking design. I have the original Momentum wired headphones and love them but they are still a bit to plastic like and I don't like that they don't fold flat. When around your neck I like the headphones to rest flat against your body so you can easily move your head left and right without chin interference of the headphones. Upon arrival and unboxing I was very happy. These look and feel top notch in every way. I really liked the color combination, the brushed metal is gorgeous and also extremely important they looked great on my bald head while feeling comfortable. The style part is A+, no doubt about it. I have the Galaxy Note Edge and the bluetooth pairing was easy. The touch controls are average in functionality but a great idea. I had no trouble circling the ear cup for volume up and down, no trouble pressing the middle for play/pause but I had all kinds of trouble swiping up and down to activate and deactivate the noise cancelling function. It worked about every 5 swipes in either direction and more often than not paused the music instead of doing what it's supposed to. This part was very annoying. At this point I am still liking the headphones. Music playback initial impressions we very good. I played Today's New Hip Hop music station via Google Play Music and they sounded really good over bluetooth. Punchy bass and wonderful clarity, I couldn't ask for more...until I started walking. I'm a Realtor and like to listen to music while I measure a home and photograph it, makes the time involved more enjoyable. Having no wires to trip you up or get caught while moving around is even more enjoyable. So when I began to walk with these I noticed immediately a thumping sound that coincided with my steps. Surprised at first thinking it must be something simple or will go away and it never did. With each step I got a thumbing feedback through each ear cup and it ruined the experience. Sure if I cranked up the volume it overcame the thumping but for $500 this wasn't going to cut it. I asked for a replacement and one was sent out while I shipped these back. The 2nd set arrived and within 15 minutes the exact same thing was present. One reviewer who rated these very well said they aren't for walking about halfway through his review and had I known this I wouldn't have wasted my time. What's the point in my opinion to have a convenient bluetooth headphone if you have to remain stationary? I cannot recommend these for that reason alone. I will also add I experienced some pretty severe distortion during J. Cole's G.O.M.D. at 4:00 through the song. These are really gorgeous headphones but the odd thumping feedback while walking and their distortion are not acceptable for the price point. I think for now I will stick to wired until manufactures get the kinks worked out.

text: I wanted a physically robust headset with good Bluetooth range for teleconferencing calls (this is not an audiophile review). I owned or tried several other headsets before this one (Sony DR-BT50, JBL E50BT, Anker Soundcore Life Q20, V-Moda Crossfade Wireless), and ran into Bluetooth problems or physical disintegration with all of them. A lot of headsets rely on plastic bands being willing to flex indefinitely, but the plastic eventually crumbles. This Pioneer device is designed to flex. It has active noise cancellation, but I don't usually use it, because the passive cancellation is really pretty good, and obviously extends the battery life. Room for improvement: 1. The controls could be better. The giant easy-to-find button is for Google Assistant, which I am a dissenter from. The power button is also used to switch among modes. The device always turns on in noise-cancellation mode; to get it into "just headphones" mode takes two more presses, which elicit non-obvious beep codes. The three-way volume-down/call-control/volume-up button is arguably too close to the power button, and arguably the middle call-control nub feels too much like the power button. These controls are much less convenient than the four-way rocker panel that the JBL E50BT had. 2. This headset is not very nimble at switching connections. I use it with a phone, an Android tablet, and a laptop, and I basically need to disable Bluetooth on whichever two devices I am not using, and sometimes also need to power-cycle the Pioneer headset, in order to force it to connect to the device I want to use. Three months in, this seems like a reliable workhorse. Bluetooth range is quite good, battery life is quite good, and it seems like this headset will last years. Those are what matter most to me!

text: These are nice overall. I had to chuckle at all the reviews I read before purchasing where people were talking about putting the headphones in upside-down - and then complaining about the cables sticking up in the air. Hello? Don't turn them upside-down... Simply swap the right and the left and you'll accomplish the same thing while leaving the cords hanging down. This works very well for me because the headphones take a much lower profile and stay in my ears more securely (your mileage may vary). This reverse insertion technique also works particularly well when wearing these with my motorcycle helmet. The range is great, as is the noise isolation. Unfortunately, there is a lot of "thumping" to be heard when the cord bounces or rubs up against something. They ship a little clip that attaches the cord to your clothing, which should help mitigate the problem - although I'd rather not have to fuss with such a clip in my active lifestyle. All this said, I think these are about twice the price they should be. 2010 July 7 UPDATE: A few weeks ago, I noticed that the cord sheathing had pulled out of the connector, which exposed the wires. I had seen other reports of this in a review or two before I purchased, so this seems to be a known defect. Klipsch issued an RA and I shipped them back at my expense. They've had them for 1 1/2 weeks now. I just called for a status check. After waiting several minutes for the guy to get the information together, he told me that they're "set to release" but that it will be a FEW MORE WEEKS before they have more inventory!!!! No apology of any sort - just matter-of-fact. Even after I calmly told him how I felt about the situation, he remained unsympathetic. I deducted one star for the defect and resisted the urge to deduct another for the lousy customer service (because we rate the product, not the company, right?) 2010 Dec 23 UPDATE/TIP: The problem with the cord sheathing eventually occurred again with the replacement pair that I received. Clearly a manufacturing defect. When I first noticed it occurring this time, I remedied the issue by pushing the sheathing back into the connector as best that could, then applying a very very light bead of super glue where the connector/boot meets the cord sheathing. Your mileage may vary, but it's held up great for the past several weeks.

text: WOW, these were a disappointment. I have not previously sprung for Bose because they're so expensive. I expected that price came with some kind of audiophile level of quality, but these earbuds would not satisfy any audiophile. They sound like you'd expect from $10 earbuds at the grocery store. I have $15 Chinese G-Cord earbuds that sound much better than these. The earbuds that came with my phone sound much better than these. Bose's "StayHear" rubber tip design prevents the earbuds from going all of the way into your ear. The result is a drastic loss of bass, and mediocre mids/highs. Shifting the earbuds around can't solve this issue. I tried removing Bose's rubber tips and replacing them with more typical ones designed to fit snugly inside your ear. They stayed on better than Bose's "StayHear" tips, and gave me all of the bass - only, with regular tips, you get way TOO MUCH bass. It's clear that Bose tried to compensate for their bad tip design by drastically boosting the bass, but the end result is that these are never going to sound great no matter how you wear them. Save $85 and go with G-Skill; they'll fit better and sound better.

text: Just turn on your headphones, connect them like you would any other bluetooth device. I should note I was connecting it to my iPhone 10. They then prompt you to download the specific Bose app from the app store. I rejected the download to see if the headphones worked without the app, and they did. Sound quality and noise cancelling worked fine without downloading the app. I subsequently searched for the app on the app store, and the first one I downloaded worked. I then agreed to sign my life away to Bose, because everyone else owns it anyway. The only real perk of having the app is fine control of the noise cancelling—arguably unnecessary—and battery life monitoring. I chose not to set up the voice control with Alexa/Google because who wants to be that jerk yelling at their electronic devices in public. You know who you are. Stop it. I found the walk throughs on the app rather intuitive and the swiping mechanism is no more difficult than Mac swiping controls. My grandma would probably have difficulty with the touch commands, but anyone accustomed to touch computer interface should be fine. Sound is amazing. I'm not particularly complex when it comes to audio, but to my untrained ears these sound excellent. Did Bose try to pack to many bells and whistles into these? Maybe one or two, but you're not force to use them, unlike one angry reviewer on here falsely declared. Don't download the app and put these on over your tinfoil hat and no one will be able to track your important secret phone conversations. Looks great, sounds better.

text: I loved my old bebens I purchased in 2020 before they changed the listing to the faux airpod style so much. I was extremely disappointed when they were no longer available after delivering consistent quality for 2 years, but I decided to give these a chance because I needed a second set to switch out while working. The sound hits just the right amount of bass for decently loud music, but the longevity and quality just isn't there anymore. The 10$ price drop really shows. I didn't think it would be so different, I was sadly wrong. While charging, they will try to reconnect to whatever source they were last connected to, taking your audio randomly and repeatedly to the point of me having to remove the device from Bluetooth connections while charging. text: Summary: a well-designed pair with good sound quality and noise cancellation, a simple user experience, and solid build quality, but also a few very annoying choices and misleading marketing. These are comparable with the higher end Sennheiser (PXC-550, and HD-1) and Bose models (QC35), all of which I've tried. There's a lot of info on these headphones in other reviews, so I'll just add a few problems/details (conveniently?) not mentioned in the product description online. These were ultimately reasons for me to return this in favor of the [[ASIN:B01E3XLNA0 Sennheiser PXC 550 Wireless]]. My DEALBREAKERS: 1. NO SIMULTANEOUS CONNECTIONS TO TWO DEVICES - *PAINFUL* FOR APPLE USERS You can only really connect to one device at a time – with all the others I've tried you can connect your computer and phone at the same time, and phone calls and music just switch between devices seamlessly. This also means all available devices connect automatically on powering on the headphones. The H900Ns don't do this. You can indeed pair more than one device, but only one can be a "phone-call-capable" device: this is only really possible with Android devices and only after turning off music connectivity (i.e. A2DP) through the device settings. (Apparently Sony's rationale for this is that you can connect to a "music player" and a "smartphone" at the same time. I don't know how many people still have a dedicated bluetooth capable music player. You may be this unicorn). If you have an iPhone and/or Mac you can have to go through the rigmarole of disconnecting from one device and connecting to another, which is painful if you're using this headphones for both video chats on your computer and phone calls. On practically every other bluetooth audio product I've tried, attempting a connection on a second device disconnects from the first and switches to the second. This Sony pretends to successfully connect on the second device for half a second, then just fails silently. What this also means is that if you want to fine-tune the audio settings while playing audio from your computer or other device, you have to switch to and back from your phone. Fun! There is a downside to simultaneous connections: in an environment with lots of bluetooth signals you can get audio dropouts, and if this is your environment you'll find yourself with the opposite problem - having to constantly disconnect from connected devices. If this is you, the Sony is a great choice. 2. YOU CAN'T USE THESE WIRELESSLY WHILE CHARGING On one hand they have great battery life, but once you look at the real battery life numbers in their manuals it's not significantly different from the Bose or Sennheisers. Basically, all of them clock in between 20-24 hours of play time with NC on. If your primary use is as a wireless headphone, then the fact you can't use them while charging could get annoying. Sony doesn't make it clear if you can use the mics while connected through an audio cable in order to be able to take a phone call while charging. I couldn't be bothered to test this to find out. 3. THE AUDIO ENHANCEMENTS ARE MISLEADING You do have access to some fine-tuning using the Sony Headphones Connect app, BUT - the spatial enhancements (VPT) are only available when using the lower quality SBC mode, which kind of defeats the purpose of having aptX and AAC compatibility. When turning on the spatial enhancements the app forces the connection to SBC. - Sony claims to have technology that upsamples (or something) lower quality MP3 audio (encoded at more than 248k) such that it is equivalent to high quality audio (i.e. near lossless and/or studio quality sampling). BUT this cannot be used simultaneously with the equalizer or spatial enhancements. Since most audio at 248k or above is pretty decent already, this feature is meaningless for most people who are not audiophiles, and if you do a web search for "Sony DSEE HX" you'll realize even the audiophiles don't seem to understand what this is. And Sony doesn't explain it at all on their manual or help pages. PROs, or small things I liked about this I wished were on other headphones 1. Tap the power button to have battery level announced at any time. The Senns can only do that when not playing audio. 2. Double tap to play/pause (is less twitchy than the Sennheiser PXC 550 I tried) 3. Cover the right headphone to temporarily reduce music and bring in outside sound 4. The volume up gesture is done right: drag and hold up and it keeps increasing the volume 5. The app allows you to determine whether you want sound quality (aptX etc.) or connection stability (SBC). Ideally the headphones should just do the right thing, but if you're having bluetooth connection issues then this setting might make all the difference. 5. The headband on these is the most comfortable I've tried, with the Bose a close second. 6. The buttons and the touch controls are on different sides, so you don't accidentally play or disconnect calls while you're trying to adjust NC or check battery. SOUND and NC QUALITY: Sound: - great sound! Noticeably better than the Bose; the Sennheisers sound more balanced and less punchy than these but you really can't fault the sound. Minor, but annoying – this is the only of the four headphones to NOT come with an airplane adapter. Noise cancellation: I tried really hard to believe that these cancel more sound than the PXC 550s but I was hard pressed to tell any real difference.

text: Anker got a lot of things right with the Soundcore Liberty 2 Pro. But some of the really big things just aren't good enough. First, setup was a bit fiddly. For some reason my iPhone 11 Pro (iOS 13.1.3) Bluetooth only found "Soundcore Liberty 2 Pro-L" which I assume meant the left earbud, though both left and right worked fine after pairing. That was a bit strange. Eventually, it showed both Soundcore Liberty 2 Pro and Soundcore Liberty 2 Pro-L in the Bluetooth settings. Deleting the "L" version made no difference to functionality, and the earbuds both worked. I'm pleased to see that the set reports its battery life (of the earbuds) to the iPhone. However, you don't see each earbud individually in the iOS battery widget or in control center - just the pair (what I assume is an average). If you download the Soundcore app it will show you both earbuds individually. After the setup, you'll still want to use the Soundcore app to tailor the EQ. I found bass booster to be the best for my particular ears, even with the largest inserts to ensure a tight seal in my ear. The bass isn't overpowering to me on this setting at all, though it might be for some depending on their ear shape. e.g. I can push the earbuds further into my ears (they don't stay there when I let go), and the bass is way more intense. So I imagine ear shape is going to play a massive factor here. But there are issues: 1.) These are fatiguing. There's no getting around it for me - if I'm using the larger inserts to ensure a tight seal and a semblance of bass, they fatigue my ears in ways the AirPods don't. Yes, the music quality etc is a little "better" with these over the AirPods, but AirPods I can wear all day and not be bothered. These? 20 minutes is hard work. Even after trying multiple different sizes and types, I couldn't find any inserts that worked for me without fatigue. 2.) The biggest issue: the "static" sound. I have absolutely no idea why these behave like there's ANC (active noise cancelling) present, because there isn't. On quieter pieces you're always aware of the static sound if you're sensitive to it (and probably even if you're not) and in between tracks it's really present. Pausing a song/movie etc, and the static goes away after a few seconds (a form of earbud sleep mode, no doubt - to conserve battery). I've no idea what's going on here, but I don't like it. Not one bit. 3.) Phone call quality. I tried using these for a Skype and FaceTime call, and the quality is truly dreadful. First, because your ears are "plugged" by these earbuds, you'll find yourself talking too loudly anyway, and it's just not comfortable to talk with your ears plugged, either. Second, phone voices are presented to you in tinny fashion, and callers on the other end said I sounded tinny/thin, too. Switching back to AirPods is revelatory for phone calls, either WiFi-based or cellular, for both me and my callers. These Anker earbuds are hopeless (in my testing) for phone calls of any sort. Both earbuds have a microphone, but there's no beamforming between then that I could tell. With both in, I found that only the left earbud's mic was active. 4.) Connection stability: Zero issues staying connected to my iPhone 11 over many hours. 5.) Case quality and charging: I like that you can wireless Qi charge the case/earbuds or charge via the USB Type-C to USB A cable (included). Also, I love the way the earbuds magnetize themselves into the case (like AirPods). This is very satisfying, as is the sliding mechanism to open and close the case. The case is much, much bigger than the AirPods case (over twice as large when you take into account height and width). 6.) iOS integration: I really like how you can pull an AirPod out of your ear, and the music etc pauses. Super great if someone needs to talk to you. No such integration with the Ankers. Overall, I prefer the AirPods by far. Contrary to the popular opinion, AirPods actually sound pretty darn great for what they are - (and no, they do NOT sound the same as wired EarPods, which are not great at all). For some, the Anker set will do it better, but for me they don't in pretty much any way. While many of my issues are subjective, the static sound really isn't, and this was a major deal killer for me even before anything else. 3 stars out of 5. OK.

text: The VAVA MOOV are light and comfortable truly wireless ear buds. In the box it has the charging cable, user manual, varying size earbuds, and headset. The packaging is designed well to fit the headset with an additional box nested with the charging cable, extra ear buds, and manual. The units powered right up when received and I used for a few minutes before charging. It takes about an hour to charge and you get roughly 3 hours of playtime. I did read about the total playtime, but was still a bit shocked when it required recharge so soon. My other wired headsets get 8-10 hours before recharge. Pairing via Bluetooth is simple, but varies a bit from standard Bluetooth set up. You start with the main receiver (right earbud), when that is paired you power on the left and it syncs with the other ear bud. If the main receiver loses signal, the other will go out as well. Music sound is very clear with rich sound. Phone call clarity is good on my end and I am told it sounds kind of tinny on the other. Connection range is very impressive. I used them at work so I would only keep the left one in place so I can use the phone or converse with co-workers using my right ear. I walked ~60 feet away and still had reception in the left bud. It started to break up after that. I do many training runs with walk intervals. I don’t have much issue with them staying in place during the walks, but always feel like I need to adjust and keep pushing back into my ear during the run intervals. Always on guard to catch one as it jiggles out during the run. I was hoping to use during bike rides, but not going to risk losing one or both on the ride. Each bud has its own multifunction button for power, volume control, forward, and back. You will need to review the instructions and practice a bit to get the controls down. One side will control volume up and forward, the other will control volume down and back. You also have control to initiate a phone call if you are not listening to music. Overall, this is a nice set of truly wireless Bluetooth headphones and a good way to break into this technology. If battery life were longer, would get 5 star. Tested with Apple and Android products.

text: I've had the Soundcore Q35's for about a year now, and I remember that WOW! factor when I first put them on and firing up Amazon Unlimited music with the upgraded HD Amazon music service. When you combine Amazon's HD upgraded streaming with the Q35's and using LDAC (high res streaming service both headphones are capable of) its a winning combination. What really impresses me so much about the Q35's are the punchy, well-defined bass combined with very clean mids and highs. Oh, and they get plenty loud enough though one should use common sense and keep loudness in a safe zone as to not damage one's ears. Okay, so on to the new Soundcore Q45's. For me, no wow factor. The bass, even with my phone tuned to LDAC codec is just flat. Even after custom tuning the equalizer to my liked settings, just not enough bass. Now, that's not all. If you go on YouTube, you'll find a lot of influencers who review the Q45's as having a "more balanced sound" with a "natural bass response". Well for me, that translates to boring. The Q45 sound quality, overall, just sounds a bit more muddy to me. I was really surprised, thinking they'd be at least a modest sound upgrade. I was not expecting anything substantial being that the Q35's and 45's have the same size drivers, but I did hope for a modest upgrade. Also, they just don't seem to get quite loud enough even with tweaking my smartphone to allow louder sound. What I will say positive about the Q45's is the earcups seem a little bit larger and the ear cushions just a bit softer. Sadly though, after a few hours of tinkering with all the settings and equalizer, I finally decided I'm going back to my awesome Q35's. I'll be returning the Q45's for the main reason as actually inferior sound to the Q35's. Final thoughts are if you already have the Q35's and sound is the most important thing, I'd stick to your Q35's. If you purchase the Q45's never having any of their previous headphones, you might be quite happy with them. I just feel you can actually spend less (purchasing the Q35's) and get superior sound vs. the Q45's which cost more and get inferior sound. These are just my thoughts.

I got all these things and I'm pleased with the purchase. Connectivity was seamless. Sound quality is excellent for my purposes. Sound adjustment is easy too as is accessing the microphone. But best of all, these buds stay secured in my ears during workouts, walks, hikes, whatever. With the Bose earbuds I was constantly picking them up off the gym floor and sidewalk and I was sure they would be lost down a storm drain before long. But not with these ZIUTY Wireless Earbuds. 3 different rubber bud inserts come with the buds - the medium size came installed and that size works fine for me. The bud case is well constructed and a lit battery life indicator scale on the outside of the case is very helpful. My buds came well charged. I've had these earbuds for several weeks now and use them daily and this week was the first time I charged them, which was also seamless. So, if you are looking for an easy-to-use, good quality pair of everyday wireless earbuds at a great price, I don't think you'll be disappointed with buying a pair of these ZIUTY Wireless Earbuds. I recommend them.

text: **Update June 2021** I originally purchased these in October 2020, and they worked well for about 4 months when one of the earhooks broke off. I used them lightly, and was not rough with them, especially for earbuds that are designed for use during exercise. I used them in general listening situations, and rarely for exercise. Customer service was responsive and offered to replace them in warranty, and asked only that I send back the broken ones at my cost. I agreed and received a replacement pair which I have used since February. Now, 4 months after receiving the replacements, another earhook from the replacement pair has broken off, and I have to conclude that the plastic earhook design is weak and prone to breakage. All my statements below in the original review still stand, but if you are considering buying these earbuds, you should not expect them to only last more than I few months. For less than $15, it's not so bad a loss, but it's a little sad from an e-waste perspective. Given their tendency to break, I cannot recommend them any longer. ---Original Review--- My ideal earbuds are truly wireless, have decent sound quality, comfortable, don't fall put, and most importantly, do not seal or block my ear canal creating that unpleasant stuffed up sensation that makes all talking and chewing really loud while wearing them. These earbuds are they closest to that ideal that I've tried it date. Even the galaxy buds live, which claim to be "open" and they rest in your ear, but don't go into the canal, still give you that stuffed up feeling of an in-ear bud. The part that goes in your ear is are shaped like the regular airpods, and does not seal fully. The earhook is fairly comfortable and keeps them from falling off. At times, the earbud part does shift and slide in my ear a bit, which does mean I have to adjust them to get the best audio quality, but it's pretty minor. The buds themselves come with a removable silicon cover or boot that goes over the part that goes in your ear. Some have complained that the buds are too big for their ears, so removing that may help in that situation. However, I found the covers to be helpful in keeping the earbuds from moving around too much, since they help to grip the skin better than the smooth plastic of the uncovered earbud. Sound quality is decent, but there is a noticeable static hiss for a few seconds before and after the audio starts playing. I don't notice it when the audio is actually playing though. I have worn these for an hour or two at a time, and they have been perfectly comfortable. I've used them with and without glasses without any problems. The only comparable product I've seen is the skullcandy push ultra true. But they normally go for more than double the cost of these. For me, aside from a few audio quality gripes, these have been great for me. Keep in mind that the case for these is twice the size compared to something like airpods or galaxy buds. So it's not going to win any awards for portability. Obviously, if audio quality is your number one priority, and the sealing sensation is not a big deal to you, you should go with a set of sealing buds that go into your ear canal since that will give you better noise isolation, blocking out outside sounds and providing better sound quality. That is the more common design so you have plenty of options and choices for that.

text: I have had these phones for about 10 months. From first listen, I was not blown away. They have a delicate sound to them like they were made to play wind chimes and flutes all day. The bass is scared to come out and play. Its there but with no authority whatsoever. I tried pushing more than 100mw through these things at the 20-40 hz range and they protest with awful harmonic distortion. The mids are clean. The highs are a bit elevated and slightly unbalanced. I (sometimes) use for mixing and mastering. Unfortunately these don't give me a super clear picture of the bass region. My work typically contains a lot of bass down to the 20hz range and I need cans that can reproduce this with as much power and clarity as the rest of the freq range. The results are decent. An engineer working on other types of music may find these more acceptable. I would suggest using these as a step in the mixing process when you need to listen critically at low low volumes. The build quality is above par. I like the cable with volume control and the leatherette ear pads seems nice for this price point as well. These are the phones that your gonna put back in the box when your not using them because you don't wanna scratch them up. . You might occasionally wipe them down with the included cloth, then you will forget you own them for a few months. I bought these really to complement my KRK Studio monitors. The monitors have bigger balls than the headphones. If you play your tunes quietly, don't yearn for ballsy bass, like it a little bright, you may like these. they do sound nice overall but they are not perfect. I am going to keep these, but more as a trophy than a tool. KRK's first headphones. $150 dollars for some headphones. My friends wouldn't do that.

text: For the price, these are a good set of earbuds. Just that there are some lingering issues with the headphones. I am on my second pair of earbuds. Anker's customer service is top notch, is the reason I purchased these in the first place. Both sets of earbuds have had issues charging after a few months of use. I clean them every week or so, to make sure that the contacts touch in the case and will continue charging. The first pair of earbuds, the right ear stopped taking a charge. I cleaned the contacts on both the earbuds and the charging case and I could never get the light to flash to indicate a charge was being made. This is where the customer service comes in. I'm sure they get a lot of contacts and you do need go through a few steps before a new pair is sent to you. They sent me a new pair and these have lasted about 2 months longer than the first pair and I am now having issues charging the left earbud on the second set. Which is fine since the right earbud is the one that pairs to the device. It looks like I will need to go a different direction on my next earbud purchase. I was hoping for as much as I use these (maybe 3 times a week) I could get a couple years of use out of it. It's unfortunate. 4/15/2020 EDIT: Anker reached out to me and offered a replacement pair of earbuds. This gains them another star to put it to 3 stars. Although the product is great out of the box, the issues with the previous 2 pairs lie within 3-5 months of use. This updated pair does seem to offer a bit more grasp in the charging case. Also the contacts are inset a little bit on the earbud, which I have noticed that is different from the other pairs I have received. Let me sweat in these things for a few more months and I will reevaluate my review then. I also want to reiterate that their customer service is top notch. This is a top reason I purchase their products.

text: Let me start with telling how long these should last for in my experience with 3 of them thus far: about a year and a half tops DEPENDING on if they get snagged on something or pulled a few to many times in the wrong direction. 2 of my 3 (i intend to get more) after know experienced an issue where only one of the 2 earbuds plays audio now with one playing for both ears if i screw with the cords angle a bit. This does NOT mean they are bad in anyway, it just means this will happen EVENUALLY and you should keep spares on hands for when it occurs. This also have 2 semi-annoying issues that happen often, 1 being even if you stop listening to something for like half a second they will disconnect for a few seconds (i voice tells you this and when its connected or pairing) than reconnects but it can be irritating just to note especially when you try to play your music/audio afterwards and it won't play via you clicking the button on the set OR it takes 5-10 seconds to register the push happened (not all the time mind you but sometimes). The second issue is randomly with all of them the audio semi-glitches as if you aren't close enough to the device its linked with (it will stutter if you are around 10-15 feet away SOMETIMES for a short period of time or randomly play perfectly find when your like 30 feet away for around 1 and a half minutes before it realizes your not close by and cut in and out), like even when its right in your pocket you'll be jamming to a song and it will gabble for a few milliseconds like your only half way plugged into the earbud socket if it had a cord. Its not a MAJOR annoyance but its something to keep in mind. An issue users may have is with it charging. If you have the right cord and make sure its not charging at a werid angle you should be good, but what constitutes as a "good cord" got confusing for me when my cords work for about everything else fine. I'd suggest having a separate cord it doesn't come with around JUST IN CASE else you'll hear it say its still got a low battery. The charge on these from what i can tell will last for around 9 to 9 and a half hours if you let it go until its fully dead that is and not just when it says its low. text: I have all four Pioneer Bass Exciter headphones. CX7, CX8, CX9 and CL751. Pioneer claims this has a Bass Exciter 2. It's the same thing as Bass Exciter 1. The only thing that really changes between these headphones as far as the bass exciter goes, is how much rumble the bass exciter provides. In that case, all four are different. CX8 is the loudest, CX9 is the second loudest, CX7 gets third and CL751 gets quietest but it's still plenty loud and it is also the cheapest option here. In terms of sound/feel, the bass exciter is the EXACT same thing. Bass Exciter, Bass Exciter 2...same thing. Just different amounts of rumble. Technically, this should be Bass Exciter 4. Since they all sound a tiny bit different in terms of amount of rumble. Now onto the actual headphones overall, the CX7 is the newest one, it sits in between CL751 and CX8 on the Bass Exciter model chain. But the CL751 is extremely cheap at $35-$65. While the CX8 is also cheaper at this point for what I feel is better bass exciter quantity and equal overall sound quality. The overall sound is nearly the same. In terms of overall volume....CX7 is the quietest of the bunch. I had to put the volume knob very high to get these to be as loud as the other ones. Now as far as build quality, CX8 and CX9 are virtually identical. CX7 loses to them in every way except the cord. The cord was improved, made smaller, less stereophonics but it is not detachable unlike CX8/CX9. The CX7 is overall better than the CL751 as far as build quality however. Right now the price of these is simply because they are new and imported from Japan. Newer isn't always better. Get a CX8 which is the loudest at the best price right now with virtually the same sound, same Bass Exciter gimmick. Get a CX8 and be done with it. You get better quality all around. The CX8 has a detachable cable, the CX7 doesn't. CX8 is cheaper, CX7 is more expensive. Bass Exciter 2 is just a lie. I think the choice is clear. Unless these go on an extreme sale of less than a hundred dollars. Just go with the CX8 or even the inferior but much cheaper CL751. It's just more sensible. There is nothing here to make the CX7 worth it at this point. This will be my last Pioneer earphone though. They are all too similar to really be worth owning any more. Their false advertising has also turned me off their earphone brand.

text: I bought these at bestbuy, where I think these are exclusively available. I'm posting this review because it was very hard to find reviews of these buds, and I'm looking to help out anyone whose interested in trying these out. First of all, they do sound very good. I think they have great bass response, if you're into that. I normally have the bass on my phone's equalizer set to high, but with these I had to turn it down all the way. Sometimes, there's still too much bass, so if you don't like bass (muddy perhaps, though i'm not an audiophile), then you won't like these buds at all. Fit is pretty good too. The buds include lots of fit options, including foam and silicone covers, and I ran with them for three miles and they didn't budge. With that said, the reason why I'm giving them three stars is: [1] battery life; [2] bad connection; and [3] the charging case. Battery life is poor. Websites reported four hours, but the box only said three. I just got a 20% battery warning after using them for an hour and five minutes. I'm assuming they were completely charged, because they were in the case and the case was charged, but there's no way of knowing how much battery life is left because neither the buds nor the case have a battery level indicator. I'm shocked that they omitted this. Anyway, such short battery life is borderline useless to me, and that's the main reason why i'm returning them. As for the connection, walking through city streets my the buds lost a connection to each other and my phone often when i turned my head. It also didn't matter which side of my body my phone was on. So that was annoying. The charging case is HUGE! its like three times the size of the samsung gear iconx 2018 case, and four times the size of the apple airpods. There's no way the case would comfortably fit in my pants pocket, so that sucks too. Some last points, you can use the left earbud while the right one is in the charging case, but you can't use the right one with the left bud in the case. Finally, I knew that the buds only had four controls on them, power on, play/pause, and voice assistant, but not having a way to change volume or play the next song seems kinda silly. I could live without these controls, but why??? (You're supposed to be able to reject a call too, but I couldn't get that to work).

text: They're fine headphones. They do what they're supposed to and the optional noise cancellation is really convenient and effective. You are going to drown in the music in the best possible way. JBL has a reputation for amazing sound quality, and these headphones aren't any exception. The over-the-ear design is really comfortable for extended listening. I could sit at my desk all day with them on and have no discomfort whatsoever. And this means a lot to me because my ears are physically sensitive (like wearing facemasks can get uncomfortable after an two hours and painful after three). I really don't like that they will disconnect themselves from my phone or laptop at random points in time. It disrupts my listening experience and I can't figure out why this happens/how to stop it. These headphones also have blips of no sound when you move around in them too hard. This stinks because I'll turn the volume up and jam out, just to be in and out of sound when I headbang. The headphones have added bass to them that REALLY kicks. As a music listener, I love them! As a music producer, I hate them. Definitely wouldn't suggest this for music producers and audio engineers because the enhancements can't be changed and you won't hear the audio as it was created to sound. I would really wish that these headphones could auto-power-off themselves after being idle for some time. The battery last for a very long time, but it's no point if I go to use them and realize they've been on for the last 6 hours. You'd be surprised how easy it is to leave the headphones on when you think you'd come back to them later. It makes me nervous because the way I keep draining them will decline the battery life quicker. The fold-in design isn't really practical for me. It should have a little bit of resistance when you want to fold them in, to make sure users are intentionally folding them when they want to. If you just hold the headphones, the ear pieces just dangle since there isn't any resistance. It makes them look frail and easy to break. I don't like that. For what they do audio-wise, it is worth the money. You will like how they sound. For the tech engineering and design, more bad than good for me. Enough to not recommend them to others, but not enough to immediate replace them myself. If I were you, I would look for some higher-end JBL products. They'll more likely be built better than these and have the same sound quality (if not better).

text: There's no doubt these can't possibly compete with the ATH-M50x (which I also own and unreservedly recommend), but for about $120 less, these will do just fine for casual (or disposable) listening. In my case, I ordered them for a trip overseas where, if I lost or broke them, I wouldn't cry. But dang, these are mighty, mighty fine for their price point. Comfort: A -- no complaints. These don't have velvet earcups or cushioned headbars, but you won't miss them. You'll always vaguely know they're on your head, but you won't mind--at all. Sound: Great for rock and pop. A fairly narrow soundstage (think just barely outside your ears, but no wider); however, a clear, punchy, well-balanced presence. Nothing supersonic, but pleasant and middle-of-the-road. Solidly central. For benchmarks, "Only You" by Yaz is perfectly balanced--vocals and percussion in the middle, synth dancing beautifully across the stage; "Bend and Break" by Keane is lusciously all over the place, as it should be--vocals just left of center, beats as well, with flourishes left to right and deep of center. Gorgeous, and perfectly balanced. Sting's "Jeremiah Blues" hits you perfectly from left to center to right, but without the sensuous depth and breadth of more expensive alternatives. Classical music fails on these headphones. They just don't have the depth of expression. The instruments are almost all at center. Unpleasant and harsh. Jazz does slightly better. But only slightly. You're still presented with the instruments at mostly center. No soundstage to speak of. "So What" by Miles Davis is an uninspired assault. No depth, no layers. Just intense sound--gorgeous sound, but dense and heavy and in your face, with barely marginal expressions. Treble: Fine. Less than perfectly crisp, but not at all mushy. Mids: Okay. I would have liked vocals with more authority, but reduced just a tad behind the instrumental layer. Bass: Definitely lacking, but not unpleasant. There's no profound density here, but with the right equalization, you should find the sweet spot. In a nutshell: Depth is mediocre; tonality is decent; sonic balance is excellent. As volume increases, quality diminishes, as is to be expected for middle-of-the-road cans. Price: Holy moly, at $29, totally worth it. Nothing to brag about, but at this price, absolutely no complaints, either.

text: The quality of the stereo signal is excellent. However, depending on the input source, you must sometimes make sure that you have the sound source set to a VERY HIGH volume (or the "hiss" that others have mentioned will be more pronounced). The "hiss" that is experienced with this headset can be described as a kind of windy sound that's added to the transmitted sound. It kind of sits far in the background of all other sounds. It doesn't distort the signal, it's just very distracting at times. It's an indication that the input signal isn't at high enough of a volume. An example of input sources; Connecting to my PC required me to adjust the PC sound output to a VERY high level. Connecting directly to the RCA outputs on my DVD player delivered excellent sound. I also purchased the Acoustic Research AW722 headphones as a comparison. There is less of an issue with "hiss" with the AW722, but the RCA headphones are more comfortable AND in my opinion deliver more of a FULL stereo sound (when configured correctly). Also, the AW722 has the WORST battery recharging method I have ever seen (induction). They stopped recharging properly within one day of owning them, meaning that you will have to resort to charging the batteries using an external charger. An interesting note; The AW722 headphones (Acoustic Research) will work with the RCA transmitter (because the headphones can be manually tuned). Tuning the AR headphones to the RCA transmitter did not exhibit ANY hiss, which leads me to believe that the "hiss" on the RCA headphones is caused by the receiver in the headset. If you already own the AR headphones, you might find it usefull to know that you can still use them with the RCA transmitter (at the same time as the RCA headset if you wish). There are certainly better wireless headphones out there, but if you get a good price on these (in the $10-$20 range), you'll probably find them to be fairly decent. JM

text: [[VIDEOID:2b283c0a6c6a8631ff05fffbbdc7358c]] The Beats Studio by Dr. Dre are amazing over-ear headphones. They provide great comfort, very good sound, and the ultimate style in head phones. Having said that, they need to be great headphones, because they are faaarrrrr from cheap. There are plenty of options for shoppers including Bose (which I am not a fan of), Sennheiser (such as the HD238 - which I feature in the review), Sony MDR-NC200D (which I have not tried), Sennheiser PXC 450 NoiseGard, VModa, Nyrius, Audio Technica ATH-ANC7B - just to mention a few options. Having mentioned those competitors, I am sure you will agree that the Beats Studio by Dr. Dre deserve your attention. My Observations - Very good sound - just short of great. Clearly, the Beats Studio have great bass that is both deep and clean. The result is bass that has extraordinary depth. It is difficult to explain, but it is the difference from being in a room surrounded by speakers compared to standing in front of a speaker. The high range sounds good, but it is not exceptional. Therefore, I give sound quality a 8 out of 10. - Noise canceling - Very effective at canceling out all ambient noise. This allows the listener to completely disengage for their environment regardless of their location. You can wear the Beats Studio on a plane with no fear of hearing engine noise.One thing to mention s that the noise canceling seems to require music playing through them (not a big deal) 9.5 out of 10 - Comfort - The Beats Studio wear lighter than their actual weight. The headphone cups completely enclose you ear, and are so comfortable that you forget that you are wearing them. 10 out of 10 -Durability - The headband seems very well constructed, in fact everything about the Beats Studio seem to be top-notch. 10 out of 10 - Phone compatibility - I can't speak for anything but iPhone, but the Beats Studio work great with the iPhone. The headphones offer great clarity for the listener, and the microphone works much better than the typical headphone mic - most sound like your driving in a car (regardless of your location) this is not the case with the Beats Studio. However, to be honest, this is not that important of a feature for me. 10 out of 10 Value - The Beats Studio are super comfortable, very good sounding, and allow the listener to completely disengage from their environment.. however, is that enough to justify the selling price.... for me it is still debatable

First, remove the requirement to create a login before you can use it. I can’t really see any reason this is necessary, so it just seems like kind of a grab for personal info. It also doesn’t have a native UI for iPad, so it displays smaller iPhone UI on the screen, and forces my iPad into portrait mode which is super duper weird when I’m using the iPad with an Apple keyboard. Outside of that, the app does what it’s supposed to and lets you control the noise cancellation features, and select amongst several preset EQ curves or create your own custom EQ settings. text: Like others I had the Jaybird Bluebuds X - what people call the X1 - and I loved them. They died on me after over three years and I wear these things every day in all weathers so for me, anything over a year is good. They were great - with one issue, being that they stuck out from the ear so in the winter I couldn't use them under ear protection, or on a plane if I wanted to sleep. In 2013 that was state of the art though. I'd been waiting to see what Apple would do, and I like a proper seal so expect I won't love the AirPods. There will be the Beats X, but I thought the battery pods at the collar would just snag on clothing - and they also stick out from the ear. (And they're not yet available.) So I got these. As others report, I have used every bud type - and they include Comply tips now too - and still getting a perfect fit has been elusive. The weight of the controller is also an issue - I don't find it pulls out of my ear but it does drag the cable behind my neck. That's fit. The build quality seems excellent, with the earbuds themselves and parts of the controller being metal. They look good. I find the sound good though it seems obsessed with its own app and customizing the EQ. In practice, I have found I like the bass-heavy sound because it compensates for the less-than-perfect seal, though that's really one compromise fixing another. The other thing is that the volume range is narrow, and also has steps: for podcasts I always feel I have to choose between not quite loud enough and too loud. It is not the same as the wired phones, or the old X1s. I actually thought I would like the battery clip as I had in mind long flights: it seemed like a good way to have the battery when I needed it, but not when I didn't. The problem is that the charger connects to this battery, not the earphones, so most of the time this works as a base station, connected to the charger. I don't really like charging a battery indefinitely, and I setting the earphones in the clip needs to be precise: it's just a bit fiddly, for something you need to do at least every day. It makes sense now I see it but I had assumed that the phones would be charged directly - and this means I can't plug them in to charge at work for example, as I don't want to carry around the little battery pack. In practice I find battery life is fine so it's not an issue, but it will be towards the end of their life when the battery no longer holds enough charge - this is inevitable. My conclusion is that Bluetooth earphones are in a difficult space: becoming mass market, and with requirements from consumers for no cut-outs, great battery life, and a slim profile. The state of the art isn't there. But for a list price of $149, there is not enough in these to justify the premium over some probably rubbish non-name earphones to tide you over till the next generation. I didn't return them because I wasn't convinced that any competing product would be better, but that is not a recommendation.

text: I've had these ear buds for about 3 weeks and so far, they are fantastic. While I'm not an audiophile, I like my music to bump and not sound like a tin can. My current headphones/earbuds are Sennheiser HD25 Aluminum DJ Headphones, Ultimate Ears Triple-fi 10, PowerBeats 2, and now the Samsung IconX. I primarily use my headphones/earbuds for the gym, work, and as a headset when talking on the phone. The music source was my Note 7 :( and now using my replacement S7 Edge using the following apps; PowerAmp for mp3s, Amazon Music for mostly every type of genre, and occasionally iheartradio. After the initial use, I found a firmware update. Upon the update, I didn't notice anything but at least it's current. IconX PROS: 1) Unique (truly wireless) - first time out in the gym and two people stopped me and asked what they were. 2) Sound - Not bad.. I ordered comply foam tips for these since that's what I had on my other ear buds which improved the sound/loudness. Also when used as a headset for phone calls, the other party says I sound clear. 3) Fit and comfort - headset doesn't hurt my hears after an hours use and most importantly it doesn't fall off. 4) Comes with a portable rechargeable dock for a quick recharge. 5) IconX app is pretty intuitive and allows you to select which notifications you want read. 6) Range - my powerbeats2 barely reached the three point line in my gym.. Today I tested the IconX and it easily reached full court. 7) SHealth integration Cons: 1) Priced at $200 is a bit much. I think the perfect price for this item is $149.99 with a sale price of $99-$129. 2) Not a fan of all of the touch controls. Keep it simple with pause/play and answer/hangup.. not a deal breaker for me. 3) Not a fan of dual volume controls. The icon app has it's own separate volume control for the ear buds. Perhaps I missed something since I never read the instructions, but wished there the phones volume rocker was the only way to control the volume.

text: I bought the Black Sennheiser Urbanite XL Galaxy. Starting out with the bad: -Description claims "Massive Bass" but, unless you set the equalizer to rev up the bass and you play a song with extremely heavy bass, you will not feel the vibrations of it. Either that's a misleading claim, or I interpreted "Massive Bass" in a completely different way. -On the images provided, the volume/mic/play&pause control looks like it will be facing towards the inside of the headphones. The ones that I received have this apparatus facing the outside. Although that does not affect performance, I think it's an aesthetic issue. -Whenever I use them with my Galaxy S3 cell phone, I need to constantly push down on the rubber base that is on the jack that connects to the phone to create diagonal pressure that will force the jack to touch the receptor on the phone, otherwise there will be no sound on the right side headphone. Surprisingly enough, I used it with my 3rd Generation iPod Touch and it played just fine; however, I can't blame the phone as I've recently used headphones/earbuds brand Bose, Beat, Skullcandy and Yurbuds and they all worked without a problem. On to the good: -Clear sound, actually better than the Beats. Listened to songs that I've listend to for years and I heard new "hidden" soudns that I had never heard before. It just lacks bass. -The twist-in feature for connecting the cord to the headset is a 75/25. It prevents the cord from coming out of the headphones whenever the cord gets stuck somewhere, so there is no interruption to your music. Bad thing is that I'm pretty sure that one day the force might be too great and I might break something. -The aesthetics of the headphones are conservative. Black on white without excessively big logos or designs. On the left side there are three bumps in the shape of dots to help you figure out which is the left side and, by process of elimination, the right side, without having to look for the letters. Pretty useful if you are in a dark place. Overall: 3 Stars Reason: 1) Claim of "Massive Bass" when the bass is loud enough to be heard with a complete lack of the vibrations caused by bass. 2) The cord, but that's more to my personal experience. For all I know, I received a faulty erroneously produced cord. I have already opened a ticket with Sennheiser and hopefully they will answer soon and they'll be able to get me a replacement cord.

text: I've had these for almost a month and have mixed feelings. The sound quality is superb. Listening to these after my last $65 earbuds was a revelation. Over time my ears have adjusted to the quality, but I doubt I could ever listen to cheap earbuds again. That said, I do think they feel very fragile. The earpiece itself is milled aluminum and seems to be very high quality, and is comfortable. The cord, remote and plug are not substantial at all. With only one months use I have not had any actual issues, but I have suspicions about their durability. The remote is my only serious complaint. The design is quite poor if you use the skip song or call answer functionality as I do. The problem is that the remote has a single flat button that "tips" one way another to change volume. You need to press this button straight down to pause, play or answer calls. This is quite finicky to do, as the button really wants to tip, not go straight down. It's hard enough to do once, but you have to do it twice in a row to skip a song, or three times to go back. This is nearly impossible. You end up raising or lowering the volume, or pausing, or some combination of the two. If you don't use the remote for this then you will have no issues, but if you do it's quite infuriating. Just bad design. I gave them 4 stars because they really do sound fantastic and that's what most people want in expensive earbuds. The durability concerns are only a suspicion. As I have had no actual problems yet it's not justified to rate them poorly for this. I will update the review if problems do develop in the future. The remote really is a terrible design and this failure is reflected in the rating. I hope this helps some of you who are considering this purchase.

text: As other reviewers have noted, the sizing/adjustability/fit and comfort on the KPH14 is nowhere near as good as on the sadly discontinued Sony MDR-W08s which I think many of us would rather buy. 1) The KPH14s are much less compliant, stiffer, in width than the Sony product. So they poke into your ears pretty firmly. I've worn one pair or another of the W08s for hours at a time for years without really noticing they were there. I don't think I could do that with these as they become irritatingly tight in minutes. This pressure might make them better for running in the sense that they won't come off (but not in the sense of they will be comfortable); I can't say for sure because I don't use them that way. 2) The KPH14s are much less adjustable in size than the Sony product. At max extension, they barely fit me and I'm sure I don't have a 95th percentile head. By contrast, I wear the W08s at about half of their extension range. I'd wear the KH14s one notch further out if they had that notch. (Attached images show first, comparison at the extension I wear the MDR-W08s and the max extension of the Koss KPH14s, and, second, both at their max extension. I couldn't figure out a good way to demonstrate their comparative compliance in width.) 3) The KH14's sound quality is "good enough" but not as good as the W08s. Lacking a better term, I'd say they just don't have the low- to mid-range fullness of the Sony. They also have less efficiency--less volume at same setting, at least when used with my 24" iMac. Finally, a problem unique to the color I ordered. I ordered the "blue" KPH14b. The listing images shows this blue as a mid tone, neutral blue. The actual product blue is much closer to a turquoise than the images led me to expect. This was true across many different devices I have viewed the listing on (iPhone, iPad, Windows, Mac, Chromebook) so I don't think it's just a device color accuracy problem. The listing images just aren't representative. (Attached are a crop of a screenshot from the product listing and a photo, from an iPhone 12, of the product shown in front of that same product listing on screen.) I'm keeping them only because I have no better choice for the use case. But it sure would be nice if Sony brought back the MDR-W08s or Koss made a better copy of them.

text: I've been looking for the perfect headphone for me. I've auditioned Focal Clear, Utopia, Hd800s, Edition X and a few others. Clear vs Utopia is no contest - Utopia has a richer immersive experience - Clear is just too bright. Hifiman's X just felt flat compared to the others. Now the tough one - HD800s vs Utopias - Both are great but both are different. The simplest way I can explain it is with the HD800s it is like sitting in the best seats listening to great musicians where as the Utopia is like being on stage with the musicians - you can hear every nuance and in some ways this can also be distracting to the music. With the Eutopias you "see" the weave of the music and the HD800s you see the fabric of the music. Again very different experiences - both great. The Utopias allowed you to distinctly separate out (and taste)all the instruments and voices unlike any headphones I've ever heard. HD800s make it all come together into a great overall flavor. I was listening to a remastered Rider on the storm (Doors - 24/192) with the Utopias I could hear the vibrato of the guitar strings and the thunder was intense. With the HD800s it felt more like I was sitting on the front porch listening to the rain falling and the band was across the room playing for you. Both can give you deep "wrapped around you" sound. It also may be that I have to get used to the richer(?) more detailed experience of the Utopias at which point my hearing will adapt to the headphones? Possibly. Not sure, though I do think it is completely normal for your ears to get used to a new set of cans. My day to day has been SE846s and it took a while to fully appreciate them over my other Se2xx. So in short - your mileage may vary - you have to listen to them and make a judgement for the kind of "sound" you want. Personally I'd skip everything and just go to the HD800s and Utopias and see which you like better.

text: I bought this set as a replacement to my HBS730s I've used for years. Those had amazing sound, and the sockets were designed to make it simple to store the ear pieces. I figured these were just this year's version of that amazing set of earphones. First of all, you need to understand that I am not an audiophile by any stretch of the imagination. If I can hear my tunes, I'm a happy man, for the most part...So imagine my surprise when I fired this set up, and found that I couldn't hear the bass in my music, people speaking in podcasts just seemed...shallow, and the ear pieces are difficult to insert into the magnetic holder due to the way they lay around my neck. Oh yeah, did I mention that the magnets seem a lot weaker, as well? Maybe this is due to the way they are stored in this version, but I have found the ear buds dangling on more than one occasion in the last few days as a result of them falling out of the magnetic holder. At the end of the day, this product works as described. The battery life is excellent so far, and the unit is comfortable to wear and use. Voice activation works fine, and the buttons are easy to find and use by touch. But the poor audio quality, weak magnets, and odd placement for the holders means I'm going to look into returning this unit and upgrade to the next one up in search of better audio quality. For the price, they're fine. If you are going to be using this set mostly for calls and voice-related stuff, I'm sure they're fine, but I'm looking for something more.

text: I bought this pair of earphones after owning the [[ASIN:B0009Q4PHO Ultimate Ears SuperFi 5 Pro Noise Isolating Earphones (Black)]] for about 2 years. I had been very happy with the SuperFi 5 earphones until the wiring finally gave out and I lost all sound in the left ear. This was disappointing, but they definitely didn't owe me anything as they had provided me with thousands of hours of incredible listening enjoyment. As I was looking for a pair to replace my first UE purchase, I decided to buy the 700 series for 2 reasons: 1) I wanted the same kind of sound quality that I was accustomed to from the SuperFi 5 2) I wanted something that would fit futher into my ear so I could listen to music while laying my head on a pillow (this was not possible with the SuperFi 5 Pro) After using for several weeks, I concluded that the fit was definitely better, and the sound quality was almost identical to the SuperFi 5 earphones. Overall, it's a great set of earphones and I would highly recommend them to any serious musician or audiophile. Pros: - Excellent sound and VERY impressive bass/low end. - Very comfortable fit, stays in when running, comfortable while sleeping, etc. - Ultimate Ears provides outstanding customer service. Any issues with the product will be fixed quickly & free of charge (see below). My only complaints are: - Considering the price tag on these earphones, they have surprisingly cheap wiring. You need to be very careful not to put ANY undue stress on any of the cords, or it will very likely damage the unit. I owned these earphones for about 5 weeks when the plugin jack almost broke off. What was I doing to cause such damage to the jack? Did I drop it off a cliff? Did I drive over it with my car? No. I was holding it in my hand with the jack pressed firmly against my palm for about 2 minutes. I simply HELD it. I don't know why a $200 set of earphones would have such cheaply designed wiring, but it's something you should be aware of BEFORE you purchase these. That being said, Logitech was extremely accomodating and provided unsurpassed customer service. They gave me an entirely new set of earphones in less than 2 weeks (and they paid for all postage). Given this, it's hard to stay mad about the incident. - When these earphones are referred to as "noise isolating", that is only a half-truth. They do a great job of isolating noise for the listener, but if you have your volume turned up to 50% of higher on an ipod, anybody who is sitting next to you will hear everything that is being played. I never had this problem with the SuperFi 5 Pro earphones (which didn't fit quite as well), but it seems to be an issue with these. When I'm laying in bed at night, I literally have to have my volume at 25% of lower because if it's any higher, it will wake up my wife. Is this a huge problem? Not really, and it probably wouldn't affect my decision to purchase again. It was just a slight annoyance when I was expected to have TRUE noise isolation from both ends.

Sound isolation still solid but the Elite Active 75t's and the Elite 85t's are substantially more effective. TL;DR -- In their current state they're unusable to me and I've returned them. It feels like they spent a ton of time and money in hardware which is legitimately impressive. But the execution and the firmware is a disaster. Stick to the 75t's or 85t's until they work out the kinks.
