text: I've tried a lot of headphones. I'm a borderline audiophile. I listen to every type of music (acoustic and classical to hip hop and films). My go-to in ear headphones are the Klipsch S4i. They produce great sound and block out most of the ambient sounds. But it is hard to wear them for long periods of time. Even though they are relatively comfortable, I just can't wear them continuously on long plane trips. But I really like the quality of sound and noise isolation from the Klipsch. So I have been looking for on-ear or over the ear noise isolating or cancelation headphones for about a year. I own or have owned many. Here's a quick take of all of them and then my final take on the Marley Destiny - which I like the best: - Marshall: just started making headphones. They are on ear. Too tight even when loosened and fairly uncomfortable. Sound quality is flat - not punchy or what you'd expect from an on ear headphone. Lackluster and uncomfortable. - RocNation/SkullCandy Aviators: Love these. Great sound. Look cool (but they are big and draw a lot of attention). Obviously great for rap and hip hop but also do a great job with mid-range. Very comfortable. But they let in a lot of ambient sound and the Klipsch in-ear do a much better job with noise isolation than the Aviators. But these headphones look very cool (cooler than the Beats IMO). - Beats HD: Sound fantastic and are very comfortable but leaks sound and doesn't do a great job with noise isolation, which is important for me. While we haven't broken ours, it always feels like the plastic headband is going to snap when you unfold them. My kids love the Beats. - Beats Studio: These are the big over the ear phones that have active noise cancellation. I've purchased two of them on eBay and neither worked. Probably my own fault so I can't give a fair review but the fact is that these headphones feel too plasticy and cheap to pay the $300 that they go for at retail. So I guess my bottom line on the Studios is that I think they are overpriced even though I think a new pair (from an authorized dealer) sounds pretty amazing. Bose QC 3: These are the smaller on ear noise cancellation headphones. I have not owned them like the ones above but have demo'd them at the Apple Store. Really comfortable and amazing job of noise cancellation. But again - $320-340. Too much for an on ear headphone. Bose QC 15: The big Bose noise cancellation headphones. The best at everything but they are so big and ugly. Can't see using these regularly. And they're still $300. But they are excellent quality. So that brought me to the House of Marley Destiny's. Honestly never heard of them before I read a quick review in Uncrate a few months back. For me they hit the sweet spot after a lot of hit and miss. I use headphones frequently so I've really looked around! The set up for these headphones is very similar to the Beats Studio or Bose QC15. They take batteries and you need to power it up before you can listen to music. I like the size of these headphones. They just fit over the ear but they aren't gigantic like the Beats, Bose or Aviators. Similar to the others in this category, they fold flat and come with a case with extra long cords, mic, plane jacks, etc. In terms of noise cancellation, they are very good; perhaps not as good as the Bose, but still very good. In terms of sound... they sound great. Punchy bass, maybe a little too much, but that's easy to ratchet down with the EQ settings in any IOS or Android device (just click "bass reducer" in settings). Once you do that, you can listen to any type of music or movie and it sounds fantastic! With the EQ off on an IOS device it also sounds good but the bass will definitely be dominant, which is fine for most genres of pop music. I found the midrange and treble to be just right for me. I especially liked the fit, quality and construction of these headphones. They look like they are on ear in terms of size, but they are just big enough to go over the ear. They don't bulge out too much. I like the combination of recycled aluminum and black headband. They are listed on Amazon at $299, but I found them in a local retailer for $228. At that price, they are 25% less expensive than the Bose or the Beats, and I think all three are pretty close in quality. So the Marleys at that price are a much better value. Personally, I like the way that these look better than the other two as well. Highly recommended after lots of trial and error.

I would like to point out that it is more flexible with USB-C cables where even a fast charger can be used, other models will not allow that option. The model has two drawbacks. The first is fit. Going a size down is more comfortable for ear pressure, but are prone to falling out even with subtle head movements or yawns. I just wish that there was a more happy medium for the two options. The other drawback is battery life. According to customer service from the manufacturer, the seven hours of playtime would be with a single bud, no phone calls and below 50%. So, for real-world use, I get about 4.5 hours playback and about four hours if I throw in a phone call or two. I can't say how long all talk will last because I have yet to use them for that purpose, for a full charge. In the end, they are a good buy when in sale. text: Background- This will be my second set of MicroPro's. My first set, lasted me around 6-7 years until they fell out of my pocket on a crowded night downtown, and were lost. I was devastated, and really couldn't bear the idea of spending the money again, because I really considered them an investment. But, after a couple months of using some Klipsch Image S4-II's and Kilpsch R6's, which were just sort of kick-around pairs, I decided I absolutely needed to have the Ety's back. I'm not an audiophile, but I do know a fair bit about good sound. Review- I'll start by addressing a few things I have seen frequently in other reviews: ---"Flat" or uninteresting sound"--- I "know" what people mean when they say this. These do have a "cool", and perhaps a slight, but not overt, "brightness" to them. The thing is, the detailed resolution that the ER4P's have makes it impossible for me to go to any of the more "warm" or "colorful" (mostly cheaper) earphones I've tried. It may take some getting used to, but I think anyone who purchases these who has a similar background as myself, and wants REALLY good sound, high isolation, and wants to drive them very frequently direct with only an iPhone, Macbook, or iPad, will come to love these. I can see how "audiophiles", musicians, studio engineers, etc, may prefer different or more expensive options, but these are really great earphones for $300--so much so that I have bought them twice at around that price. ---"Lack of bass"--- Yes, compared to perhaps 80% of consumer-oriented earphones (especially cheaper ones like Klipsch and Bose), the bass on the ER4P's will seem underwhelming. However, the bass that is there, is tight and accurate, with absolutely no boominess. I really have become accustomed to the sound signature of ER4P's and find that I don't miss the exaggerated bass that most ear/headphones have. Additionally, it must be said that there will be absolutely NO bass audible whatsoever if the wearer isn't truly getting an adequate seal, and placing the phones deep enough in the ear canal. ---"Cables transmit a lot of microphonic noise"--- This is also true. They do, plain and simple. For me, using the provided clip to attach the plastic "barrel" (where the cord separates into individual L/R cables" is a must. I always clip this barrel to my shirt or collar, to "lift" the portion of the cable closest to the ears, and relieve it of any tension or it's own weight. That being said, honestly I run long distances with these in all the time. ---"Poor build quality, breaks easily"--- Like I said, my first set still worked fine until I lost them. I did have the cable replaced for free once under warranty, and I think the replacement cable (the current design with the red/blue dot), is better than the original (which had red/blue plastic where it connects to the can). I take good care of them in general, however, and am very careful never to tug or place strain anywhere on them. I also wind them neatly and carefully each time when I am done with them, and never "ball them up" or cram them in pockets. If you don't plan on being able to handle these with at least a reasonable degree of care, then they aren't for you. They aren't designed to be used in a gym or during active use; more like for when sitting still in a room. But I use them all the time, and love them.

text: Previously, I used 3 pairs of the KOSS KPH30i. Those have good sound, but are too brittle for normal use. 2 pair broke while putting them on my head. another, broke while pulling from a jacket pocket. These KPH40 seem more durable, so far. Durable enough for normal use. Like the KPH30i, the KPH40 offers a lot of sound quality, for the money. However, they do sound different. The KPH40 has noticeably better bass extension. If you focus on hip-hop, R&B, or other genres which showcase true bass response, these are strictly better than the KPH30i. That bass extension also tends to add more depth to the soundstage, in general, for all types of music. KPH40 doesn't quite have the same energy in the mids, as the KPH30i. Certain rock songs will have a bit of a different feel to them. A little less texture and punch for guitars. However, the bass extension can still keep the KPH40 in the overall lead, especially if the music has some dynamic drums. For bass guitars, You would need to compare song by song. Depending upon the mix, either headphone could be favored. The true weakness of the KPH40, is in the high mids and highs. They lack a bit of texture in the high-mids. And highs can sound a touch compressed. However, that weakness in the highs is not drastic. overall, these headphones sound very good. Especially considering their price. KPH40 does not have an in-line microphone, like the KPH30i. I wish it did.

text: Pros: - Probably one of the most secure fitting, if not the most secure fitting wireless earbud on the market. The wing tips ensure these will never fall out, no matter how hard you rattle your head. - Personalized EQ is fantastic. The app will create a custom EQ tuned to your ears, and you can manually adjust it after or reset it any time you like. Every audio company should be doing this. I found my EQ setting to be fun, exciting, and brilliant with a nice but not overbearing bass boost. - Carrying case is rather small. - Thorough app support. There's a guide built in, EQ with presets, control customization options, and more. - Solid water resistance - Slim profile in your ears. To my eyes, these are quite attractive looking buds, unlike the protruding designs in the Airpods pros or Bose soundsports. - Voice prompts on startup tell you the battery of the buds (not including the case) and if they're connected Cons: - Sound quality, even with fine tuning the EQ, is a bit meh. It's not bad, but compared to the premium buds out there (like the Sony WF 1000xm3), it's a little congested. There's not much soundstage or track separation, but it's good enough to enjoy on your runs. In some genres I really enjoy the way these sound (especially pop and EDM), but in more nuanced tracks the sound can kind of fall apart. I would've expected a little better for $180, but it's still decent. I'd say it's like a $150 level audio experience. - Carrying case feels cheap and easy to break. The hinge creaks when I apply even a little pressure past its maximum opening point. I get the feeling I could snap the lid off if I tried. It's also made of a not-so-premium plastic. - No ANC or ambient mode, which is odd for a pair of workout buds. - No matter how you customize the controls, you can only go forward on your playlist. There is no back song option. - Call quality is absolute trash. - Physical buttons on the sides cause you to press them into your ear canal whenever you do an input. A little painful. Can be mitigated by holding the buds in place with your thumb and middle finger, and using your index finger to press the button. In my opinion, the major selling points of these are their immaculately comfortable and secure fit, wonderfully implemented EQ, and extremely portable case. If those matter to you, these will be a great option. But if you don't have much of an issue finding earbuds that stay in your ears, you can probably find a better value.

text: I have tried skull candy headphones, bose headphones, beats headphones, apple in ear headphones, etc. Honestly, any head phones you have are more about style than sound. The differences in sound are really not that substantial to make your music listening experience that different. And even the price difference does not matter. What is the difference between 25$ and 500$ in the big scheme of things? Not that much. Sure, if you are a poor college student or whatever, well get a pair of the in ear apple headphones. If you have more money, get whatever you want. Don't confuse yourself. Also, if you want to have the simplistic, minimalist look, wear apple. If you wanna be cool and modern, wear bose, if you wanna go with what's good in mainstream, wear beats, and lastly if you wanna feel like an environmentalist hippie (which I can be at times), wear house of marley. It does not matter. With regards to how these feel, they feel perfectly fine after wearing them in for about a month of normal listening. They don't break unless you freaking jump on them. They have a little sound leakage, but as long as they are on your ears (where they are supposed to be) and you listen at a normal volume (like you should to not cause hearing damage), your friends will not be able to hear what you are listening to and you will be in your little, isolated noise-cancelling world (I promise you if you have these at full blast, and a song has a loud intro, your ear drums will feel like they want to burst because the dynamics are extremely strong in these). And lastly, I like how it sounds with hip hop, reggae, blues, folk, singer/songwriter, indie, pop, and... oh wait, everything. ***UPDATE: Literally a day after I give these a 5 star rating and try to be all "honest" about them (although maybe slightly naive), the right earbud blows out. After listening to "beats music" (the new streaming music service rivaling iTunes and Spotify) and probably being subliminally messaged, I started watching Jimmy Iovine interviews and just looked into everything Beats was aiming to be, not just what its mainstream reputation is. I am not ashamed to say that I do appreciate people like Steve Jobs who promote lifestyles and beautiful products no matter what. Jimmy Iovine, Dr. Dre, and Beats might be just that, and it is my prediction that beats music and beats headphones will be a HUGE company in the future (despite the fact that they already are), and with all of its talent and people in the music industry backing it, I think I'm going to start putting my faith in Beats. *** UPDATE 2: So, decisiveness over headphones has never been my strongpoint, but for some reason my beats order got cancelled today and I went to the apple store at my school and picked up a pair of in-ear apple headphones (80$) and, despite some negativity about the ear buds breaking or whatever, they sound perfect and they give you a choice of small, medium, and large earbuds. I have small ears and the small ones fit perfectly in my ear and have the crispest sound I've ever heard. So much respect for those folks at Apple in CA and China.

text: These comfortable SleepPhones are exactly what I have been looking for- if only this company had an interest in quality control. The first pair came with a defective left speaker. And although a medium size is supposed to "fit most heads", it was far too large. It was the wrong color too, although that didn't matter to me. The second pair are a little grubby, have obviously been used, and came with a large opening in the back that should have been sewn up. I don't know if the speakers work, because I am not willing to try to fix the gaping plastic gripper. They are going back tomorrow. First of all, AcousticSheep needs to offer more detail on head sizes. I had to choose between "medium" and "extra small". I have a normal-on-the-small-side head, so extra small fit me. But I had to guess, and the first time I guessed wrong. Secondly, these are much too hit-and-miss in terms of construction, as reviews amply demonstrate. One is either lucky- or not. But effective quality control exists in order to minimize the misery, eh? It is quite off-putting to receive an exchange that is in bad shape and flagrantly used. I am not necessarily against the wide-spread practice of replacing new returns with slightly used items: it all depends on the result. If I can't tell the difference, and everything works well, I can live with it. I will try one more time to buy these, for the same reason other people also keep trying. If I can get SleepPhones that don't have anything terribly wrong with them, I am fairly sure I will like them very much. And I will change my ratings if the third time is the charm. But no matter how much I like them, I won't give more than three stars because the quality control level is inexcusable. This is a very simple and clever device, and rather expensive for what it is because of the cleverness. But no amount of potential utility makes up for junk you have to keep sending back.

text: I had really high hopes for the earbuds. I have been a long time user of the wired Panasonic Ergofit earbuds. They always fit my ears better than any other earbuds I've ever used. I was thrilled to see about two weeks ago that Panasonic finally came out with these! Pros: These earbuds sound great and are just as comfortable as the wired version I'm used to. They're light and are almost unnoticeable when they're resting on my neck. Cons: They do NOT stay powered on when used in a stand-by mode. If I'm playing audio through my phone and decide to pause or stop playing the audio, the earbuds disconnect from my phone and turn off after less than 10 minutes. My routine during the day is listening to podcasts off and on throughout the day. My old wireless earbuds allowed me to keep them powered on for the entire day and start or stop playing audio whenever I wanted. They also allowed me to receive a phone call during this time and use the earbuds as a microphone. These Panasonic wireless earbuds make this style of listening impossible. It also makes them impossible to receive a phone call on them unless you're using the earbuds while you receive the phone call. I can no longer wear these around and answer a phone call whenever it comes through. I had really high hopes for these earbuds, but I sadly don't think I'll be able to keep them. text: My favorite features of these headphones are the materials they are made of, the ear cushions, and the sound. My least favorite part of these is the cord. The materials: I have a big head, so I go through over the ear headphones rather quickly due to the stress I place on the band just putting them on and taking them off. With these headphones, the band is metal with helpful size markers on the band. The actual cans look like and mixture of plastic and metal. The headphones do not creak at the seams like many cheap plastic ones do, and they feel sturdy and durable even after six months of me using them every day. The ear cushions: To add to my big head, my ears are very sensitive, which adds to my trouble with over the ear headphones. Most headphones press on my ears and irritate them after wearing them for only a half hour, but these are so incredibly comfortable that I've worn these for several hours without feeling any pain or irritation. The cans swivel, too, which helps keep the pressure off the top part of my ear. These are easily the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn, more so than any in the Beats, Audiotechnica, or Bose lines of product that I've tried. Also, they don't make my head sweat :) The sound: I've owned and tested many speakers and headphones over the years and JBL has been the most consistent brand that I've had the pleasure of using. I have yet to encounter a product of theirs that was not worth the money they charge. These headphones definitely carry on the JBL legacy with their sound, however I have to agree with some of the other reviewers that the mid-ranges are a little lacking. I still enjoy using them so it isn't a deal-breaker, but I would have liked to have that final piece of an otherwise perfect package. The cord: Okay, so almost perfect package. This cord do not hold up the the rest of the headphones. I have not had any connectivity issues, so it functions as it should, but the remote is a cheap plastic. It has a 3/32 inch plug at the end that plugs into the headphones, so it won't be easy to replace either. I only hope that it continues to hold up over the years. I highly recommend these headphones. Of the ones available in this price range, these headphones are hands-down the best value for your money. You will not regret buying these, I promise. :)

text: I have been using the Westone Bluetooth cable v2 for about a week now. Previously I was using the v1 for about 2 years. Westone has made some very welcome upgrades to the v2, but there is one large problem. The Good - The upgrade to Bluetooth v5 has eliminated lip sync issues with certain video platforms, increased sound quality, and reduced if not eliminated audio drop out when waking outside. With the v1 I often had lip sync issues with the YouTube app on my iPhone 7 and audio dropped out dozens of times throughout the day. - the added battery life/charging cradle means I am charging less. I do not like the requirement of using the cradle to charge, since it means I have to have it with me, but the fact that I can extend my battery life is well worth it. -build quality is slightly better than the v1; however, this is at the detriment to shure IEM users as the mmcx plug now has a larger rubber lip meant to reduce water infiltration, but instead it makes it very difficult to interface with shure IEMs. If you keep this cable and use shure you will likely need to trim this rubber down. - the ends of the cable near the mmcx connectors are now more rigid and rounded. This keeps the headphones in place and more secure. The Bad The biggest issue with this cable, and the reason that I have returned it despite the many notable upgrades, is that a rhythmic, beating, buzzing type noise is very audible in the right channel from low to medium volumes. At normal to loud listen volumes the sound is not audible (likely masked), but if there is a quieter section or silence between tracks the sound is again audible. I have contacted westone and they admitted this is an issue with the google pixel, but I am using an iPhone 7 and two different laptops. They exchanged the cable, but replacement suffers from the same issue. Additionally the noise is documented on several forums, leading me to believe this is a problem with the design or firmware.

text: If you want noise-cancelling headphones for your next flight, these are a good choice. The amazon.com price kind of fluxtuates, but you should be able to find these for around $100. Noise cancelling: excellent, used these in a building with a loud a/c system, and they did the trick. I also have used these on two flights, they definitely block out a lot of the engine noise, but not 100%, but enough to make a big difference. The over the ear design also gives pretty good passive noise cancelling. Comfort: It's not advertised anywhere, but the ear pads are memory foam and extremely comfortable. However, I did notice with extended wear (after several hours) these headphones get a little warm around the ears. The headband is not too tight, but not as loose as the Bose. I don't have a huge head so this doesn't bother me much. They're over the ear headphones, but they're not overly bulky and don't weigh too much. Sound quality: I am not expert, but the sound with the noise cancelling on sounded great. With the noise cancelling off, it didn't sound nearly as good, but I got these suckers for the noise cancelling. Compared to other noise cancelling headphones: there is definitely much less "hiss" compared to some of the other noise cancelling headphones I have used (old JVC and old Sony models). My only complaint is that if you turn up the sound really really loud, there might be some sound leakage. I turned up all the way up and could hear sound coming from the headphones without wearing them. But when I put the earpads facing down on a table, i could barely hear any noise, so maybe the sound leakage isnt too bad if you're wearing them. Just don't crack up the volume all the way up (I haven't had any issues at the volume level I listen to music at). Other thoughts: it comes with a nice case and adaptor plugs. They are kind of big to carry, so if you want something small and compact, these are not for you. Verdict: a very good price, and excellent sound with the noise cancelling on. Definitely worth picking up a pair if you don't want to spend too much for premium NC headphones.

text: I had noise-canceling earbuds on my Wish List and actually ended up with a choice... "Keep the ones you like best." It took me a while to test them out. After I decided, I thought I'd share some notes. All comments are my personal opinions only! Models: - Sony MDR-NC100D; ~$100-160 on Amazon - Panasonic RP-HC55; ~$45 at Costco Test: - Standing in front of kitchen range hood fan on high. I felt this is similar to airplane engine noise. Noise canceling, no music: - Mid-low range: Good for both Sony & Pana. - Lowest range: Most remains for both Sony & Pana. - Mid-high range hiss: Sony is lower. Music: Natalie Merchant, Carnival - Bass: Much better for Pana. - Treble: Slightly better for Pana. Design: - Cord length: ~5' for both Sony & Pana. - Cord design: Sony has shorter cord to L ear (bad if feeds are on R); Pana cords are same to L & R ears. - Controls weight: Same for both Sony & Pana. - Controls size: Sony is smaller than Pana and positioned a little lower on cord (i.e. more length between controls and ears). - Volume control: Pana has volume control; Sony does not. Sony has 'monitor' function that pauses all music. Sony allows music to pass when unit is off (e.g. dead battery); Pana does not. - NC settings: Sony has 3 settings and automatically chooses best; Pana has one setting. - Earbuds: Pana rubber is softer and more comfortable than Sony. - Battery life: Sony publishes 22h; Pana publishes 40h. Summary: - Sony has better NC tech and sound pass-through when battery dies. - Pana has better bass, comfort, battery life, and price. My personal decision was for the Panasonic. I fly cross-country every other week and will use it mostly on long flights. I'll just carry an extra battery. It was hard justify Sony's ~3x higher price when I liked Panasonic's sound so much more.

text: These Sony XB950B1 headphones are somewhat of a mixed bag for me. In the end, I like them pretty well despite a few issues, but I'm not sure they're worth the price of admission. Design wise, I really dig these. They look super sleek and have a very Sony-esque smooth techie kind of vibe. The blue color is definitely eye-catching. The headband frame is metal, but alas most of the rest of the parts are plastic. They are lightweight but feel sturdy enough, though for $200 I'd really love to see more metal used in the construction. I do find these headphones to be very comfortable, and I get a great fit thanks to the swiveling earpieces. I find that fixed earpiece headphones don't give me nearly as good a fit, but the rotating earpieces here allow just the right angle to cover my ears properly. The padding is very comfortable and provides a good seal to block external sound. These are not noise canceling headphones, but I find that they block external noise really well on their own. The controls are easy to learn and work well for me. Within a few minutes I was able to control playback and volume by feel using the right side controls, and the left side controls for extra bass and power are equally easy to use blindly. In terms of sound, these are definitely heavy on the bass, all the time. In fact, I can barely tell any difference with the "extra bass" on or off because there is already so much bass presence. They don't sound bad, but if you don't want enhanced sounding bass all the time these aren't for you. I find the overall sound to be very pleasant, rich, and warm, though I find them lacking a bit in the highs, which aren't especially crisp or sparkling. I can definitely enjoy using them with about any kind of music, but they're ultimately good but not great in the sound department. I am glad to report that there isn't a hint of background hiss or noise, which I have found with some other bluetooth headphones. I am pretty disappointed in the Headphones Connect app. It has only two features: surround sound (with arena, club, outdoor stage, and concert hall settings), and bass enhancement control. I don't like surround sound effects (though these are certainly distinctive and effective), but I do appreciate the bass control - primarily for the ability to dial DOWN the bass. I wish, however, I could do that without having to use the app. Unfortunately, the "extra bass" button on the headphones doesn't have a low bass setting like the app, so you have to use the app to listen with a decreased amount of bass. I also wish Sony had put a full blown graphic equalizer in the app, but they didn't and it sure feels like a missed opportunity. My Android phone has one, but it would be much more convenient if Sony put more control and power into their app. The bluetooth connectivity works fine, and the range is solid - good enough for me to be in one room with the headphones while my phone is in another room. Battery life is excellent. All in all, these are good but not without caveats. If you love bass, they have it in spades and offer a pretty nice sound all around despite lacking some clarity in the highs. If you like a more natural sound (without super enhanced bass), the only choice is to open the app and dial down the bass, which is a hassle and only goes so far. The app is also disappointingly sparse. On the other hand, these look great and offer a fantastic fit for me. At $200, I'd only recommend them if you really want that bass. Otherwise, I think you can find better sound for less.

text: TLDR: Specialist headphones, great for playing loud rock. The materials and design do not at all match the price point, and the NC is of mediocre quality but at least does not mess the music up. Long battery life, and great single button playback controls. If these were a bit cheaper, they would be great. Three Way High End BT Headphone Review Compared: Marshall Mid ANC ($277 at time of writing.) Master Dynamic MW60 ($550 ATOW.) AKG N700 ($350 ATOW.) Occasionally I will reference comparable products I have used and owned, from Bose, Sony, and VModa. Noise Cancelling: The MW60 does not have this feature. In general, I find NC to be at best an unnecessary added option – I like the feature on two occasions. First, when listening to music on airplanes (I fly less than 10 times per year.) Second, when I feel the urge to listen to low dynamic acoustic music on the subway or in a noisy café. (Happens a bit more frequently, but generally prefer other sorts of music for those settings.) Comparing the two phones that have the feature in the roundup? The Marshall is acceptable, as it does not ruin the music in the way Bose’s NC does, but also does not mute sound all that well. Good for cutting really noisy background noise by a little bit, especially low pitched rumbling, without wrecking sound quality. AKG noise cancelling is much more effective and also allows setting two different modes, one typical NC and the other oriented towards allowing conversation that pares back the noise reduction when it detects what it thinks are human voices. A fairly sophisticated system, and one that works better than both Bose and Marshall. No impact on music tone at all, but peak volume seems a tad reduced, though this may be the result of other design choices. However, both Marshall and AKG are worse NC systems than the very sophisticated and excellent performing system found in the Sony MX1000 series. I have one of the second series models in that line, and it remains my go-to for plane and subway travel, having excellent battery life, added features like temporary muting with touch control, and virtually no impact on music tone or dynamics. So noise cancelling, worst to best: MW60 (none) >>> Marshall >>>> AKG. (Though Sony MX beats all these!) Not scoring this category as it is not essential to me. Materials / Ergonomics: MW60, oddly, feels like a very expensive AND a very cheap product at the same time. The frame and cups of the MW60 feel ultra premium, and the unit looks very high end. Then I ratchet the frame open a bit to fit on my large noggin… and the teeny metal slide feels stressed and reluctant to open, and I worry the arm is going to come right off the frame. Obviously it has not done so over many hundreds of extensions, but it still FEELS flimsy and bothersome, very unfit for a close to $600 product. $50 Koss units have felt sturdier in hand (though $300 Grados have not…). Also to single out the most shameful gaffe by MD: the carrying “case” for the MW60s is utterly dreadful. Made of cheap canvas / nylon, it is thin skinned, flimsy, barely fits the folded headphones, has an awful jammy zipper, and attracts every speck of hair and dust from hundreds of yards away. This is perhaps the worst and cheapest carrying case I have ever seen with any headphone – the cheapo drawstring pleather bag used in many mid ranger Japanese designs (e.g. ATH M700) seems like the height of luxury in comparison. A baffling downscale move for a very costly product! The MW60s also have the nerdiest look to them when worn – the frame sticks out the most from the head and makes one look like a sonar console operator in a submarine war movie. The frame feels solid (well, except when you slide the arms in and out!) but looks like a 20 year old design when compared to the BT VModas. Control buttons on the MW60 are well done – with all buttons having distinct tactile feel and confidence inspiring reliable operation. Functions are logically placed, buttons are the right size, and everything feels solid. All in All: MW60 gets a B in Materials / Ergo. Some stuff feels really well done – materials and controls – but the awful carrying case and uninspiringly rickety frame ratcheting action for the driver arms take away many points. AKG in comparison gets things mostly right, and hits the price point properly. Design feels solid in terms of materials – a bit more plastic used in the frame, but the cups look and feel upscale. The arms slide smoothly and feel much less flimsy than the MW, and larger headed users can be accommodated more easily. (Some slider space left even on my XL head.) The buttons feel good enough, but placement is odd. Volume and track control is on the left while power and NC is on the right. Being right handed, I prefer the opposite arrangement. The buttons also are a bit small and overly flat, and worst of all, do not feel much different from each other. A bit more work here would have made these easier to use. Carrying case is OK. Sturdy enough, spacious, a bit bulky, and the loose webbing used to retain wires and what not allows anything carried in there to work its way out and rattle around the case. Looks awful compared to the compact, efficient, and almost literally bulletproof cases VModa uses… but looks infinitely better than the carnival prize giveaway quality case that Master & Dynamic offers on their 50% costlier MW60s! K700 gets a B+ in Materials / Ergo: A bit lower quality materials but a sturdier feel gives a good start to the score, but then the mixed control quality takes a few points off. All in all, AKG meets its lower price point admirably in terms of quality to dollars, but the controls will take some practice to get used to, especially for righties. Marshall Mid ANC: Another mixed bag. I have non NC Marshall Mid BT phones – and the quality of these much cheaper phones virtually matches that of the ANC Mids which cost more than twice at much! I feel as if the premium price has gained me exactly zero percent increase in materials or build quality, not a good feeling. That said, the base level Marshall ANC quality is not awful. Lots of reasonably high quality pleather, slider feels sturdy enough (thought at max extension for my big noggin) and the controls are very well done. Marshall has their trademark single button joystick for on / off and volume / track control (along separate axes) and that little gadget offers perhaps the most intuitive operation of any headset controls I have used, even though it is mounted on the left cup. To make up for this excellence, Marshall offers a weird and dysfunctional noise cancelling button. Located on the right cup, the NC switch has no clear marking as to whether the function is on or off (red is on… I think!) and worst of all, the NC does not turn off when the rest of the set is turned off, so you will need to switch this off separately to avoid running your battery down while the phones are off. I guess in theory you might want to use the mediocre NC when the BT function is off, but this “feature” could have been implemented more effectively and clearly. Marshall Mid ANC gets a B- in Materials / Ergo. Really good controls, marred by the exact same build quality as the sub $100 Mid BT phones. Though the Marshall is the cheapest set of phones here, using the exact same build as a much cheaper offering in the Marshall product line is not a win for anyone. The bizarre NC control also costs some points. Materials / Ergo, worst to best: Marshall Mid >>> MW60 >>> AKG K700. Bear in mind, the Master Dynamic has the most superficially attractive choice of materials by far out of the box, so if you are getting this as a gift for a millionaire or some such, this is the best choice. The deficiencies in arm extension feel and the dollar store carrying case may not matter to some buyers. AKG wins overall IMO by best matching buyer expectations to materials and build quality at the price point. If AKG cost as much as the MW60s, they would lose the category. Sound Quality: All are pretty good, about as good as a decent wired headphone, which is saying something, given the notable quality gap in BT phones as little as two years ago. Marshall Mid: Most “sculpted” sound, emphasizing mids (guitars and vocals) with a prominent low end. These sound great with rock and pop, and reasonably good with acoustic music that does not emphasize a treble presence (e.g. jazz). Not awful with classical, but the trebles are rolled off a bit, which may bother you if you want absolute accuracy in playback. The noise cancellation does not distort the sound too much, maybe narrowing the soundstage a bit. Like the other contenders (and like most closed back headphones in general) the soundstage is pretty narrow already, so you are not getting many directional based sound cues. Everything sounds centrally miked, which is the way that most popular music tends to be recorded anyway, but acoustical music fans that want to hear where the instruments are on the sound stage will fine the sound here congested and central. Of note, the Mids get very loud, louder than the other two phones by a significant degree. Bottom Line: if you like rock, metal, etc and never listen to acoustical music, these make a compelling claim for best sound in the trio, especially if you like your music loud. I’ll give the Marshall Mids a B+ in sound, as I like rock and metal – but also classical and jazz, so the A- rock sound and B level acoustical sound even out. MW60: Kind of the polar opposites of the Mids. Better at acoustical music and very accurate, but also do not like to go loud. The equalization here is very minimal – slight bass boost – and all sorts of music sound good and accurate. The sense of energy many like in popular music is missing to an extent due to the flat equalization curve, but if you want detail and accuracy, the MW60s are probably the best headphones here. The soundstage is smallish, maybe a bit broader than the Mids, but you will not be mistaking these for Grados. I found myself playing music back at higher volume on these because sensitivity seemed lower, though on paper seemed comparable to the others. Bottom Line: If you want accurate music playback and headphones that are equally strong in all genres, the MW60s are excellent. Definitely the best acoustical music playback in the roundup, and if you like your rock, metal etc to be finely detailed, these are also great. There is a lack of mid range dynamism, and the low end thump is mainly absent, but whether these are good or bad points depends on your musical tastes and what you expect from headphones. I’ll give the MW60s a B+ in music quality mainly because I tend to listen to rock and metal when commuting, and that endeavor is mainly where I use BT headphones, saving the acoustic stuff for home listening. The MW60s are decent for my commuting needs, but the other phones sounded better for my music tastes during those occasions, and the rather lower volume output was also bothersome. Still, if you are Niles Crane and want to listen to Satie while sipping sherry, these could conceivably be your top choice. K700: The happy medium in sound quality, but also the jack of all trades and master of none. Better with classical than the Mids, better at rock and metal than the MW60s. The mids have a slight boost, bass moreso (but less than the Marshalls) and there is a modestly bright treble presence that brings most orchestral music to life. Soundstage is still narrow in the scheme of things, but ends up being better than the Mids, somewhat less than the MW60s. Dynamic volume is also between the two – does not get as loud as the Mids, but a bit more vigorous than the MW60s. Bottom Line: For me, if I was going on a long trip and wanted to listen mainly to classical or jazz, I would bring the MW60s. If I was making that same trip, but wanted to hear mainly rock and metal, I’d take the Mids. If I was on that trip and could not decide ahead of time exactly what I might want to hear, I’d take the K700s. Given the elevated price points here, I am thinking the K700s will be the sweet spot for most people as well, given the generalist nature and mid range pricing of the design. I’d give the K700s an A- for sound quality.

text: I was taken in by the specs of this headphone. Quality wise and sound production wise, it's OK. I compared it with Bose QC3 Noise Cancelling headphone (bought from Amazon). Surprisingly, the audio output quality when using it in the wired mode is (in my opinion) better than the high end QC3. However, when I switched it to bluetooth mode, the outstanding audio reproduction in the wired mode is completely lost and the superior quality of the QC3 is immediately obvious. I am not an audiophile but in my opinion, the BTH3 surpasses the QC3 at both the bass and high frequency range of the sound output - when you are using the BTH3 in the wired mode. The sound reproduction in the bluetooth mode is not the same as what you get in the wired mode, so much so that I don't feel like using it in the more convenient Bluetooth mode again. I used my travelling scale to weigh the two. The Photive wighs 0.4 lb (181.4g) while the QC3 weighs 0.28 lb (127g). Of course the QC3 is outstandingly more comfortable. The controls on the BTH3 are easy to locate and use. However, the characters are not very bright to read. text: Alright, when it comes to the JBL Quantum One Headset, it was my first choice. I could not justify the original price ,as i do not game enough, until there was a $100 price drop and then i snagged them. I did wait through a few shipping delays, (to be expected as i ordered them in the beginning of December.) but then they arrived. I ripped the box open to find a very hardy and very nice quality box. I'm a sucker for a nice box and the unboxing experience was rather premium. Anyway, onto the headset. First impressions: Pros- Very nice weight- Very weighty headset. Memory foam cushions- Very comfortable memory foam that forms to my head, but has enough rebound to not sink into my head. Very solid woven cords- I have abused these cords on accident and I have yet to see a single sign of fraying from them Very nice materials all around- Very premium plastics and metals to obtain a finish fit for the value. Little to no material squeaking- Materials fit together nicely and mesh well together, unlike my Razer headsets of the past. Very Sturdy- Doesn't bend in ways that seem precarious to fit around my unfathomably Brobdingnagian cranium. Very Comfortable- I have worn it for hours and haven't noticed any fatigue from my ears or my head. Amazing Audio Quality for Gaming in General Music quality is far above average as well. It has a very even tone all around and doesn't overly accentuate highs or lows. I honestly prefer them to my first generation AirPod Pros. Bass is a little lacking, but that is generally adjustable on most platforms to your liking. The microphone only picks up sound from you. It auto isolates your voice and doesn't pick up my ear shatteringly loud bass coming from the subwoofer directly next to my desk. As for the quality and volume of the microphone, it's nothing short of fantastic. My teammates and buddies can hear everything clear as day, even if there is background sound. I consistently get compliments from randoms on my audio quality from people asking if i play on PC and have a dedicated standalone microphone. Outstanding Directional Sound. Noise Isolation and fit is Astounding. Cons- I really love this headset but i must bash it for JBL to improve. Noise Cancellation is Sub-Par comparably to headphones of the same or similar values. The ambient sound in ANC is quite nice, but not when gaming. Its incompatibility with MacOS has become a bit of an issue as I wanted to experience the full headset, but I am limited to what is immediately out of the box. This, though, is not an issue as I originally intended for the use to be on my XBOX full time. Overall, I would wait for a price drop until buying as you can be just fine with a $70 headset instead of something at such a premium value.

text: I believe these headphones shouldn't be taken outside. They are expensive. I have a cool hanger thingy that looks like a banana hanger where these hang on, and they never leave my home. The sound quality is insane. I cannot stress how amazing the sound is. I went from a 120$ pair of Sony headphones which I didn't have any gripes with, but I didn't know what I was missing until I popped these on and pressed play. These headphones are the way apple justifies being an apple nerd in the sound quality department. It just makes sense if you own apple products already. Did I mention they are expensive? The noise canceling is mind blowing. I can vacuum with these and still hear what im listening to quite clearly. My girlfriend gets completely blocked out when I have these on, I literally cannot hear her because the noise cancelling is insane. My neighbors dog who never stops barking? Bye bye didn't even struggle canceling that out. It basically makes you beyond legally deaf which is what it should do. You can push a button next to the Apple Watch style volume crown which turns on transparency mode, which is surprisingly good as well. It basically lets you keep the headphones on and hear as if they weren't on, actually you can hear a bit better than normally from my personal experience. Its weird how good these functions perform in practical use and I find myself using transparency mode as it is easier than just taking them off. I gave this review 5 stars after debating in my own mind the battery life. My old Sony headphones which were only $120 which isn't necessarily cheap, but it isn't $450. Those headphones, the Sony, had over 30 hours of battery life. HOWEVER I decided to still give 5 stars even in the battery life department. The reason is simple and it is because of how the noise cancelling is just insane. I just figured (idk if im right) that the insane noise canceling must require more power. The way I figured this isn't necessarily scientific so idk. These headphones have really blown me away and they are super comfortable, they sound amazing, and I never really find the battery life as some kind of issue that im always running into, so I just put 5 stars. If you are on the fence, just ask yourself, do you like nice stuff? If you are like me and have a MacBook an iPad an iPhone an Apple Watch a house full of HomePods, AirPods, ect. Your deeply enslaved in Apple at this point. There isn't any turning back from the plane of higher existence that apple is selling myself and those like me. Ease of use is unmatched, just pop them on. The headphones even know wether it should connect to my phone or my laptop or iPad as it connects to whatever device im currently using, which is super nifty. I don't have to even push a button to go from laptop to phone, I can just pause whatever is on my laptop, grab my phone and start playing music and it automatically switches. This is standard of apple H series microprocessor powered headphones however, so its not necessarily something new compared to any of the other AirPods, but I have noticed that it has superior range compared to the normal AirPods earplugs. This last section of my review will be a summary. I listened to all my favorite songs with these on and they sounded almost unrecognizable. If your in the apple ecosystem, and you are on the fence, just buy them. Treat yourself to amazing noise canceling, insane sound quality, and apple ecosystem no-effort compatibility. Sure the case sucks but it looks cool on a desk. Mine is blue and it does look slick and modern but function is just cosmetic and serves to magnetically shut off the headphones while inside the case. If your going to travel with these, yeah you gotta buy a sturdier case for sure. Dont throw these in a bag without a hard case. There are many good hard cases on amazon, and that is something to take into consideration before you make your purchase, it is not going to last long on the go without one. Hope this review was somewhat helpful, I have owned these for 5 months now and I love them.

text: It can be hard to judge how something will sound just from reading impressions online - especially with all of the vague and confusing terms floating around. I've read every review and watched every video related to these headphones prior to buying them (how can you not for this price) - and none of them prepared me for what I've just experienced. In short: These are incredible, miraculously detailed in every aspect of the sound, and most of all - these sound HUGE! The presence of the sound hitting your ears, it's almost overwhelming at times. NOBODY talks about what bass monsters these are! I didn't even know headphones could capture the presence of a home theater, ESPECIALLY in an open back. If you can afford it, you should do yourself the favor of experiencing this. In long: You hear the same thing over and over from people who aren't into audio. Why would someone spend $1.5k on a headphone? How good can it possibly sound? Yet they have no problem spending the same mount on a higher end TV. It's because everyone has seen a high end TV compared to a low end TV in passing, it's obvious what the money gets you... Almost nobody has heard a $1.5k headphone, therefor they can't possibly understand, having no frame of reference. Honestly, neither have I until I got these, I bought them on blind faith that they would be better than everything else I have. Boy am I glad I took the jump. The difference is huge with these. I was concerned that a $1.5k headphone wouldn't be worth it (diminishing returns and all). I am happy to say I was wrong. Overall, I feel lucky. Lucky that I get to experience music so deeply. I wish everyone could have these to enjoy music with. I don't know how much higher this audiophile journey goes. Is an Abyss AB-1266 that much higher of a jump than these? Only one way to find out. - PS: If you spend enough time researching, the audiophile world really has people believing that amplifiers and DACs have as much difference between them as one headphone to another. This is dead wrong at best, and nefarious at worst. This sentiment is pushed by equipment manufacturers looking to cash in on the subjective nature of this hobby. It has people spending $400 on a Amp/DAC stack for their $200 headphones, where the money would be much better spent on a $500 headphone and a $100 Amp/DAC. Save up for a good headphone, that's where the real differences are. - My comparison items: Sennheiser HD 6XX. Bayerdynamic 880 DT 250ohm. HiFiMan HE-400i. Sony MDR-MA900. Blue Monkey Flyer Mod T50RP. Philips X2. Beyerdynamic T1. Paradigm Studio 20 v5 Speakers. Sources: JDS O2, JDS OLDAC, CmoyBBv2, TheBit Opus #11, ifi hipDac, ifi iDSD Signature

With music on, I seriously doubt I would hear sirens and I only hear my engine towards the upper RPM limit, but wind noise is nonexistent. I know many riders claim this in dangerous, but in the past few months I've been using these while riding all through Los Angeles and have yet to be surprised by a car because I did not hear it. text: The SMS BioSport Earbuds could have and should have been a boon to runners using the Sony SmartWatch 3 to track their runs on their smartwatches, except: 1. SMS Audio did not implement the BTLE standard which would have allowed their HRM to work with almost any Heart Rate Monitoring Android Wear app (e.g., Ghostracer). 2. SMS Audio did not work with Ghostracer (which displays heart rate with other running stats on the SmartWatch's display) to make sure it supported their HRM (it does not). 3. RunKeeper does not bother to display HR on the SmartWatch's display. So if you want to monitor your heart rate while you are running you must use RunKeeper AND either: 1. run with your phone in your hand, continually looking at RunKeeper on the display, and trying to read it in the bright sunlight as you run OR: 2. enable current HR in the RunKeeper audio cues and wait for the audio cue to hear your current heart rate. However you have to wait for the audio cue (every 5 minutes? every mile?) and if you miss it when it comes up, you'll just have to wait for the next audio cue! This is not very useful and may be even more annoying than trying to read it from your phone as you're running. The opportunity to make this a great tool for runners has been squandered by SMS Audio and RunKeeper. Although I have become accustomed to using it with Runkeeper and the audio cues, it would be so much more useful if either: 1. Runkeeper displayed average and current HR on their SmartWatch 3 app display, or 2. SMS worked with Ghostracer or other SmartWatch 3 running apps that display HR info In spite of these shortcomings, I like the SMS Audio BioSport Earbuds because I don't have to charge them. I listen to Pandora while I run so I have to have my phone with me anyway, so plugging the earbuds into my phone and not having to charge them is a major advantage. They also have a very good sound. If they would fix the problem of displaying HR on my Sony SmartWatch 3, they would get 5 stars. ADDED 12/06/2015: I just got a new phone, the Nexus 6P. Runkeeper will not connect to the heart rate monitor at all on this phone. Occasionally the headphone jack does not even register the Biosport as being plugged in at all and the music comes out of the speakers. This does not happen with other earphones. But even when the music does come through the earbuds, Runkeeper does not display the Heart icon on its Start page at all, indicating that it is not connected to the BioSport's HRM. For this reason I am changing my rating from 4 stars to 1 star. Check the SMS Audio FAQ page at for compatible devices. It is currently a very short list: Apple iPhone 4S, Apple iPhone 5, Apple iPhone 5S, Apple iPhone 5C, Apple iPhone 6, Apple iPhone 6 Plus, Samsung Galaxy Note II, Samsung Galaxy Grand II Duos, Samsung Galaxy S4, Samsung Galaxy S5, LG Nexus 5, and Motorola Moto X (2013)

When I listened to my music with background noise I tried the different modes of noise cancellation, using them both with and without the noise machine. Things obviously were blocked out to different degrees when I switched modes - the background noise from the noise machine was just about totally gone under one of the modes but the other two modes just had changed the noises so it was softer in the background, it seemed constant and manageable now and there was no music or tv noise coming from anywhere - just the background noise very soft in the distance even though it was on my nightstand (the music I was softly listening to as I fell asleep did not have to be loud). So I saw different modes did block out different things. When in bed, if I fairly quietly turned on the background noise, listened to some softer relaxing music and then I could not hear any of the annoying sound(s) sometimes echoing thru the walls... I do not know if the background noise from the noise machine is needed, but that is the only thing I can remotely hear, other than my music. Pressing the talkthru button does stop the music and make it so there is a constant sort of noise in the background in which it is easy to hear people's voices but it sounds to me like I am speaking louder than I actually am. The CXC700 are good for playing music but I could not get it to put the outside world on mute if their were a whole lot of different things around me.

text: The Sony CD-180 is a very unimpressive headphone, even at (dollar amount). Then again, most closed headphones at this price are a poor choice. Deep bass is lacking badly, but upper bass is exaggerated somewhat, giving them a boomy, fake bass sound. Mids aren't much better - some midrange frequencies are very prominent, and voices drill into my head in a rather fautiging manner, and smear together with insturments to my displeasure. They also have a very hollow quality that probably has something to do with the closed headphone design. Treble is very muted, but lower treble is exxagerated, and it makes the CD180s sound at first like they have a lot of detail, which they don't. Imaging (Placement of insturments) is poor. Everything sounds like it is either coming from the center of my head, or the right or left side, there isn't much in the way of seperation otherwise. They also have a fairly cheap feel, although they are reasonably comfortable - they don't clamp down on your ears overly hard, and they are circumaural (Go around your ear, not on top) so the pressure is put on the area around your ears. They do sound better then other closed Sony headphones in this price range like the MDR-v150,200,250, but sound somewhat worse then the Koss UR-20s which are also closed, and much worse then the open Koss KSC-50s which can be had for the same price. The next step up from the Koss UR-20s with a closed headphone is the Sony MDR-v7506, which is around (dollar amount) - there isn't anything worth buying in between. As always, keep headphone listening volume reasonable - you can damage your ears very easily. As a general rule of thumb if you can't tell someone is talking to you when you are not engrossed in the music, they are up too loud.

text: There are so many earbuds to pick from it's hard to decide. Bottom line, this is a good company, not a no-name knockoff, and it shows. I first bought a less expensive no-name pair that fit my need for running, biking, etc and the reviews were good, with respect to sound as well which is important to me. I don't want to generalize and I'm no audiophile but the sound in the less expensive buds was tolerable but not good at all. They produced noise like a low end car stereo (which many people are ok with). They were consistent with the less expensive ones my kids and wife have who are ok with hearing noise rather than music. They also paired the left one as a slave to the right and I couldn't get it connected right. I'm a tech guy and I think it was faulty so I returned. I wanted something better. Many may be ok with a less expensive pair if you get a working pair but for the 20 bucks extra, these things sound fantastic comparatively and well worth it. Again, no audiophile here but for perspective I run some pretty high end equipment in my home and car. I was really shocked at what these produced. Maybe you can get better sound by spending even more but to me it might be negligibly better, might just get other features. I see no reason for my needs. Pairing was much easier too, I've used one earbud, right or left, depending if I'm running or biking with zero issues. I haven't memorized the controls yet but I think you do lose some control just using one which seems obvious but I'll mention it. That said, while biking I took calls with one bud in and the other person could hear me fine. They said I sounded a little distant but I also had a thin hat on a gator over my mouth and ears so I was impressed they even heard me. I have had no issues with them coming loose running, biking, circuit training, etc. They are packaged well with multiple choices to fit. Wings or no wings, multiple sizes, etc. I thought about the waterproofing but after researching, if Bluetooth doesn't work under water like for swimming, waterproofing became less important to me. These are waterproof enough for me and I haven't had an issue. Just something you'll have to consider for yourself. Couldn't be happier with these.

text: ***NOTE: My review previously incorrectly stated that IconX earbuds do not work with iOS. They do pair with an iPhone and other iOS devices and play sound without any issues. Touch playback controls work, however, there's no support for fitness features. I apologize for misreading the spec sheet without actually trying them out with an iOS device.*** I am an avid runner and a martial artist and have always been on the lookout for truly wireless earbuds that would allow me to fully engage in my workouts without worrying about them falling out or getting displaced. Thanks to Samsung, I have finally found them! But it's not to say they're perfect or without compromises. I should also mention that my previous go-to earbuds were Jaybird X2 and I will compare the two below in some areas... On to the main points... Build Quality & Design: solid, hard plastic. They look like they are built to last. Solid case that doubles as a charging dock and has a battery of its own that is good enough to recharge the earbuds about 3 times. A clever move by Samsung given the battery life is one of the IconX's major weaknesses. Fit: The earbuds fit exceptionally well. I have medium sized ears and ended up using M-size tips and L-size wings (there are 3 pairs of each included). They never fell out or came loose during running, heavy bag workout or anything else I threw at them. Easy to put in and take out of your ears as well. Exceptionally light. Colour me very impressed, Samsung! Look: While visible in your ears, they're not sticking out too much. I like the look of them far more than my Jaybird X2. Compatibility: Only Android 4.4+ is officially supported per spec sheet, though they do pair with iOS and play sound as your regular Bluetooth headphones. I had no issues whatsoever connecting my Samsung Galaxy S7 to it and listening to music/podcasts via Bluetooth. Samsung Gear app found it instantly and connected without any probs. Also successfully tested with an iPhone 6 for music/podcast playback. Controls: I have mixed feelings about touch controls. In casual use, they're simple and quite reliable once you get used to them, but can be finicky during workouts when you're moving and your hands are sweaty. All in all, they work pretty well. I like the fact that either earbud responds to touch commands. The automatic pairing/start once you put them in and the auto-stop once you take them out are nice touches as well. Activity Tracking: This is where we get into some negatives... IconX fails miserably as an activity tracker. It cannot track distance accurately due to lack of GPS. It told me I've run 2km after completing a 4.5km run which is just cruel. :) The heart rate monitor, as is the case with many other trackers, is unreliable. I really wish they'd concentrated their efforts on sound quality and audio player features instead... speaking of which... Sound: No issues with sync between the earpieces or sound cutting out as reported with some other similar wireless headsets. Sound quality is pretty good for a Bluetooth headset. It can be described as "warm" with bass present but not overpowering. Highs and mids are somewhat lacking but not to the point where you won't enjoy your music. Jaybird X2, in comparison, does sound a little better but not by a huge margin. Noise Isolation: Superb! They cancel out all the noise around you which can be a good or a bad thing, depending on what you're doing. There is an "ambient sound" mode that allows you to hear the surroundings, but it is a bit weird as the sound is fed through the built-in mics. Music Player: IconX have 4GB of internal storage to store your audio files (each earbud has 4GB capacity and audio files are copied to both during transfers, in case you're wondering). Unfortunately, the built-in music player is very limited. You can jump back and forth between tracks, randomize their play, pause/play and that's about it. No skipping, no playlist support which makes them terrible for podcasts or any similar large audio tracks. You do have an option of streaming podcasts directly from your phone but that diminishes the already limited battery life -- its single biggest weakness... Battery: Obviously you can't have something this light without compromising battery size... I generally found the battery life claims by Samsung accurate. 1.5 - 3 hrs depending on enabled features. My average workout length is 1.5 hrs and I use them as a standalone MP3 player (with Bluetooth / activity tracking off) which works quite well. Streaming Bluetooth will drain the battery very quick, you'll be lucky to get 1.5hrs out of them. Another major issue that I've found with the related to battery life is that they drain battery when left unused (in case or otherwise) for a day or two. There are many reports of this on various boards, including Samsung support forums. I've contacted Samsung support about this issue and they say this is not normal behavior and the earbuds should not be discharging *while in the case*. Still not decided whether to take them in for repairs or exchange at Costco where I bought them, but I will update the review with regards to this problem. Overall, a decent first effort by Samsung. Given the fact this is a first truly wireless headset from a major manufacturer, I am willing to accept some compromises. I took off 2 stars for the rather useless activity tracking features, the limited playback capabilities and the battery life issues. I am sure the next iterations will bring the much needed improvements and I am curious to see what other manufacturers come up with.

You have to choose one of the two unless you use a voice assistant. However not being able to control volume isn’t a big deal to me. What is a problem is that I can’t pause and play unless that earbud is assigned that function. The capacitive touch buttons are ok. They are a little bit finicky especially if your hands are wet. However that’s Expected with those controls. Case: case is thick. It’s small however due to its thickness it might be a little trouble for some to Cary them. However it’s not a deal breaker. It’s decently built nice mate rubber finish. Connectivity: the connection has been not the best at time. Most of the time it works fine. However it unpairs at random times and and only one bud connects. Bugs: there a few I’ve encountered. The app is a bit buggy. When I open the app it takes a couple of seconds for me to see my buds. It constantly closes and opens up the bud profile. Also the most annoying and funny bug that I’ve encountered is when I put them in the case they emit a high pitch ringing sound. I assume this is the ambient mode in each bud interfering with each other. It’s really annoying sometimes however putting them back in the case and closing it a couple of times usually stops it. Final thoughts : These right now go for about 200$. For that price these buds are not worth it. For android users there are plenty options that are better than this at this price. And for apple users AirPods Pro are infinitely better than these. However, I did get them around 100 and for that price these buds are a good value. Only thing is the comfort is a bit lacking. Reasonably I wouldn’t pay more than 130$ for these.

text: I’ve been interested in trying bone conduction headphones since the day I saw someone wearing this technology in the grocery store. After I asked him what that device on his head was, his explanation intrigued me. So I decided to ask for one for Father’s Day with a lot of hopeful expectations. This device small, lightweight, and comfortable. I wore them for about two hours and there was no pain. When the volume is high, there is a noticeable pulsing, it feels like they’re lifting off the skin slightly, but it isn’t too annoying and since this is my first time with bone conduction, I can’t say for sure if this is typical with this type of headset. Another reason I was interested in bone conduction was to see how well they perform in a loud environment. With ear buds, I always have a problem with fitting in my ear and slipping out when I sweat. I grew up in Wisconsin and now live in Florida, so as you can imagine I sweat a lot. Also with ear buds, I can’t hear what’s going on around me. This product has solved both those issues. When I’m operating a forklift I’m still aware of voices and noises around me and I don’t have any problems with the slipping out of position. The squeeze on your head just right. Today I used them while I mowed the lawn. I couldn’t hear anything through ear buds and to my disappointment, I couldn’t hear with this device either. I did try using earplugs hoping they would muffle the ambient noise and would be able to hear my music. It turns out that the earplugs worked to lessen the outside noise, as well they should since that’s what they’re designed for, but also damped the music making it sound like I was listening underwater; however, I was able to hear it. I asked for this headset because of the good reviews and reasonable price. With that said I’ve been happy with this product and I would recommend them. If anyone has any advice on my lawn mowing issue, please let me know!

text: The RCA WHP141B 900MHZ Wireless Stereo Headphones are fine for casual TV watching. If, on the other hand, you are looking for high fidelity headphones for high end home theater, you are looking in the wrong place. These headphones are fine for your average TV watching experience, but the sound quality is really sub par for music or other applications that require a little nuance. As long as there is sound being fed into the base unit, the headphones sound alright, but in quiet spots, the system's power saving kicks in and you get audible "pops" as the amp cycles on and off. You also get a little hiss if the volume is turned too far down on the source output. Fot the money the RCA WHP141B 900MHZ Wireless Stereo Headphones will work for many situations, but if you are picky about sound quality, you may want to look elsewhere.

text: I bought this direct from Headset Buddy and am very happy with it. I read the negative reviews before purchasing, so I was ready to be disappointed, but after using it, I just don't understand the complaints, as mine works perfectly fine. I did various test calls with noises in my office and found that the mic worked great, with very little background noise being picked up. Just like the Bose headphones themselves, the noise cancellation is best for constant or relatively non-intrusive noises, particularly those that are not in the normal voice frequency range. The noise cancellation is great for filtering out a leaf blower or lawn mower outside, or server fans in a data center, but terrible for a crying baby sitting next to you at an airport or loud voices in the background. I have had zero issues with feedback, buzz, or other audio issues when using the mic with my iPhone. The only limitation I've found is that I cannot use this with my Panasonic cordless phone at home. For some reason, the Panasonic phones produce a loud "amplifier buzz" sound. I tried with 3 different models of Panasonic phones, and 2 out of 3 were unusable, while 1 was barely usable. Since the mic works perfectly fine with my iPhone, it's something about the cordless phone. The boom is highly adjustable and does not move at all for me once I position it. The boom can only be bent in a limited radius--it doesn't bend at 90 degree angles, but it is more than adequate for me to get the mic anywhere I want near my mouth, cheek, or chin. Zero issues. I don't understand the complaints about the mic flopping down or not staying in position. The jack that plugs into the Bose headphones is not a perfect fit--the plastic isn't flush and the connector isn't as snug as I would like, but it's not a major issue. If the cord gets pulled, it can pull the mic out of the Bose headphones, but I have only had it happen once. The benefit is that if the cord gets yanked, it will pop out and should reduce damage to the cord or the headphone plug. The cord is thinner than the Bose inline mic cord, but who cares? Could they have used a larger wire? Sure. Maybe a heavier cord would make it more durable, but the cord works fine, and isn't much different than typical headphone wires. If you peel open the cord for iPhone earbuds, most of the cable is comprised of the plastic sheath--the wires inside are thinner than thread (literally--they are like fine hairs). So the Clear Mic cord really isn't that thin. Overall, I'm perfectly happy with the mic. I've taken many calls on my iPhone with it, and it has worked flawlessly. Yesterday I took a call while waiting at the noisy gate at the airport. Worked great, the caller could hear me just fine. UPDATE: December 2014: After using this headset lightly for about a month, I found that the headphone jack that plugs into my iPhone is either damaged or poor quality. I accidentally pushed on the jack while on a call and it disconnected the call. Apparently the jack has a poor connection to the phone and when it loses the connection during a call, it hangs up the call. After this happened twice, I stopped using the headset. While I really like the headset, it does seem that there is a quality or durability issue. Some have complained that it is relatively expensive, but I would pay $20 additional, or more, for a higher quality version of this headset. If Bose made a version of this for $70 that was high quality and durable, I would buy it. UPDATE 2: February 2015: I e-mailed Long Tail Products / Headset Buddy and explained the problem with the headset disconnecting if I moved the jack while using it with my iPhone 6. I shipped the headset back to them and they sent me two replacement headsets. (They were responsive and had very good customer service.) Unfortunately, the new headsets have the same issue with my iPhone 6. So it likely wasn't a damaged headset jack in the unit I returned.. I then tested the standard Bose QC 15 microphone / cord, and that works fine with my iPhone 6, along with the standard Apple headphones. So the problem doesn't seem to be with my iPhone 6. But strangely, I tested the Headset Buddy on my wife's iPhone 5S and it worked fine. So whatever the problem is, it seems to be with the combination of Headset Buddy Clear Mic with my iPhone 6. Perhaps the jack is slightly out of spec or there is something about the electronic / electrical properties of the ClearMic that the iPhone 6 doesn't like. I will have to find someone else who has an iPhone 6 and test the ClearMic on their phone to see if it is just my iPhone 6, or all iPhone 6 phones that have the issue. Whatever the cause, the end result is that I'm unable to use the Headset Buddy Clear Mic with my iPhone 6, so I now have two of them sitting in my office. I'm bummed, since I really liked it. Again, given the price of the Bose QuietComfort headphones, I would now gladly pay a lot more than $30 for a high quality noise cancelling boom microphone.
