text: Okay, the main points first: 1. The noise-cancellation works fairly well, but has some problems. 2. The overall sound quality is good, but not exceptional. 3. The ear-pressure effect is there, but it's not that bad. 4. They cost $300. First off, there's the noise cancellation. The effect is so subtle at first that I missed it completely, and thought there was a problem with my headphones. With a little experimentation, though, I figured out exactly what it was doing. (Disclaimer: I haven't been on a plane with them, which is apparently exactly where they shine the brightest.) The upside: in certain environments, they'll actually filter out a great deal of ambient noise. They're pretty nice at home. I live in a noisy apartment in a noisy neighborhood. They dampen out the sound of cars on the street, people talking outside my window, and (fortunately or not) they entirely kill the sound of my doorbell. So far so good, but there's a drawback. While they cancel out some frequencies beautifully, they leave others virtually untouched. Specifically, human voices carry through the NR circuitry almost undiminished. When I tried these in the cafe down the block, it was pretty unpleasant. They killed all the regular background noise, but left untouched the sound of conversations. This is really weird, because normally, human voices in public places are muted by background noise. With the QC2s on, I could hear everyone around me talking, and they were all talking really loudly, to overcome background noise that I couldn't hear. The effect was really annoying, and I found it impossible to concentrate. As far as sound quality, it's fine, but nothing special. The sound is probably far better than the headphones that came with your walkman, but it's not even near audiophile quality. Compared to any number of reasonably good under-$100 headphones from Grado or Sennheiser, these are muddy and indistinct. Not a huge problem for most people, but folks who are used to good headphones will be disappointed. The ear-pressure effect is definitely real. Anyone who's having trouble noticing it, try putting on the headphones without any input and turning them on and off while you're wearing them. You'll feel it. Unlike other reviewers, though, I don't find it uncomfortable or annoying, just weird. It's a little like your ears popping at altitude (or, rather, your ears not popping when you'd like them to). Finally, there's the cost issue. I gotta tell you, these just don't sound nearly as crisp and detailed as much, much cheaper phones without the NR circuitry. Beyond that, though, a good set of closed-earpiece headphones will block out almost as much background noise as these do, and an in-the-ear set like Etymotics (I had a set of ER6s) will block out more noise and sound better for less money. Bottom line - these are great headphones if: 1. $300 is not a lot of money to you and you like gadgets, or... 2. You travel a lot on airplanes, or... 3. (Like me) you have several pairs of headphones, and you don't count on any one set to do everything for you.

text: You can find full reviews on Head Fi and other audio sites and forums so I'll be brief. I've had my fair share of quality headphones and listened to many others and the Focal Elear is among the best I've heard and it is the best $1000 and under headphone imo. The dynamics are some of the best I've heard and the depth of field and imaging is also fantastic. They are comfortable to wear and build quality is what you'd expect from a $1000 headphone. If you can only buy one headphone and have the money to spend these are it (unless you can spend thousands on something like the Utopia). I like them so much I'm going to sell most if not all of my other headphones and that's something I never thought I'd ever do. Update 3/1/17, After having the Elear now for about 4 months I couldn't be more happy with them. I have well over 150 hours of use on them and the sound better than ever, though I think the Modi Multibit DAC has something to do with that. The mids have come through quite a bit more than in the beginning and that's without them being EQ'd. I do have the bass turned up 2.2db to give my electronic music that extra kick it needs but its still not basshead territory imo. Highs are nice and crisp without any harshness and I think the overall detail retrieval is very good though not in the HD800 realm. The soundstage to me has more width to it now so it's not as narrow sounding and the depth is as good as ever, they really do have the best depth of field I've heard from a headphone. The only downside to the Elear is that my other headphones don't get used much, I'd say only my Nighthawk gets picked up every now and then when I'm in a more basshead feel (not saying they are basshead cans but they do have a nice kick to them). Build quality is perfect with no rattles or loose fittings anywhere and they are a very comfy headphone. For a thousand dollars these really are a bargain, so if you want top tier sound quality for a mid-fi (top end of mid-fi) price the Focal Elear is they way to go, unless you like a more analytical detailed sound sig then the HD800 or T1 is the better choice.

text: Update Four: It's almost been a year since I bought these and I'm glad to say these earbuds have held up fine. My case has a few minor scratches from drops, but otherwise they look aesthetically the same and work operationally the same as when I bought them. Sound quality is still good. Overall, I still recommend, although I haven't read other reviews so there might be some flaws I haven't run into. Again, these aren't top notch earbuds, but they're a solid sub-$50 pair for people who don't use them all the time or want a cheaper set. ---- I don't know if this is already in the Q/A section, but I wanted to explain how to resync the two earbuds. I've had to do this once every couple months, and I don't know what the cause is, but eventually it happens and it can be a struggle to fix. In the manual, it gives the following instructions: 1) Turn off earbuds. 2) Wear one in ear, hold button for 12-13 seconds, wait for "deng deng" prompt and release. 3) Wear both, hold each for 2 seconds at same time, left should flash red/blue and right should be blank (no led). In personal experience, I'd like to clarify these directions for what works for me most of the time. 1) Turn off both earbuds and keep out of case. 2) Go into bluetooth settings and forget the device. 3) Hold right earbud down for 6ish seconds (not 12-13) and you will hear the "deng deng" prompt. Release. 4a) Place both earbuds in charging case and close, then remove again and place in ears. Listen for "power on". 4b) Hold both earbuds for 2 seconds in ear and listen for "power on" from both. 5) Then hold them for a second to look at lights. The left should be flashing red/blue, right should have no led on. 6) Open bluetooth and reconnect to the earbuds, you did it. If at step 5 they aren't blinking correctly, try it again, and try different step 4 options. They should practically do the same thing, but I don't know, I've had both work and not work. The red/blue blinking indicates that that earbud is in the independent mode. The non-blinking one is in dependent mode. Normally this issue happens for me when the right is somehow tricked into going independent, and with two independents only one can connect because they are both giving bluetooth prompts. This is their "monaural mode" according to the manual, and when this happens to both earbuds it can cause issues. Hence why I only use the left earbud in these situations. If you can get the right earbud back into dependent mode, the earbuds should be able to reconnect together and step 6 should always work. If not, but the light setup is correct, try simply putting them back into the case for a few seconds and try again, left earbud out first, then right. The left should detect the right and you'll be aight. ---- Update Three: I've had them for 4 months now and they're still holding up great. Dropped the case on the sidewalk last week and yep, still no problems. Sound is still solid, same with battery life. Great option for discount wireless earbuds. Update Two: Shortened the first update and the battery problem has been solved. The problem was in my charging brick, got a new one and now they’re working fine again. Also, I did a full battery test, and after fully charging and playing music continuously, they lasted 4 hours and 41 minutes off one charge. Update: *removed battery issue* I realize I never commented on how they physically fit and felt in your ear. In my experience it’s been comfortable, nothing luxury but it’s never been outright uncomfortable in my ear. I’d agree with the statement someone else made in a review: it fits well if you have small ears. I have average sized ears and they work fine for stationary use and moderate activity (mowing the lawn, lifting at the gym, taking the bus, etc). However, running or jumping can cause them to come loose and wiggle out. I don’t know if these difficulties are because I don’t have smaller ears, but I’d say for the average eared person, these aren’t quite active-wear headphones for running. Additionally I believe down below I had a quote about the multi-touch navigation features that was something like “they work well enough”. No they don’t. Pausing/playing is alright with just one click, but clicking the button 12 times to raise the volume by 3 is not fun or convenient. Just keep your phone in your pocket or nearby. It’s much easier to control. All in all what I’ve said in the original post has held up, and the quality is still there. These are good wireless earbuds for anyone on a budget. Original Post: I’m just going to do a brain dump on every detail I can think of. I bought this during a flash sale for $30, and they’ve exceeded my expectations. They’re smart, automatically disconnect when put in the case for each ear and vice versa by automatically pairing when taken out. The sound is good except the bass can be a little grainy, but otherwise clear and detailed. The range is also fair, when I tested outside it reached roughly 30-40 ft. Material wise, the headphones feel cheap, but that is to be expected with discount Bluetooth earbuds. The one-button multi-click navigation features take a little to get used to, but they work well enough. It’s eaider to just keep your phone nearby or in your pocket though. For the case, however, it is of great quality and feels very sturdy. I’ve dropped it twice, once onto tile and they still work fine. The light indicators make each earbuds charge status clear and the case as well. The battery in my experience lasts for about 4 hours if fully charged, which in my case is more than necessary. The cable that comes with it for charging also feels cheap, but it should work fine to simply pump power into the batteries. I wouldn’t trust it to transfer data. I haven’t yet tried the microphone. They’re also comfortable in the ear. Would I recommend buying it for $30? Absolutely. For $50, the normal cost? If you are looking for a cheap pair, this will work. text: First off, let me start by saying that this is probably the best sounding new headphone that you are going to get at the 25 and under price range. Postives + good bass + strong full-bodied midrange + very good sound isolation; much better than the similarly priced Sennheiser HD201 in this department. + light for a fullsize headphone + detacheable cable. Super-easy to replace if needed. + solid construction for headphones made of all plastic. Seems less flimsy than the HD201 + highly flexible headband and great range of pivoting. + foldable for maximum portability. Negative - rolled off highs, which is quite noticeable due how much these phones emphasizes the midrange. - because it is so light and made of plastic, you can hear sound being transmited through the cable if the cable rubs against anything. - very uncomfortable headband after about 15 minutes. The padding is small and segmented into 3 sections. This creates small areas of contact which adds extra pressure to top of the head. Not good for someone with a sensitive scalp. I'll have to find a way add extra padding to them. - The use of vinyl material for the ear cushions. I would have prefered some softer cheap pleather instead which would be more comfortable. However, the vinyl material does aid quite a bit in sound isolation. That's why they tend to use this material for hearing protecting earmuffs. In many ways, this headphone is the opposite of the Sennheiser HD201, which another bang for the buck contender. The HD201 was shy on bass, and good at everything else. These Monoprice headphones is a bit shy on the treble, but good at everything below. The HD201 was kind've thin sounding, but the Monoprice phones sound more fullbodied while not needing as much power to drive. You still hear the highs with these, but they are recessed back while the midrange takes center-stage. It is very good for vocals and bass. Things like hi-hats and cymbols will take a backseat. Not necessarily a bad thing though because you can listen to these longer without being fatigued. My biggest gripe by far is the uncomfortable headband.

Thought nothing of it until I noticed it was getting very loose on my head and had it slip off. I don't believe I have a large-shaped head, and my other wireless headphones have never had this issue, so it's hard to tell what caused it. Plantronics was helpful with the warranty process and sent me a brand new pair, but it's been a little less than a now and the headband's broken again. This time I probably won't go through the trouble of doing another warranty cycle and toss it into the donation box. TLDR: Very good wireless headphones, especially for the gym and doing active things. Doesn't cancel out too much sound, so keep that in mind. If you think you have a big head maybe the headband will deteriorate over time and break.

text: The LG Electronics Tone Ultra (HBS-800) Bluetooth 3.0 stereo headset, made in China, comes with a charger, two ear gel sets, user manual, quick start guide, and the warranty card. Most of the headset rests comfortably on around the neck, with the ear buds attached by wire. I’m not particularly good at remembering which side has what controls. Fortunately the left side has a phone shaped button while the right has a play/pause shaped button so I can feel what side I want to work on. Music controls are on the right and phone controls on the left. The only variation is the ANC button being on the right. Voice dialing is activate by briefly pressing the call button. This only works when not using an app like Pandora. Pressing the call button for a second will automatically redial the last person called. For the most part, the controls are easy to use and learn. I find the LG Electronics Tone Ultra (HBS-800) Bluetooth 3.0 stereo headset works all day on a single charge. I tend to listen to audio more than I use the phone features, and have yet to run out of power. However when not in use, the headset seems to run out of charge overnight. If I don’t plug in the headset before going to bed, I won’t be able to use the headset the next morning. Considering there is supposed to be 20 days standby time, this makes no sense to me. Listening to music or podcasts on the LG Electronics Tone Ultra (HBS-800) Bluetooth 3.0 stereo headset is pleasing to the ears. There are no equalizer controls, but I don’t feel like I have to have them. The sound quality is good, and the headset is comfortable to wear. On my end, taking phone calls are equally pleasing to the ear. Although people on the other end can tell I am talking on an earpiece of some sort, they still report that they can hear me clearly. When testing the ambient noise cancelation, it was reported back that they could not hear a difference between turning it on or off. The LG Electronics Tone Ultra (HBS-800) Bluetooth 3.0 stereo headset is effective, pleasing to the ear, and comfortable to wear. If you’re looking for an easy to use headset, the LG Electronics Tone Ultra (HBS-800) Bluetooth 3.0 stereo headset is definitely worth considering. PROS: 10 hours talk/music time Auto reconnect Ambient noise cancelation A2DP voice compatible Advanced multipoint Voice activated dialing JBL Signature sound One year limited warranty CONS: 20 days standby time not reality

text: I'm a music lover, but also enjoy music production in various forms. I enjoy a lot of genres of music. I do love to sit back and get lost in the music but I also like analytic and critical listening as well. It's a little hard for to me to review these, since I'm not the targeted demographic for these. They seem to be designed for more laid back listening or for those that enjoy a more colored sound to their music. Not even an eq (which I don't think should be necessary for a $499+ headphone) is going to make these work for me. I own quite a few pairs of headphones, the AKG Q701 / K702 / 271MKII, the Beyerdynamic T1 / DT 770(80ohm) / 880(600ohm) / 990(250 ohms), the Grado 325is and the Sennheiser HD600. I have had a chance to compare them all to the HD 650's and felt like the 650's didn't do anything that some of my other headphones didn't already do better. I tried the 650's on several different headphone amps and just didn't feel they did anything special. The main reason I didn't fall in love with them though is the HD600's. I purchased a pair of HD600's about a year ago and I loved them after I spent 10-20 hours. When I reached 30-40 hours in I knew I would never part with them. If I had never heard the HD600's maybe I would feel differently. They are very similar in design and have a lot of the same sound characteristics. The HD650's have a bass boost and they are not as clear as the HD600's to me (I guess "veiled" is as good a description as any). I feel like by DT 990's already fill that niche with a much tighter bass response (although the higher frequencies will bother some). Now everyone has their own tastes and everyone hears music differently. Some would say the Grado's and Beyer headphones are too harsh and grating when it comes to the higher frequencies. If you feel this way, the HD650's might be for you, although I don't find the HD600's to be remotely harsh. I really thought having the HD650's and the HD600's both would give me the best of both worlds, but to me they are too similar with the main difference being the HD650's are more veiled and bass heavy. The head phones sound a little "slow" and at times even a little bit murky on the lower frequencies. On some records it can feel like the bass is seeping into the mid-range. Some people love a colored headphone with an enhanced bass sound that is more forgiving on lower quality music formats. It works with a lot of types of music and I can see why some people prefer them. If you are a bass head, this head phone may still be a little too analytical for you though. There is also no question that the HD650's are the better looking headphones, the HD600's paint look like a bad pair of hammer pants from the early 90's. The HD650's are a huge step up for most people and are a great mid-fi headphone. I just wish I would have had the opportunity to listen to them both side by side before purchasing both. I had to get both to see what everyone was talking about, but it was an expensive "adventure." I just don't think you really need both, if you like one, it's not worth getting the other. Either way I have to take off two stars. One because they are severely overpriced for a mid-fi headphone. You can usually pick up a pair of the 600's for around $280-300. You could even find a high end set of headphones like the T1 or the HD 800's used around $800-900 if you are lucky and they smoke the 650's. I'm not sure why the 650's go for $499. The other star is because even though a colored sound may be what some prefer, I don't think you should label them "reference" headphones or audiophile headphones. To me, getting rid of the 650's was an easy decision. To sum it up: PROS: *Cosmetically, this is a stellar headphone *It is very sturdy and parts are interchangeable between the 600's and the 598's *The cable is detachable, why don't more companies do this????? *It comes packaged in a nice sturdy box that you can use to store them in *Great for people that like an enhanced bass curve CONS: *$499 is far too much for a mid-fi headphone, especially when the HD600's often go for around $300 *The colored sound disqualifies this from being Audiophile or Reference in my book *The foam in the box smells funky, but I find this is the case with the HD600's as well

text: I ordered these after searching for bone conduction headphones. These are like regular air conduction headphones (mini speakers outside of the front of your ear) BUT not bone conduction. There is a difference in the method of how sound signal relays. These definitely work for what I needed. My inner ears are sensitive to earbuds or earplugs sitting in them as they make my ears feel warm and or itchy after about 10 minutes. I am averse to over the head headphones that encompass my ear or rest on the whole ear. Tactilely I just can't. These are very light weight and I forget that I have them on if I am not actively listening to something. The material is soft and I have not noticed any weird smells. Suggestions for improvements: 1. *** Battery life - They are quick to charge but they don't last long enough ESPECIALLY if I am actively using them often throughout the day. I will have to set to charge then wear my in-ear active noise cancellation wireless earbuds. 2. *** Calls/Voice control - the headphones do not have a mic. I'm mostly ok with this UNLESS a call comes across while I am listening to music and I am not near my phone. You can hear with the headphones, your voices still uses the phone or laptop mic. This also means if I am away from my phone and give a voice command to change song or screen, the phone cannot hear the command. Minor inconvenience. 3. *** Volume control - I am ok with using my phone for volume control. The issue is that as I am at work and listening to a book or music while multi-tasking or if laying in bed drifting off to sleep the lowest volume setting is potentially still too loud. It would be nice to turn the volume down even further in smaller increments. 4. *** Headband length - While upright the headband length is not super problematic. in laying down, the stiffness of the band pushes the earpiece forward putting pressure on my ears. I have manually manipulated the band to rest more flat and turned the earpieces at the band inward a little more by manually flexing the band and it is less irritating. I would enjoy a way to shorten the band or if the band were more easily manipulated the issue could be sorted. 5. *** "BATTERY LOW" - this repetitive, automated, loud voice scared me out of sleep the first night. The volume of the robotic voice could use lowering and maybe after the verbal warning if an audible short beep or tone could be played once or twice before it cuts off, it could be much less startling. I won't mind if I wake and they are off because they died. I'll know when they don't turn on or if a tone is played if I try to turn them on to signal they need charging. In all, I am happy with the band and quality for what I need. I would have loved them to be actual bone conductive, but am happy nonetheless. This is a good product so far and I will update if one is warranted.

text: I bought these purely for sound, I expect all bluetooth headphones to at least have connectivity down by now and some degree of portability and comfort. So that's what I'll lead with. Sound: My first impression is that the soundstage on these is wide, surprisingly so. Close to other open headphones I own. My second impression is the present but controlled bass in the upper mid bass region, but the real lack of extension. The bass bleeds into the mids without really extending to a point where it's exciting. The mids are up front here, and vocalists are easily heard (especially male vocalists) and generally sound accurate. The highs have a relaxed delivery, no real sibilance but symbols and hihats sound a tad dulled. Overall, I found these to have good detail retrieval (better than both the XM4 and QC35II) but the tuning is poor. They work well for vocals focused music, acoustic music, and some kinds of hip-hop, but overall lack dynamics on things like prog rock or electronic music. They sound much closer to the QC35II with a wider soundstage, the XM4 is a significantly more exciting headphone to listen to with better dynamics and bass extension. Most of the sound issues improve significantly when wired, but that's not what I bought this headphone. You can do better with a wired headphone at this price point. Comfort: The ear pads touch the edges of my ears but they're plush enough that it's not a huge bother, but every hour or so I have to give my ears a bit of a rest. The QC35II wins in this department. The XM4 press my ears in a bit and get hot sometimes. Build: These take the cake, the metal in the construction and real leather have a vastly more premium feel than either the QC35II or the XM4. However they are not as portable as the XM4 and have a slightly larger profile on the head. Features: I am constantly accidentally pausing or skipping tracks with the controls on these. The wear sensor is absolutely poor and ruins the experience often. Bluetooth connectivity is fine and I haven't had any problems with it. The XM4 is the winner in this department. The ANC is good, the XM4 is noticeably better but this cancels out fan sounds and airplane noise to a point where it doesn't matter. The QC35II is good if you want tactile buttons, but the XM4 has it beat in multi device connectivity, the wear sensor, and ambient mode. The battery time claims are accurate and hasn't been a concern. Overall, the strange tuning on these make them hard to enjoy on all music, and the spotty implementation of things like the wear sensor make it a hard sell over the XM4.

text: Build: The headphones are poorly built using cheap plastics. It creaks and rattles, and is quite noticeable. The top of the headband is plastic. Headband detents for the adjustments are nearly non-existent and the headphone does not hold your fit adjustment. Comfort/Controls: The headphones are pretty comfortable with large memory foam earcups and an Alcantara padding on the headband. The weight is okay for me not too heavy like the B&W PX, however the headphones are bulky with large gaps between your head and the headband. The headphones use physical controls which are small and hard to differeniate. You have to read the instructions as the controls are not intuitive. Bluetooth: There are some issues on what Bluetooth version the headphones are using. The AKG website and spec sheet indicate that the headphones use Bluetooth 4.2, but the "Quick Start Guide" states that the headphones use Bluetooth 4.1. Range is pretty good, I can go about 75 feet and through walls before connection drops out. You cannot connect to two devices at the same time like the Bose QC35 II or Sennheiser PXC 550. Audio Codecs: There is no documentation on what audio codecs the headphone supports. After some research, it seems that the headphones only support SBC and AAC codecs. Sound: The headphones seem to be tuned towards the warm side with vocals a little recessed and the volume seems to get louder than some competitors. The headphone's EQ can be adjusted in the AKG app. Noise cancelling: The noise cancelling is not as strong as the Bose QC35 II or the Sony WH-1000XM3, but it is adaptive and adjustable. App: The headphones have an IOS and Android app where you can adjust the EQ, noise cancelling and get firmware updates. Accessories: The headphones come complete with airplane adapter, headphone cable, USB charging cable and hard travel case. The case is bulky for travelling since the headphones do not lay flat inside the case. Conclusion: These headphones did not meet my expectations, there are too many compromises and no standout features. At $350 I cannot recommend these headphones. You are better off getting the Bose QC35 II, Sennheiser PXC 550 or the Sony WH-1000XM3 headphones at the same price point.

text: As a hard of hearing 35 year old customer, finding a good set of headphones is a difficult task where at a reasonable volume I can hear everything. Some are all thump and you can't hear the vocals, the highs and lows, some are "tinny" and sound like the old string and 2 used plastic cups tied together. After doing WAY more research than I probably needed between Beats, Aviators (Skullcandy), Vmoda Crossfade LP's, these, and the M80 (which by the way are the exact same headphone), I opted for these as the price was a good bargain and after Christmas I had some spare cash to roll towards an audio solution. While I am no audiophile, I have tried many types and brands of headphones. Skullcandy Ti, VModa Remix, Skullcandy Skullcrushers, Shure SE115, Beats Tour, Skullcandy Hesh, and probably a couple I forgot about. Through all of these I looked for comfort and great sound quality. While they may have one, they often didn't have the other... Today I received my V80's from Amazon.com, I was very pleased with the entire package as VModa really goes the extra step towards the presentation of these products. I haven't burned them in all the way but I have been running them for the past 11 hours and the sound is getting warmer. I can hear all the parts of my music plus parts I never had heard before. The bass isn't so heavy it rattles your brain out your nose, but it's there and blends nicely with the ambiance of the music. The vocals, highs, and mids are very smooth and it all sounds uniform together. I have been sucked into my own little world for the past many hours and haven't taken these off yet. They sit lightly on my ears (ON the Ear), and can be twisted around for a better fit, but I have a small head with small ears so I didn't have to move things around much. Types of music played on the headphones already at 50% of the volume on my 5th Gen. iPod Classic and my Macbook Pro Guns n Roses Tori Amos Soundgarden The Beatles Jimi Hendrix Joydrop Sneaker Pimps Eminem Ice Cube Weird Al Yankovic Nine Inch Nails Warrant Nirvana Courtney Love / Hole Smashing Pumpkins Deftones Poison Cinderella Led Zepplin Pink Floyd Faster Pussycat Primus Mother Love Bone Godsmack Sixx AM Tribe Called Quest My Life With The Thrill Kill Cult Beastie Boys Motley Crue Seether Red Hot Chili Peppers and quite a bit more music If I were you and you had the cash to invest, I would for sure give these a shot, VModa has a test drive program, if you don't like these within 60 days you can return them, no questions asked and Amazon is an authorized dealer. What have you got to lose. Just remember, my opinion is mine, and with music and headphones, it is all based on user experience, to take ANY feedback with a grain of salt. Good luck shopping and if you get these I hope you enjoy them as much as I do.

text: I acquired a couple of these directly from UE in July 2010. Nine months later they're still going strong. The UE 700 is a dual-driver design that uses one balanced armature driver to deliver the lows and another to deliver the highs. Using balanced armature drivers instead of a conventional mini-speaker has several advantages. First, the mass of the drivers is much lower, allowing the driver to start and stop vibrating faster, translating into greater detail and accuracy. Second, they're quite efficient; most of the time I have the computer set for the lowest sound level and it's more than adequate. Third, because the armatures are small, the entire housing (even though it's a dual-driver) can be made smaller than many single-driver mini-speaker units. In addition, using a two-way system allows each component (low frequency and high frequency) to act on the sound spectrum that it's tailored for, rather than a single unit trying to produce all frequencies. As mentioned earlier, these things are quite small - about 5/16" diameter. I don't remember if I had to change out the tips from medium to small to fit my ears but they fit very well. I gave a pair to a friend of mine who has small ear canals and usually has trouble finding earphones that fit; they fit her ears perfectly when using the smallest (XXS) tips. The included kit contains six pairs of tips so you should be able to get a good fit. The cable is also very thin and flexible, allowing it to coil up compactly when you want to store them in the included case. Note that you'll want to treat the cable nicely; don't just wrap it around your iPod or other device - take the time to store it correctly and it'll last a long time. You can wear the cable hanging down for casual listening or over-the-ear if you'll be in a more active situation such as working out at the gym. The UE 700 is also sound-isolating which means that it blocks out sound from entering the ear canal. This means that background noise is greatly diminished and allows you to listen to your music at a much lower volume. In turn, this can save your hearing since you don't have to turn it up as loud to drown out the background noise, plus you won't get listening fatigue as easily. Make sure you get a good seal as this is critical to getting sufficient bass response and blocking out noise. Sound-isolating is different from sound-cancelling in that it doesn't require batteries (since sound-cancelling is active) and it doesn't introduce sound artifacts (since sound-isolating is passive). All you hear is your music and not much of anything else. I haven't tried using these as in-ear monitors (I have a pair of UE Custom 10 Pro for that purpose) but I'm sure they'd work well. Plugged into my computer at work (I can't use speakers because I share an office) they sound great. The bass has plenty of punch without being overwhelming and the highs have lots of detail. I've purchased several pairs of UE earphones over the years starting with the super.fi 5 Pro back in January of 2006. A few were for me, some were gifts for friends, and everyone who has used them has been impressed. I wouldn't hesitate to buy UEs again.

text: For the last few years, I have been blessed with the opportunity to work with audio equipment of all levels and prices. I am a slight audiophile, but learn more towards the budget audiophile/DIY guy. I do not blow hundreds of dollars on ear monitors, but rather find well-priced equipment and make it sound better through amps, using high quality music files, and yes, custom EQ to make the device accurately mirror the song's recorded quality. All the above options were tested, yet still I could not get decent sound out of these IEMs. Pro's: -multiple ear pieces for a perfect fit -comfortable -airplane jack -I got them for $30 Con's: -sound canceling tends to amplify ambient noise -any cord movement is nauseatingly loud and is amplified through the speakers -treble is nonexistent, even when boosted through custom EQ -mids are muffled, muddy, and hollow, almost as if you are listening to music through a long pipe. -bass is loose, muddy and often overpowers the rest of the music. -does not take well to EQ -packaging is laughable... does Phiaton really think they are going to fool us with "this is a $120 value for $30" with packaging equivalent to $10 WalMart headphones? I'll leave this review short, simple and to the point. I really wanted to like these IEMs, and for $30, I thought they would be a steal. I tried everything from my iPhone, MacBook Pro with expensive audio and DJ programs, my church's $100,000 sound stage, headphone amps, and even hooked it up to my personal recording setup with which I used them to monitor direct guitar and vocal feed- even with the sound canceling off, these cannot replicate neither true nor "trending" audio. Save yourself the headache and take a look at some REAL IEMs from brands like Klipsch, Etymotic, Beyerdynamic, Sony, Sennheiser, Shure, etc. All of these brands have IEMS in this same price rage that can offer way more than Phiaton.

text: I really wanted to like these! The sound skips pretty often, either completely dropping or only coming out of one headphone for a split second. It seems to be happening in some areas more than others, like if I'm in a more crowded intersection or sometimes when cars drive by. It's really distracting. It also happens less if I take my phone out of my pocket and hold it closer to my head which makes me think that they've got some kind of bluetooth field issue that can't handle a layer of fabric when walking around outside. They work great indoors! No skipping issues at all when I'm inside. It just sucks that I can't use them outside walking around in a city. ---------------------- The fit is kinda strange too. The arms do hold the headphones in place pretty well - I've never felt like they were gonna fall off just from me moving around. They work really well for exercise and I don't feel like they get in the way while I'm lifting weights or riding a bike. The problem comes when I try to put them on - due to the arms retaining shape, I need to sorta undo them to fit them over my ears and then readjust them to get the fit right. Also (and this may just be a problem because of my weird ear shape) but I have to undo the arm fitting in order to get them charging back inside of the case - one of my headphones seems to magnetically lock in place but the other has to be eased into position or it won't charge. Lastly, the way they sorta sit right on the edge of the ear canal, not inside like traditional earbuds fit or surrounding the ear like over-hear headphones fit, is just really strange. I've gotten more used to it over the last few days, but it's...unique.

From a common sense perspective, muffs are the only real option for ensuring maximum hearing protection. I should have known better, but I read every word on Axil's website and took their word for it that these earbuds are superior to muffs. At this point, I'm not a fan of the company in general. text: I just sent PSB the following note. I'm giving the headphones two stars because they combine superb sound quality, in both passive and amplified modes, with a severe defect in noise-canceling mode that makes that mode effectively unusable. But I'm baffled that many others do not report similar issues, even while I'm skeptical I received two similarly defective headphones, or there's something about my usage that is triggering this issue. I'll share PSB's response when they respond. I previously wrote you about a pair of PSB M4U 2 headphones that appeared to be defective due to suffering from what I thought was interference in various environments. But the replacement pair I got is at least as bad, possibly worse, and I've come to realize this must be a design defect. The issue effectively precludes the use of the noise-cancelling function (which is a central feature of the headphones). I find it odd that a majority of users do not report this issue, but I'm skeptical I could have gotten two similarly defective models. I also don't think the issue is a function of how I'm using the headphones, because it occurs regardless of which source is feeding them, or for that matter even with no source connected at all. The issue is that small external noise inputs will trigger a chain reaction of rather loud pop-pop-pop-pop noises when in active noise-canceling mode. The easiest way to set this off is to tap the headphones with a finger while they're in noise-canceling mode, but the click of the button as it goes from amplified mode to noise-canceling mode is enough to trigger it (quickly clicking from passive mode straight to noise canceling mode avoids triggering it), as is chewing food, walking while wearing the headphones, road vibration while in a vehicle, or even just the jaw movement of yawning. Even sitting perfectly still, after a few minutes, random environmental noise in an airplane cabin will trigger it, and certain sounds reproduced by the headphones, such as while watching a movie, will also trigger it. It's extremely unpleasant. Sometimes the pops will resolve on their own, sometimes the only way to resolve them is to switch out of noise-canceling mode, in part because they seem to be self-reinforcing, i.e. each pop triggers another pop, and so on. The headphones otherwise function superbly, as I would expect from a company with PSB's reputation, so I am very disappointed this apparent design defect requires me to return them. My only modest additional feedback is that the hiss of the amplified (non-noise canceling) mode is on the louder side, depending on source impedance and content, but that's manageable, especially since passive mode is available as needed. And it appears the case could be a little thinner and still fit the headphones, the current case barely fits in a briefcase, which is a shortcoming for a travel-oriented device. But these are minor points, whereas the defect I described is a severe shortcoming. I hope you're able to address it in future models! And if you think something else might be going on, or you regard this as acceptable headphone function, I'd be very curious to hear that, too.
product_title: PSB M4U-2 Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones - Black
experience_rationale: The reviewer praises superb sound quality but reports a severe defect that makes noise-cancelling unusable, leading to a low overall experience

text: Why would you consider these? 1. You listen to music at a low volume (below 65-70dB). 2. You value comfort and build quality over 'even' tonality (sound signature). 3. You appreciate definition between bass and midrange in your music. 3. Unfortunately, EQ can't fix the shortcomings mentioned above. Alternatives at ~$200 or less: AKG K361/K371 [*quality control issues] - Better all-arounders, more balanced frequency response, flimsy built. Sennheiser HD25 [*on-ear, fixed removable cable] - Also v-shaped sound with better mids, bass definition and less sibilance, not as comfy. text: First of all the good things: 1. Case is small and compact 2. The earbuds are tiny and comfortable to sleep in even for side sleepers 3. Unlike most sleep earbuds, you can use these to play other audio than the sleep sounds (music, podcasts) 4. They sound quite good for a single BA; decent bass and pleasant overall across the frequency range 5. They have clear and understandable LED indicator lights It should be noted that while these can play music, they don't have any controls and they don't have a microphone, so these probably can't replace your regular earphones in a pinch. The case also doesn't have wireless charging even though from the outside, the case looks almost exactly like the case for the Colorbuds 2, which do support wireless charging. For me, there is really only one major con that means I probably won't use these very often and it's the battery life. They're rated for 3.5 hours. That means they won't last through a full night of sleep and for me that's a deal breaker. While I understand and appreciate that some people just benefit from some white noise to help them sleep - and these do that very well; the selection of sounds (btw, you can have only 6 loaded at a time, not the total 30 and transferring new sounds is sometimes a painful time consuming venture) will probably work for most people - but I sleep in earplugs because my husband snores and I'm a light sleeper. So although I can attest that these do provide pleasant background noise to help one fall asleep, they don't block much sound so if external sound is what's keeping you awake, these won't help. I haven't seen any other sleep buds that provide such a short battery life. It's very disappointing. However, as I said, they don't block much noise so perhaps considering their intended use, the battery life isn't that big of a deal for people who just want help calming down and falling asleep. But as for me, I'm going to have to keep looking.

text: TAKEAWAY There's still a lot of room for improvement in these headphones, but being able to wear them for hours with minimal discomfort makes them far more useful than headphones that are painful to wear. They are presently the only option I've been able to find on the market that I can wear relatively comfortably, so I'm keeping them. If you have large ears, these are the headphones for you. By the way, I found the QC45s to be more comfortable than the previous QC35 II model I tried on in a store. COMFORT I spent a long time trying to find true circumaural wireless ANC headphones in the up-to-$500 range and tried a number of pairs on, including the Bose QC35 II headphones. While the Bose QC45 headphones aren't completely circumaural, the deeper ear cups allow ears to fold into them with far less discomfort than other headphones I've tried. Bose care enough about comfort to put it in the product name and they deliver pretty well on this. The only improvement I'd make to the fit is to have slightly larger openings in the ear pads for a true circumaural fit. ACTIVE NOISE CANCELLATION (ANC) This is my first pair of ANC headphones and the ANC wowed me. The dome of silence is incredible in "Quiet" mode. The ANC drowns out a lot of background noise, especially if voices are in another room. Voices/TV/radio in the same room isn't as good, but still better than nothing at all. Road noise in the car is considerably reduced. Airplane background noise is still audible, but significantly reduced, except they crackle and pop loudly for about 10 to 30 seconds on take-off and landing. I think it's just too much for the ANC to keep up with. I do wish there was a way to turn off ANC altogether (to preserve battery life, for instance), but that's only possible in wired mode. The "Aware" mode seems to not be useful for listening to music in, as it seems to amplify outside sounds obnoxiously. For that reason, it would be nice if turning on "Aware" mode automatically paused the music and resumed it when switching back to "Quiet" mode. SOUND QUALITY I wasn't blown away by the sound quality. It is certainly better than my old $40 pair of wireless headphones, but the sound isn't as full and rich as I would expect from Bose. It came off a bit tinny at times, especially when listening to harder rock music. Just a tad more bass would be appreciated. Being able to set at least the treble and bass myself would be better yet. These also lack support for the aptX codec. BATTERY The battery life is good, but I wouldn't call it great. A 15-minute fast-charging feature like the Master & Dynamic MW65s would be awesome. Having a standard USB-C port for charging is nice, though, so I don't have to bring a special cable or adapter with me when I travel. The prevalence of USB ports on planes is helpful but, annoyingly, you can't charge the headphones and listen to them at the same time. DESIGN The design of these is pretty boring, but it is serviceable. All the hinges that make it comfortable and fold up compact make the headphones feel a bit flimsy in hand, but the build quality feels good when they are in place on my head, and they are light enough to wear for hours at a time with minimal discomfort (due to the ear cups not being quite large enough). The carrying case is great and the fact that it is included makes the value of these headphones even better.

text: This is the second pair of Skullcandy headphones that I have purchased. These Skullcrusher over-ear headphones are an exceptional value for the $56 I paid for them. When I have the added bass turned off, the sound coming from my music is clear and crisp, equalized to how I have the track set on my portable device. When I turn the added bass on, it is simple to adjust to user preference and liking. I love the little vibration you can feel when you turn up the bass and let the headphones do their thing. Here is a brief list of pros and cons: Pros: 1) Very portable because they fold up to about the size of a softball and come with a carrying pouch. 2) For the price they are high quality head phones with a decent bass subwoofer system. 3) Although not marketed as noise cancelling headphones, they do a good job of getting rid of background noise. Cons: 1) It can be a challenge to exercise wearing them for two reasons: your ears sweat and the subwoofer control flops around alot when clipped to my shorts. (I know they aren't made as exercising headphones) 2) If any of your audio files are lower quality audio files, you WILL hear the difference! This isn't a con of the product, but I consider it negative because it makes me want to purchase higher quality tracks of songs I already purchased. 3) My experience is that if you turn the bass all the way up, some of the other audio will become distorted. Overall for the price, they are a great pair of over-ear headphones. If you are looking for high end DJ'ing headphones, these probably aren't your solution. You'll need to look into their higher end line of headphones. But for the average guy like me who wants to create a soundtrack to his life, they work great!

text: Me: I've been a musician for 30+years. I've fronted a rock band, sat first chair in a symphony and performed with all kinds of groups. I do instrumental and vocal work, as well as DJing and producing music. I spend more hours in headphones than anyone I know and I have lots of different kinds. I DJ with in-ear monitors, so I bought these for casual listening, backups/consumer references for tracking and mixing, and situations where I'm playing with another electronic artist and I need to hear the mains directly. I hoped these would have enough sound quality to be up to the task, but be cheap enough that I could use them as backups and not worry about leaving them at a venue. Model reviewed: I bought the Pro-30 Upgraded Standard version in silver and brown. First, the good: These headphones sound great, especially for the price. They've got a V-shaped "consumer" tuning, as you would expect, but not as extreme as Beats or Monsters. It's actually pretty accurate if you're looking to reference quality consumer gear tuning profiles, not "audiophile" or studio reference profiles. The soundstage and separation are good, the clarity is good, mids are full and forward but balanced, treble is clear but not peircing or sibilant, and with the volume turned up, the bass really rumbles without getting muddy. Overall, they're nice and warm, but still detailed, full, and not overly colored. I don't think you could get better sound at this price or even 3x this price. They may or may not be up to audiophile standards (I don't consider myself one) but they certainly reach the hi-fi bar. They'll also please any bassheads without muddying up the music. They're great casual listening headphones and with some EQing, depending on your preference, would be useful for mixing or tracking. I've found for hip hop and EDM they don't need any adjustment for music production. The tuning isn't skewed for bass, but they're not thin, cold, "reference" headphones either. I actually like them much better than the AKG K92s that sell for $20 - $30 more, and I like them better than the Monster DNA 40s. I also tried them out for DJing and played about half a set with them. No issues at all with that application, although I switched back to my in-ears after a couple hours and since that's my preference, I can't give a full review specifically for DJ purposes. The double-sided cable and audio pass-through features are very smart and quite useful. I found that I used it as a built-in headphone splitter for casual listening and movie watching with my partner much more than I thought I would. I also used them connected to two audio sources to mix tracks from my DAW and listen to references tracks from a music player. I also listened to music while having a phone conversation. It's a brilliant feature! The fact that two removable cables and a bag are included at this price is awesome. The earcups are incredibly plush and comfortable and provide a good seal. I cannot overstate the comfort of these earpads. It's like a broken-in kidd leather couch on your head. I can only describe them as "buttery". They're the most comfortable cushions I've ever worn and I don't think you could find much better at any price. Ditto on the comfort of the headband. If you have big ears though, they may not be a good fit for you as the inner diameter of the cups isn't that large. Perfect for my tiny ears and peanut head! They look very stylish and I really dig the retro brown colorway and matching cable. The bad: Build quality and QC could be better. My pair has one side where the adjustment notches are nice and snug and one side where they're a bit loose and mushy. It's not terrible, but noticeable. Also, I've only had these for maybe a couple weeks and I've only used them a few times and been gentle with them. I was jamming with another DJ yesterday and went to remove the cable to fold them and put them away. I pulled on the knurled connector cover just like you're supposed to, not the cable or the strain relief. The cover popped right off the connector. I was kind of surprised to see that it's only held on with a tiny bit of weak adhesive. Bummer, because I actually thought the strain relief design looked pretty beefy. A couple days later, the right side driver started dropping out intermittently. I'm hoping I just got a defective unit and that the overall durability of the brand is better. Sadly, I wouldn't use them as main cans for DJing. I don't think they'd stand up to hard use. Perfect for backups or spares though, for casual home listening or as budget reference cans. I'll contact the company to see if they can help me out and update this review with my results. Update 2/8/19: The company actually contacted me before I got a hold of them to offer a replacement! Great customer service there. I asked them about buying a replacement brown cable (I always need extras on hand). They let me know that they don't sell the brown cable separately, but they sent me a red one free of charge. Solid. No issues with the replacement cable. I think I just got a bad one. I haven't gotten the replacement headphones yet, but I'll update my review when I do. Update 2/13/19: I got the replacement headphones a few days ago, in about half the time they estimated! Unfortunately, they sent the wrong ones. I got the cheaper Pro-10s instead of the Pro-30's I originally bought. I snapped a pic and emailed the company and got a reply literally within minutes. They apologized for the mistake and immediately sent me a replacement for the Pro-30's. They told me to keep the Pro-10s and enjoy them. Fantastic customer service and I'm upgrading my original 3-star review to 4-stars just for how good OneAudio is to deal with. Since I get to try the Pro-10s, I'll go ahead and review those and report back. I'll also update this review when I get the replacement Pro-30's and get to spend a little more time with them. Update 2/26/19: So I got my replacement Pro 30's just a few days after OneAudio sent them out. Very timely. They work great. No issues with the driver or the cable. I've been spending more time with them; producing music, listening to music, preparing tracks for DJing, watching media and listening to podcasts. I'm appreciating them more and more. The comfort is incredible. The sound quality of the large, 50mm driver is very good, and especially impressive for the price. They are clear enough for critical listening but they're not fatiguing, which is unusual. The warmth and richness of the mids are really pleasant and the thickness of the bass is a treat. The treble is slightly recessed in the tuning and while clear, it's not sparkly, magical treble, if that's your thing. The upside of that is that you can listen to these phones for hours without your ears getting worn out. OneAudio has been excellent to deal with and has shown a real commitment to customer service. The 24 month warranty is very generous and they actually stand by it. They definitely earned my future business. I've updated my review from 4 to 5 stars for the replacement set and for OneAudio's customer service. Update 02/01/20: One year later, I still love these headphones to bits, I still enjoy listening to them, and I still use them all the time. My AKGs are still gathering dust. I've since bought a pair of Nuraphones which retail at $400 and I still reach for my OneOdios when I'm gaming, relaxing on the couch, watching Netflix, or referencing how tracks will sound on midrange consumer headphones. They don't outperform my Nuras in sound, but they're still enjoyable to listen to and the comfort is unmatched. The earpads have only gotten better as they've broken in. I haven't been gentle with them at all and they've held up. If you're looking for a comfortable, high-value headphone that sounds good, I still recommend these and would happily put them up against headphones at the $100 mark. If you want wireless, check out the OneOdio A70 Fusion, which I think an excellent all-around, workhorse headphone.

For anyone wonder what it's like, it's basically a wallet. I really couldn't figure out to how to use it, so I didn't really like it. 2. The comfort is great, if you get the right size cushion. I can wear these for hours and sometimes forget I even have them in my ear. 3. The construction is certainly more logical on these, with many other pairs the jack is straight and when you want to pull it out, it tugs on the cable which can damage it later on. Other things like the cable splitting in the middle, rather than at the jack, prevent it from getting damaged as well. I can't say the cable is all that strong, but we'll see... (SPOILER ALERT) It wasn't. 4. The sound quality is excellent, it seems a bit muffled or something, that might wear off, not sure, but I hear parts of the music that I didn't hear before, whether good or bad. The bass is there, (really there). I've lent it to friends and compare it to my other earphones, and it generally has the most bass of the lot. edit: You could take out the little foam cushions which seems to get rid of the slightly muffled sound, they then become a slightly brighter pair of earphones. (Because as we learned, treble has a harder time passing through objects, so the higher frequencies get blocked) People had downgraded these earphones because of some "microphonic issues" where tapping the cable could be heard inside the earphone. This is true, but it's not as noticeable on these as it is on my other earphones. So I wouldn't give a downgrade for this. If you want earphones with 0 microphonic interference, you'll be looking into earphones like TF10 & shure Se series in which you wear them over your ear to prevent that. 5. Sound Isolation: Decent. it may take awhile to get adjusted, but if you get a good sized earbud and stretch your ears a little, it blocks out a good amount of sound, not nearly as much as my triple fis. I would've honestly given these a 3.5 but there isn't one, so I'm rounding up. The reason for that mainly, is the price. I saw these originally on amazon for $92.99 2 weeks later they went to $102.99, a week later $109.99 then they jumped all the way to $129.99 I payed $119.99 for these, which is a bit (very) steep. These, all in all, are about a $60 pair of earbuds. I still do regret paying that much, but I guess it's sure "beats" buying beats. Alright, well I hope I've covered it all. Edit: After 7 months They've finally broke, the sound in the right earbud cuts out when the part of the cord near the jack moves. It's happened to every pair of earbuds I've had so far. However, Sennheiser has a fantastic policy where you can send them in to be repaired, free of charge, for 2 years. I'm still waiting for them to be returned, and I'll rate how their policy really is. How I feel about these now: Currently, they are $99.99 on Amazon, and at this price. I'd say they're still not worth it. But honestly, I'd recommend the Shure se215, se315 or UE triplefi10, the removable cable is a huge perk at this price range. And you can buy another cable that includes an in-line volume control, a microphone, and a pause button. 2nd Edit: I sent them in for repairs after 7 months. In first class shipping it took about a week and a half to send them in and receive them back. Fairly prompt. What I wasn't expecting was they gave me an absolutely new one. Not refurbished, unopened, 100% brand new. As a brand I feel I'll be buying from Sennheiser a lot more now.

text: GOOD The sound is good. Many reviews indicate or suggest it's light on bass, but I didn't find that was the case, rather, it was light in the mid-bass and high-bass regions, but low bass was good. This gives the headphones an overall clean presentation, in fact, the sound signature mimics a live jazz performance. Quite good. BAD The description indicates the headphones have "soft leather headband and form fitting ear cushions", neither of which is true. The headband is not leather, it's vinyl (protein leather in marketing speak), while the ear pads are not at all form fitting; they are a firm non-memory foam that does not conform or form to anything. It just rests there, which is absolutely horrible because it does not create a good seal, so slight movements of the head will "break the seal" and lead to constant readjustments. The description further indicates the materials were "carefully selected", which of course is pure marketing lingo. Also, the mic does not pick up your voice well during calls, so you'll sound muffled and a little distant. This could have been a good headphone if actual form fitting memory foam was used and they didn't falsely advertise the materials. There is a fundamental difference between "leather" and something that is not leather. They cheaped it out then falsely claim the materials to be premium and "carefully selected", when they are not. It is also is mediocre for calls, another area they could have improved. Definition of Leather 1 : animal skin dressed for use 2: the flap of the ear of a dog — see dog illustration 3 : something wholly or partly made of leather Definition of Vinyl 1 : a monovalent radical CH2=CH derived from ethylene by removal of one hydrogen atom 2 : a polymer of a vinyl compound or a product (such as a resin or a textile fiber) made from such a polymer

text: Have this headset since 2 months back (used a Logitech H800 before this). I use it for work and some occasional gaming. I'd say overall it is a good headset, but slightly pricey given shortcomings. (honestly I'd give it a 3.5 rating). If they were to fix the quircks I'd give it 5 stars. Pros: > Overall build & comfort is good. > Battery duration is very good as well - so you don't need to recharge that often. > Folds up nicely for say a laptop bag > The sound is good & the noice cancelling is pretty good too (my first noice cancelling headset, so not really able to compared on that aspect - can only state that it's a good noise reduction whilst on an airplane) > You can connect to two seperate devices (say phone and laptop), there's a caveat (ses in the cons). > If it's not connected to anything it'll shut off after appx 10 mins / ie powersaving feature. > Comes with a smartphone app (me having a Windows Phone - impressed they made one for that too). > Good Bluetooth range. Cons: 1) Cannot use noice cancelling w/o using a 3.5mm cable. Unfortunately the design is poor if you want to use Noice Cancelling only (say if you want to use it on an airplane) since bluetooth cannot be turned off on the headset. The workaround ( ) is to attack the line-in cable that comes with the headset (my guess is that this disables Bluetooth). If you don't have the cable with you.. the headset (and noice cancelling) turns off after 10 mins due to the powersaving feature. 2) Cannot charge it whilst speaking. Albeit the battery time is very good mini USB port hidden behind the wishbone shaped arms that hold the speakers/earmuffs with the effect you cannot wear the heatset and have have a USB Cable attached. 3) Sensitive touchplate/lack of tactile feedback. Since there's no tactile feedback when you use the buttons (to turn up/down volume, receive call and similar) you might accidentically start/stop music instead of turning volume up/down. 4) The mute button, is too small. Using it frequently for business calls where being able mute/unmute quickly is desirable. 5) When it's connected to two devices, sound is bad :-S. Example if you're playing a game on the computer (use a PC) and use the headphones, then the sound is poor if somebody calls on the mobile phone. I'm not sure if this is an issue with the Bluetooth standard or the headphones. Net result I only connect one device at the time (shame). 5.1) in Windows it shows up as two seperate devices one being "SHB9850NC hands-free" and SHB9850NC Stereo", which adds a slight usability issue as there's two devices when controlling the volume. Example if you call in on say a Skype call then the taskbar in Windows might only show the 'stereo' volume control - whilst the audio come through the 'hands-free' part.. ie you can turn the volume up and down w/o any effect. My guess is that it's how they allow it to be connected to two devices at the same time. Suspect the design idea was that you listen to music from one device (ie 'stereo') and then take a call from say a smartphone (the 'hands-free' device). Hope this helps someone else.

text: While I consider myself an audiophile (I have expensive headphones on my computer that requires an amp), I'm not a snob about it. This has allowed me to relax my requirements for on the go audio, such as for work, working out, or just generally not home and in need of some music or podcasts. While these headphones don't reproduce the audio the best, they are still pretty good for the price. I have enjoyed them so much that I have purchased 4 sets of these after enjoying the previous model (white) for a long time. Why have I bought so many? Is it not durable? Out of the 5 total sets, only one set has failed, and it's the set that received the most manhandling abuse. The first set is still running strong and has become the set that lives in my car (I don't use them in my car, but they are accessible if, for example, I go to the store). I have another set for home use for when I'm not at the computer. I have another set for the office (I don't like leaving expensive stuff there as there is a theft problem). The office set had to be replaced as the years of wrapping and unwrapping the wire created a break and short. When I ordered its replacement, I ordered a spare. How do they fit big heads? I have a big head. They fit well enough to not cause pain. I've tried many neck wrap headsets and most of them cause pain on the ears due to their pulling on the ears. While these don't seem to be any larger than other neck wrap headphones, they don't pull on the ears, and I can get hours of listening out of them without discomfort. Sometimes I have to readjust them as they can move around a little in the course of wearing them and moving my head around, but that is because they do not grab on the ears. I'm okay with readjusting headphones if it means they don't cause me pain. I have not seen any other headset that were as portable and compact as these and provided decent sound reproduction. They get sufficiently loud and have sufficient frequency response for music. They are relatively durable, very portable, and relatively comfortable. I recommend them to anyone looking for a good on the go set.

Jaybird X3 - Pretty solid headphone but the isolation factor made it a no go for me. Great for around the house but you are tempting fate to take this on the road. 3. Bose Soundsport - I love the sound of these. Can't swim with them but amazing sound. If that's the number 1 criteria for you in a wireless headset then Bose soundsport is a solid choice. I do hate how much they stick out from your head. 4. Bragi- the headphone. Not bad at first. Maybe still a good option. The buttons are definitely superior to the "touch" system of the dash. The sound is still mediocre but I still like how small they are compared to the Jabra and the Bose. 5. Bragi - The Dash (away from it?) - I really wanted these to be a winner. I ordered them and when they showed up I made sure to update all the software to the latest version(not easy but we figured it out). I never got to try them in the pool but they were terrible on a bike ride. The "windscreen" created a static mess. Sound quality was terrible. The touch controls are a hot mess of technology. Constantly bumping them and then when I did want to do something, they fought me the whole way. Battery died super quick as well. Overall, one of my top worst experiences with a purchase from Amazon. Not Amazon's fault but this thing is beta at best. Not ready for prime time. Thank goodness for Amazon's return policy. For now I'm going to sit on the sideline and see what comes next. text: I spend around 2000 minutes per month on my phone for work, mostly with an BT earpiece stuck in my ear. My previous earpiece was the Jabra JX10 (1st gen), and it was a small device that worked really well most of the time. After a couple weeks of using the V1, I can say the same about this headset. I had some initial issues with sound clarity (re-pairing helped) and with keeping it in my ear reliably (removed the black nub used for the over-ear plastics). I am not a fan of plastic over my ear, and with the Jabra I was able to use Jabra softgels to put that earpiece in my ear - and it stayed all day if I wanted. With the BlueAnt V1, I had to work harder but finally found the solution. Softgels don't fit, and the included Comply soft tips alone were not enough. I use Comply tips with Shure headphones on my iPod, so I am already fine with foam in my ear. However, I couldn't get the foam tips far enough in my ears to stay put. Once I took off the black rubber nub that sits in the middle of the nice-idea-but-useless-in-practice 'tie clip,' I am finally able to get the V1 to stay in my apparently cavernous ear. That nub simply kept me from getting the last little bit I needed for the Comply foam to stay put. As a user for a couple of years, I know these Comply tips wear out with any kind of regular use. They are dirt magnets no matter how clean you try to keep them and your ear, and so far they are not available from BlueAnt at the site mentioned in the included documentation. It's a very new product, so that's fair, I just hope they get them out soon. Contacting Comply directly has not elicited a response, although these tips seems to have the same larger hole as the Whoomp Earbud Enhancers for the iPod's standard mediocre earbuds. The ones from my earphone have a hole that is far to small to fit the V1. Other critiques include the fact that pressing the button occasionally does nothing. It's as if the V1 is asleep. I try to answer a call and the V1 does not notify me nor does it respond to the press of the ant button. Or, sometimes I'll press the button and the V1 does not say "Say a command" as is normal. These are overcome with a reset or a few presses to 'wake' it back up. Still, it's a flaw as I see it. In all cases, I am offended by the fact that many BT earpieces on the market feel they need to flash that they are active. As the wearer, I can't see the flash going on in my ear, and it does nothing but annoy other people - especially at night. The V1 and other BT headsets may be seen as a fashion accessory by some, but I bought it for the size coupled with the technology. I don't care to advertise that I have it in my ear. So, on the one hand, many thanks to BlueAnt for giving me a way to turn it off. Unfortunately, it's an annoying fact that when I turn that flashing blue square off through the voice prompts, the device forgets and starts flashing again once it is turned off for charging. If I shutdown via voice prompts (a waste of time) it seems to remember. BlueAnt, if you're reading, please fix this... that flashing square with an ant on it is huge. At least on the Jabra XJ10 it was a tiny square. Although I couldn't turn it off, a black marker took care of it. I was thrilled when I found the V1 allowed control, but less thrilled now that I have to repeat the action over and over. Before I say anything else, let me pay a compliment that the voice quality on the other end and noise-canceling appear to be stellar. That said, I also hope BlueAnt will consider tweaking the V1 firmware updates, per the documentation, so I can just press and use my phone's internal commands if I want. With my old earpiece that was what happened with a press. The BlueGenie voice control is cool, if a bit of a gimmick since you can only answer or ignore calls completely hands-free as others have pointed out. However, calling numbers by pressing the ant and saying what speed-dial you want to call (after memorizing them) is limiting. I have hundreds of contacts I can dial by name if you pass me through to my phone and Microsoft Voice Commander. I know I can say 'phone commands' - but why not add another voice-activated setting to just pass the button press through to the phone's internal commands? Those of us with Windows Mobile devices and VC are not a minority. Also I want replace these canned and limiting voice-recognized names... 'office' - 'favorite' - 'home' - I don't even have a home phone, and I'm not alone. So, I've set my wife as 'home' - but I'm calling her mobile. If I make her 'favorite,' who would be home? If I make her home and leave favorite empty, I wasted one of the limited voice shortcuts available for speed-dial (voicemail, favorite, home, office, goog411, speed-dials 6,7,8 and 9). Locking me to Goog411 as speed-dial 5 is a waste of an entry. Again, if I could just pass through to my phone with a press, I already have Goog411 as an option. To me it appears the beta-testing group was a small sample. Don't get me wrong. This is a great device with next-gen features for a BT headset. But give me a few more business-class options (and retain all settings) at this end of the price spectrum if you want to retain my business long-term.

text: These are by far the worst headphones I have ever purchased. Not just in the premium, in-ear, $95 retail range, but of any price range. I purchased these on Amazon for $60 bucks on sale after hearing many very good reviews about the S4, it's predecessor. I read about the cord noise and decided since I usually listen to my music at a decent volume it won't really affect me too much. Amazon Prime shipping was fast as always and I was eager to put these to the test. Immediately I noticed none of the earbuds stayed in my ear. I tried every single size that came with the headphones and EVERY, SINGLE, ONE just fell out. These headphones weren't even usable until I splurged $20 on Comply TX series medium foam earbuds. After putting down $60 on a pair of headphones, I shouldn't have to spend another $20 just to have them be operational. Whichever moron designed the one button controller should be fired from product design immediately. Why would ANYONE want premium headphones that cannot control the volume or change songs without downloading an app from the play store? Seriously. Even the S4i's of the very same generation of headphones by Klipsch, made for iphones, had 3 buttons. To do something simple like skipping a song and then increasing the volume you have to tap dance through many double clicks and long clicks and triple clicks and single clicks. You have to tap dance because if you don't get the timing exactly right of your clicks, or don't click on the exact spot on the button it won't recognize your click and you end up repeatedly pausing and playing your songs. Thus far, these headphones have completely failed at the 2 main functions of headphones: listening to music, and being able to control the music you listen to. The fact that these headphones are made with a flat cord that helps with keeping it untangled isn't even a plus because the cord noise is terrible, even at a normal volume. If you don't plan on moving your head AT ALL while you're listening to music, never bother using your controller to change songs or volume, have miracle ear canals that keep these earbuds in, go for this heap of crap. If not, stay FAR FAR away.

text: In short: Excellent/ immersive sound, very well made, keep for a lifetime. I am listening to music again because of these speakers. Really *listening* -- in a comfortable chair, eyes closed, not thinking about anything else. I frequently listen to music from local bands that I have seen perform live and these speakers do a good job of making me feel like I'm there. I got lucky. I live near Vanatoo. One of the engineers that designed the speakers actually delivered the speakers. We talked for about an hour. I mention this because it is now clear to me how much Vanatoo cares about the sound. I'm an engineer too, but frankly I was overwhelmed by his knowledge on speaker design. I'm not an audiophile, but here are my impressions: - When I close my eyes, I can see the stage/studio position of the individual musicians - Vocals are strong, clear, and deliver an emotional wallop - Horns are sharp and energetic - I can hear bits that I haven't heard before e.g. the lower frequencies of an upright bass - I don't feel the need for a subwoofer for music (more below) My biggest criticism is that there is no remote control. Some sources do not provide volume control e.g. Kindle Fire TV movies, Apple TV movies, Apple TV iTunes cloud music play. My work-around is a DAC that has a remote control such as ASIN B00JKBMXCI (I also reviewed that device). A subwoofer is supported. If you really like action movies, you might want a subwoofer. For music though, I don't think a subwoofer is needed. So far, Ode to Joy is the only piece of music where I wished for a subwoofer, but maybe that is because I recently saw that performed by symphony and a remarkable 100-person chorale :-).
