text: The Good: The battery life is fantastic. I was on the phone, in the cold, for a good long while with these. I did not lose connection or experience any issues hearing the other person. When I got home and checked the battery I expected significant drain. Nope! These babies were still at 100%. Color me impressed! Another thing I enjoyed was the premium feel. The packaging was nice and not incredibly hard to unpack (more or less frustration free). The headphones look and feel very high-end — which makes a lot of sense given the over $100 price point. The cord that connects one bud to the other was one of those new-fangled flat ones which, as by design, didn't tangle when thrown into my giant laptop tote. I also really liked how they came with two different choices for the ear buds. I'm not a huge fan of the silicon tips that are so common and have come to obsess over foam earplug style headphones. I did appreciate them throwing in some Comply foam tips, even if I didn't really think they were as effective at canceling out noise as I had hoped. And finally, connecting them to my phone was really simple and I did enjoy the "Jenna" voice prompts where some woman whispers into your ear that you are connected to a device. The Bad: The first thing I want to do with any gear I purchase is immediately set it up. One thing I noticed with these is that there was no quick start guide or any indicator of how to turn the friggin things into music listening devices! After setting them to charge, I did see in small print that I should go to their website and grab a guide from there. I have to admit, once I did get the guide it was very simple but it was really annoying to have to go to a website (and then hunt for a PDF!) to learn how to play with my new toy. This was especially frustrating because they could've just included an insert that instead said "hold down the middle button to get started." Fit was also problematic for me. While I read a review that said a woman could fit these, I still think they were large for my ears. The actual tube that provides music to your ear was actually quite wide even without the Comply tip attached! That said, I acknowledge I have somewhat small ears relative to the rest of me so this might be more of a personal problem than anything else. I have problems with the new in-ear Apple headphones (more than my husband and other humans with reasonable ear canal size) so this doesn't come as a shock. I also have to say I really disliked the "fins" that are supposed to keep the headphones in my ears. Maybe I'm behind the times or again, tiny ears, but I had no idea how to make those work. I did not get a chance to test them while running so could be that the fins are more relevant in that case but even still, I felt like they were a distraction and more something that would cause them to fall out rather than stay in. Finally, the most troubling problem with these was the sound quality. This is what disappointed and surprised me most! Every single review I read indicated that the sound quality was phenomenal and for me it was truly unlistenable. Again, this may depend on the ear but for me they sounded way too tinny as opposed to "bright" as they were described by some. I tried really hard to make them work. I went and adjusted the equalizer presets on my device but I just couldn't get the music to a tolerable place. I did some digging and found that this could be a fault more of the tech than of the actual device I received. Bluetooth audio is by definition compressed which could account for the lousy sound when I'm listening to streaming or my own MP3s (which, by definition, are compressed). In other words, perhaps I have too high expectations for wireless audio. This means that my quest may actually be like searching for a unicorn. This audio issue coupled with the high price tag made these completely not worth keeping for me so I ended up returning to Amazon, which was a very easy process.

text: Updated review, May 2017, after Phaiser customer service contacted me with the following advice about my headset randomly turning itself off every few minutes: "You will have to do a reset. This will delete all previous pairings from the pairing list of the headset, so that you can start over. You will have to keep all 3 buttons pressed for about 10 seconds. You will hear a low tone and the headset will restart and go to pairing mode. Now the issue should be gone. You will need to delete the entry for BHS-530 from the Bluetooth menu of your connected phones, scan and pair BHS-530 again." I did as they said, and I used the headset problem free for 2 months, and then had to do the hard reset again. Knowing how to fix the problem made it not a big deal. I appreciate the customer support. I use these while working out, gardening, studying, or even watching a movie on my Ipad in bed. One star lost for bulkiness, sticking out of the ear, and for not having this problem clearly talked about with a solution anywhere that I could easily find. The sound quality has improved with use, as good earbuds are want to do. I love that my cat can't eat through them, as she has with so many very expensive headsets. The microphone is still no good for calls. I love the small, square case that they come in. It's compact, and I'm able to put these, plus two USB charging cords and two corded ear buds (one for my Iphone, the other for my Android) into the case neatly when I travel. .................... Feb 2017 I got these because they have a "Sweatproof Guarantee", and I wanted them for the gym. They randomly power off when I use them at the gym, and I've no idea why. When you're working out, the last thing you want to do is to stop every 3-5 minutes to put your music back on. Strangely, if I use them at home while I'm working around the house, there isn't a problem. The sound is decent, even if the mic is not good enough for calls. Perhaps it's a faulty set, I don't know. I can't seem to find where or how I would contact the company about a replacement, or if that would be covered in their guarantee. They do stay on my head comfortably enough, though they are a little bulky, and stick out awkwardly if I want to wear a hat in winter. It's not a deal breaker though, because they are fairly sturdy. ------------------------------------------------- Preliminary review: I got this primarily for use at the gym, not for calls. It's fairly comfortable, and the sound is dynamic with Netflix shows. Slightly less so with music, but still quite decent out of the box. There are three equaliser settings: bass, treble, and normal. I hesitate to write anything about sound quality and music until I've used it for awhile, as earbuds need to be worn in before you really know. Controls, simple: 1 multi-function button, and a volume +, volume - button. The variety of tip sizes is good, with one extra, "high quality" dense foam one which blocks sound if inserted all the way. It comes with a case, which is perfect for throwing it in your bag. It plays for hours, and charges quickly. Call quality is impossible. There's a delay, and the mic eats my voice. The incoming sound is much diminished, and even a bit robotic. One star lost for that failed feature. All in all, if it holds up to gym use (read that as, sweating and staying on my head), I'll be happy.

text: These are great BUT... Update after a month: I sent these back. The problem is a very slight graininess. It's slight, but it keeps music from being well musical. I wouldn't call them sterile or analytical. They do have a nice detailed sound. They are slightly revealing of poorly recorded music or low bit rate. They need a little bit of volume to sound their best. I have about 25 songs I use to audition speakers and headphones. While using these I found myself skipping to the next song instead of forgetting that I was auditioning headphones and getting lost in the music. And while using them that bit of graininess on horns or grating vocals (think Bob Dylan) would pull me out of what I was doing. They are very light and I wasn't crazy about the angled cord but it wasn't a big deal either. Another pair of phones might be better if you wear them wire over the ear but these are so light you may not feel the need to wear them over ear. Knocking a star off for the slightly irritating sound on some music. Original review First let me say these only have about 20hrs of time on them so I would not call them fully broken in yet but they should be over that new out of the box sound. Like a lot of people I'm looking for all the sound I can get in cheap headphones. And technically these are very good and the internet is filled with great reviews. The highs are good and just walk the line of sibilance. If sibilance is there you can hear it, but it's not going to make you want to scratch your ears out. Mids are nice but not particularly impressive. Mid bass is not as controlled as I'd like but it's not smeared either. Drums are handled adequately. I'd like to hear a little bit better separation between kik drum and bass guitar, but it's not bad either. There is a very subtle bloom/extension on the bass. You don't really notice it but you would notice if it was missing. The bass is quirky. If you like a big emphasised bass it's not here. If you like super controlled bass (like hearing the beater on the kik drum and the pluck of fingers/pick on bass guitar strings) it's not here either. But for many people, I think they would find the bass handled well overall. The level of detail on bass I'm talking about just doesn't come on sub $50 headphones. They do a very good job with acoustic guitar. Where I think they do best is on details like cymbals, and other things with 'ring'. Don't get me wrong these are very nice phones, i'm just being super picky for people who are trying to pick based on the sound signature. I'm not a soundstage guy, but I would say that soundstage on these is barely adequate. There is no sense of space around the instruments and all the instruments sound like they are in a straight line. There is little sense of the room the instruments are being played or and/or you can't hear much of reverb on the instruments. I'm not saying that these things aren't there at all, but they don't stand out. What I'm saying is they do a very nice job, and do a nice job for the price, but I'm not hearing the $100+ headphone beaters some make these out to be. But I can see where some people would really like these, and many people do if you read reviews They just are not super impressive in ways I look for. While I could make a case that these are technically better I liked my Vsonic GR02 Bass Edition more. And I liked my old NUFORCE 700M's (about $90 at the time) much better. At times they are a touch forward and a bit unforgiving of poorly recorded music. Not bad, just a bit unforgiving. A case can be made that is a good thing in 'phones because that is accuracy. And I agree but sometimes it is enough to take me out of the music. If something is bit blaring, like a trump, you are going to notice it is blaring. If you hate Bob Dylan's voice you will really hate it with these. LIke right now I'm listening to Miles Davis and the horn just doesn't sound right. Yeah it should be raw and in your face and it is, but it lacks a certain depth of the horn that would/should balance that out. They can be a tiny bit dry, a bit sterile? By that I mean they lack a bit of musicality that makes me want to listen to more music. When I was first auditioning with my music I found myself skipping to another song instead of getting lost in the song and forgetting that I was auditioning headphones. I suspect that these might benefit from a headphone amp, but I"m not going to buy a $50 amp for $50 headphones. I'd rather put that money towards a bigger budget for the phones themselves. I wanted to try these to see what I think of these and if your budget is less than $50 they are probably hard to go wrong with for a balanced sound. Not flat, not V-shaped, and not too fatiguing. If you told me I had to keep these I would not cry myself to sleep but I plan to up my budget a bit and find something that suits me a bit more. text: I bought these as well as the Beyerdynamic DT 1990 Pro to compare the two. The latter lost, easily. The HD 660 S is incredible. No frequencies pop out like the Beyerdynamics (too harsh in the high end), everything is very even. Excellent in the mid-range for sure, unlike many headphones that try to push the higher frequencies to come across as "super pro." It's natural for our brains to go "ooh" when we hear bass, or crisp highs, but you don't want these things when judging a mix! Bass is quite good (but not ear-rumbling), about as good as my Shure SRH1540's. If you want a good pair to judge bass and sub-bass, definitely grab the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x in addition to the HD 660 S, and prepare to be amazed—I've never heard such good subs in a pro level headphone. Don't get the ATH-M50x as your sole pair of headphones, they're problematic in the mids and mid-highs. Some things to keep in mind with the HD 660 S: - These are pro level open-back headphones meant for studio use, so you must be in a quiet environment to use them properly. Also, don't wear them in public because external noise will ruin it for you, and you'll annoy people around you because they'll be able to hear everything. - Headphones sound a little better after a brief burn-in period (48-72 hrs). Plug them in, put them on your ears, and fire up some heavy rock or electronica at a volume that's loud, but not painful. Then remove the headphones and let them sit for a few days. This loosens up the material around the drivers. Some people think this is a myth, but some of the best mix engineers in Hollywood disagree. In short: get these headphones, they're incredible!

text: I replaced the $1700 Audeze LCD-X with the $180 NAD Viso HP50, so I'm clearly a believer in Paul Barton's "RoomFeel" headphone tuning philosophy. Naturally I was curious to see how that sound translated to in-ears, but unfortunately these didn't sound much more spacious or open than the [[ASIN:B004PO10E2 Shure SE215-CL Sound Isolating Earphones with Single Dynamic MicroDriver]]. I've been using in-ears for many years, so I understand the importance of getting a proper seal. As is so often true, none of the included silicone tips fit, but fortunately the [[ASIN:B01EH0MKGU SpinFit CP100-L - Patented Silicone Eartips for Replacement (2 Pairs, Large size) (3.8mm Nozzle Dia.)]] I had on hand fit perfectly. Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the overall housing and wire design. The non-moldable ear loops are fiddly and annoying, and the multi-driver design results in a housing that's too big to rest comfortably against the concha and a massive nozzle that can't be inserted deeply into the ear canal. So what about the sound quality? I was prepared to forgive all weaknesses in fit and finish if the sound was spectacular, but it wasn't, at least not played straight out of a phone. I found these earphones to be extremely recording-dependent: on some recordings, they blew the Shures straight out of the water (treble micro-detail and bass impact are both very impressive), while on others the Shures actually sounded better. Played directly from my phone's headphone jack, the PSBs struggled to get loud enough across all frequencies, leading to an unpleasantly recessed midrange, which made vocal and instrumental music sound cold and strange. My suspicion is that these require an amp to really sound their best, but I didn't bother to try that because I'm not going to commute with a headphone amp in my pocket. If you're in the market for earphones for desktop listening with an amp, I'd say these are worth checking out, but for commuting, the Shure SE215 is still the gold standard: they get loud easily and evenly, they're great for all genres of music, they're light, comfortable, and durable, and they isolate from outside noise exceptionally well.

text: Ok, first of all I want to point out the price increase on these headphones. I bought them through amazon from the seller atonline_com for $65.60. Now the price is $105.93. Do your research on the price before buying these headphones. Background information: I live in a college dorm and my neighbors have a surround sound system so when they play movies I can hear the base thumping every time a car crashes or every boom. I can also hear them talking when they have friends over past midnight. The walls of the dorm are extremely thin and at night sound is magnified as it is. My roommate likes to go to sleep with the tv on low volume at about 11:30pm. I unfortunately have to be up by 6:45am. In an effort to protect my neighbors from myself, my solution was to find a good priced noise canceling headphones that a grad student can afford. Rating the noise canceling: When going to sleep with the headphones on I found that I need to either put my hands behind my head or arm over one end of the pillow to keep my pillow from squishing the headphones. (Which, is pretty easy to do and still be comfortable). So last night my neighbors decided to have their friends over and watch movies again. I figured it would be a perfect chance to test the headphones. Without the music but with the noise canceling feature on it took away about 50% of the noise. With the music on it was about 85-90% quieter. Trust me it's a lot easier for me to ignore my neighbors when I only hear about 15% of what I used to hear. For the tv being on, if it is low it completely cancels out the noise with the music on so experiment with the volume when you buy them before deciding if they don't work. Rating on the music quality: With the noise canceling feature on these are the highest sound quality headphones I've ever listened to music with. You can hear parts of the song you didn't know were there. I had to go back and listen to my favorite songs to see how they were original supposed to sound with the headphones.

text: Let's get one elephant out of the room right up front: setting this thing up SUCKS. More on that later. For now, let's begin from the beginning, shall we? The packaging on this product is outstanding. It arrives in a classy cardboard box, nicely printed and trimmed to give it a much higher-end appearance. If you're used to seeing cheap electronics from Amazon come tossed into plastic bags, you're in for a pleasant surprise here. The extender is packed with an ethernet cable, a user manual and a quick installation guide, both printed on thick cardboard stock for a really nice appearance. That said, the packaging is a bit like the beautiful plumage on a Norwegian Blue. There are still some very serious problems with this parrot. The quick start instructions are pretty straightforward, so I wasn't expecting any headaches. I chose the laptop method of installation, which is much like any other router. Plug it in, connect, point your browser to a dummy IP address and set things up. This went off more or less without a hitch until I was just past the point of selecting the network to repeat and entering the password. After entering my desired SSID name and the password for the existing network, the page errored out with a connection reset message. The install guide does say that the router will reset, but the router wasn't behaving as expected. The repeater network's name was to be "Bedrooms", but instead it retained the "Coredy 300_EXT" moniker. Even more frustrating was that the dummy IP address *and* the local URL given by Coredy to access the repeater's setup would not load. Like, at all. The rest of the Internet worked, but the admin site did not. So, scorecard for attempt one: yes to Internet, no to the right SSID, no to the admin site. Attempt two, using a smartphone instead as Coredy suggests, went exactly the same, but with an added twist at the beginning. Per Coredy's manual, holding a reset pin, paperclip, etc. in the reset button's slot for 2-3 seconds should restore the unit to factory defaults. So I tried that...and it didn't reset. I tried it again, being absolutely certain that the lights were flashing as the manual said they should before letting go, but no, the thing still would not reset. Finally, I tried unplugging it from the wall and holding a pin on the reset button while plugging it back in. It reset. All of that for the exact same result at the end of this trial: wrong SSID, no admin site. Rather than continue chasing my tail on a setup procedure that clearly just didn't want to do what I wanted it to, I gave up and used the WPS button instead. To the device's credit, the WPS button setup worked instantly...but I still don't have the right SSID or access to the admin site. Let's move on to results from here: I moved the repeater to the location I'd intended for it. The little thing's a bit garish and purple, but it's small enough that it's only really noticeable if you look straight at it. Mine's underneath a table, and though it's perfectly visible, it doesn't bug me at all. Some baseline results from speedtest.net testing: my speeds are generally right around 90Mbps down. I moved the Coredy back next to the router and tried running two tests each per network on my computer and phone, using both the network being fed to the Coredy and the Coredy's network itself. The results were, ahem, telling: Computer averages: -Home network: 89.13Mbps down -Coredy network: 25.37Mbps down Phone averages: -Home network: 83.42 Mbps down -Coredy network: 22.42 Mbps down Ouch. The first bullet point on Coredy's product description advertises "up to 300Mbps" speed. I suppose they're technically being honest when they say "up to", but I don't think this repeater could hit 300Mbps if you put four million volts through it. I moved the repeater back to its outlet in the living room to test the phone at the distance where the home network frequently doesn't quite reach. The good news is that the signal off the Coredy was strong and stable, with no dropping issues. The bad news, eh...the average download speed from the bedroom on the Coredy network was a whopping 5.23 Mbps. Yes, that's right, the "up to 300Mbps" repeater managed to pump out about 1.5% of that--around 5% of the network's usual speed at the repeater's outlet--with nothing between it and the phone but 20 feet and a half-closed wooden door. To say that I'm unimpressed would be an overstatement. So to recap, setup is a pain, changing your settings is impossible and the promised speeds are but a pipe dream. Yeah, not gonna lie, it's pretty terrible. So why did I give it a second star? Well, at the end of the day, it technically does what it says it will do. It extends the range of a network by quite a bit, and puts out a strong, reliable signal. As this thing was squeezing out 5Mbps in the bedroom, the signal was -57dBm. Consider my mind blown. A signal more than strong enough to hold up anywhere in the house, and it's running at 1/4th the speed of an HSPA+ cell network. Perhaps it was pining for the fjords? I feel as though I'd be disingenuous in my review if I didn't acknowledge that in the most basic of ways, at the most primal level, Coredy has technically put out a product that successfully completes its essential function. It's just not particularly fast about it, or particularly user-friendly. Would I buy this again? Not a chance. Am I going to use the one I've got? Why not? I did pay for it, after all. I paid for it at a reduced price in exchange for this honest review, and I hope the team at Coredy doesn't take this one personally. Sometimes a spade needs to be called a spade so that people know up front that they're buying a spade. This is one of those times. Hopefully the next Coredy product I get my hands on will raise the bar back up a bit. I received this product at a discount in exchange for my honest review. Sorry for being so honest, Coredy.

text: This headset has become the answer to my long quest for a high quality sound in a small, on ear headset. Based upon the acoustic accuracy as perceived with my ears which have many years of listening experience with a focus on blues, jazz, vocals, opera, classical, rock n' roll, folk, acoustic, ballads, C&W, Cajun, Tejano and more, I rate these headphones as a 5 star audio product. I compared them to Sennheiser 280 Pro, various Bose headsets, Bowers and Wilkins, Dr. Dre, Bang and Olufsen Form and others. I was amazed at how much musical clarity, range, brilliance, bass and presence the AKG Q460 provides compared to the other headsets I compared. It is important when testing these using an iPod Classic 160 GB - my music source in this case - to select the EQ, or equalizer, setting that is most pleasing to your own ears. The form factor of the Q460 makes them easy to carry, comfortable to wear indoors or outdoors (except for wind noise). I found they exclude enough external sound so that I can enjoy my music while someone is listening to a nearby television set. When I first tried this headset, I was blown away by the range of sound that came through clear and crisp. For example, bell tones, fingers on guitar strings, background talk between musicians, and I also experience the full side to side breadth of the sound spectrum across the recording studio or live stage. Very enjoyable and not expected in this price range. The cord is a super design and it can be disconnected from the headset and is strain relieved and well made. The ear pieces feel comfortable and are much preferred for bus and plane travel compared to ear buds. Quincy Jones must have approved this headset personally and he is a stickler for the quality of his arrangements and of his recordings - which span some sixty plus years and 27 Grammy awards. I have enjoyed his 4 CD Musical Biography on the Q460s. So, all in all, a great headset, but why did I have to take away one star from my 5 star rating? The biggest reason is that the in line control on the long cord corrupted some of my music. This - I expect occurred when I was fast forwarding to the next song. Perhaps I accidently clicked the control an extra time, but whatever I did, there is no excuse for a product to corrupt the data in the iPod. The buttons on the control are tiny and my fingers are big so I may have hit two buttons at once. See photos. But, the end result was that a number of songs would play for a few seconds and then skip to the next song all by themselves. I had to delete and reload some 40 pieces of music to my iTunes library and to my iPod. Fortunately, I caught this early. If anyone can explain this, I will be glad to modify this review. I do not know the exact cause but it seems to be related to the long cord's integral control. The male plug also is different than that on the normal ipod headset as it has one extra insulated section. I cleaned up my corrupted iTunes files, stopped using the in line control, place the iPod on "lock" when inserting and removing the male plug and the problem seems to have gone away. Be very cautious before you invest in one of these headsets for use with an iPod Classic as AKG does not list them for iPod Classic use. In fairness, many iPod Classic users have complained on line about a similar song skipping problem, but have not blamed it on their headset. The second reason for the loss of a star is that the warranty that I received is not good in the USA or Canada. Amazon or the seller should so state in its advertisement that this is a "gray market" product if that is in fact the case. Some people have noted that the ear piece can come loose when adjusted. I found it is necessary to grip the headset by the slider and the steel backed band and not by the ear piece in order not to stress the swivel joint which can break if you put too much force on it. I did not run any tests with an iPhone or other phone. The headset comes with a six inch phone adaptor cable. It also comes with a short cable which I found less useful and a long cable which is excellent except for the switch (which you do not have to use at all), but be careful if you loan out your iPod Classic and headset. If someone plays around with the switch, your music collection will suffer. PRICE ALERT! Since the product is made in China - a low cost manufacturing country - I would have expected a lower price even though it is designed in Austria. I was right! To my chagrin, I purchased my AKG Q460 Headset from Amazon direct on April 2, 2011 for $151.47. Now, lucky buyers may pay $119 or less direct from AKG via Harman Kardon with free shipping too. How low will it go? All in all a great small profile headset well worth your time to consider.

text: These are undoubtedly some of the coolest looking cans out there. The pictures do not do these justice. They are sexy, futuristic, and the contrast between the red leather and the carbon fiber is striking. They are attention getters. They're the only headphones/IEMs I've worn where somebody interrupted my listening to ask me if they could look at them. Now what about the sound? Audiophile flat? No. Not at all. The highs and the lows are definitely pushed forward with a slight recession in the mids. Not the cans you listen to your Chesky Records on. But, if you're hooked up to an iPod and are on the go you'd be hard pressed to find a better pair with which to enjoy your music. They sound great hooked up to the less-than-stellar amplifier on most portable devices but run through a Fiio E7 or similar portable amplifier they really shine. The difference is notable but if you only have enough room to carry your portable device then don't fret, at 32 Ohms they are easy to run. There is a slight burn in period needed but 60 hours or so should do. The highs smooth out, the mids come slightly forward, and the bass stays nice and tight. They're great rock, pop, rap, and metal cans covering everything from The Byrds "Sweetheart of the Rodeo" to "Prowler in the Yard" by Pig Destroyer to "Labor Days" by Aesop Rock and for some reason they really love Massive Attack's "Mezzanine". The carrying case is fairly standard thick paper walled covered with nylon and it has a nifty little plate in the center that says Phiaton. Compared to most carrying cases it is definitely meant for on-the-go. In other words the cans, 6.3 mm plug, a little extension cord, and an iPod nano or mini will fit. But that's all one really needs, right? The only downsides I see are the Y cord and the clamping force. The Y cord is a little short and a less thick than I care for. I just don't trust thin cords and the MS 400's cord is definitely thin and about six inches too short. The headphones are comfortable to wear for a bit but after 30 minutes or so my ears start to hurt a little. Granted, I have a head like a bowling ball. I wear between 7 5/8 and 7 3/4 in hat size if that explains anything. They have loosened up a bit since I first started using them so maybe it'll just take some time for them to become second skin. I've listened to and owned a a large number of headphones and IEMs and I can honestly say that I will never get rid of these. While not my first choice for home listening they are my go-to cans for road trips, flights, and for listening to music at the book store/coffee shop. Put down the Beats cans and get the MS 400s.

text: My car does not have Bluetooth but it does have a 3.5mm jack / AUX connector. Since this device has a 3.5mm jack in it I purchased this device and a 3.5mm male to 3.5mm male cable. Now I can connect my iPhone via Bluetooth into my car's sound system. Since I also have an iCloud account my music selection is almost limitless now and this works almost flawlessly. I also use this device in my office with my iPad. It has excellent range; I can literally go anywhere in the office and still hear and control the music on my iPad. Since I work in a cubicle I am able to use this to tune out the various distractions and focus on my job. I'm very happy with the sound quality and ease of use. It's almost 5 Star worthy, but there are just a few minor things that cause me to subtract one star. Due to the very compact nature of this device, the buttons are by default also compact and you may find yourself turning the volume up or down when/if you are trying to skip ahead and/or back in the music. Also, likely due to the compact nature it doesn't hold a very long charge. Probably not enough room for a bigger battery. Pros: Sound quality Range Multiple device connection On screen info is very well done Cons: Compact nature of device causes "fat finger" mistakes Switching between calls and music not intuitive At around 6 - 8 hours not bad, but would have liked a little longer battery life Indifferent: Radio

text: My first impression out of the box was that the charging/carrying case looks nice... then I picked it up. The plastic isn't super high quality and it feels lightweight despite being .2 ounces heavier than my Bomaker Sifi earbuds at 1.6 at 1.4 respectively (we'll be comparing to those a lot here). It must come down to the density - these are a little bigger, but still pocketable. USB C and wireless charging are a great point in favor of these, as you'll be able to find a way to charge them practically anywhere. What matters most here are ergonomics and sound quality. On the first point, I'd say these do pretty well. They're lightweight and comfortable in my ear and don't feel like they'll easily fall out (quick note: don't forget to size your ear tips). I like the touch controls since they don't require hard pressure on the ear like the tactile buttons on my Bomakers, but at the same time they do seem a bit oversensitive. I accidentally un-paused my music a couple times in the hour I've used these. It's likely that given enough time with these, I would adjust and start holding them by the stems, so I don't see this as a massive problem. What I do see as a massive problem, at least for me, is the sound. The bass is boomy, no doubt, but it's not well defined. It really overshadows everything else, and I can barely find the mids in there. Even Steely Dan doesn't sound as crisp as I'm used to. Listening to these with them well-seated in my ear canal feels like I've had a subwoofer implanted in my skull. My ear is not the most practiced, but it sounds like a v-shaped EQ: bass and treble are pumped up to the max and the mid-range is treated like a middle child - cold, alone, forgotten. The sound profile reminds me a lot of old-school Beats by Dre, so if you liked those, you'll probably like these. Coming back to the Bomakers, though, there is a reason those are so well-regarded: the sound is much more even and less fatiguing to my ear. I could listen to my Bomaker Sifi for hours and not get tired of it. On the bright side, I did notice the VEAT00L can get louder. Sifi can only barely get as loud as I want it. These buds just aren't for me, but at $25 I can't say they're a bad value. Just consider what you're giving up: there's no active noise cancellation and no aptX of any sort. Which means if you're using them in a loud place, you might hear more background noise than you might like, and the sound quality and latency aren't going to hold up in comparison to wired earbuds. Of course, there are earbuds four times the price and higher that don't have those features, but I paid $35 for my Bomaker Sifi set two years ago and they *do* support aptX. At least mine do. Therein lies a problem - I own the original Bomaker Sifi, but now you can only get the Sifi II which comes in a larger case and lacks the aptX codec. Given that, I don't really have an alternate recommendation for audiophile-types like myself. I can't afford to compare all these budget offerings myself and no one seems to be interested in reviewing the cheaper stuff with a critical ear. My conclusion is only what I have concluded for myself: the only benefits to these over my other earbuds are the touch controls and more options for charging. They aren't the upgrade I hoped for. Edit: It does appear someone is reviewing budget wireless earbuds. Check out Scarbir.

text: Sound is okay. I'm not an audiophile so I can't give you specifics, but music is a little muted. I use it mostly for phone calls and the sound is fine for that. No problems with the other side hearing me, either. Battery life is good, I can go all day on a full charge. Comfort is a mixed bag. It fits comfortably against the ear without excess pressure, but the earpads will get sweaty when its warm. A nice feature most other wireless headsets don't have is a 3.5mm stereo/mic jack, so you can use this as a wired headset with your laptop or non-bluetooth device. My complaint is that the headset is charged via a proprietary USB cable that plugs into the 3.5mm headset jack on the headphones. I suppose the manufacturer thought this an innovative space-saving design, but the weakness is the proprietary cable. Misplace that cable, as I have done mine, and you cannot charge the headset. Would have been better to put a mini or micro USB connector on the other earpiece so standard cables can be used to charge.

text: For the price, I was not expecting Air Pod quality, but I was expecting a little more. The visual appearance is nice and was designed well, but that is where the good stops. There were a few things that I just couldn’t get past. They are “Noise Cancelling” ear buds, but I suppose that means when loud enough everyone else hears what you are listening to, canceling out everything around you. I have had other earbuds and this really hasn’t happened before. I am not sure what the issue was, but no matter what set of ear tips I used, music was still loud enough for others around me to hear. Then there is the sound quality in general. I expected maybe some distortion as I turned up the volume, but it was little more than I was ready for. Oddly enough, call clarity was decent, but I might attribute that to not having the volume up to loud. Granted I was indoors in a quiet space, so I am not sure how it would be outside or on transit. They felt comfortable, they just didn’t perform as I expected.

text: I bought the Beats Studio buds refurbished and received a set of buds that look and sounds like new. Great way to save a few bucks. The sound profile is much better than any of the Beats cans that I bought years ago when they first came out. Deep punchy bass, crisp highs and decent mids. That’s where sound quality falls a little short is in the mid range. You can play with the different EQ settings to get better mid range sound but it’s not going to get a lot better by changing EQ settings. I haven’t had any battery issues. After about the 2.5 hour mark, my ears hurt slightly but popping them out for a minute or so solves that problem. I have owned countless pairs of headphones and these are the best true wireless headphones I have tried. I’m a big skullcandy fan and the sound quality of the Beats is superior to any of the skullcandy headphones I have had. I like the fact that you can find lost buds with the find my app.The minimalist design paired with the clean looks of these buds make these fashionable. The ANC is adequate as well is the transparency mode. These will be my go to buds for the next year or 2 until something better comes down the pipe at the same price point
